papers.fulltext: On Interfaces to Support Agile Architecting in Automotive: An Exploratory Case Study Rebekka Wohlrab, Patrizio Pelliccione, Eric Knauss, Rogardt Heldal Chalmers University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden Systemite AB, Gothenburg, Sweden University of LAquila, LAquila, Italy Western Norway University of Applied Sciences, Bergen, Norway Email: wohlrab chalmers.se, patrizio.pelliccione gu.se, eric.knauss cse.gu.se, heldal chalmers.se AbstractPractitioners struggle with creating and evolving an architecture when developing complex and safety-critical systems in large-scale agile contexts. A key issue is the trade-off between upfront planning and flexibility to embrace change. In particular, the coordination of interfaces is an important challenge, as interfaces determine and regulate the exchange of information between components, subsystems, and systems, which are often developed by multiple teams. In a fast-changing environment, boundary objects between teams can provide the sufficient stability to align software or systems, while maintaining a sufficient degree of autonomy. However, a better understanding of interfaces as boundary objects is needed to give practical guidance. This paper presents an exploratory case study with an automotive OEM to identify characteristics of different interfaces, from non-critical interfaces that can be changed frequently and quickly, to those that are critical and require more stability and a rigorous change process. We iden- tify what dimensions impact how interfaces are changed, what categories of interfaces exist along these dimensions, and how categories of interfaces change over time. We conclude with suggestions for practices to manage the different categories of interfaces in large-scale agile development. Keywords-large-scale agile development; agile architecture; interfaces; boundary objects; case study; architectural change; automotive; empirical software engineering I. INTRODUCTION The interaction of software and systems architecture with agile development has received increased attention in the last decades 1 . A core challenge with architecture in agile development is to deal with the tension between upfront architectural planning and agile development embracing change 1 , 2 , 3 . Change is an important aspect, as the rate of change impacts the adoption of the architecture- agility combination 1 . In architecture-centric agile environ- ments, developing the architecture in a lightweight way and keeping the architecture flexible to change is challenging but necessary, especially with respect to interfaces 4 . Interfaces determine and regulate how two or more entities exchange information. Oftentimes, the entities connected by an in- terface are developed by different teams 5 . It commonly happens that blocking issues arise along interfaces among agile teams, especially if they are ambiguously specified or based on wrong assumptions 6 . To enable teams to work in an agile way, islands of stability are needed 7 , which can be facilitated by the creation of boundary objects that maintain a common identity 8 , 9 . In this context, better ways of supporting the coordination of interfaces are required 9 . To address this issue, mechanisms are needed to under- stand what architectural entities can be flexibly changed and for which parts stability is needed, especially as the complexity of systems grows 3 . Focusing on interfaces as key architecture entities, this paper contributes to an understanding of islands of stability in agile development, which interfaces can or should be particularly stable, and how they can be coordinated. This paper presents an exploratory case study to analyze categories of interfaces and dimensions influencing their change in practice. We conducted a case study together with an automotive OEM that aims to improve the agility of their architecture practices. We present dimensions of interfaces, categories of interfaces, and suggestions for industrial prac- tices to manage interfaces in an agile development context. Our research questions are as follows: RQ1: What dimensions impact how interfaces in agile automotive contexts are changed and how are the dimensions related? RQ2: What categories of interfaces exist in the context of agile systems engineering with respect to the dimensions? RQ3: To what degree does an interfaces category change over time in agile automotive contexts? To get a better understanding of the problem in our case study, we conducted an initial literature review and four pre- study meetings with architects at the case company. In order to collect better insights and derive guidelines, we explored the topic further using 12 semi-structured interviews with stakeholders with different roles. Our findings indicate that multiple dimensions impact how interfaces are changed, e.g., the number of affected components and the criticality. We found three relevant categories along the identified dimen- sions: (i) commodity interfaces, (ii) early stage interfaces, and (iii) central vehicle interfaces. An interfaces category 161 2019 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA) 978-1-7281-0528-4 19 31.00 2019 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. can change over time, but typically becomes used in more components, slower to change, and less frequently changed the longer it exists. In the discussion, we provide suggestions on how to manage interfaces. We propose to leave stable and flexibly changeable interfaces up to the teams, but to control change for central vehicle interfaces. For all categories, we advise to establish interfaces to create boundaries that enable independent development, set an interfaces abstraction level as high as possible, and to assess interfaces early on. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: In Section II, we describe related work. Section III introduces the case company and Section IV presents the research method. We present our findings related to the dimensions of interfaces (Section V), related to categories of interfaces (Section VI), and related to how categories change over time (Section VII). In Section VIII, we conclude this paper with a discussion of our findings and suggestions of practices to manage interfaces. II. RELATED WORK The combination of architecture and agile development has been studied from different angles 1 , with several reported challenges, practices, and lessons learned. There is still a lack of guidance of using agile practices with architecture, and the evolution and continuous change of an architecture merit further research 10 , 1 . In this paper, we focus on how architecture is stabilized and changed, based on influences of product, process, and people in a large-scale agile context. Nord et al. 7 have identified the need for the creation of islands of stability in which teams can operate in a mode that is closer to the agile sweet spot, and possibly at a faster iteration rhythm. At the same time, one aims to enable teams to respond to change quickly and capture aspects of emergent architecture 3 . This paper relates to the allocation viewtype at it is concerned with how tasks are assigned to groups in the development organization and influence both process and people aspects 11 . Concretely, this paper deals with in- terfaces, which are natural boundaries between agile teams developing parts of a software or system. An interface is a form of relation between two or more distinct entities ... such that it ... selectively allows a transmission or communication of force or information from one entity to the other 12 . An alternative definition is that an interface is a boundary across which two independent entities meet and interact or communicate with each other 11 . The notion of interface change and evolution has already been included in early works on interfaces 13 , pointing to the need of leaving room for future expansion and considering design decisions that are likely to change in the future. Interfaces capture the relation of a providing entity to a consuming entity and ideally, both are considered during the establishment and maintenance of the interface. In this study, we focus on how they are changed, from their creation until an eventual deprecation or removal. In the context of APIs, the focus often lies on the side providing interfaces that are used downstream 14 . The consuming entities are not necessarily known; instead, the focus lies on attracting more potential users of the interface as a business strategy. While APIs are mostly written for developers using the interfaces, interfaces in general can have stakeholders of several roles and can be documented using several notations 15 . III. CASE COMPANY The case company is an automotive OEM located in Sweden. The company has had a focus on agile architecture for more than four years. The SAFe framework 6 is used widely in research and development areas across the company, across around 50 release trains with approximately 500 teams in total. Large parts of the architecture work have been moved from centralized teams of architects to the release trains and solution trains. Architects operate as a shared service in the organization. Moreover, local train architects take care of the architecture developed in particular release trains. Parts of our interviewees work on the core system plat- form, representing a new, centralized vehicle architecture. The idea is that the vehicle architecture is not based on hundreds of Engine Control Units (ECUs) communicating with each other, but that a central platform is used, taking care of the communication to other ECUs via a device proxy. The core system platform is currently still under develop- ment. It will contain the most critical parts of the software, will facilitate continuous integration and deployment, and be controlled by the OEM. Microservices on a high level are used to increase decoupling between hardware and software components. An example is a microservice sending out information about the vehicle speed and it can be processed by hundreds of applications for a variety of purposes. IV. DIMENSIONS OF INTERFACES We identified several dimensions of interfaces and rela- tionships between them. We consider dimensions as measur- able characteristics of interfaces and how they are changed. In this section, we answer RQ1: What dimensions impact how interfaces in agile automotive contexts are changed and how are the dimensions related? An overview of our findings is displayed in Figure 1. The arrows represent implications between dimensions and the dimensions are directly proportional to each other, i.e. the higher one dimension, the higher the other. This increase can be due to the direct conceptual relations between the dimensions (e.g., a higher criticality implies a longer time to perform a change because of additional overhead) or because of decisions taken or actions performed by stakeholders (e.g., if the time to perform a change is high, typically an interface is kept more stable by architecture stakeholders to reduce the overhead of changing it). The text on the arrows indicates the core motivator behind the relations. The level of abstraction refers to the nature of an interface and how closely related to hardware it is. The criticality relates to safety and security criticality. The distance to affected parties relates to the distance between people (e.g., geographical, organizational, or cognitive distance), related to artifacts (e.g., semantic distance), and related to activi- ties (e.g., temporal distance) 19 . The time to perform a change relates to the time it takes to plan and implement a change. The number of affected components relates to how many logical, software, or hardware components need to be adapted because of a change. In the automotive domain, functions of different natures exist that are more or less established. We found that the maturity of the affected functions of an interface is relevant. Another dimension is the interfaces position in the lifecycle. As any artifact, an interface has a lifecycle from its creation to its first use to its maintenance, its potential deprecation, and removal. Finally, the stability of an interface indicates how steady it is over time. We describe each dimension in the following, together with its outgoing relations shown in Figure 1. Each dimen- sion is marked with its subsections letter. A. Level of Abstraction Interfaces at our case company were typically signals and communication interfaces between ECUs, interfaces between software components, or application programming interfaces (APIs) on a higher level of abstraction. Signals and interfaces between ECUs are managed in a signal database. The intention with hardware-related inter- faces is to stabilize them early on, as stressed by Intervie- wee 7. However, currently, the signal database is constantly changed. Change requests come with an overhead as a signal database team needs to approve and perform the changes. Interfaces on a software level (e.g., APIs) are intended to be reusable over time and make the company less dependent on the implementation (e.g., provided by suppliers). Several interviewees reported that changing an API on a high level of abstraction should be avoided. With APIs, its difficult to change or remove things, its easy to add. If you think this is good for now, we will see later if it will change, that will be problem- atic. (Interviewee 12) We identified that a higher level of abstraction typically implies a higher level of stability. This is mainly motivated by the broader applicability of a high-level interface. In- terfaces on a high level of abstraction, e.g., APIs, can be generic to be usable for different applications and have the potential to be stable. Interviewee B. Criticality Eight of our interviewees pointed out that criticality is an important factor that requires to keep interfaces stable. Interviewee 2 reported that since we have safety-critical functions in the car, we need to have stable interfaces, and Interviewee 1 stated that costly validations need to be performed when changing safety-critical interfaces. A core motivator for the stability of safety-critical interfaces is the need to do the certification and security safety analysis again. These additional steps increase the time to perform a change. Additionally, practitioners are afraid that a change could have unpredictable consequences, which is why they prefer to have stable interfaces. For this reason, a higher level of criticality typically implies more stability. C. Distance to Affected Parties This dimension relates to the distance between human stakeholders, semantic distance, and the distance between activities 19 . Organizational distance is relevant both within the same company and to suppliers or other com- panies. Another relevant aspect is whether involved teams have the mandate to prioritize tasks in a common way. Interviewee 3 stated that its tougher to change interfaces ... when you are affecting teams and components outside of your scope where you dont have control. All interviewees mentioned that performing a change takes more time if several (distributed) teams are affected by a change. The more stakeholders are affected by a change, the higher will be the coordination overhead. Interviewee 9 stated that if only two teams are affected, resolution of changes is bilateral, independent, and quick. Sometimes its just two teams, then they talk. Then one team takes over the concern and discusses it with the other one. And the architects give directions. (Interviewee 9) D. Time to Perform a Change Our interviewees mentioned that the speed of implement- ing a change also impacts how often a change can be made and how stable an interface is required to be kept. It clearly depends on the type of interface how long a change takes, but can be up to half a year (Interviewee 12). Because of these constraints, engineers sometimes try to come up with workarounds to avoid making a change. As time is related to cost, several interviewees see it as desirable to reduce the time to perform a change and increase the stability. You want to be able to change the API fast. If you have a slow process, then you get problems in agile because the teams get blocked. (Interviewee 10) To foster efficient development, practitioners try to keep these interfaces as stable as possible. E. Number of Affected Components The number of affected components relates to how many parts of the system need to be adjusted because of a change. Several interviewees pointed out that the number of affected components or subsystems by an interface change strongly increases the time a change takes, because of the adaptation effort per component. Interviewee 4 stated that the time to change an interface depends on the change, how many subsystems are affected and what actions need to be taken. It is common that these components are also managed by different teams across a distributed organization: a high number of affected components typically implies higher distance to affected parties. F. Maturity of Affected Functions A variety of functions are developed in automotive com- panies, e.g., infotainment, powertrain, or autonomous driving functions. We found that the maturity of affected functions has a strong impact on the stability of their interfaces, due to less frequent changes occurring for these functions. For instance, Interviewee 2, working with the hybrid control system in the powertrain department, stated that they mainly have stable interfaces overall. On the other hand, Intervie- wees 812, working within new functions, stated that the frequency of change is very high and the interfaces are very unstable. We have different parts and different features of the car with different maturity periods. Today a lot of functionality is quite mature. ... So we dont need to change those interfaces. Those are related to traditional car functions. The commodity functionality, what the customer expects. (Interviewee 1) Several interviewees stated that the surrounding layers of functionality impact the number of interface changes: After some time, when the layers that are using your interface are not really subject to change, then you see that it is stable. (Interviewee 10) All interviewees stated developing new, immature func- tionality, the frequency of change is higher. In the early phases, it is more unclear and tech- nology decisions will change a lot. While in the end, its just nuances of which interfaces to change and how often. (Interviewee 5) G. Position in the Interfaces Lifecycle An interface can be at different points in its lifecycle, from its creation to its deprecation or removal. The later it is in its lifecycle, the more stable it becomes. Interviewee 11 stated that an interface undergoes many changes at first , then some rework, and then hopefully it will stabilize over time. Interviewees 6 and 7 stated that the period of change is typically two to three years. Then, the stability increases due to less frequent changes. Categories of interfaces with their dimensions Our interviewees pointed out that the longer an interface exists, the more components are likely to use it and rely on it. An interface gets more widely adopted with time. As a consequence, the time of making changes and the stability as a whole increase. Before everyone else uses it, ... update it daily, every hour, I dont care. But when you work with people who use the API, you need handshakes between the provider and users. Stability Many of the mentioned dimensions impact the stability of interfaces. Stability is understood as the opposite of the frequency of change. The stability of an interface can be a consequence of the development context or actively enforced by stakeholders. Our interviewees use different formulations to talk about stability. It can be observations of changes, e.g., it becomes rather stable (Interviewee 6). However, practitioners also intervene as there is a need to stabilize an interface (Interviewee 9). Interviewee 2 stressed that we want to have stable interfaces, then we can make our own internal development. Interviewee 5 pointed out that there exist interfaces that are naturally stable (e.g., because the affected components do hardly ever change), as well as interfaces that are kept stable in an artificial way (because the process to change is so rigid or because suppliers are involved). VI. CATEGORIES OF INTERFACES This section answers RQ2: What categories of interfaces exist in the context of agile systems engineering with respect to the dimensions? We used the interview data to scrutinize examples of interfaces and arrived at the following categories: (i) com- modity interfaces, related to mature functions, (ii) early stage interfaces, used in few components and being changed quickly and often, and (iii) central vehicle interfaces, which are very critical interfaces that are used across a large distance and affect many components. Interfaces can be at different positions in their lifecycle and all dimensions can change over time. According to our findings, one interface can only belong to one of these categories, although it can change its category with time. The dimensions are shown along the axes, with Low, Medium, and High as the dimension values. While the abstraction and maturity impact the (potential) stability of an interface, the main influencing property of central vehicle interfaces is its centrality, as many components are affected. Commodity Interfaces Commodity interfaces relate to very mature functions that have been developed and used for several years. Intervie- wee 7 mentioned signals for the headlamps technology on a rather low level of abstraction. An interface needed to be adjusted due to minor changes in the technology, but implementing the change took a high time effort. Intervie- wee 7 stated that the stability is high now, and that the interface affected a medium number of components and only organizational units across a manageable distance. The criticality of the interface is neither particularly high nor low, but undergoes the same procedures as typical vehicle interfaces. The team has a strong focus on actuators and controllers for them, on a rather low level of abstraction. Only groups inside the same department are affected by the change, across a medium distance. They develop 3-4 nodes, i.e., a medium number of affected components. The interface is stable now, as Interviewee 2 mentioned: We came up with a common interface that could take care of both gearbox types. Interviewee 8 mentioned an interface between two components: the vehicle interface unit that is connected to an ECU, and the core platform itself. Central Vehicle Interfaces Central vehicle interfaces connect a high number of criti- cal components developed across large distances, and take a long time to change. The main concern with central vehicle interfaces is the lack of flexibility and the high impact of change. Due to the high distance and the high criticality, changes have to be performed in a very controlled way. To increase the interfaces stability, the trend is to increase the level of abstraction and support a larger number of applications of the interface. However, Interviewee 6 pointed out that the interfaces still need to be revised all the time because the different teams ... find a lot of details that nobody thought about. We found three subcategories that we describe in the following: critical Cross-company interfaces, a service API, and infotainment head unit interfaces. 1) Critical Cross-Company Interfaces: Interviewee 6 mentioned interfaces related to connectivity, both inside of our case company, but also to other organizations. The distance is high: 17 architects are involved in-house to manage these interfaces, plus additional ones from other companies. Due to the large number of stakeholders, the time to agree on and perform changes is long. The number of affected components is high, which is why the intention is to keep the interfaces as abstract as possible, so that they can be used for different purposes and applications. The interfaces are highly critical, both as they provide safety features and because of security and privacy constraints. The stability is on a medium level, but typically increases over time: Usually, in the first three years it changes a lot and then it becomes rather stable. The interface is at a late position in its lifecycle, with only 6 months before production. The affected functions are on a medium level of maturity, i.e., neither very early nor very established. Interfaces are especially complicated if they are used to exchange data with externals: For interfaces to other companies, you try to keep them as minimal as possible. ... We try to focus not only on the technical interfaces, but more on the data structure as such. So that we are not bound to a certain technology, its still changing so fast. (Interviewee 2) Service API: A service API has been mentioned by In- terviewees 812 and represents interfaces to microservices. Software service interfaces are on a high level of abstraction. Interviewee 10 pointed out that they are security-critical, as not everyone should have access to all signals. Intervie- wee 8 mentioned that some interfaces affect a high number of components: If we make one change, maybe we need to change 100 applications. There is a large distance to affected parties, both be- cause of different backgrounds and different geolocations. According to Interviewee 8, the time to perform a change is high, due to a high overhead of interface governance. So far, the maturity of affected functions is very low. Also the position in the interfaces lifecycle is in its definition phase. Interviewee 12 stated that eventually, it will become very hard to change and to remove interfaces in the API. It should be really stable (Interviewee 8), because of the large impact on other teams. Currently, however, it has a low level of stability. 3) Infotainment Head Unit Interfaces: Interviewee 5 mentioned interfaces to and from the central head unit within infotainment. These interfaces allow users to activate and use functions in the car. It has a high number of affected components and also affects different departments across large distances. Interfaces are often on a signal level (i.e., low level of abstraction). The criticality is high, and certain signals need to be prioritized more than others, as Interviewee 5 stated: We can delay features like a shuffle function. But warnings for the safety system are more important, for instance. Changing the database takes a long time, as all changes are performed by a signal database team. It is a concern, as its not really scalable if you want to change your system rather often (Interviewee 4). The maturity of affected functions is low, as infotainment needs to adapt quickly to market trends. The interfaces position in the lifecycle is currently under development, but has passed the initial definition phase. The stability is currently on a medium level, but the interfaces still undergo change. VII. CHANGE OF CATEGORIES OVER TIME This section answers RQ3: To what degree does an interfaces category change over time in agile automotive contexts? Our overall observation is that an interfaces category can change over time, but typically the values of the di- mensions increase rather than decrease. The position in the interfaces lifecycle inevitably changes over time and moves from Early to Late. Our interviewees named interfaces across all lifecycle positions. An increase in the position in the interfaces lifecycle affects three other dimensions (Section V-G): More components are affected, more time is needed to perform a change, and stability is increased. Early stage interface, in particular, change values in several dimensions: At one point in time, you should try to be careful with interface changes. ... We have a year of a lot of changes, but then we want a release so that others can rely on this. (Interviewee 9) Commodity interfaces are already at a stable level and our interviewees did not expect their dimensions to change, except if new, immature functions affect the interface. In- terviewee 2 reported that interface changes are motivated by new technology or new functions that put requirements on us. For the central vehicle interfaces, the criticality and dis- tance complicate change. Several interviewees mentioned a point of increased stability that will be reached with an increasing use of the interfaces. Interviewee 12 motivated this as follows: Once it comes to a point where people will use it, other people, other groups, then it wont be easy to change it anymore. The goal is to aim for stability in certain time periods: We dont change constantly but have a heartbeat. So that the API should stay as stable as possible between two points in time. (Interviewee 10) The interviewee recommended to keep the API stable and continue the development on a separate branch that is merged later on. Interviewee 10s idea is to start with one or two users at the beginning. ... With a small set of users, it is easier to get the standard in place.. VIII. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION This paper describes dimensions of interfaces that impact change, categories along the dimensions, and an analysis of how these categories change over time. We conclude that interfaces play a central role for the architecture, especially when developing multiple compo- nents that exchange information. Related work confirms that challenges with agile development are to foster information exchange across teams and to deal with distance between teams 19 , 20 , 21 . Our findings indicate that practitioners aim for stable interfaces to enable flexible and indepen- dent development inside agile teams 7 . In this context, architecture models and descriptions have been considered boundary objects 9 , 8 , i.e., artifacts establishing a com- mon understanding across sites, while allowing each of the teams to maintain its interpretation of the object 22 . Our understanding is that interfaces as an integral part of the architecture can also be considered boundary objects be- tween teams developing different parts of the system. Teams interpret them from different angles, based on the concerns of the component they are currently working on. Architects have a broader scope and work with interface or architecture descriptions to communicate with several teams 15 . The findings presented in this paper help to understand the Table III SUGGESTIONS FOR PRACTICES AND RELATIONS TO DIMENSIONS Practice Dimensions 1 Select what interfaces need to be managed cen- trally, and leave other interfaces (especially those in an early stage) up to the teams. Time, position in lifecycle 2 As soon as the lack of stability impedes that teams can work autonomously, involve stakeholders with architecture expertise to establish interfaces that set the boundaries. Stability 3 Increase an interfaces level of abstraction if you have the flexibility, so that you can support more users. Abstraction 4 Assess interfaces in the early stages with one or two users before its position in the lifecycle and stability increase. Position in lifecycle, stability 5 For central vehicle interfaces, establish controlled change mechanisms and a strategy for versioning. Number of components, stability different dimensions relevant for managing interface change and assessing these boundary objects relevance and usage over time 8 . Based on the mentioned examples in the study, we identi- fied three categories of interfaces with respect to dimensions and main concerns: Commodity interfaces, related to mature functions. They only affect teams across a manageable distance, but changes take time to prioritize, assess, and agree upon. Early stage interfaces are in an exploration phase and can be changed flexibly, although too frequent changes result in undesired rework. Central vehicle interfaces, that play a role for many architectural entities. They are more difficult to manage than the former two categories, being very critical and affecting many components and teams. Table III shows suggestions for practices that we deduced based on the findings and how they relate to the dimensions. The practices are based on our interviewees experiences, their suggestions, and reasoning based on the collected data. In the following, we motivate the suggestions based on a re- elaboration of our findings. First practice: Select what interfaces need to be managed centrally, and leave other interfaces (especially those in an early stage) up to the teams. Currently, the tendency at our case company is to control interfaces from a central point, involving architects or the signal database team. This results in a large overhead of managing interfaces and long times to perform a change. To be scalable and competitive in the future, a more lightweight approach can be beneficial to manage early stage interfaces impacting only a few teams. Interviewee 8 mentioned that should be up to the teams to decide on these interfaces . Second practice: As soon as the lack of stability impedes that teams can work autonomously, involve stakeholders with architecture expertise to establish interfaces that set the boundaries. Several interviewees suggested that if an interface concerns only one or two teams, they can agree on changes themselves, keeping the architects in the loop. The suggestion is also confirmed by related work 6 . As lack of stability often results in rework (Section VI-B), boundaries as islands of stability 7 need to be set. Third practice: Increase an interfaces level of abstrac- tion if you have the flexibility, so that you can support more users. More general and abstract interfaces often lead to higher stability 13 . In the case of interfaces for gearbox types, a more abstract super interface was created to ac- commodate two types of gearbox interfaces (Section VI-A). A similar observation was made in the cases of central vehicle interfaces and the abstraction from details. Fourth practice: Assess interfaces in the early stages with one or two users before its position in the lifecycle and stability increase. When examining the change of categories over time (Section VII), we found that flexible interfaces likely reach a point where change becomes more compli- cated. Our interviewees idea was to leverage the freedom in initial phases and assess interfaces with a few users before more stability is required. Fifth practice: For central vehicle interfaces, establish controlled change mechanisms and a strategy for versioning. Central vehicle interfaces that have become used by many components should be carefully changed (Section VI-C). Also in agile setups, stability is needed to enable teams autonomy, as confirmed by 7 . To conclude, the study presented in this paper contributes to an understanding of architectural change in agile contexts. The described dimensions of interfaces and their relations can help to understand characteristics of interfaces and how they can be managed in agile development. While certain categories can be managed in a very flexible way, other cat- egories of interfaces should be stabilized for agile teams to work effectively. The presented categorization showed that the dimensions are useful to describe differences between interfaces. We observed that over time, dimensions rather increase than decrease. It should be noted that the extracted categories are based on an initial exploratory case study and that more research is needed to systematically examine categories of interfaces. We expect that there are more general categories of inter- faces that are not specific to the automotive domain. Practitioners can understand dimensions and categories of interfaces to reflect on how interfaces can be established as islands of stability to enable agile teams to flexibly develop systems and software 7 . Our findings suggest that interfaces with different characteristics require different ap- proaches to managing change. The suggestions for practices can help as a starting point to create and change interfaces that allow as much stability as needed. The study was conducted in the automotive domain, characterized by very diverse functions, criticality, slow pro- cesses for non-software parts, and large distances between stakeholders. We expect these findings to be valuable also for other companies and industries, but further research is needed. Based on this study and the suggested practices, researchers can assess interfaces in other companies and domains, and develop tools and methods to support interface change in agile environments. papers.fulltext: Mitigating the Influence of Embedded Software Development Environments and Toolsets (ESDT) on Software Architecture Jasmin Jahi c Embedded Software Engineering Fraunhofer IESE Kaiserslautern, Germany jasmin.jahic iese.fraunhofer.de Peter Enbrecht beyerdynamic GmbH Co. KG Heilbronn, Germany enbrecht beyerdynamic.de Uwe Mayer beyerdynamic GmbH Co. KG Heilbronn, Germany uwe.mayer a-oben.org Pablo Oliveira Antonino Embedded Software Engineering Fraunhofer IESE Kaiserslautern, Germany pablo.antonino iese.fraunhofer.de AbstractOne of the first tasks in engineering embedded systems is the selection of the hardware; more specifically, the MicroController Units (MCUs). This selection is driven by business, technical, organizational, and legal constraints. Often, the hardware is delivered together with proprietary environments in which the software to be deployed has to be developed. This imposes architecturally significant constraints that are usually communicated inappropriately (in terms of time and format) to the engineering team. Examples are the usage of proprietary data types and programming language constructs (e.g., macros in C) and limitations to the reuse of existing software assets. To overcome this challenge, we propose an approach that has two main constituents: (i) the Embedded System Checklist, which aims at guiding the selection of MCUs according to the architecture constraints; and (ii) the Em- bedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) Architecture View, which connects the software design view with the technical view, describing hardware-related development environment limitations and their influences on the software architecture. We evaluated the application of these concepts in two industrial projects and show that making these dependencies transparent saves a lot of effort during software system development. Keywords-architecture; embedded systems; embedded hard- ware; proprietary environment; I. INTRODUCTION Architecture-centric techniques have played a key role in managing the inherent complexity of Embedded Sys- tems Engineering. For example, the SPES 1 modeling framework is a widely accepted approach for architecture- centric engineering of embedded systems on top of which more customized frameworks, like the Fraunhofer Embed- ded Modeling Profile (EMP) 2 have been designed. The reuse of software across multiple hardware platforms is very common in industrial environments of embedded sys- tems. As embedded systems are migrated to new hardware, the same legacy code and the same features need to be reused. Hardware manufacturers, especially manufacturers of MicroController Units (MCU), tend to provide Em- bedded Software Development environments and Toolsets (ESDT). An ESDT comprises an integrated development system (i.e., IDE), a proprietary compiler, build systems, proprietary data types and programming constraints, and libraries, among others. The impact of such a provided ESDT is that embedded systems engineers rely heavily on it when developing their software. Therefore, the architecture solution of the software to be deployed is heavily constrained by manufacturer-specific proprietary software assets, making some features not possible on new platforms. Although ES- DTs influence the software architecture, they are hardware- specific, and their influence is commonly neglected by existing approaches. Ideally, hardware-independent and generic ESDTs would resolve this issue. However, previous research (e.g., Bulajic et al. 3 , Yagi et al. 4 , Hussein et al. 5 ) has identified several major challenges for the development of generic ESDTs. The origin of these challenges is the strong coupling between embedded software and specific hardware. Since the challenges of generic ESDTs have not been solved yet, we investigate how to manage the influence of proprietary ESDTs on embedded systems, relying on architecture principles. We have designed guidelines aimed at avoiding common pitfalls like critical dependency on proprietary data types and software assets. We created a list based on the analysis of the current state-of-the-art regarding the suitability of generic tools for the embedded domain and on the results of an industrial survey in several em- bedded systems companies in Germany. Besides this initial guidance, there is a strong need to explicitly express the dependencies of the software architecture on manufacturer- specific ESDTs in order to ease future migrations. Therefore, we suggest an extension view to the SPES- 1 -based Em- bedded Modeling Profile 2 : an embedded system ESDT dependency (SED) architecture view. The SED shows the deployment and dependencies of library functions supplied with the BSP (board support package) from the vendor. The constituents have been developed in a cooperation with our industrial partner beyerdynamic GmbH Co. KG 1, which is a German company specialized in engineering audio equipment and manufacturing professional audio products. The results show that it is possible to for avoid many pitfalls 1www.beyerdynamic.de 111 2019 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA) 978-1-7281-0528-4 19 31.00 2019 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. when designing such systems, which leads to potentially large effort savings. This paper is structured as follows. In section II, we present related work, starting with industrial challenges (section II-A). These challenges were gathered via a survey performed in several companies from the embedded systems domain. In this section, we will also present state-of-the-art challenges and provide description of bare-metal systems, a sub-group of embedded systems, which are the target area of our work (section II-B). In section III, we will summarize how selected hardware, through ESDT, constrains the soft- ware architecture and present our guidelines in the form of items of an Embedded System Checklist for capturing these constraints. In section IV, we will present the extension Em- bedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) Architecture View with examples. We evaluate SED in section V, conclude, and discuss future work in section VI. II. STATE-OF-THE-PRACTICE AND STATE-OF-THE-ART A. Industrial Survey To reason about the challenges engineers face with Em- bedded Software Development Environments and Toolsets (ESDTs) and the influence of ESDTs on the software archi- tecture, we performed a survey in a number of different com- panies and application fields 2. The survey was conducted within the authors personal network of contacts, within 19 different participants (embedded systems developers and architects) from a number of companies and business sectors in Germany, during the period from February to March 2018. The survey questions considered: Company size, application field, and educational back- ground of the engineers; MCU selection criteria; Continuous software integration practices; Usage of ESDTs and related challenges; Software architecture and software reuse practices; The size of the companies that participated in the survey ranged from less than 50 to more than 500 employees, in the areas of automotive industry, telecommunication and con- sumer electronics, industrial and manufacturing engineering, and Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASIC). We did not distinguish between software architects and software engineers (as these roles in industry are not always strictly separated), but surveyed individuals developing embedded software systems. Around 94 of the participants were electrical engineers and 6 mechatronics engineers. The results of the survey (Fig. 1) show that two thirds of all participants use a variety of MicroController Units (MCUs) from different families or manufacturers. More than half of the participants claimed that they select MCUs mainly based on hardware features and price, while 37 of the participants consider compatibility with existing ESDTs 2https: goo.gl Figure 1. Results of the survey regarding MCU selection process, usage of ESDTs, continuous integration practices, and ESDT challenges in related business sectors. ASIC - Application-Specific Integrated Circuits. and their software code repository when selecting MCUs. Most of the participants (58 ) use the ESDTs provided by the MCU manufacturer. The fact that two thirds of all participants work with different MCUs explains why very few of the participants use the same ESDT for most of their projects (21 use only commercial ESDTs and 32 exclusively use open-source ESDTs), and confirms the dependency of the ESDT on the MCU. In addition to these results, roughly half of the participants claimed that they develop a software blueprint before the actual implementation, but that the architecture emerges with the evolution of the software (i.e., the architecture grows naturally) (Figure 2). We also gathered several custom statements from the participants regarding their experience Figure 2. Results of the survey regarding the usage of architectural practices in industry. with ESDTs. We analyzed these and integrated the con- clusions into our model, which represents the influence of the hardware on the ESDT and the software architecture (section III-A). When it comes to software engineering, independent of the hardware, only one participant (from the automotive industry) claimed that their software depends only on the hardware abstraction layer. When it comes to understanding software dependencies imposed by the hardware, only one participant (from the telecommunication and consumer electronics industry) claimed that they plan the overall system and explicitly specify which features are implemented in hardware and which in software. B. State-of-the-Art Each software system is unique and has its own special requirements. An additional challenge in embedded systems is the tight coupling of hardware and software, which occurs predominantly in bare-metal systems (i.e., with no abstraction layer introduced by the operating system). The lack of the insulating layer provided by the operating system (i) changes the hardware abstraction view and (ii) allows direct hardware access to peripheral devices. Bare-metal systems are often characterized by (iii) considerable resource scarcity. These attributes propagate to the software engi- neering level. Researchers have identified several challenges regarding Embedded Software Development environments and Toolsets (ESDT) that are associated with engineering software for embedded systems. In practice, embedded soft- ware system engineers can choose between in-house ESDTs, manufacturer-proprietary ESDTs, and generic ESDTs. The choice of ESDT impacts the software under devel- opment, and potentially limits its evolution and migration to new hardware platforms. Bulajic et al. 3 state several factors involved when selecting and setting up an efficient ESDT: The development process facets (requirements, docu- mentation, system design, implementation, integration and testing, configuration management, change man- agement, and maintenance). Software development is a team effort. Separation of the process responsibilities (facets). Yagi et al. 4 describe the existing situation regard- ing ESDTs as ...the lawless wild west. With no clear methodology .... As the main reason for this claim, they name the challenge of combining platform model, hardware abstraction layer, and development tools. To manage the rising architecture complexity at the hardware and software levels, Hussein et al. 5 claim that there is a need for an environment that eases the development of such systems. According to Dixon 6 , the development of embedded software systems is demanding due to limited resources and the lack of software infrastructure support. Lefebvre 7 noticed that in-house ESDTs often support only a narrow set of embedded platforms and may, therefore, make it difficult to upgrade the hardware in the future. Guo 8 reports that in embedded systems, software archi- tecture best practices are often ignored. As a consequence, there exists language incompatibility between the application and implementation domains, leading to discontinuity gaps arising in the development process. In addition to technical challenges, Antonio et al. 9 explore the challenges in the education of computer scientists and embedded systems engineers. Their conclusion is that the knowledge of com- puter scientists regarding embedded systems concepts such as controllers and actuators is usually limited. As a result, the role of embedded software architect is often played by engineers from other fields who have a limited education in software architecture (such as electrical or mechanical engineers). Regarding the state-of-the-practice conceptual limitations, we investigated a report from DESIGN ELEKTRONIK 10 at a Tech-Talk held in October 2016 about the complexity of MicroController Units (MCUs) in embedded systems and their software. The participants were representatives from many big semiconductor manufacturers and distributers (NXP, Atmel Microchip, Silica, EBV, Infineon, ST Micro- electronics, ARM, Renesas, and Texas Instruments). One of the conclusions is that semiconductor manufacturers today mostly differ from each other in terms of hardware pe- ripherals, memory architectures, and software (development environments and libraries). Each vendor offers its own unique solution. ESDTs and hardware driver libraries serve as assets for customer retention since the effort to change to a different software environment might be high. It is fair to assume that, to certain extent, MCU manufacturers base their business model on the individuality of their peripherals and their software support, both of which directly influence the ESDT. There exist very few examples of open-source ESDT solu- tions. Hussein et al. 5 describe a model-based development methodology using open-source development platforms and virtual platforms to simulate the target hardware. Hadipur- nawan et al. 11 designed a virtual development environ- ment for embedded systems (VDEES), which provides tools for building virtual platforms according to the hardware specification. VDEES is implemented by exploiting open- source software packages. However, Yagi et al. 4 reason that for virtual platforms to be useful, they have to (i) model a full end-user system, (ii) be neutral in terms of vendors for the modeled hardware as well as the software tools attached to the virtual platform, and (iii) combine system-on-chips and cores from many different vendors under a single roof. Software development challenges that are present in infor- mation systems are mostly present in embedded systems as well, as listed by Bulajic et al. 3 . In addition to these, the hardware dependency of embedded software and its ESDTs (including the hardware abstraction layer) is one of the key challenges when designing a useful and effective embedded software and system architecture. There exist a variety of generic ESDTs. However, due to the discussed challenges, it can hardly be expected that there exists one single ESDT for all controllers manufacturers. Modern development en- vironments exist that are suitable for embedded system development, with compilers with varying architecture back- ends, flexible build systems, etc. However, there is a lack of proper abstraction that would allow engineers to assemble and automate ESDT processes. These processes require a lot of in-depth knowledge. Therefore, engineers turn to in-house solutions and manufacturer-specific ESDTs. Embedded en- gineers have become so used to this that they rarely ask whether there is another way at all. Additional aggravating factors are the costs and limited resources of embedded systems for which the engineer has to find a usable alloca- tion of resources. From the state-of-the-practice report 10 we can assume that there is no great business interest in ESDT standardization and interchangeability. Besides these imposed limitations, embedded software systems engineers are often not familiar with architectural practices that could help them in designing appropriate solutions 9 . Since it is clear that in most cases engineers need to use either limited in-house or provided manufacturer-specific ESDTs, there is a great need for solutions to manage hardware and ESDT dependencies of software. There is also a need to formally manage the hardware selection process (specifically the selection of the MCU) while taking into account its ram- ifications regarding ESDTs, embedded system architecture parts influenced by ESDTs, and hence the complete software engineering process influenced by these factors. The inputs for the process of selecting an MCU are the requirements of the existing system (under the assumption that they already exist) and the requirements of features that are on the road map for the future. In order to avoid common pitfalls while selecting an MCU, we provide guidelines in the form of an Embedded System Checklist (section III). For the concrete migration, we provide the embedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) extension architecture view for modeling those parts of the system architecture that are dependent on the ESDT (section IV). Our results show that there is a benefit in integrating this extension into existing architectural views. III. EMBEDDED SYSTEM CHECKLIST GUIDELINES The industrial survey (see Section II-A) and the state-of- the-art investigation (see Section II-B) on the suitability of generic development tools for embedded software systems uncovered numerous challenges - primarily that it is neces- sary to understand and minimize the influence of Embedded Software Development environments and Toolsets (ESDT) on an embedded system and its software. Based on these, we deduced a generalized process model for engineering an embedded system or for migrating an old system to a new hardware platform (i.e., MCU). Both use cases are directed towards selecting an MCU for an embedded system and mitigating its influence on the software architecture (Figure 3). As we see a great need to help engineers in the process of choosing new hardware while also considering software constraints, we have designed a guidance checklist to avoid common pitfalls. A. Influence of Selected Hardware on ESDTs and on the Software Architecture In this section, we will provide details on how a Micro- Controller Unit (MCU) influences the software architecture (Figure 4). Build tools (e.g., compiler, linker) are only one of many components in the value chain of the software development process. In the ideal case, it would be possible to use a single package of tools, under the assumption that the system and the tool provide high-level abstraction interfaces with low-coupling between them. The cost of the interfaces, however, is the abstraction of the underlying tool in question and assumptions of their functionality. All is well while these assumptions are met and the tools function according to commonly accepted standards. However, if these assumptions are violated and failures are caused by them, the engineering costs increase as the project advances. The later the inadequacy of a tool is established, the more time-consuming and more difficult it is to find an appropriate replacement. It is thus essential for software engineers to understand the proprietary limitations of the build tools. However, in industrial environments, invested effort is directly proportional to cost. An MCU is supported by a group of build tools. In-depth knowledge of one tool can, due to time restrictions, only be traded for shallow concurrent knowledge of many other tools in the same area of application. It is thus prudent for any software engineer to have a shallow overview of available tools within the same area of application and to specialize in only very few of them that suit their purpose in the best possible way. If a team uses software-in-the-loop simulation, the existence of a corresponding virtual model of an MCU can be a hard Figure 3. Generalized model of software system migration process from old to new hardware. Figure 4. Influence of Embedded Software Development environments and Toolsets (ESDT) on software architecture. requirement. We strongly recommend considering the re- usability of software build tools as a driver for the MCU selection process. As we have established, MCUs selection directly deter- mines the compilers that support it, as well as available hardware-related software assets (e.g., libraries, hardware abstraction). The compilers, in turn, determine the available proprietary programming language constructs (e.g., vendor commands) and may support non-standard data types, im- plemented for their optimal use of hardware resources. The available data types are also influenced by secondary MCU constraints, such as memory layout. In embedded systems development, the C language practically is the standard. Writing a compiler is a really difficult venture. All kinds of mistakes can happen: (i) Support for the minimalistic C standard is related to the fact that the initial C standard was published in 1989. Although there have been several updates (e.g., in 1999 and 2011), MCU vendors ship their own compilers and provide language support for something that is three decades old. Many functions from the standard library are not implemented or only implemented with limited functionality, creating (ii) omissions from the C standard (because of the bare-metal nature of the problem). Deviations from the C standard depend on the version of the MCU and or the compiler vendor. Defining custom commands for accomplishing something in an MCU-vendor- specific way has led to (iii) add-ons to the C standard, mostly related to optimization issues. There do exist subtle language issues that are allowed by the standard, but these can lead to (iv) unexpected behavior. Finally, there exist (v) platform- specific issues, which refer to hardware-related specific issues; for example, cannot use pointer arithmetic across 64k boundary size. Over time, developers get accustomed to whatever MCU and C standard they are using. Every time the MCU changes (or the compiler version upgrades), all these issues may change and the developer must be aware of all of them. The SPES 1 methodology and related work extending it (e.g., the Embedded Modeling Profile 2 ) place a great emphasis on modeling data, acknowledging that the software architecture is highly influenced by the (supported) data types. Besides compiler-related limitations, software assets and their interfaces exist as a part of the manufacturers pro- prietary software package that have a direct influence on the software architecture. Some already developed software components might become obsolete, while others might need to be adapted to new hardware or software abstraction levels. Side effects may also play an important role (e.g., namespace pollution, forced dependencies). Finally, it is very beneficial to explicitly express drivers regarding software reusability (e.g., for maintaining legacy). It could be that some components must be re-used for legacy reasons, while others could be replaced by newly developed components. The set of factors from an ESDT that influences the software architecture consists of proprietary data types, proprietary programming language constructs, proprietary software assets, and any explicit requirement on software assets reuse. B. Embedded System Checklist Items The checklist that is intended as guidance for the process of selecting the most appropriate MCU (Figure 5) consists of twenty items. Items 1 to 7 are related to dependencies on the MCU hardware; items 8 to 16 are related to development tools and the build system; items 17 to 20 are related to existing software assets. The individual items of the checklist are known in practice. The novelty of our aproach comes from summarizing them and establishing a process. The reasoning behind each item is described below: 1) We recommend selecting an MCU (or an MCU family) with which the software engineers already have ex- perience. By selecting a familiar MCU, the engineers will have a first impression of possible software re-use (e.g., target source code, build system) and potential limitations upfront. 2) Understand whether the intended MCU requires a manufacturer-specific compiler and find out which compilers (both manufacturer-specific and off-the- shelf ones) are supported. For those compilers that could be used, check whether there exists a manu- facturer support. 3) Some MCU impose memory limitations. Therefore, it is necessary to understand whether the MCU sup- ports volatile memory, linear address space, and inter- nal external memory. These directly influence block size access limitations, access timings, dual access memory constraints, the ability to rewrite program memory during execution (customer update), data erase options, and the MCU boot process using boot- loader technology. 4) Check if the MCU fulfills hardware synchronization requirements (i.e., DMA, buffers, timers, clocks, com- munication buses). Check against the related product requirements. Details often found as relevant con- straints are listed in the footnotes of the MCU manual. 5) MCU performance needs to meet existing hardware requirements (i.e., clock frequency, memory, and I O ports), as well as the requirements of features on the road map. It is common to consider system re- quirements with 50 more performance or headroom Figure 5. Checklist for guiding the process of MicroController Unit (MCU) selection. than estimated in order to allow for bug fixes, late requirement changes and life cycle maintenance. 6) Check MCU hardware debugging capabilities: which tools and hardware interfaces are necessary? Are these compatible with the intended build system? 7) Check the available documentation for the MCU and other relevant chipset devices for proprietary limita- tions. Design defects or errors documented by the manufacturer are known as errata. 8) Select compilers with which the teams software engi- neers already have experience, and which are widely used in the company. The latter is particularly impor- tant, as long-time usage of a certain compiler implies the existence of a knowledge base about its common defects. 9) It is important to understand the compilers (i) com- pliance with programming language standard(s), (ii) proprietary programming language constructs, and (iii) proprietary programming language instructions. Some MCUs support proprietary data types (e.g., 24-bit data types, long long as 40-bit data type). As it is often not possible (although it is recommended) to use only standard programming language instructions, the goal of this item is to document mentioned specifics in order to reduce the usage of proprietary types as far as possible to restrict their usage to localized places in the source code. 10) Which datatypes are offered by the MCU compiler combination? Do these datatypes comply with the current programming language standard(s)? 11) Some MCUs require a post-build step in order to transform the compiled binary file into a bootable image. It is possible to implement this process within a script-based build process or to consider further integration steps (e.g., production deployment files customer update files). 12) Considering the previous items, in cases where the engineers intend to use a manufacturer-specific ESDT for the selected MCU, it is important to consider whether it is possible to use an existing ESDT (e.g., in-house) or some other generic ESDT. 13) Does the development team utilize automated build, test, and continuous integration systems? If not, con- sider implementing a generic automated build, test, and continuous integration system connected to a source code revision control system. In other systems, this is a default requirement. In some systems, this requirement becomes explicit only after a product is well under development. 14) Which new build chain tools need to be introduced to the team for the intended MCU? Do these new tools support scripting (command line execution and configuration by human-readable text files)? Are these new tools compatible for integration into the existing build chain and continuous integration model? Check the quality of the intended tools. 15) Check if a virtual model of the product or MCU emulator is available for software tests prior to the availability of the target hardware. 16) Check the release notes of development tools for unexpected limitations. Sometimes the documentation contains explicit limitations. 17) List potential dependencies of external software assets (such as third-party libraries, frameworks) on the MCU hardware and the compiler. 18) Check if the MCU manufacturer provides a specific hardware abstraction layer (HAL) library: Do the li- brary functions work for the intended hardware ar- chitecture (consider details!)? In certain cases, the li- braries might not cover the intended usage completely or might not be compatible with the planned chipset of the product. 19) Based on the previous items, conclude which software assets from existing projects or from the companys internal asset base can be reused in this new product. Which modifications are necessary? 20) Which questions are still open regarding the software architecture for the new product? Only implement those software features that have no open questions regarding the architecture or regarding requirements. For those with open questions, consult an appropri- ate field expert (e.g., computer scientist, information technician, hardware engineer). The information captured by this list provides, to the best of our knowledge, the most complete summary of relevant dependencies when choosing a new MCU for an embedded system. The information related to the existing assets (items 17 to 20) includes cost estimations and is important for making the final decision on the suitability of a certain MCU for the target system. IV. EMBEDDED SYSTEM ESDT DEPENDENCY (SED) ARCHITECTURE EXTENSION VIEW In order to plan, document, and integrate dependencies of the software architecture on the Embedded Software Devel- opment environments and Toolsets (ESDT) as standard ar- chitectural artifacts, we present an Embedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) Architecture View as an extension to the Embedded Modeling Profile EMP (Figure 6). The Embedded System Checklist guidelines presented above (section III) capture in detail relevant dependencies of an embedded system on the ESDT, and consequently the influence of the targeted MCU on the software architecture. It is not necessary to use the checklist as input for the SED view. However, this is the most efficient combination. The SED view has a dual purpose: On the one hand, it relates development tools, assets, and constraints of the development environment from the ESDTs perspective. On Figure 6. Embedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) Architecture View - an extension to the Fraunhofer IESE Embedded modeling Profile. the other hand, it also serves as a binding framework, as it relates to the bridging dependencies between the ESDT and the architecture design. We extend the EMP with appropriate elements (blocks, stereotypes, connectors) to be able to capture dependencies on the ESDT and the impact of these dependencies on the target software. In this section, we will first introduce new modeling elements and then show examples of applying the SED view to real examples from industry. A. Building Blocks of the SED View The SED extension reuses elements introduced by the Technical View and Software Design View of the Embed- ded Modeling Profile (EMP) 2 and elements from other methodologies (e.g., SPES 1 ) upon which the EMP builds. Specification blocks include Business Driver, Organizational Constraint, Technical Constraint, and Architecture Decision. Building blocks include Device, Build System, Execution Environment, Logical Data, etc. Additional stereotype ele- ments include blocks for build chain tools, blocks for build scripts or tool configuration files, and constraint blocks. We also propose new relationships between elements: determine, constrain, and impact. The determine relationship specifies a certain trait or fea- ture from the source ESDT element to the target architecture block (result of the decision of using a particular ESDT element). The constrain relationship expresses a certain property that reduces the flexibility of the target component. The decision of using an element with a certain property will constrain the functionality or possible options of the target element. The impact relationship puts focus on the effect that one component has on the other element. Elements of the SED view aim to (i) model the ESDT architecture and (ii) the connection of the ESDT to the embedded system architecture. The first view type includes a model of the build tool chain, the input output code transformations, configuration files, deployment, and test systems. The reason for modeling the build system is that in many cases a compiler uses preprocessor directives to configure compiler-built-in macros. This is not necessarily a bad thing. It is bad, however, that directives to the linker are integrated as preprocessor directives. This way, build system responsibility is mixed with application logic. The second view type models the dependencies of the software architecture on the ESDT in detail. It captures the impact of proprietary data types, components using proprietary data types, language dependencies, third-party libraries, code generators, and other architecturally relevant limitations. It models the dependencies between the software architecture, the development tools, and the existing software assets. B. Application of SED View In order to start capturing the dependencies between the software architecture of an embedded system and the Embedded Software Development environments and Toolset (ESDT), we recommend modeling an overview of the embedded system and its ESDT (similar to the Context view of EMP). Interfacing blocks represent the influence of the ESDT on the software architecture (as explained in section III-A, Figure 4) and include proprietary data types, proprietary programming language constructs, proprietary software assets, and any explicit requirement on software assets reuse. Figure 7 illustrates an example of such an overview. The embedded system under consideration is a battery charger project developed with a MPLAB 12 based ESDT from Microchip. Each interfacing block represents a set of dependencies. We recommend at least one view instance for each of the listed interfacing blocks. The view on proprietary data types should include a determine-relationship between parts of the ESDT and the types. If a component uses a proprietary data type, it is necessary to model the impact. Figure 8 illustrates an SED view example with proprietary data types. The same analogy applies to proprietary programming language constructs (Figure 9) and other interfacing blocks. Each dependency should be connected to a block in the software design view or in the technical view. V. EVALUATION AND DISCUSSION We applied both conceptual solutions in an industrial context in two projects (Battery Charger and Microphone Control software), in cooperation with our industrial partner. A. Evaluation Setup The first industry project was a Battery Charger em- bedded system, consisting of one widely used single-core, 8-bit, bare-metal microcontroller (MCU). The project was completed within six months. One engineer was working on the project, and the result was a C software with 1000 lines of code (LOC). Figure 7. SED view overview example - Battery Charger product with intended developed with MPLAB-based ESDT from Microchip. Figure 8. Embedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) Architecture View example - modeling dependencies of proprietary data type. Figure 9. Embedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) Architecture View example - modeling dependencies of proprietary programming constructs. The second industry project was related to a piece of microphone control software based on one widely used, bare-metal, single-core, 16-bit MCU. Four engineers worked on this project, for 18 months, producing C software with 20 000 LOC. B. Effort Overhead for Mastering the Proposed Solutions Learning how to apply the Embedded System Check- list and the Embedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) Architecture View requires some effort. This effort counts once per engineer, assuming that the engineer will be able to reuse the acquired knowledge. Getting familiar with the checklist contents and understanding the idea behind each checklist item involves reading and understanding each of the twenty items. Based on our experience in the setup of this evaluation (section V-A), engineers require an average of twelve minutes per item. This leads to a total effort of four hours for understanding the checklist. The SED view is an additional view within the Embed- ded Mmodeling Profile (EMP). Our evaluation showed that engineers with an electronic engineering and computer sci- ence education background need an average of two days to learn and understand the theoretical idea behind the SED view. Two additional days are allocated for acquiring practical experience with the SED view by modeling random projects (this overhead adds up to four working days, around 32 hours). In total, an average effort for adopting the proposed technology per engineer is 36 hours. If engineers work in team, it is enough for one team member to take up the role system architect and invest this effort. C. Benefit when Using the Proposed Solutions The process of understanding the MCU and its ESDT involves reading MCU datasheets, programming specifica- tions, and compiler user manuals. This overhead must be calculated per project and is project-specific. Gathering all the relevant information for the Battery Charger project required around eleven hours of effort, while for the Mi- crophone Control project the invested effort was 22 hours in total. The significantly higher effort in the second case was the consequence of a more complex project setup, including more detailed documentation. It is fair to argue that engineers would need to invest most of this effort as part of their previous workflow. The effort for applying the SED view depends on the number of generated models. In case of the Battery Charger, the engineer created a SED view overview, details regarding the deployment, a build system view and dependencies, pro- prietary data types and language constructs, and dependen- cies on the hardware abstraction layer (HAL). This required around two working days of effort (approximately 16 hours). In the case of the Microphone Control software, for similar tasks, the engineers invested around three working days in total (around 23 hours). In the case of the Battery Charger project, the engineer faced the following issues: datatype signedness (a blatant violation of the ANSI C standard), compiler migration issue (the new compiler implemented the short data type as bool), different implementation and usage of timer interface com- pared to the previous MCU, and incompatibility of compiler macros. The engineer estimated that five weeks could have been saved if the information provided by the checklist and the SED view had been available. The total saved effort is estimated to be five weeks of the estimation, reduced by the one-time action of understanding the technology (36 hours), understanding the documentation (11 hours), and modeling using the SED view (16 hours), resulting in around 137 hours of potentially saved effort. In the case of the Microphone Control project, the issues were more severe. The incompatibility issues of the new MCU and its EDST with the old solution resulted in many hours spent on finding the reason why some features would not function properly. In the end, these incompatibilities resulted in the re-implementation of several features. The engineers participating in this project estimated that they could have saved around 3.5 months of effort if they had all the information that our solution captures. The total effort saved is therefore estimated to be 3.5 months, reduced by, in this case, the relatively small effort for the one-time action of understanding the technology (36 hours), understanding the documentation (22 hours), and modeling using the SED view (23 hours). The results of the evaluation are, of course, specific to the project and to the microcontroller. However, the evalu- ation results reflect experience from real industry projects. We argue that it is prudent to integrate our methodology into standard architectural and development procedures. The benefit of using the described techniques might vary from project to project. However, it is certain that not using the proposed practices will cause significant overhead. VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK Embedded systems engineering is an interdisciplinary challenge. Embedded systems have a strong coupling on hardware through Embedded Software Development envi- ronments and Toolsets (ESDT), which limits the resusability of software and make the ESDT constraints not obvious to all engineer types. To overcome related challenges, we presented a guideline in a form of Embedded System Check- list and an Embedded System ESDT Dependency (SED) Architecture View for mitigating the Influence of Embedded Software Development Environments and Toolsets (ESDT) on Software Architecture. The guidelines drive the process for choosing an appropriate microcontroller while exposing the origins of common pitfalls and capturing the ESDT constraints. The SED view models these constraints and integrates them into existing and commonly used modeling methodologies in embedded systems (e.g., SPES, Embedded Modeling Profile). The evaluation in two real-world, produc- tion, industry projects showed that there is a benefit in using these two approaches. At this point, the Embedded System Checklist captures the most important ESDT dependencies, but its interpretation is left to the engineers, as they need to asses how critical the dependency is. In the future, we plan to focus on providing thresholds for quantifying the generic outcomes of the Embedded System Checklist. REFERENCES 1 M. Broy, W. Damm, S. Henkler, K. Pohl, A. Vogelsang, and T.
