papers.abstract: Situational Aware (SiA) Cyber-physical systems (CPS) harmoniously integrate computational and physical components to being aware of what is happening in the surroundings and using this information to decide and act. Architecture description of SiA-CPS can be a valuable tool to reason about the selected solutions, and to enable code generation and simulation. This paper presents an architecture framework that automatically generates from a SiA-CPS architecture description, an executable code used to simulate the architecture model and evaluate it in terms of data traffic load, battery level and energy consumptions. The framework makes use of a model transformation approach where, three SiA-CPS domain-specific modeling views are automatically transformed into the input language of CupCarbon, an open source tool supporting the simulation of sensor network architectures.

papers.fulltext:
1 IntroductionAn architecture description is the practice of recording software, system, and enterprise architectures so that architectures can be understood, documented, analyzed and realized [1]. Accordingly, a number of architecture frameworks, architecture description languages, and different views and viewpoints have been proposed in the years [2,3,4,5], each one focussing on a specific application domain, set of views and viewpoints, or concerns. As clearly remarked since more than two decades, an architecture description is essential to the analysis of the high-level properties of a complex system [6]. It can expose various kinds of problems that would otherwise go undetected [7].This paper proposes a means to simulate situational-aware cyber-physical systems, based on a multi-view architecture description.Situational-aware cyber-physical systems (SiA-CPS) are cyber-physical systems that, by transforming sensed data into actionable intelligence, has the ability to observe the (user’s) surroundings and make detailed assessments about his environment. SiA-CPS involves being aware of what is happening in the vicinity to understand how information, events, and one’s own actions will impact goals and objectives, both immediately and in the near future [8].Architecting SiA-CPS requires the description of novel architectural views, were the physical environment, as well as its cyber dimension, plays a key role [9]. Software components, implemented on top of SiA-specific hardware IoT devices (e.g., sensors and actuators, CCTV cameras, beacons), are required to interact in a prescribed open or closed physical space (e.g., a parking lot, a classroom, a hallway) under observation [10]. In previous work [11], some of the co-authors presented an architecture description for SiA-CPS. Designed according to the IEEE/ISO/IEC 42010 standard [1], the CAPS architecture description supports an architecture-driven development of SiA-CPSs, and comprises three (plus two) modeling views, and namely: the software architecture structural and behavioral view (SAML), the hardware view (HWML), and the physical space view (SPML). The latter implements an architecture description for what typically referred as cyber physical space [12,13,14]. In order to create a combined software, hardware, and space view of SiA-CPS, the three proposed modelling views are linked together via two auxiliary views, denoted as Mapping Modelling Language (MAPML) and Deployment Modelling Language (DEPML).This work builds on top of [11] by proposing a code generation framework that, by transforming CAPS models into the CupCarbon [15] simulator input, will support the CAPS architecture simulation in terms of data traffic and load and battery consumptions. The framework, through a group of code generators, transforms SAML model (and then, HWML and SPML) into a completely functional code. This paper will focus on the CupCarbon simulator language named Senscript. The CAPS modeling and simulation framework is realized by exploiting advanced Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) techniques, such as metamodelling, model weaving and model transformation.The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

A technical process, comprising four main processes (parsing, analyzing, generating script, and generating project) to manipulate CAPS models;


A set of model to text transformations, that transforms SAML, HWML, and SPML models into CupCarbon files;


The initial application to the UnivAq Street Science situational awareness application.


The rest of the paper is organized as follow: Sect. 2 provides background information on the CAPS modeling framework, the CupCarbon Simulator, and the UnivaAq Street Science application scenario. Section 3 details the code generation framework: its process and the transformational approach. Section 4 applies the CAPS simulation approach to the NdR system, while simulation results are presented in Sect. 5. Section 6 concludes the paper.2 Background2.1 The CAPS Modeling FrameworkThe CAPS modeling framework supports the engineer of SiA-CPS. It is based on a multi-view architectural approach designed according to the IEEE/ISO/IEC 42010 standard [1]. The aim of this framework is to support the architecture description, reasoning, and design decision process.The CAPS is designed and implemented taking into account three architectural views: the software architecture structural and behavioral view (SAML), the hardware view (HWML), and the physical space view (SPML). We decided to have all things related to Software in one view (as well for HW and SPML) in order to provide a cohesive modeling environment. In addition, the CAPS has two auxiliary views, denoted as Mapping Modeling Language (MAPML) and Deployment Modeling Language (DEPML), are used to link together the three views. While details are provided in [11], we here summarize the main modeling elements.The software architecture view supports architects in the definition of the software architecture of the SiA-CPS application through the SAML modeling language. This view looks exclusively to software elements, with a specific focus on the architecture structure and its behavior [16]. Briefly, the SAML view describes how components and connections exchange messages through message ports. Each component in SAML model can declare a set of modes, and each mode can contain a list of events, conditions, and actions, that all together represent the behavior of the component (an example is provided in Sect. 4). Moreover, application data manipulated by actions are defined inside the component.The hardware view describes the hardware characteristics of each hardware element to be used within a SiA-CPS. A model in the hardware modeling language (HWML) encompasses specific low-level, node-specific information, like its memory, energy source, processor, installed sensing units and actuating units. A description of the HWML metamodel is reported in [11].The physical space view describes the physical site, in the real world, where the SiA-CPS equipment will be deployed. The space modeling language (SPML) provides support for developing 3D model editors. The CAPS modeling framework enables engineers to specify 3D syntaxes for SPML in a declarative way which will reduce the amount of effort and need for low-level expertise. It aims to support the standardization of a language for declarative specification of 3D concrete syntaxes for SiA-CPS. This view is especially useful for developers and system engineers when they have to consider the network topology, the presence of possible physical obstacles (e.g., walls, trees) within the network deployment area, and so on. More details are available in [11].2.2 CupCarbon SimulatorCupCarbon [15] is an open source simulator dedicated for wireless sensor network. It is used for scientific and educational purposes. It assists scientists in testing their wireless topologies and protocols, while it assists trainers in clarifying how wireless sensors work. Moreover, in CupCarbon, a network can be designed and sensors can be deployed directly onto the map by using OpenStreetMap that is provided through its interface. For more specific sensor nodes configurations, CupCarbon provides a scripting language called SenScript that can be used for this purpose. Moreover, its environment allows users to design mobility scenarios through which they generate different events. After deploying sensor nodes, one can use CupCarbon to simulate the energy consumption.In this paper, the CupCarbon simulator will receive the input files generated by the CAPS code generator. Those files, encoding information coming from CAPS in the SenScript language, will be used to simulate energy consumption, battery level and data traffic of model nodes associated with the CAPS architectural model.2.3 UnivAq Street Science SystemThe UnivAq Street Science is the European Researchers’ Night (NdR) event organized by the University of L’Aquila. In this event, the research community and public are brought together from the afternoon until late at night to share a combination of entertainment and information. As an exemplification scenario we will take the NdR held in L’Aquila city center, in which performances, lectures, demonstrations, workshops take place in its squares, main streets, and buildings. From our experience in organizing this event in L’Aquila, we captured some source of evidence. First, about 20,000 visitors are coming to the NdR every year. Second, late hours usually have more crowded than early hours. Third, the weather changes the visitor’s preferences in what to see and where to stay more. Forth, visitors are unable to easily locate activities and though they miss some of them.Our research group has been invited to provide new services to improve the quality of the visiting experience. For this purpose, we developed (and we are refining for the 2017 edition) a SiA-CPS with a mobile application as the first step towards a better NdR experience. Through the environmental physical sensors that we are deploying in the NdR area, and the mobile application used by visitors on their smartphones, we are providing the following services: (i) access control to rooms, laboratories, and parking lots, (ii) open and closed spaces monitoring, (iii) balance people crowd among different events and spaces, by using the mobile app to inform visitors about the degree of crowd in a place, (iv) make a planner that creates a tour while minimizing the waiting time and crowd in an area, (v) urban security, specifically in the case of earthquakes, fires and over crowd.In this paper we focus on two situational-aware services that are planned for the NdR. These services are related to rooms access control and safe airflow. A SAML model will be presented in Sect. 4. We will also describe the related HWML and SPML models. By using the CAPS code generator, the models will be transformed into CupCarbon Scripts. After all, the model generated code will be sent to the CupCarbon simulator in order to evaluate the architecture’s energy consumption, battery level, and data traffic.Fig. 1.CAPS automatic code generation frameworkFull size image
3 CAPS Code GenerationCAPS code generation framework is a framework in which CAPS models pass through different interpretations in order to build a code project that is able to be inserted in CupCarbon simulator. By running this code project on CupCarbon, we will be able to evaluate CAPS architecture in terms of data traffic load, battery level and energy consumptions of its nodes. This framework starts from interpreting SAML model and its components into Senscript files. Then, HW specifications and the deployment locations of nodes will be extracted from HWML and SPML models, respectively, and used to set up configuration files. All files result from CAPS models will be used in building CupCarbon project.As depicted in Fig. 1, the framework has four activities: parsing, analyzing, script generation and project generation. These activities are detailed in the following sections.3.1 ParsingIn this activity we use as input the SAML model that is typically stored in XMI file. This file encompasses a lot of information that are not needed for code generation. Thus, this information needs to be filtered out in order to acquire a relevant subset of SAML model values that conforms to SAML meta model. These values are used to instantiate templates. Templates and filtering pattern is one of several patterns that are usually followed in implementing code generators, as described in [17].The parser is in charge of parsing the SAML XMI file to get all the information needed based on templates definitions. Templates are defined based on SAML meta model, and there are different templates defined for different SAML sub models. For example, there are templates for Software Architecture elements (SAML components and connectors), ports, modes and data. This parser, will create an object of software architecture, that in turn carries the SAML model description in java.Accordingly, the resulting software architecture object contains the structural and behavioral part of the model. For the structural part, it contains the declarations of components, their data, their ports (as defined in the SAML meta model). Moreover, according to the definition, each port can be an IN message port or an OUT message port. The IN port defines APIs for messages to be received from other components. The OUT port defines a set of APIs for messages to be sent for other components [18].For the behavioral part, each component has a group of modes, or states. The mode is represented as a method that carries the name of the mode. The mode method can contain if statements that perform logical tests. If a test evaluates to true, the mode method performs an action. The action can change variables values defined in the component scope and/or can call another mode method. Exit and entry modes are represented by calling methods of different types. Furthermore, this behavioral part of the code generator provides helpers to navigate through the diverse SAML metaclasses that are responsible for modeling the behavior.The assumption we have in this work, that, each component in CAPS must be built to have at most one sensing unit (humidity sensor, or temperature sensor, or etc.). The reason of this assumption is, in the current state, CupCarbon is able to manage one sensing unit inside its sensor node. Hence, CupCarbon sensor node can contain many radio modules, a battery and a sensing unit. As it will be shown later, the component in CAPS will be represented as a sensor node in CupCarbon. More complex representation for several sensors in CAPS component will be handled in the future.Fig. 2.Part of CupCarbon template and analyzerFull size image
3.2 AnalyzingThis activity takes as an input the software architecture object and the SAML model description in java, that result from the previous parsing activity. The input must be transformed into CupCarbon compatible information, in order to build CupCarbon Senscript files.The Analyzer (ModelAnalyzer) depicted in Fig. 2(b), represents the core section in code generation. The method analyzeModel takes the Software Architecture object as a parameter and analyzes each element to create the corresponding objects that will be used later for generating CupCarbon sensors and scripts. The CupCarbon template depicted in Fig. 2(a) represents the structure of CupCarbon element that will be used in this conversion.The Analyzer is composed of two main parts:

(1)

Element Analyzer: this part of the code (line 10 in Fig. 2(b)), takes an SAElement object as a parameter (that retrieves the parsed SAML software architecture elements) and then checks each element type and creates new objects that will represent the element in CupCarbon. For example if the element is a component, it will create an object from the Component class. If the element is a connection, it will create an object from the Connection class. Another important task of this part, is the mode analyzer. It is responsible for analyzing each mode in a component.
Modes (that were represented as methods) and mode transitions (represented as calling methods), will be interpreted as a group of while and if statements (a Senscript code, that result from a component of two modes, is described in Sect. 4, Fig. 5). The behavioral elements (event-condition-action) contained in the mode will be interpreted into other objects (composite objects) for a component. Thus, the result from this step, is a list of CupCarbon components, each CupCarbon component (CupCarbon element) has a sensing unit, radio module parameters and instructions that will be used in the creation of SenScript file for this CupCarbon component.


(2)

Connection Analyzer: this part of the code (line 13 in Fig. 2(b)), is used to check the connection between components that already have been generated, in the previous part, and deciding their target and source components (connected components). Moreover, it denotes connections that occur between two components on the same platform or separated by a network, and it can decide how messages are controlled when they are moving between two components on different communication channels. The communication over these connections can be synchronous and asynchronous [19]. Asynchronous communication is acquired through using buffers (declaring communication array), while synchronous communication is acquired through using the buffer and setting its size to 0. For the sake of simplicity, the communication on the connection is made unidirectional and one communication is used for each different exchanged message. The buffer size is set into 1 in asynchronous communication, but during the code generation, the user can change this size of the buffer depending on the requirements of the application to be analyzed.


Finally, the result of analyzing activity is a list of CupCarbon components defined with their connections. The object that carries this information is shown in Line 3 on Fig. 2(b). These objects represent CupCarbon elements description in java, and will be an entry to the script generation activity.3.3 Generating ScriptThis activity takes as an input the list of CupCarbon components objects produced from the analyzing phase. This activity is in charge of preparing the Senscripts code. A Senscript file for each component will be produced.Part of the code responsible of Senscript generation is shown in Fig. 3. Figure 3(a), Lines 5, 6, 7, and 8, show how each component in the list of CubCarbonElement is sent to SenscriptGenerator. Figure 3(b), Line 10, shows the generateSenscript method that receives the component. This method uses several helpers and command instructions to translate the content of component object into Senscript code. In Fig. 3(c) an example of helper methods that translate read and write variables statements are shown.Fig. 3.Part of generating senscripts codeFull size image
The script controller in Fig. 3(a), is responsible for putting all the translated statements for each component in a distinct Senscript file.For each component, the script controller depicted in Fig. 3(a), is in charge of storing all the code translated for a component into a senscript file (.csc). The name of the file is distinguished by the device id (component id).Thus, the result of this activity is a group of SenScripts files that represent all the components in the CupCarbon simulator (the CupCarbon component is represented as a CubCarbon node in the CupCarbon simulator).3.4 Generating ProjectThis activity is responsible for creating files readable by the CupCarbon simulator. These files include configuration parameters and radio modules needed to run a CupCarbon project. Examples of device parameters are: device type, device id, device longitude, device latitude, and device elevation. Examples of device radio modules are: radio standard, radio radius, and radio data rate [15].The location parameters for each device (device longitude, device latitude, device elevation) will be automatically extracted from the SPML model (XMI file). Other parameters and radio modules will be extracted from the HWML model (XMI file). Then, an automatic generation of parameters and radio modules files are created. Each device has parameters file and a radio module file. An example of parameters and radio modules extracted from these models into CupCarbon files are shown in Figs. 6 and 7 in Sect. 4.Parameters and radio modules files, along with the generated Senscript files, will form the final project to be loaded in the CupCarbon simulator workspace.Finally, after loading the project and before running the simulation process on CupCarbon, few more configurations are needed to be done through its interface. First, set some device (node) parameters through its interface (like, setting up the energy max value that represents the initial energy of the battery). Second, create natural events for each sensing unit. This in turn will create a natural event file for each sensing unit and store it in the natevent folder in the project workspace.4 Application of CAPS Models, Code Generation and Simulation to the NdR Case StudyIn this section, we will simply represent a partial example of NdR case study introduced in Sect. 2. A simple scenario describes the monitoring of people count and oxygen level in a NdR room will be introduced. We will show its SAML model that plays a major role in SenScript code generation. We will show the needed part of its related HWML and SPML models that will be transfered to CupCarbon configuration files.Fig. 4.The Software architecture of simple scenario in NdR case studyFull size image
Figure 4 shows the SAML model of the CAPS. It is important to note that this figure is actually a screen-shot of our CAPS tool [20]. From a structural point of view, the shown SiA-CPS model is composed of five main components; OxygenSensor, RoomPeopleCounter, RoomController, EntranceLockActuator, WindowsLockActuator, and Server.The OxygenSensor component is responsible for monitoring the Oxygen breathing percentage in a room. It includes two modes: (1) Normal mode: in this mode the oxygen sensor reads Oxygen breathing percentage (O2) in a room every 100 s. A timer is set in this mode to schedule the reading from the oxygen sensor. A message carrying the O2 value is sent from the output message port of the OxygenSensor component to the in port of the RoomController component. Moreover, if the reading of O2 is less than 0.19 that means the state of the room will enter the critical mode. (2) Critical mode: in this mode the oxygen sensor reads Oxygen breathing percentage (O2) in a room every 1 s, since this mode indicates the unsafe level of oxygen. Also in this mode, a timer is set to schedule the reading from the oxygen sensor. A message carrying the O2 value is sent from the output message port of the OxygenSensor component to the in port of the RoomController component. Moreover, if the reading of O2 is more than 0.23 that means the state of the room will go back to the normal mode.The RoomPeopleCounter component is responsible for counting the people in a room. This counter work all the time to count people in a room. But, it updates this information to the RoomController only every 5 s. When a timer is fired, it sends a message containing the people count in a room (count) from the out port of the RoomPeopleCounter component to the in port of the RoomController component.Fig. 5.SenScript generated by CAPS code generator for OxygenSensor componentFull size image
The RoomController component is responsible for receiving sensors data in a room and take decisions based on its values. The decisions in this example are related to send a control messages to the actuators to open and/or close, windows and doors. The description shown in RoomController component is a simplified version of its supposed work. In this example, RoomController component receives two types of messages from its out ports:

(1)
Message contains Oxygen breathing percentage: if the received value is less than 0.19, this component sends through its out port a message to the in port of the WindowsLockActuator component. This message contains a Boolean variable (open), the value of this variable is set to true. Otherwise, if the received value is more than 0.23, this component sends through its out port a message to the in port of the WindowsLockActuator component. This message contains a Boolean variable (close), the value of this variable is set to false.


(2)
Message contains people count: if the received value is less than room capacity (rCapacity = 35), this component sends through its out port a message to the in port of the EntranceLockActuator component. This message contains a Boolean variable (open), the value of this variable is true. Otherwise, if the received value is more than rCapacity, this component sends through its out port a message to the in port of the EntranceLockActuator component. This message contains a Boolean variable (close), the value of this variable is false.
The RoomController component is in charge of sending a message contains the values of the Oxygen (oxy), people counter (pCounter), and ID of a room (roomID) to the Server, in port, from the out port of the RoomController.
WindowsLockActuator component is the one responsible for performing the correct action of opening or closing the windows. If it receives from its in port a message containing a true value coming from the out port of the RoomController component, it enables the actuator and thus it opens the windows. Otherwise, if the value received from the out port of the RoomController component, to its in port, containing a false value, the actuator closes the windows.
EntranceLockActuator component is liable for performing the correct action of opening or closing the doors. If it receives from its in port a message containing o true value coming from the out port of the RoomController component, it enables the actuator and thus it opens the doors. Otherwise, if the value received from the out port of the RoomController component, to its in port, containing a false value, the actuator closes the doors.


Finally, Server component is liable of processing the different data received through its in ports from other components. In this example, we restrict the Server component responsibility in sending updates to the users running NdR mobile application. This update indicates the rooms state if they are full or not, depending on the roomID and pCount received from out port of RoomControllers.For the sake of space, we show in figure 5 the code generated by CAPS generator for OxygenSensor component. Line 3 and Line 20 represent the normal and critical mode respectively. Line 14 and Line 27 represent the timers in the normal and critical modes, respectively. Line 4, 10 and 23 represent the instructions of reading the current oxygen value from the oxygen sensor.Fig. 6.An Example of HWML model and its representation in CupCarbonFull size image
According to the HWML model, we take the OxygenSensor component as an example to show the configuration information needed for it in CupCarbon simulator. Figure 6(b), shows part of HWML model that represents hardware specifications for OxygenSensor component in CAPS. This OxygenSensor is equipped with O2 sensor for sensing the percentage of oxygen in a room. It uses Texas Instruments ChipCon 2420 RF transceiver and it uses batteries of two AA with up to 19159 Joules. The sensor radio standard is 802.15.4 and radio radius is 20. Figure 6(a), shows a screenshot for an Oxygen Sensor radio modules configuration file.Referring to SPML model. The example, depicted in Fig. 7, represents part of the physical environment of our NdR scenario. Figure 7(b), shows part of the SPML model that describes the deployment physical position of OxygenSensor device. Figure 7(a), shows CupCarbon parameters needed from the OxygenSensor SPML model, these parameters are: device longitude (x), device latitude (y) and device elevation (Elevation).Fig. 7.An Example of SPML model and its representation in CupCarbonFull size image
In addition to the described models, there are two auxiliary models: (i) MAPML is Mapping Modeling Language used to link SAML and HWML, (ii) DEPML is Deployment Modeling Language (DEPML) used to link SAML and SPML. For the sake of simplicity, they are not described here. For better details about these auxiliary models, please see [11].5 ResultsIn this section we will describe the results of running our project in CupCarbon simulator. We applied three different behaviors for the NdR case study example. These behaviors are, first, the OxygenSensor runs with normal mode only. Second, the OxygenSensor runs with critical mode only. Third, the OxygenSensor runs in normal and critical modes, that is originally described in Sect. 4. These three different behaviors are applied in our CAPS modeling framework tool. Then, we used our CAPS automatic code generation framework tool to produce three CupCarbon projects. After all, we ran the simulator under the three behaviors and compare data traffic, energy consumption and battery level of it nodes.Fig. 8.Running NdR project on CupCarbon simulatorFull size image
For all simulation experimentations, we fixed simulation time to 6000 s, and energy max for all nodes to 19159 J. For OxygenSensor natural events, we selected random generation between 0.10–0.35. For people counter natural events, we selected random generation between 15–45. The Fig. 8, shows a screen shot of running the NdR project (applying third behavior) on CupCarbon simulator.Table 1. Messages exchanged in components during simulationFull size table
In all the behaviors applied, the OxygenSensor and RoomPeopleCounter components are always sending messages and they don’t receive any. While, WindowsLockActuator, EntranceLockActuator and server components are always receiving messages and they don’t send any. But, In RoomController, the traffic is in both direction, it sends and receives messages. This explains some zero values appear in the table depicted in Table 1, this table shows the exchanged messages through the IN and OUT ports of the components during running the three behaviors in CupCarbon, it also shows the data traffic in Kilo Bytes that occur at each component.Further, from Table 1, we conclude that the data traffic of OxygenSensor, RoomController, and server node receive the highest traffic when we run the critical mode behavior. This is due to the high messages they exchange during this mode. The normal mode receives a low amount of traffic but it could be not safe enough for detecting Oxygen level in a room. Thus, we can notice that using the critical and normal modes give also a low range of data traffic compared to using only critical mode. Moreover, using critical and normal modes together is still a safe behavior. Thus, this proves how small changes in the architecture can affect on the efficiency concern.Fig. 9.CupCarbon results for battery level and power consumption in different modes (Color figure online)Full size image
According to the battery levels and power consumption. The Figs. 9(a), (b) and (c), show the battery level when running the simulator under the three behaviors. The Figs. 9(e), (d) and (f), show the energy consumption when running the simulator under the three behaviors. From these figures, if we want to consider for example the two nodes, OxygenSensor (S1 in blue) and RoomController (S3 in red), we notice that S3 received the highest battery level drain when running the three modes. That is expected since the controller receives the highest data traffic among them. A minor improvement is noticed on RoomController when running the two modes together. While, for OxygenSensor we can notice how it experience the lowest battery level drain when it runs only the normal mode, the highest drain is when it runs critical mode, but we can also notice that running the two modes together gain better battery level improvements than critical mode. If we notice also the same nodes in the energy consumption charts, we can see how running critical and normal modes together shows a good improvements comparing to running only critical mode. Moreover, we notice how the energy consumption in normal mode is close to energy consumption in normal and critical modes together.Therefore, to recognize the tradeoff between safety, energy and data traffic concerns. We notice that using only normal mode achieves energy efficiency by having the least data traffic. The energy efficiency is inversely proportional to the data traffic size (number of messages exchanged). However, in normal mode, the safety concern will be less than it in critical mode. Therefore, using normal mode with critical mode provide a better compromise between those concerns.Our simulation results show that by using CAPS modeling framework, CAPS code generation framework, and CupCarbon simulation for SiA-CPS, we can get the early evaluation for energy and data traffic savings while developing SiA-CPS. This vision of testing the architecture in the early stage will improve the process of architecting such systems.According to the real experimentation, it is a work that we are planning to do. It requires a long process of deploying sensors and actuators. We will use the arduino code, that result from cubcarbon, to be installed in real sensors. The Ndr event runs in L’Aquila every year in September, so our first experimentation is supposed to be in September 2017.6 Conclusions and Future WorkIn this paper we proposed a modelling platform supported by a code generation framework, and integrated with CupCarbon simulation for engineering situational-aware cyber-physical systems.This frameworks allows engineers to run a trade-off analysis between energy consumption and performance indices like sensor nodes throughput, reliability and network latency. The modeling framework, automatic code generation, and simulations represent only the starting point of a series of goals we are willing to achieve in the mid-term.The code generation framework functioning and simulation has been tested by applying an energy and data traffic-related simulation of the NdR SiA-CPS.In future work, we plan to make these frameworks used by practitioners involved in the development of SiA-CPS. We wish to record and analyze their usage patterns and collect their feedback for further improvements. We are also working to realize an analysis that, while getting in input a series of environmental configurations options, can tell us which configuration can increase the network life-time.Moreover, we will expand in the near future the Ndr case study to real experimentation that includes different architectures of massive size and real events. Thus, the real evaluation will be compared to the result from the simulator and this will clearly state the efficiency of our work.

papers.fulltext: Mapping Features to Source Code through Product Line Architecture: Traceability and Conformance Yongjie Zheng, Cuong Cu Department of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering University of Missouri Kansas City Kansas City, Missouri, USA yzheng umkc.edu, csc326 mail.umkc.edu Hazeline U. Asuncion School of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics University of Washington, Bothell Bothell, Washington, USA hazeline u.washington.edu Abstract Existing software product line approaches often develop and evolve product line features, architecture, and source code independently, which makes it difficult to manage the relationship and conformance between these artifacts. This paper presents a novel approach using the architecture as a pivot to address this problem. It consists of a modeling mechanism that integrates features specification into an architectural model, and an architecture-implementation mapping mechanism that combines code generation with annotation processing. The approach can trace a product line feature to the architecture and source code, and automatically update the architecture and source code to maintain their conformance when feature changes occur. We implemented an Eclipse-based toolset to support the approach, and conducted a case study with the Apache Solr open-source system. The result shows that our approach is both applicable and capable to support the development and evolution of real-world variations of a software system. Keywordsarchitecture-implementation conformance; feature traceability; architecture-centric development I. INTRODUCTION A software product line is a family of software products that have extensive commonality. Software product line engineering (SPLE) 1 focuses on development and maintenance of the artifacts that can be reused among the products of the product line, such as product line features, product line architecture (PLA), and product line code. Product line features represent the user-visible characteristics that distinguish the products in the problem space 2 . The PLA and product line code both contain variation points 3 (e.g., optional architecture components and code fragments), which represent product differences in design and implementation respectively. Each variation point is defined in terms of the related product line feature(s). An existing problem with SPLE is that relating or tracing a product line feature to its corresponding variation points in the PLA and source code often requires manual effort. In addition, the product line features, architecture, and source code of a system can easily become inconsistent in terms of variability definition during product line evolution 4, 5 . For example, the PLA and source code may contain variation points related to a feature previously removed. A variation point in the PLA model and its implementation may also be erroneously related to different features. All these difficulties are primarily because product line features, architecture, and source code are typically developed and evolved independently using different techniques and tools 2, 6, 7 . When a product line feature is changed, a developer often manually inspects the PLA model and source code to identify the related variation points and update them accordingly. A number of SPLE approaches and tools 8-13 have been developed to automatically manage the relationship (i.e., traceability) and conformance between product line features, PLA, and product line code. They can map a feature either to a design model 8, 9 or to product line code 11, 12 , mostly relying on traceability links. However, automatically creating and maintaining traceability links across different software models and development tools is a research challenge, and is not yet practical in complex system development 14, 15 . In particular, none of existing approaches supports feature- architecture-code mapping at the same time, since an architecture-implementation mapping mechanism for SPLE is still missing. Existing work in this area can maintain conformance between a single systems architecture and source code along the criteria such as communication integrity 16 , behavioral conformance 17 , or quality concerns 18 . None of them can ensure that a variation point in the PLA and its implementation are consistent in terms of the related features (i.e., variability conformance). Further, a variation point in the PLA may also be changed (e.g., due to a feature change). None of these approaches can automatically update product line code, especially code manually developed by a programmer (i.e., user-defined code) to maintain variability conformance. In this paper, we present a novel architecture-centric approach to automatically mapping a product line feature and its evolutionary changes to its PLA and source code. The approach consists of a PLA modeling mechanism and a PLA implementation mechanism, which address the feature- architecture and architecture-code mappings respectively. The modeling mechanism leverages an extensible architecture description language (ADL), xADL 19 , and integrates features specification into the PLA model. This enables product line features and architecture to be developed and maintained in a single model. Their relationship and 2017 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture 978-1-5090-5729-0 17 31.00 2017 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. conformance can then be automatically managed with tool support. The PLA implementation mechanism combines an existing code generation and separation technique that we developed previously 17 with a novel architecture-based code annotation technique to implement variation points in the PLA model. It separates the generated code and user-defined code of each architecture component into two independent code modules. The user-defined code uses architecture-based code annotations to indicate code fragments corresponding to product line features. Different from existing annotative approaches that usually require independent development and manual maintenance of annotations 12 , an architecture-based code annotation contains the information (i.e., the related features) that is automatically extracted from the PLA model. When the PLA is changed, the separated code can be automatically updated via code regeneration and annotation processing to maintain the variability conformance between the PLA and code. Overall, our approach has two main capabilities to support feature-architecture-code mapping. First, it can automatically trace a product line feature to its related variation points in the PLA and source code. In particular, identifying feature-related code is based on an automatic analysis of the annotations embedded within source code, and does not require creation or maintenance of traceability links from the PLA to source code. Second, and more importantly, the approach can automatically update the PLA and source code to maintain feature- architecture-code conformance when an existing feature is changed. As a result, the related architectural variation points defined in the same model as the changed feature are updated. Further, the implementation of these variation points (both the code and annotations) are processed based on the updated PLA model. We built an Eclipse-based toolset named xLineMapper to support the approach. The video demo of xLineMapper is available online 20 . The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II briefly describes background information about PLAs. Section III introduces details of the approach. Section IV presents our support for traceability and conformance. Section V covers the implementation of our approach. Section VI describes a case study that we conducted with an open-source software system to evaluate the approach. Section VII discusses related work, and Section VIII concludes the paper. II. BACKGROUND: PRODUCT LINE ARCHITECTURE A software systems architecture is the set of principal design decisions made about the system 6 . It is typically modeled as a configuration of components using an ADL. Each component encapsulates a subset of the systems functionality and or data, and communicates with other components via interfaces. The interface pointing to the inside of a component is a provided interface. It contains the operations implemented within the component. The interface pointing outwards is a required interface. It includes the operations that the component expects other components to implement. The PLA is an important application of software architecture in SPLE. It consists of core elements common to all products of the product line plus variation points representing the architectural differences among the products. Each variation point contains a guard condition, determining when the associated architecture element should be included in terms of related product line features. In this work, we mainly focus on optional variation points in the PLA model. We model and implement alternative variation points (e.g., alternative interfaces) as a group of optional elements with mutually-exclusive guard conditions, so that only one of them can be selected for a product. Figure 1 shows an example of a PLA model, which represents a chat application that allows clients to exchange chat messages via a server. For simplicity, only some essential elements are included. The PLA model has four components (represented by rectangles) connected via interfaces (represented by triangles). The text next to a provided interface is the operation included in the interface. The elements drawn with solid lines are core elements. The elements drawn with dashed lines are variation points that are related to three product line features respectively: uploading files, saving chat history in different formats, and sending chat messages (e.g., a smiley face) that are pre-defined in a message library. Fig. 1. Example of a PLA model. III. CONNECTING FEATURES TO SOURCE CODE THROUGH PRODUCT LINE ARCHITECTURE Figure 2 provides an overview of the approach. The rectangle at the top represents a PLA model consisting of both architecture specification (based on the existing definition of the xADL language) and feature specification (based on a xADL extension we created). The rectangle at the bottom represents product line code implemented using an object- oriented programming language (e.g., Java). It separates the source code of a PLA component into two independent code modules: generated code and user-defined code. The generated code can only be updated via code regeneration. The rounded boxes in the figure represent examples of using the approach to model and implement Component Chat Server of the chat application described in Section II. Between the PLA model and product line code in Figure 2 is a programming construct (e.g., a Java enum) that is generated for every component containing variation points. This programming construct, which includes the names of the features related to a component in the PLA model, is also used in architecture- based code annotation. This annotation is attached to a feature- related code fragment in the components user-defined code. The four directed arcs next to the rounded boxes in the figure highlight the activities to maintain feature-architecture-code conformance. The approach also supports feature traceability. They are discussed in detail in Section IV. Chat Client Chat Server Chat History Message Library saveMsg loadMsg sendMsg fwdMsg uploadFile Fig. 2. Overview of the approach. A. Integrating Features into Product Line Architecture Our approach bridges the abstraction gap between product line features and a PLA by integrating them in a monolithic architectural model. This makes a PLA model self-contained in the sense that the information (i.e., the related features) required for variability modeling is defined in the same model. This integrated model avoids the difficulty of maintaining consistency between two different models that evolve independently. In addition, product line features and architecture are relatively close in the software abstraction hierarchy 21 , and both of them are free from implementation details. Therefore, the integrated model can stay simpler than source code. This integrated model requires (1) an ADL that can be used to specify product line features, architecture elements, and their relationships, which is not yet available; and (2) a modeling tool that supports development and evolution of both features and architecture. We address the first requirement by leveraging the technology of extensible architecture modeling 6, 22 , which emphasizes extensibility of an ADL to capture new concerns that different stakeholders of a software system may have. We chose to use xADL, an XML-based extensible ADL in this project. The existing definition of xADL includes a set of XML schemas providing language elements to model PLAs. The architecture specification shown in Figure 2 is an example. It defines an optional interface that belongs to Component Chat Server of the chat application. The optional element (Lines 4- 13) is a variation point embedded in the interface specification. It includes a guard condition defined as a Boolean expression, specifying that the interface is related to the uploading files feature. If a variation point is related to multiple features, Boolean operators such as AND, NOT can be used to represent a more advanced existence logic. We extended xADL and developed new language elements for specification of product line features. The extension was based on the general definition of product line features in a feature model 2 . It supports both optional and alternative features. An optional feature only exists in some products of the product line. An alternative feature exists in all the products of the product line, and each product may contain different variants of the feature. A feature can be further characterized in terms of some other properties (e.g., default value, binding time). The rounded box at the top left of Figure 2 shows an example of defining the uploading files feature using our xADL extension. It includes a new xADL element (i.e., Features specification Architecture specification Generated code of a component Annotation processing Code regeneration Feature changes Architecture pruning Architecture-based code annotation Code generation and separation 01 public class ChatServerArch 02 IServer imp new ChatServerImp(); 03 IChatHistory history; 04 IChatClient client; 05 public void sendMsg(String msg) 06 imp.sendMsg(msg); 07 08 public void uploadFile(File f) 09 imp.uploadFile(f); 10 11 ... the rest of the code 12 01 class ChatServerImp implements IServer 02 ChatServerArch arch; 03 public void sendMsg(String msg) 04 arch. client.fwdMsg(msg); 05 Optional(Feature.saving history) 06 arch. history.saveMsg(msg); 07 08 Optional(Feature.uploading files) 09 public void uploadFile(File f) ... 10 ... the rest of the code 11 User-defined code of a component Enum Feature uploading files, saving history 01 archStructure 02 component id ChatServer 03 interface id FileIntf 04 optional 05 guard 06 booleanExp 07 equals 08 s uploading files s 09 v true v 10 equals 11 booleanExp 12 guard 13 optional ... 14 interface ... 15 component ... !--other components-- 16 archStructure 01 archFeature 02 feature id uploading files 03 type optional type 04 defaultValue true defaultValue 05 displayColor red displayColor 06 relatedElements 07 link xlink:href FileIntf 08 ... !--links to other PLA elements -- 09 relatedElements 10 variants 11 !--alternative features only-- 12 variants 13 feature ... !--other features-- 14 archFeature Product line architecture model Product line code archFeature), which is parallel to the element (i.e., archStructure) that contains the architecture specification. The new element further includes a list of child elements (i.e., feature), each of which defines a product line feature. In particular, the feature definition contains the links (i.e. relatedElements) to its related architecture elements defined in the same model. Additionally, we built a modeling tool to support integrated modeling (the second requirement mentioned earlier). The tool supports side-by-side development of product line features and architecture in a graphical environment, and encapsulates reading writing xADL specification from the user. The tool is discussed in detail in Section V. Our approach currently does not support feature relationship, such as mutual exclusion or dependency 2 . We focus on feature-architecture-code relationship in this work. Modeling feature relationship is not a research challenge, and mainly involves engineering effort (e.g., to further extend the xADL language). A research question for us to investigate in the future is how to automatically map the modeled feature relationship to the architecture and source code. B. Code Generation and Separation The code generation and separation pattern shown in Figure 2 is a technique that we developed previously to maintain architecture-implementation conformance in single system development 17 . It separates the generated code and user- defined code of an architecture component into two independent code modules, and integrates them through method delegation. We reused the technique in this project given that it can automatically map architecture changes to source code with code regeneration, and preserve the programmers manual work during this process. In particular, it was revealed 3, 7 that code generation is effective in implementing product line variations. A remaining challenge, however, is supporting variability implementation in the user- defined code. This is addressed by the architecture-based code annotation technique introduced in the next subsection (III.C). The product line code shown in Figure 2 is an example. The generated code (e.g., Class ChatServerArch) implements the externally-visible information of Component Chat Server, including the operations defined in its provided interfaces (e.g., sendMsg, uploadFile) and the references representing its required interfaces (e.g., history, client). Both core elements (e.g., sendMsg) and variation points (e.g., uploadFile) of the component are implemented in the same way. All the operations in the generated code redirect (i.e., delegate) request to the corresponding operations in the user-defined code (e.g., Class ChatServerImp), which represents the internal implementation of the component. The user-defined code contains implementation details of both core elements and variation points in the PLA. All the feature-related code fragments in the user-defined code are attached to architecture- based code annotations. C. Architecture-Based Code Annotation Architecture-based code annotation is a novel technique we developed to support manual implementation of variation points in a PLA model. This annotation addresses variation points that cannot be implemented by code generation alone, such as use of an optional required component interface in the middle of a method. A code annotation is a tag or metacode attached to a program element in the user-defined code to indicate the product line features related to a program element. The annotations (Lines 5 and 8 of Class ChatServerImp) in Figure 2 are two examples. The first annotation is attached to a single line of code, while the second is attached to a method. They are both specified in the following format. Optional(Feature. feature name . variant , ...) An architecture-based code annotation is represented as a programming language annotation. In our example, it is a Java annotation (i.e., Optional) wrapped by a block comment (i.e., ... ). This annotation can be used in all applicable places, including classes, interfaces, methods, fields, local variables, and method parameters. In addition, an annotation can also be applied to a single line of code and a control structure (e.g., if- else), which are not supported by the standard Java annotation. We built an annotation processor to automatically identify and process an annotation and its corresponding code fragment (see Section V). As shown above, the format of an annotation contains a list of comma-separated features enclosed by a parenthesis. In our example, each feature is represented as a predefined value of a Java enum (i.e., Feature shown in Figure 2) in the form of Feature. feature name . The variant portion will be included for alternative features that have multiple variants. As mentioned earlier, this Java enum only contains the features that are related to a component in the PLA. This prevents an annotation from including unrelated features or typos that cause PLA-code inconsistency. The annotated code will be removed if none of the features or feature variants is selected for a product of the product line. Architecture-based code annotation only requires manual entry in the user-defined code during the initial (i.e., first- round) implementation of a product line feature. After that, both the existing annotations and the corresponding code fragments can be automatically updated when the feature or the related PLA elements are changed. This not only reduces the maintenance cost of the annotations, but also increases PLA- code conformance. In addition, architecture-based code annotation plays an important role in feature traceability introduced in the following section. IV. FEATURE TRACEABILITY AND VARIABILITY CONFORMANCE This section presents the capabilities of our approach to support feature-architecture-code mapping, including feature traceability and conformance maintenance. The approach can also automatically derive the architecture and code of a product member from the feature-integrated PLA model. This is not the focus of this paper (please see 23 ). A. Architecture-Centric Feature Traceability Our approach can automatically trace a product line feature to the PLA and source code. It uses the PLA as a pivot, and divides the entire process into two parts: tracing a feature to the PLA first, and then tracing from an identified PLA component to source code. In this way, only the code of the identified components (instead of the entire code base) is analyzed to find feature-related code. Tracing a feature to the PLA is straightforward based on the related information (i.e., relatedElements in Figure 2) defined in the integrated feature and architecture specification. In particular, this information (i.e., the feature-architecture relationship) is automatically created and maintained by our modeling tool (see Section V). The tool can further highlight the identified architecture elements in the color (e.g., displayColor in Figure 2, top box) defined in the feature specification. Tracing from a feature-related component in the PLA to source code exploits the architecture-based code annotation technique. When a tracing request arrives, the annotation processor mentioned in Section III.C is used to dynamically parse the components user-defined code and returns the positions of all the code fragments that are annotated with the corresponding feature. A code visualization technique (e.g., changing the background color) can then be used to highlight the identified feature-related code fragments in the same color as the highlighted architecture elements. If a PLA component is related to multiple features, different portions of its code can be highlighted simultaneously in different colors. A primary advantage of our approach is that it does not store or maintain explicit traceability links from the PLA to code, since this connection is automatically provided through annotations. The annotation processor can dynamically extract the code fragments of a component that are related to a feature. Moreover, a programmer does not need to manually maintain the annotations (i.e., traceability information) in the code as discussed in the next subsection (IV.B). Note that the code tracing function is limited to user-defined code. As mentioned earlier, generated code is a code-level reflection of the architecture and is not for manual manipulation. B. Maintaining Feature-Architecture-Code Conformance Another important capability of our approach is that it can automatically maintain feature-architecture-code conformance when an existing feature is changed (e.g., removed). The entire process is shown in Figure 2 as directed arcs, and also includes two parts. Mapping feature changes to the architecture is similar to the tracing process described above, and also uses the feature-architecture relationship defined in the feature specification to identify the related architectural variation points. An identified variation point and its associated architecture element will be removed, if it is only related to a feature that has been removed. Otherwise only its guard condition will be updated. Again, all these operations are automated by our modeling tool. Additionally, the source code of the changed architecture components will be automatically updated to maintain architecture-implementation conformance. On the one hand, code will be regenerated for each of these components, including the Feature enum shown in Figure 2 that includes the list of related features. On the other hand, the user-defined code of the components will be processed by the annotation processor. An existing code annotation in the user-defined code may be updated for a renamed feature or a removed feature. Both a code annotation and its corresponding code fragment will be removed if all the related features are removed. Consequently, the PLA and source code remain consistent in terms of the design and implementation of related features. Instead of permanently removing a code fragment in the user- defined code, our approach comments out the fragment as a TODO task. This enables developers to confirm that they wish to remove this code and enables both developers and architects to provide feedback on the changes made. As an example, if the saving history feature of the chat application is removed, our approach can automatically remove the related PLA elements, including an interface of Component Chat Server that is connected to Component Chat History in Figure 1. Then, Class ChatServerArch shown in Figure 2 will be automatically regenerated for Component Chat Server. The code corresponding to the removed interface (Line 3 of ChatServerArch) will be removed in the regenerated code. In addition, the ChatServerImp class will be processed by the annotation processor. Its related lines of code (Lines 5-6) are removed or commented out as a TODO task. Finally, Enum Feature shown in Figure 2 will be regenerated for Component Chat Server. It will only contain one element representing the remaining feature (e.g., uploading files). The focus of our approach is mapping feature changes to the architecture and finally to source code (not the reverse). A programmer may still introduce inconsistencies by manually changing the source code. For example, a programmer may accidentally remove an existing annotation in user-defined code by mistake. In addition, the implementation of a component may incorrectly reference another component that is not connected to it in the architecture. This is a limitation of our approach that we plan to address in the future. V. TOOL SUPPORT We developed a toolset named xLineMapper to support the approach presented in this paper. It includes a graphical modeling tool, a code generator, an annotation processor, and a code visualizer. They are integrated in ArchStudio 24 , an Eclipse-based environment for modeling, visualizing, and analyzing xADL-based architectural models. xLineMapper can be downloaded and installed from the project website 25 . Figure 3 is a screenshot of the xLineMapper toolset. It shows an example of tracing a product line feature to its related code fragments through the architecture. One window shows (1) a product line feature tree and (2) an architectural model of an application in xLineMappers modeling tool. A feature is selected (in 1), and its related architecture elements are all highlighted in the same color (green, in 2). The other window in the figure shows (3) the feature-related code of a component that is identified by xLineMappers annotation processor and highlighted by its code visualizer. It is opened from a context menu (i.e., View Feature Related Code) associated with the component in the modeling tool. A. Integrated Development of Features and Architecture The modeling tool of xLineMapper shown in Figure editor. It supports side-by-side development of product line features and architecture based on the integrated modeling mechanism presented in Section III. The feature tree contains a list of optional alternative features of a product line application under development. Features may be added or modified within this feature tree. Each feature corresponds to a feature specification shown in Figure 2. To the right of the feature tree in Figure 3 is a graphical editor to visualize and edit an architectural model. It is built based on the Archipelago editor of ArchStudio 24 . Archipelago is a graphical architecture editor that provides a symbolic boxes-and-arrows user interface for developing architectural models. It supports operations such as creating an architecture component, removing a connection, and adding a component interface. All the changes made to the architecture are automatically saved in the xADL specification. An important function of xLineMappers modeling tool is creating and maintaining feature-architecture relationship. A user may double click a feature in the feature tree shown in Figure 3 and enter the architecture editor to modify the PLA model. All the new architecture elements that the user created thereafter will be automatically and implicitly related to the selected feature. Alternatively, the user can explicitly relate an existing PLA element to a selected feature by right clicking the PLA element and selecting Add to Current Feature from the context menu that pops up. As a result, the tool automatically updates both feature specification (e.g., relatedElements in Figure 2) and architecture specification (e.g., the guard conditions of the related variation points) to create the corresponding relationship. In addition, the tool automatically updates the architectural model when an existing feature is changed to maintain feature-architecture conformance. As mentioned in Section IV, this may involve update of the guard conditions of the related variation points or removal of an architecture element if it is only related to a removed feature. Another function of the modeling environment is mapping the architecture to source code. It can automatically update the source code in response to feature and architecture changes. This ensures that product line features, architecture, and source code are consistent. The user may also right click a component in the architecture editor and select Map Component to Code to automatically generate regenerate code for the component. As a result, the code generator, annotation processor, and code visualizer of xLineMapper will be triggered to process the generated code and user-defined code of the architecture respectively. Moreover, a user may select a feature-related component to view its feature-related code fragments as shown in Figure 3. B. Code Generator We developed a template-based code generator based on the Eclipse JET code generation engine in a prior project 17 . It can generate code from a xADL-based architectural model of a single system. We updated the templates of the code generator to extend the support to a PLA model. The updated generator generates code for the variation points of the PLA model in the same way as for the core elements. No explicit distinction is made between these two elements in the generated code. This is considering that variation points are explicitly represented in the PLA model and the generated code is not intended for manual manipulation. Another important change we made to the code generator was for extracting and generating a list of related features (i.e., Enum Feature shown in Figure 2) from a PLA component. As described in Section III, it is used in architecture-based code annotation and will be regenerated if the architectural model is changed. Fig. 3. Screenshot of xLineMapper for mapping ( C. Annotation Processor The annotation processor of xLineMapper is built based on the ANTLR open-source system 26 . ANTLR is a parser generator that generates a code processor from a user-defined grammar. The generated processor can be instructed to parse and process source code. We developed the grammar for architecture-based code annotation. After that, we further developed the processing logic based on the code generated by ANTLR. Figure 4 shows the design of our annotation processor. JavaBaseListener is an abstract class generated by ANTLR. It contains methods to be overridden to handle events emitted by the ANTLR parser. AnnProcessor extends JavaBaseListener and contains the concrete processing logic that we developed. It uses modifiers to perform necessary modifications to the code. A modifier implements the Modifier interface that has three methods: emit returns the processing result; modifyStndAnn and modifySpecAnn specify how a modifier modifies the standard and special annotations respectively. We have defined four primary modifiers: Pruner, Commenter, Refactor, and Tracer. Pruner removes the corresponding code and is used to derive the code of a product member in a product line 23 . Commenter and Refactor maintain the architecture- code conformance, as described in Section IV. Commenter comments out code fragments and places TODO tasks. Refactor rewrites annotations. Finally, Tracer records and returns the positions of code fragments related to a feature. It is used in tracing the feature-related code presented in Section IV. Fig. 4. Design of the annotation processor. D. Code Visualizer The code visualizer of xLineMapper is based on the Eclipse annotation mechanism 27 . It highlights feature-related code fragments by showing them in different background colors. If a code fragment is related to multiple features, the code visualizer can show it in multiple colors in parallel, with each color representing a feature. This is visually easier to identify than some existing code visualization techniques 11, 12 that show a similar code fragment in a blended color that may be hard for the user to recognize. VI. EVALUATION We evaluated our approach by conducting a case study on an existing open-source software system, Apache Solr 28 . We developed a PLA model based on an analysis of Solrs existing versions, refactored the source code, and finally evolved the refactored system in an architecture-centric way enabled by our approach. A. Objective The overall purpose of the evaluation is to validate that the approach presented in this paper can be applied in the development and evolution of a realistic system to support feature-architecture-code mapping. Our evaluation is focused on showing (1) the approach can be used to model and implement variations (i.e., product differences) of a realistic software system, and (2) its capabilities to support feature- architecture-code mapping are valid. First of all, we validate if the PLA modeling and implementation mechanisms of the approach are feasible. In particular, we are interested in whether or not they are compatible with a system that has its own implementation model, bootstrapping process, or dependency management system. We also measure the amount of changes that need to be made to the source code of an existing system to adopt the approach. We want to ensure that the approach will not impose significant changes on a system developed using traditional programming techniques. This is important because it is the norm rather than the exception in SPLE to convert an existing single system into a product line 1, 3 . Next, we evaluate the capabilities of our approach that are not supported by existing SPLE approaches, including maintaining feature-architecture-code conformance and supporting feature traceability. We validate if the automatic update functions correctly, if the updated architecture and code are consistent, and if the performance of the related operations is acceptable. For example, the time that it takes to update the source code must be proportional to the size of the changes made to the architectural model. B. Methodology We chose Apache Solr V5.2.1 as the subject of our evaluation. Solr is a Java-based open-source enterprise search server. It has over 50 packages and more than 181K SLOC. Solr has been through more than ten years of development and has several major releases (e.g., Versions 1.3, 1.4, 3.1, 4.0, and 5.0). A number of features have been added to it while the system evolved over time, such as query result highlighting, spell checking, caching, NoSQL support, and SolrCloud. In particular, many of these features can be enabled disabled in a configuration file (i.e., web.xml) of Solr. This provides an opportunity for us to fully evaluate the approachs support for real differences among products of a product line. In addition, Solr has its own build tool and dependency management system. It is bootstrapped and initialized by a web container (i.e., the Jetty container) based on the configuration file. All these properties have made Solr appropriate for our evaluation given the objective described above. The evaluation consists of the following three steps. JavaBaseListener AnnProcessor Commenter Pruner Refactor Tracer Modifier modifier emit() modifyStndAnn() modifySpecAnn() Step 1: Preparation and environment setup. The first task of the evaluation was to import Solrs source code in a local development workspace of Eclipse and resolve the involved dependencies. A specific issue that we met and resolved in this step was about Solrs bootstrapping process mentioned earlier. It relies on the Jetty container that parses the web.xml configuration file to initialize all the required web components of Solr. In contrast, the ArchStudio environment has its own framework managing the lifecycle of an application. We resolved this issue by writing an application to bootstrap Solr programmatically. It translates all the configuration in the web.xml file to program statements in a bootstrapping class. Step 2: Architecture recovery, code refactoring, and feature development. We first developed an architectural model of Solr that had seven components. This model was based on the information specified in the web.xml configuration file. After that, we recovered more components from the source code and added them to the architecture. For every new component, we started to refactor its code instantly: generating code from the updated architectural model; copying and pasting the existing implementation details into the user-defined code. Next, we began to identify features and the feature-related code. The feature identification was mainly based on the Apache Solr reference guide and the web.xml configuration file. The feature-related code was identified through manual analysis of the code assisted by an existing UML tool. After a feature was identified, we modified the architectural model developed earlier in this step by either creating new architecture elements or relating existing elements to the feature. During this process, the related variation points were automatically created by xLineMapper in the PLA model. After that, we modified the related user-defined code and attached annotations to the feature-related code. Step 3: Capabilities evaluation. Up to this point, we had a full-featured architectural model of Solr and the source code consisting of generated code and annotated user-defined code. Next, we evolved the refactored Solr system in an architecture- centric way enabled by the approach. Specifically, we made a feature change and used the xLineMapper tool to automatically update the architecture and source code. Then, we executed the updated system again. We assessed our approach by (1) determining the feasibility of the approach, (2) validating the conformance between the modified architecture and code using a consistency checking tool included in ArchStudio, (3) inspecting the functional correctness of the updated system, and (4) observing the performance of the tool. C. Results Assessment 1: The feasibility of the approach was validated by the fact that we successfully finished the modeling and refactoring process, and all the functions of Solr are still working correctly in the final system. The architectural model that we recovered and developed includes 40 features and 86 components. There are 27 common components, representing the kernel functions of Solr such as evaluating queries, executing commands, and generating responses. These functions are not included in the feature list as they exist in every Solr instance. In total, 224 feature-architecture relationships were created. This was determined by counting the number of related architecture elements for each modeled feature. On average, each feature is related to 5.6 architecture elements. All of them were automatically created by the modeling tool of xLineMapper during the evaluation. Table I lists and compares the sizes of Solrs code base before and after the evaluation in terms of the numbers of classes, program interfaces, and lines of code (LOC). For clarity, we divide the refactored code into four categories and analyze each independently: (1) the original code migrated from Solr without any changes made; (2) the code generated from the architecture; (3) the code manually developed; (4) Misc. (e.g., Bootstrapper, annotation definition). Note that the manual code was not developed from scratch. Instead, the majority of the manual code was based on Solrs existing code with some minor modifications made. Overall, about 91 percent (166.8K 181.8K) of Solrs code was not affected in the evaluation. The size of the code base increased less than 8 percent (i.e., from 181.8K to 196.1K) after the refactoring process. In particular, more than 60 percent (9.6K 14.3K) of the added code was automatically generated. Out of the manually written code (19.4K), 15K (181.8K-166.8K) or more than 77 percent was based on Solrs existing code. Actually, the majority of the manually written code was devoted to the 91 interfaces (3.8K) created for the definition of component interfaces in the architecture.
