1 IntroductionThe digitalization of industry is a grand challenge. The advent of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) combined with Data-Driven (DD) technologies creates the necessary infrastructure for the 4th industrial revolution, where machines and humans are interconnected in sociotechnical systems, which are business or mission-critical 
[5]. Indeed, most sociotechnical systems are organizational systems which support enterprises to achieve their goals by explicitly including all those artifacts, processes and people needed to run the business. In this context, having an accurate digital representation of the organization would facilitate the decision-making processes in the value chain by providing (i) an aggregated view of the elements affecting a decision, and (ii) a prediction of the decision outcome: namely, a Digital Twin of the Organization (DTO) 
[11].A Digital Twin of the Organization allows for representing all the elements and connections of a organizational system in virtual models, which can be perpetually simulated and analyzed to achieve continuous assessment and optimization of the organization. Employing a well-defined DTO is an important asset in positioning new developments within the context of existing processes and other assets of an organization, as it helps in identifying necessary and/or opportunistic changes. Indeed, good DTO practices can help organizations to change and innovate, thus enhancing the organizations sustainability.However, the digitalization process is far from being fast, inexpensive, or effortless. The lack of engineering best practices for developing and operating DTOs makes it difficult for industry to fully benefit from them. Many companies are currently investigating the potential use of DTOs, but provided solutions are often context-dependent or system-specific, and challenging to adapt, extend and reuse. Indeed, making optimal business/design decisions and selecting the right technology (given the considerable number of DTO, CPS, and DD technologies and platforms available) able to satisfy both current and future needs is challenging. The following main question, raised by industry, should be addressed: In fact, the adoption of DTO is, as we describe above, not straightforward and the many challenges prevent organizations from deciding to move into and invest in DTOs and related technology. Some decisions, among others, are: (1) How to incorporate CPS, DD and DTO technologies into an existing organization? (2) How to benefit from incorporating DTO in products and/or production? (3) How to define and achieve a long-term strategy for adopting DTO? (4) How to access and analyze data in real-time and enact changes based on decision support mechanisms? (5) When the organization executes structural changes, how to systematically evolve the DTO to reflect these changes?To this extent, engineering best practices suggest the exploitation of architectures (at different levels of abstraction) to capture different aspects of the system under development. Indeed, separation of concerns (e.g., structure from behavior) improves the design and eases the maintenance of the system.In this paper, we report about a first attempt made in architecting and developing a DTO, and evolving it to accommodate changes occurred at the business level. Evolvability is investigated through development. Specifically, we first investigate how to employ a DTO in an already-in-place manufacturing process (representing only a small part of the whole production system), then we evolve it by developing and integrating, new features. The paper details the development process, and pinpoints a set of concerns to be confronted with when architecting a DTO that is expected to evolve overtime according to the organizations requirements. From the experience, it emerges the need for defining an architectural framework for facilitating DTO development and evolution.The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reports our experience in implementing and evolving a DTO for a given industrial case study, whereas Sect. 3 pinpoints and discusses some architectural concerns to be addressed in order to facilitate the DTO evolution. Section 4 discusses related work, and Sect. 5 conclude the paper by addressing future research directions.2 Industrial Case StudyThis Section describes the first steps towards the digitalization of an existing production line. It provides details on the DTO development, and some examples about how the organization can benefit from the DTO.2.1 Digitalization JourneyThe digitalization journey in the organization requires the construction of the DTO focusing on its evolvability. Evolvability is a design principle that takes into account the future change and growth of the system. Within the incremental digitalization process, it serves as a measure of the ability to extend and modify DTO upon the introduction of new activities to be digitalized or new requirements to be fulfilled. We use the evolvability measure to assess the level of effort necessary to evolve the DTO and put it into operation.Fig. 1.Incremental approachFull size image
As a key requirement for a DTO is to mimic the structure of the organization that produces it, we leverage on Enterprise Architecture 
[20] (EA) to describe the different aspects of a DTO. In fact, EA is by default positioned to play a key role in realizing a DTO, as it embeds all the principles and models used in the realization of an organization: (i) the Organizational Architecture (OA) and Business architecture (BA) provide the structural and behavioral models, respectively, whereas (ii) the Information Architecture (IA) provides the data representing the actual status of the organization.We adopt the incremental development approach in Fig. 1, where each evolution step is divided into four phases: development, integration, validation, and operation. As illustrative example, consider that we start from a subsystem \(S_1\) that has already been digitalized into \(DTO_1\). We incrementally digitalize the organization by taking another subsystem \(S_2\) and developing its \(DTO_2\), implementing the necessary integration of digitalized subsystems and validating it, resulting in \(DTO_1+DTO_2\).2.2 Organization DescriptionThe organization is a supplier of articles in the automotive industry. It manufactures a product line with a large number of variants (\(\ge 1000\)). The automotive industry supply chain requires Just-In-Time production. This requirement prevents from, for instance, producing to a buffer. We focus only on one of the different activities, namely the manufacturing of a specific part P of the final product. To keep the appropriate synchronization among all parts of a product in the whole assembly line, there is an additional requirement for P: units must leave their production line in the same sequence as they were ordered.Figure 2 illustrates the OA/BA representing the production line P according to the notation introduced in 
[20], which consists of two workstations: Workstation A (WA) manufactures the product and it is highly automated with two machines working in parallel (WA1 and WA2). An operator must supervise the machines and must change their configuration between orders of a different variant of P. Workstation D (WD) packages the product. It also has two machines working in parallel (WD1 and WD2), but it is less automatized and requires two operators continuously working on it, one on each machine. The business process is supported by a legacy in-house software for Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), which constitutes the IA. Data about both the products and the production activities is collected by the operators, which are required to check the products (e.g., for identifying defects), to observe the process events (e.g., for identifying deviations in the production plan), and to report all their observations into the IA.Fig. 2.OA/BA of the case studyFull size image
This section of the plant receives orders to produce P. Each order refers to a concrete variant v of P. An order specifies the number n of units to produce. The operator in WA will configure either WA1 or WA2 to produce n products P of variant v. When an order is received and both WA1 and WA2 are busy, it waits for its manufacturing turn in a queue. When the manufacturing in WA completes, P moves towards its packaging in WD. Operators in WD create packages containing up to 30 units. If both operators in WD are busy when P arrives for its packaging, then P joins a priority queue. The queue uses as priority the sequence number of the order. Older orders have more priority than newer orders, to help preserve the in-order delivery requirement.The organization stakeholders (e.g., management and operators) want to digitalize this section of the plant. The reason is that they would like to know, in real time, the orders lead time, the utilization of resources, and the amount of work-in-progress in the line. They would also like to predict the near future of these three characteristics. These predictions will allow the sales department to give better estimations of the delivery time to the clients at the moment they are filling an order, and the production planning department can plan less disruptive maintenance of machinery.2.3 DTO Development – Iteration 1
Fig. 3.Digital twins of the organization (model for simulation) (Color figure online)Full size image
According to the IA, the monitorable data in the production line are: According to the IA, the monitorable data in the production line are:

the moment when an order is placed, and its unique identifier ID;


the type of variant v, and the number of units, n, to produce;


the moment when an order ID enters WA;


the moment when the units belonging to a given order ID are produced;


the moment when the units enter WD;


the moment when an order ID is packaged and ready to be delivered; and,


the moment when an order ID is delivered.


Figure 3a shows the digitalization of the production line P based on the monitorable points. The model, developed using the Discrete Event System toolbox in Matlab/SimulinkFootnote 1, shows the sequence of order arrival, waiting in queue for WA, execution in WA, waiting in queue for WD, execution in WD, and in order delivery. The last is modeled with a selection gate that controls the orders ID and a small storage. The small storage stocks some orders if necessary until the order with the next ID to deliver is packaged in WD.This DTO allows for observing the status of the plant –in terms of lead time of orders, utilization of workstations, amount of work-in-progress, products in queue waiting for an available workstation–, and simulating future scenarios.Figure 4 shows this type of observations. The horizontal axis indicates the observation time, 30 days. Figure 4a shows the arrival (blue line) and delivery (black line) of orders along time, and the size of each order. In the last 30 days, 59 orders arrived to the production line, adding up 3303 units to produce. The blue area that is demarcated by these two lines exposes the work-in-progress in the line. The height of the blue area in each x value exposes the work-in-progress in the line in that moment.Figure 4b illustrates the lead time of each order. The number of units to produce in a single order is variable in the interval
[1]. Since the size of an order affects its lead time, Fig. 4b puts together a bar for the lead time of an order and a bar for the number of units n in the order.Fig. 4.Observations from DTO (Color figure online)Full size image
2.4 DTO Development – Iteration 2 (Evolution)The organization would like to predict more accurately the lead time and to estimate in real time what is the optimal task for an operator. To achieve these new goals, the organization needs to evolve its DTO.The DTO evolution consists in providing a more realistic representation of what happens in the organization between the moment an unit leaves machines WA1 or WA2 and an order is ready for packaging. In the real production line, machines in WA do not always manufacture the units correctly. Sometimes they have defects and they need a subsequent rework before joining the queue for packaging. The rework is manually done, and requires one of the operators in WD. We refer to the new manual rework station as WB.This evolved DTO will enable a more accurate estimation of the lead time of an order –coming from the explicit digitalization of WB– and a better understanding of the utilization of resources –coming from the more accurate representation of operators’ tasks. In the first iteration in Sect. 2.3, the busy time of stations WD1 and WD2 also included the time that operators spent in the rework station. The separation of the operators’ tasks into their actual work in WD and their work in WB enables a more accurate understanding of the busy time and service time of packaging activities in WD. Using this improved understanding, the DTO can assist the production planning in scheduling the optimal task for an operator in a given moment.Fig. 5.Number of units in the production line that need reworkFull size image
To gain this new information, it is necessary to first obtain new monitored data. This is achieved by connecting the quality sensors in the production line that inspect units for possible defects to their digitalized representation in the DTO. The operators gain awareness of defects at a glance since each quality sensor, upon the detection of a defect, sends a notification to a control panel and raises a short audible alarm. The DTO development in this phase includes that the notifications of each sensor are also sent to the DTO (the alarm is not). In case of defective unit, the DTO receives precise information of the necessary rework and, therefore, the expected lead time of its associated order is recalculated. This dynamic recalculation increases the accuracy of the lead time estimation. As soon as the quality sensors discover that an order will need a time-consuming “extra” activity (the number of defects from WA is relatively low), the information is sent to the DTO and integrated into the lead-time prediction calculations.According to the incremental approach in Fig. 1, in this iteration we first need to develop the DTO of WB. After that, we need to integrate it with the previous DTO in Fig. 3a, considering the new data acquisition points and the sharing of human operators among WD and WB. Figure 3b illustrates the resulting model of the integration, where highlighted (yellow) areas represent the new parts that have been added to Fig. 3a to evolve the initial DTO.The evolved DTO can be analyzed to estimate the most efficient allocation of operations in each moment, and to easily control the evolution of the number of units that require manual rework (Fig. 5 illustrates an example of this information) and the number of operators in WD and WB.From the description in previous paragraphs, one can deem the DTO incremental evolution as a simple activity. However, it is not. The next section describes the difficulties and complications arose during the DTO integration and validation phases at iteration 2, and the lessons learned during the journey.3 Architectural ConcernsAs discussed in previous section, evolving the production line and the DTO accordingly is essential for the sustainability of the organization. To this end, we reported about the physical changes made in the production line (e.g., a new workstation WB, and new sensors in WA), as well as the changes made in the initial DTO to reflect the changes in the production line.3.1 Architectural Concerns in the Case StudyBy comparing the two DTOs depicted in Fig. 3a and Fig. 3b, it is clear that changes mainly occurred between WA and WD. We introduced in WA a set of different sensors, which are the quality sensors that identify defective units. As these quality sensors send different type of raw data (e.g., ASCII, Binary, Hex, and etc.) at different points in time, we added in the DTO a pre-processing entity (i.e., the Faulty_Unit_Identification in Fig. 3b), which is in charge of analyzing sensors data, tag defective articles, and aggregate data by number of defective articles in a concrete order. It is worth noticing that, due to the volume of raw data, this activity is complex and time consuming. After the analysis, the output of Faulty_Unit_Identification consists in: (i) the order ID, (ii) the number of defective articles in such an order (can be zero if none of the articles had any defect), and (iii) the predicted necessary time for reworking the defective articles (can be zero). Using this information, the DTO recalculates the estimation of the manufacturing lead time for the work-in-progress orders.An order proceeds its way to either WD or WB according to the existence of defective articles. If the order is healthy (i.e., the number of defective units is 0) it is transferred to the priority queue that precedes WD, otherwise it is transferred to WB. When entering WB, the order is buffered into a FIFO queue and waits for an operator. Once the rework is finished the order proceeds to the priority queue before WD, while the operator can remain working in WB or go to WD. The DTO records the defective order ID, the number of defective units, and the actual rework time. The DTO uses this information to increase the accuracy of the future estimations of the necessary rework time and, in consequence, to increase its future lead time predictions accuracy.Further, the evolved DTO also incorporates a policy that computes how to optimally allocate operators to WB and WD to minimize lead time. It uses the information about the status of the production line and the number of articles in each stage, including articles under rework and waiting for rework. In fact, while \(DTO_1\) (see Fig. 3a) was not aligned with OA/BA because it naively assumed two human resources continuously working in WD, the evolved DTO can also suggest the calculated optimal allocation to the operators in each moment.For example, suppose that the two operators are working in WD. When the quality sensors detect a defective article, one of the workers in WD may decide to attend the defective article and rework it. However, this decision can result in a sub-optimal allocation of resources. It is possible that the optimal allocation still assigns two operators to WD, maybe because the current bottleneck in the production line is still WD. The evolved DTO can continuously provide a suggestion about the optimal allocation operators.From this discussion, it is clear that making an evolved DTO is challenging, as it requires to consider many different dimensions. Summarizing, the main issues emerge from:

The OA, BA, and IA are misaligned, and it is difficult to understand the relationships between different resources, between resources and processes, and between resources, processes and the available data.


Both OA, BA and IA are not flexible and they are hard to evolve. When introducing/changing resource/processes/data all of the architectures need be rearranged by introducing technical debts, which will lead to architecture erosion.


DTO is not flexible and hard to evolve. When changes happen into either the OA or the BA or the IA, the whole DTO requires to be rearranged by still introducing technical debts, which will lead to architecture erosion.


3.2 Lessons Learned for Sustainable DigitalizationFrom the above discussion it emerges that, in order to facilitate a straightforward and sustainable digitalization of the structure, products, operations, and all relations tying these together, the OA/BA and IA must be fully aligned. In fact, once the OA/BA and IA are aligned, they can be straightforwardly mapped to the DTO and used for simulating and analyzing the organization: (i) OA/BA provides all the structural and behavioral models needed for the simulation and analysis of the organization, whereas (ii) IA provides both raw (from CPS) and aggregated (from DD) data representing the actual status of the organization.Unfortunately, this is a necessary but not sufficient condition. In fact, as the sustainability of a DTO is largely determined by the sustainability of OA/BA and IA, it must be flexible and able to accommodate continuous and rapid change to OA/BA and IA. Indeed, if the OA/BA requires to be changed in response to new market forces (e.g., manufacturing a new product), the IA should change as well and fulfill the new requirements (e.g., a functionality for managing the new production process). Therefore, the DTO should evolve accordingly and reflect the changes made in both the OA/BA and IA. In fact, if the DTO does not evolve and align according to the enterprise, its benefits are drastically reduced. In other words, rigid architectures restrain the sustainability and evolution of the DTO, and reduce its benefits.To this end, we need to define Architectural Frameworks, which provide principles and practices for jointly specifying, aligning, and evolving OA/BA, IA and DTO. In particular, the Architectural Framework shall include 
[4]: (1) an Architectural Pattern describing architectural elements and connectors, with constraints on how they can be combined, achieving flexibility; (2) a Reference Model decomposing functionality into elements (and data between them) that cooperatively satisfy the organization needs; (3) a Reference Architecture mapping the Reference Model onto system elements and defining the data flows between them. Whereas a reference model splits functionalities, a reference architecture is the mapping of such functionalities onto a system decomposition. The Architectural Framework should explicitly address the following concerns:Modularity – Software engineering defines abstraction as the process of identifying the important aspects of a phenomenon and ignoring the details that are not relevant. What must be considered as important and what should be considered as a detail to be ignored depends on the purpose of the abstraction. Modularity is the degree to which DTOs are decomposed and recombined in terms of abstractions. Specifically, a modular DTO should be structured into identifiable entities, which encapsulate the representation of abstractions, and are accessible through well-defined interfaces. A modular DTO can be then composed entirely from a set of constituent DTOs, where each of them takes care of a specific aspect (i.e., single responsibility), rather than having the aspect spread out over many parts of the DTO. Modularity and Single Responsibility are then important concerns, as they allow for separation of concerns, which can be applied in two phases: first, when dealing with each constituent DTO in isolation (bottom-up design) and second, when dealing with the overall characteristics of all constituent DTOs and their relationships as a whole DTO (top-down design).Granularity – Granularity defines the level of detail of a single constituent DTO. Indeed, it refers to the extent to how small the constituent DTOs are. When a DTO is split into constituents, it is important to measure the degree of componentization. On the one hand, having small, fine-grained constituents provides greater flexibility when composing them into a DTO. On the other hand, small, fine-grained constituents are more difficult to govern. In fact, the larger and coarse-grained constituents are, the easier it is to manage and coordinate them in a whole DTO. Modularity and granularity are tightly coupled and affect each other. A DTO can have multiple possible levels of granularity. The granularity of the data that the physical system can transmit and that can feed the DTO is also a factor to consider during the decision of the most appropriate DTO granularity.Decomposition/Composition Style – Understanding how to properly decompose/compose a DTO into/from constituents is relevant for defining the modularity and granularity of the different entities. A new DTO should be built by taking reusable constituents and combining them to form the required functionality. The capability of understanding each constituent DTO in isolation aids the adaptation and evolution of the whole DTO. To achieve modular decomposability/composability, and understanding, constituent DTOs must have two very important properties, namely high cohesion and loose coupling. A constituent has high cohesion if all its elements are strongly related, and they are together for a reasonable and well-defined specific purpose (i.e. single responsibility). Complementary, coupling is determined by the relationship of an individual constituent with other constituents in the same DTO. Coupling is a measure of the interdependence of two or more constituents in the form of interaction. If two constituents depend on each other heavily—i.e., they are tightly coupled—it will be difficult to observe, analyze, understand, and act them separately. In contrast, modular structures with high cohesion and low coupling allow for considering constituent DTOs as black boxes when the overall structure is described. Such constituents can be observed, analyzed and described separately.Evolution – A DTO emerges from the interactions among the constituent DTOs. Despite the adoption of best engineering practices, the DTO must face inherently continuous evolution, as well as heterogeneous and inconsistent changing elements. Changes inside an organization are the cause of continuous DTO evolution. A DTO evolution occurs when any of the following three basic situations happen 
[8]: self-evolution, joint evolution, and emergent evolution.In self-evolution, a change is introduced because of redesign, redevelopment or improvement of an existing DTO. Requirements include improved business-supporting functions, improved performance through using a new design and more advanced technologies, improved architecture for future development, and their combinations. Referring to the case study addressed in Sect. 2, an example could be an improvable production line WA able to accommodate newly designed robotic arms that best fit the product the machine is working on, or arms that are simply offering improved performance over the previous ones. Self-evolution targets a certain level of granularity of a DTO. In fact, self-evolution can occur at the highest level of granularity, or at lower levels. As the granularity of a DTO is strictly tied with its modularity, it is important to have a distinct vision of the constituents and the grains of a DTO to better locate where the evolution occurs.In joint evolution, two or more DTOs are to be integrated for improved business support. Still referring to the case study in Sect. 2: the two communicating constituents, namely WA and WD, have to deal with possible multiple changes involving, interoperability, data sharing, improved functions and services, and workflow integration. Joint evolution targets two or more DTOs at the same or different levels of granularity. Furthermore, integration between DTOs could potentially change the connectors of the constituents involved.Emergent evolution deals with the design and development of a new DTO based on existing DTOs. Requirements include new functions developed on a joint basis of existing constituents, and new DTOs supporting emerging business needs. An example could be the development of a DTO on the basis of the two constituents including WA and WD. The new DTO digitalizes the functionalities of the underlying smart manufacturing system. Emergent evolution targets two or more DTOs where the one emerging has a higher level of granularity.The previously described evolution types could result in isolated changes. However, Multiple evolutions could also come out simultaneously, with self-evolution, joint evolution and emergent evolution directly affecting a large part of the DTO. If the evolution’s complexity is not controlled the DTO will erode over time due to such changes. The laws of software evolution 
[13] state that uncontrolled evolution brings to

Increasing complexity: as a large program is continuously changed, its complexity, which reflects deteriorating structure, increases unless work is done to maintain or reduce it.


Continuing grow: the functional capability of E-type systems must be continually enhanced to maintain user satisfaction over system lifetime.


Declining quality: unless rigorously adapted and evolved to take into account changes in the operational environment, the quality of an E-type system will appear to be declining.


Hence, an open and connected DTO requires that evolution dimensions are controlled to prevent costly reconstruction. Moreover, it is important to understand why, how, when and where this evolution occurs.4 Related WorkRelated work is manifold and spans over different topics, namely Digital Twin Architectures, Architecture Alignment and Architecture Evolution.Digital Twin (DT) Architectures – Since the DT conception, more than a decade ago 
[21], pioneers have used it in the manufacturing domain in order to improve the production leveraging Virtual Factory 
[12]. In the Industry 4.0 domain, the simulation of different possible behaviors is a main enabler for construction of the desired intelligent systems 
[19]. Despite the efforts to systematize and guide the development and deployment of digital twins in companies 
[1, 9], the systematic implementation of digitalization process in sociotechnical systems remains an open challenge. For instance, DT modeling is recognized as of paramount importance for its prosperous utilization, but there is not a general agreement in the community on a general approach to build the DT models 
[21]. The implementation of DT in domains such as the Cyber-physical fusion also remains an engineering challenge due to the lack of a generally accepted framework for acquiring the data, transmit the data, building operative knowledge from data through simulation or data mining, and controlling the CPS 
[14]. Only recently, researchers have started focusing on the architectural aspects of DT 
[16]. For example, in 
[2] authors propose a layered architecture reference model for cloud-based CPS, in 
[17] authors propose a four-layer architecture pattern to design DT incorporating various types of information sources. The pattern is designed to be extensible with respect to the number of sources, and flexible with respect to the type of information. However, in spite of the increasing interest in DT, little effort has been devoted to investigate architectural quality attributes, such as modifiability, scalability, evolvability, reusability.Architecture Alignment – The need and importance for aligning the Organizational and IT architectures as been pinpointed over time by many research studies 
[7, 22], and now many points of alignment are commonly recognized. Early studies focused on linking the business plan with the IT plan, and/or on ensuring the alignment of business and IT strategies. Other approaches instead examined the mapping between business needs and information system priorities. The implications of architecture alignment have been also demonstrated through many empirical case studies (e.g.,
[10, 15]). The results demonstrate that the organizations that have their Organizational and IT strategies aligned outperform those organizations that do not. Indeed, alignment leads to more focused and strategic use of IT which, in turn, leads to increased performance 
[6].Architecture Evolution – Sociotechnical systems obey the principle of there is nothing permanent except change. The Organizational/Business Architecture will evolve and the Information architecture needs to keep aligned. In consequence, the DTO of the sociotechnical system needs to evolve too. At present, evolving the software-based DT is possible, but doing it in a systematic way that does not boost the software engineering expenses resides in the research frontier. In 
[18], the authors propose a pattern-oriented development approach, where patterns are considered as the main building blocks of the architecture and changes are applied by means of patterns substitution, i.e., design evolution is identified in terms of replacement of patterns by other patterns. Another interesting approach is proposed in 
[3], where the authors present the Evolution Style, which defines a family of domain-specific architecture evolution paths that share common properties and satisfy a common set of constraints. The evolution style specifies the set of concepts needed to define and analyze the software architecture evolution: (i) the set of operators defining the evolution transitions, (ii) the set of evolution path constraints defining whether a path is allowed or not, and (iii) the set of evaluation functions used to compare different evolution paths with respect to quality metrics.5 Conclusions and Future WorkA Digital Twin of the Organization is an accurate representation of an organization (including physical, software, and human elements), which aims at facilitating decision-making processes, and making informed decision in the value chain. However, the lack of engineering best practices for developing and operating DTOs makes industry difficult to fully benefit from this technology. Further, as current solutions are often context-dependent or system-specific, they result challenging to change, extend and reuse.In this paper we reported an initial attempt made in architecting and developing a DTO from a manufacturing industry, and its further evolution. In particular, (i) we detailed a development process leveraging Enterprise Architecture to map the organization structure/behavior (i.e., Organizational/Business Architectures) and status (i.e., Information Architecture) into a DTO, (ii) we pinpointed a set of concerns to be confronted with when architecting a DTO, and (iii) we discussed the need for an Architectural Framework enabling the specification, alignment, and evolution of OA/BA, IA and DTO.To this end, as a future work we mainly plan to address the aforementioned architectural concerns, by devising an architectural framework which specifically takes into account DTO’s Modularity, Granularity, Decomposition/Composition, and Evolution.

papers.fulltext: Testing the Implementation of Concurrent AUTOSAR Drivers against Architecture Decisions Jasmin Jahi c Embedded Software Engineering Fraunhofer IESE Kaiserslautern, Germany jasmin.jahic iese.fraunhofer.com Varun Kumar Infineon Technologies AG Munich, Germany varun.kumar infineon.com Pablo Oliveira Antonino Embedded Software Engineering Fraunhofer IESE Kaiserslautern, Germany pablo.antonino iese.fraunhofer.de Gerhard Wirrer Infineon Technologies AG Munich, Germany gerhard.wirrer infineon.com AbstractConcurrent software based on a shared-memory model is predominant in industrial applications that cannot afford to execute complex message-passing libraries. However, direct access to shared memory creates implicit dependencies between concurrently executing components. Therefore, the de- velopment and maintenance of such software is hard. In this paper, we argue the need to manage, at the architectural level, the implicitly high coupling between concurrent components that share memory. We suggest an approach that verifies architectural specifications against the implementation and finds potential mismatches. While static analysis approaches can be complete and verify all possible mismatches, they are often imprecise, leading to a large number of false warnings, especially in con- current software. Instead, we built our approach, using dynamic analysis, on top of one of the most well-known algorithms for detecting data races, Eraser Lockset, and extended its model to support features required for the verification process. Since Lockset operates on the execution traces, test cases that produce these traces must ensure proper coverage. Therefore, we argue the need to use test cases conforming to the strict modified condi- tion decision coverage criteria (MC DC). Our version of Lockset takes advantage of the fact that possible shared memory locations are known in advance. We further improved its precision by considering atomic operations as a synchronization mechanism. The approach was evaluated on industrial AUTOSAR drivers that execute concurrently. Index TermsTraceability, AUTOSAR, data race, Lockset, architecture, MC DC coverage I. INTRODUCTION In the era of multi-core and many-core computing, software components execute concurrently and independently. However, to share their execution results, these components eventually have to communicate with each other. Message passing is one of the most common communication strategies. It is present in distributed systems, and it can also be implemented between components executing on the same multi-core machine. From the architectural point of view, messages that components pass to each other express their data interfaces and their depen- dencies. As message passing is performed via well-defined interfaces supported by libraries (e.g., MPI), the dependencies between components are obvious and explicit. The interfaces ensure low communication coupling between components, making the understanding and maintenance of such systems relatively easy. In the embedded domain, however, factors such as cost, performance, and size are among the main architectural drivers of a system. Software executes on electronic control units (ECUs) with limited performance capabilities. Message pass- ing is not suitable for most embedded systems, as engineers are not willing to sacrifice performance for running additional communication libraries. Another great architectural driver are real-time execution constraints. The non-deterministic commu- nication duration of message passing and the lack of direct control over the communication between components is often not acceptable. This is especially the case in safety-critical systems (e.g., airbags in a car), where engineers prefer low- level control over executing components (hence, approaches such as OpenMP are not an option). To cope with these challenges, engineers often use shared memory for the com- munication between software components (i.e., threads), and thread libraries that provide low-level control (e.g., POSIX threads). Although such communication solves performance and control-related challenges, it introduces a new kind of complexity. Threads directly access shared memory without any specific interface. Dependencies between them are not obvious and not explicit, and are very hard to reconstruct from the code (i.e., it is difficult to identify memory shared between threads). If developers of one thread change its code to access shared memory, the change implicitly affects the correctness of other threads. Lack of proper communication interfaces leads to high coupling between threads, making the understanding and maintenance of such systems very hard. The simplest example of the high coupling in multi-threaded software systems is the synchronization of the threads access to shared memory. For example, if n readers and one writer access shared memory, there is no need for an explicit synchro- nization mechanism. However, if engineers change one of the readers to also write to the shared memory, this change affects all other threads involved in access to the shared memory. Therefore, there is a great need to manage this kind of implicit dependencies. In order to cope with this challenge and impose a certain structure, architects often impose constraints on the usage of shared memory. In industry, architectural specifications often include information about thread components and their expected operations on shared memory (e.g., a thread is 171 2019 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA) 978-1-7281-0528-4 19 31.00 2019 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. allowed to write to a specific memory range). Therefore, the main problem is to ensure that the implementation conforms to the architectural specifications. Contrary to the classical trace- ability problem, in this case there exists an explicit mapping between architectural specifications and the implementation. In industrial architecture design, we often see specifications of the operations of each executing thread component on concrete (not abstract) memory locations of a controller and names of shared states (variables) that the implementation needs to conform to. The simplest way to verify whether the implementation conforms to the architectural specifications would be static analysis. Static analysis of source code can be complete and find all violations of the specifications. However, some code statements are statically unsolvable. Consequently, some execution paths are not feasible in reality. Because of this, static analysis of the source code is prone to false warnings (i.e., false positives). In cases of imprecise static analysis, instead of fixing the real issues, developers spend more time verifying whether the reported issues are really harmful. This is especially the case for software that involves concurrency. To solve the problem of ensuring that the implementation does indeed conform to the concurrency-related architectural decisions (i.e., operations on shared memory), in this paper we propose an approach based on dynamic analysis. Our approach executes the software under consideration and uses the execution trace as primary input for the analysis. The execution trace represents a list of the executed instructions with their details (e.g., instruction type, memory address, symbol name, mapping to a source code line number). To ensure the completeness of our approach, the test cases that produce the execution trace satisfy the modified-condition- decision-coverage (MC DC) criteria 1 . A logical decision (Figure 1) is composed of logical conditions connected via logical operators (e.g., AND, OR). To satisfy the MC DC coverage criteria, it is necessary to evaluate every decision to TRUE and FALSE; also every condition in a decision must be evaluated to TRUE and FALSE. In addition, MC DC prescribes that every combination of conditions where a change of a single condition leads to a different outcome of a decision (while other conditions in the decision do not change), must be considered. For a decision with n conditions, MC DC prescribes the execution of n 1 test cases 1 . Therefore, a trace collected using MC DC conforming test cases contains traces of every statement, traces of the execution paths considering different outcomes of every decision and every condition, and relevant combinations of conditions. The strict coverage criteria of MC DC are acknowledged by the standard for safety-relevant automotive systems, ISO 26262 2 , which prescribes them as a highly recommended coverage metric for the highest Automotive Safety Integrity Level (i.e., ASIL D). To verify mismatches between architec- ture specifications and the implementation, our approach takes as input architecture specifications (operations of software components on shared memory), statically extracted debug symbols of the tested binary, and the execution trace of Fig. 1. a) Structure of a logical decision with conditions and logical operators. b) An example of a logical decision with conditions and logical operators. the binary. We adjusted the memory model of the Erasers Lockset 3 algorithm (a well-known algorithm for detecting concurrency bugs) to help us identify shared memory and shared-memory operations of concurrently executing software components. The absence of mismatches between architecture specifica- tions and implementation does not guarantee the absence of data races. In order to find data races more efficiently, our approach uses a modified Lockset algorithm with information about the shared memory from the architecture verification step. This helps us discard non-shared memory locations from Locksets analysis. The Erasers Lockset algorithm was designed to consider only lock-based synchronization. We modified the Lockset detection algorithm to consider atomic operations as synchronization primitives. In summary, this paper presents the following contributions: Approach for finding mismatches between concurrency- related architecture decisions and their implementation. Lee in his famous paper on why threads are a bad idea 4 claims that the main problem with threads is that their concurrent abstractions does not resemble the concurrency of the physical world. We investigated further the problem with threads, and complement this observation with the conclusion that the core challenge with shared-memory based computation model is the high implicit coupling of threads due to the need to synchronize them. Changes in access to shared memory, or in use of synchronization primi- tives in one thread, immediately affect correctness of other, otherwise independent threads. The proper synchronization is a condition for correctness. The lack of the standardized communication interfaces further contributes to difficulty of managing these implicit dependencies. However, threads are commonly accepted in industry. Since we have to live with this complexity, there is a need to manage it. We see a great need to specify concurrency-related intentions on the logical data architectural level and verify if the implementation is following those specifications. Otherwise, development and maintenance of multithreaded software on a large scale is very difficult. A. AUTOSAR API CONCURRENCY SCENARIOS Software functionality and complexity in the automotive industry have been growing in the past two decades. The complexity of automotive software originates from its eco- system, which consists of multiple layers of different suppliers and vendors. The automotive industry has perceived a growing demand for software and has established standardized software engineering practices, methods, tools, and specifications in the form of the AUTOSAR consortium 30 . The AUTomotive Open Software Architecture (AUTOSAR) framework defines an open architecture for automotive software. The AUTOSAR software stack is divided into three lay- ers (Fig. 2). The application software layer is composed of software components that provide end-user features. A software component (SWC) is a collection of tasks, which are composed of runnables (i.e., functions that can execute concurrently). SWCs connect through the Virtual Function Bus (VFB).The RunTime Environment (RTE) layer separates the Basic Software Modules (BSW) layer from the AUTOSAR application software layer and is an instantiation of VFB. The RTE is generated to realize the connection between different SWCs, and also between the SWCs and the BSW modules. At the bottom of the AUTOSAR stack is the BSW, a collection of software files (code and description) that define certain basic software functionality present on an electronic control unit (ECU). It contains basic services, the ECU abstraction layer, the Microcontroller Abstraction Layer (MCAL), and device drivers. The MCAL contains drivers to enable access to the on-chip peripheral devices of a microcontroller and to off-chip memory-mapped peripheral devices by a defined Application Programming Interface (API). A runnable invokes the MCAL to execute basic software module APIs either via basic services or via the ECU Abstraction layer. APIs provided by shared modules may be called by runnables executing independently on different cores. This scenario leads to concurrent execution of driver APIs. Also, several runnables can concurrently execute instances of the same API. API drivers communicate with peripheral devices through special function registers (SFRs), which are special memory- mapped locations on the overall System-on-Chip (SoC) pro- cessor memory map. API drivers also have access to the global variables of the AUTOSAR software module. Therefore, API drivers face standard challenges found in concurrent, mul- tithreaded software (i.e., data races, deadlocks). In order to avoid concurrency bugs, API drivers need to synchronize their access to the shared memory (i.e., using locks and atomic op- erations). Lock-based synchronization introduces a new source of non-determinism into the system as API drivers that use the same lock can block each other, which causes a delay to the execution of the tasks. System architects make decisions about API drivers, their data dependencies, and the operations they should perform on the shared memory (i.e., read, write, read- write). To tame the synchronization-related source of non- determinism, architects use an architecture model to reason about the necessary type of synchronization between instances of API drivers, and minimize the interleaving of critical API drivers in the scheduling scheme. For example, if it is decided that a group of drivers only writes to a shared memory location, it is enough to use atomic operations that do not cause blocking. However, if a driver reads and writes to a shared memory location, it will be necessary to use lock- based synchronization (i.e., create a critical section). It is Fig. 3. From the execution trace, Lockset finds data races by using synchronization primitive specifications. expected that developers will comply with the architecture design decisions when implementing API drivers. However, if developers make some other decisions about operations on the shared memory than those prescribed by the architecture, API drivers might influence each others execution time in a manner that the architect did not predict. The software might have a different execution time than expected and might miss real-time deadlines. Therefore, it is necessary to verify whether the implementation is in conformance with the architecture decisions. IV. VERIFICATION OF CONCURRENCY-RELATED ARCHITECTURE DECISIONS The architecture offers an overview of data dependencies between AUTOSAR API drivers. In particular, the architecture design contains the memory locations shared between the API drivers and the memory operations performed by the API drivers on the respective shared memory (i.e., read-only, write-only, read-write). The first challenge we address is the verification of specified data dependencies against the im- plementation. The verification process of these dependencies is static (no software execution). It requires a model of the software architecture and debug symbols from a binary (Fig. 3- a). The second challenge is the verification of operations on the shared memory. For this verification, our approach executes the API drivers and produces their execution trace (i.e., exe- cuted machine instructions with debug symbols). By analyzing the execution trace and the architecture design specifications, our approach finds mismatches in memory operations between the architecture design and the implementation (Fig. 3-b). In order to give credibility to our results, we conclude this section by explaining how we ensure code coverage (i.e., completeness) of the execution trace, appropriate for the safety critical embedded systems. A. Verification of Shared Memory Locations The architecture design contains two types of shared mem- ory, global variables and microcontroller special function Fig. 4. Model of an API driver with operations on the shared memory. registers (SFRs). The global variables follow the Mip Vn naming convention prescribed by AUTOSAR, where Mip is the module implementation prefix and Vn is the variable name. SFR is a special register within microcontrollers used to control various peripheral hardware devices (e.g., analog- to-digital converters). SFRs are modeled as memory location ranges. The architecture model of the API drivers specifies data dependencies as architecture decisions. Concurrency- related architecture decisions are represented as a relationship between an API driver and shared memory locations (i.e., a global variable or SFR, Fig. 4). Concurrent API drivers could theoretically share global variables, heap memory, and even a local memory passed over pointers. However, we assume that the software adheres to the MISRA-C coding guidelines 31 (common in AUTOSAR- related safety-critical automotive applications), which prohibit dynamic memory allocation. MISRA-C static analysis ensures compliance with the standard of all source files. Therefore, the only possible shared memory locations are global variables and SFR memory locations. As the compiler assembles and links the source code into an executable and linkable format (ELF) file, it produces a binary with debug symbols. The list of debug symbols contains the names and locations of memory used. Modern micro controllers generally allocate a continuous memory location range from the CPU address map for SFRs as memory-mapped registers. These memory ranges are globally defined and shared by nature. By analyzing the symbols of a binary, we extract the global variables and the SFR range accessed by an API driver. The verification process that checks whether the software implementation conforms to the design is as follows (Fig. 3- a). With the help of architecting tools, we generate a textual representation of the architectural design. We compare the generated textual representation of the architecture with an extract of the symbol list from the executable. The comparison verifies whether the source code implementation of an API driver uses only the shared memory locations prescribed by the architecture. It also verifies whether the architecture defines data dependencies and shared memory locations of API drivers that are not used in the implementation. The outcome of the static verification (Fig. 3-a) is a list of shared memory locations that API drivers of an AUTOSAR module can possibly share. Fig. 5. Modified Lockset memory model (isShared instead of virgin state), with possible states of a variable shared between drivers (a), and states of a variable per driver (b). B. Verification of Operations on the Shared Memory Besides data dependencies, the architecture design also contains information about the types of operations performed by different API drivers on the shared memory. An API driver can only write, only read, or read-write to a shared memory location. In order to verify whether the memory operations of the API drivers on the shared memory conform to the architecture design, we execute the software and record its execution trace. For each executed instruction, the execution trace contains: API driver ID (similar to thread ID), instruction operation type, and target memory location (in the case of STORE LOAD instruction types). If there are several instances of the same API driver that can execute concurrently, the API driver ID is different for each instance. By relating the execution trace and the debug information, it is possible to link the executed instructions to the source code. Therefore, we relate every memory access to a concrete variable name as well as to the location of the access (i.e., a function and a line number of the access). We verify whether the implementation is in conformance with the design by analyzing a list of shared memory locations that the API drivers of an AUTOSAR module can share (Fig. 3- a), information about the types of operations that different API drivers perform on the shared memory, and an execution trace as illustrated in Fig 3-b. In order to classify the memory operations, we used an enhanced version of Erasers Lockset memory model 3 . This model was designed to identify shared memory locations between threads (shared) as well as those memory locations that are prone to data races (i.e., a variable is shared between threads, and at least one operation is write; hence, it is in the shared-modified state). According to the original Locksets memory model, upon allocation of a memory location, its state is virgin. As long as the same thread that allocated the memory accesses that memory location, it remains labeled as exclusive. When a new thread accesses the shared memory with a read operation, Eraser labels it as shared. If some other thread executes a write operation on the same memory location, Eraser labels it as shared-modified. API drivers do not allocate shared memory; hence, we do not need the virgin state (Fig 5-a). Furthermore, if a variable is not on the list of possibly shared memory locations, it will be discarded. This piece of information enables us to instantly filter out all irrelevant memory operations. The Lockset model describes how concurrent threads share memory locations. Besides this information, we also want to track the memory operations of each API driver. Therefore, we add additional data structures to the Lockset model for each API driver (Fig 5-b). The structures read-only, write-only, and read-write exist for each API driver. Based on the first operation that an API driver performs on a shared variable, it will advance either to the read-only or to the write-only state. If an API driver performs read while a variable is in the write- only state, or write while a variable is in read-only, the state of the variable will be read-write. The verification process is performed on a set of API drivers and their instances. It discovers whether the API drivers really access the memory locations from the list of shared memory locations (Fig. 3-a). If a variable stays in the exclusive state, then it is not shared. The reasons for this could be dead code, as none of the execution paths leads to the access of the possibly shared variable. After analyzing the execution trace, the process compares the state of the variables of each API driver (Fig 5-b) with the architecture design. It detects whether the API drivers operate on the shared memory as prescribed by the architecture design. C. Code Coverage of API Drivers and Completeness of the Execution Trace The verification process for the operations on the shared memory takes as input the execution trace of the API drivers (Fig 3-b). However, generating a complete execution trace, where completeness is characterized by the execution of all possible execution paths of a driver, is a challenging task. Executing all possible paths is, first of all, time-consuming. Therefore, scientists have adopted coverage criteria which, if satisfied, are commonly accepted to ensure certain quality properties of software. For verifying the memory operations, it is enough to access every variable with every possible memory operation type (i.e., read, write). In order to find data races, it is necessary to reproduce all possible paths that can result in access to the shared memory. If an execution path containing access to the shared memory does not contain appropriate synchronization primitives, it is a racy execution path. If the source code of an API driver contains logical con- ditions, a single execution covers only one possible execution path. Test cases fulfill statement coverage if they achieve exe- cution of every statement. Branch coverage requires execution of every branch in the program. Branches depend on decisions in the code that can evaluate either to true or to false. Decisions are composed of logical conditions. Some paths depend not only on the outcome of the decision (i.e., true or false), but Fig. 6. Data structures required for Lockset. also on the combination of the decisions conditions that result in its outcome. For n possible logical conditions of a single decision, the number of possible execution paths is 2n. In order to solve the problem with path explosion, scientists have suggested modified decision condition criteria (MC DC 1 ). It requires execution of conditions that independently influence the outcome of a decision (i.e., a change of a single condition in a decision changes the outcome of that decision, while other conditions in the decision do not change). To produce execution traces, we rely on source code in- strumentation. At this level, software that generates test cases has access to the source code structure, which it relates to the execution trace. Therefore, it can extract all necessary information (i.e., control flow graph) for the quantification of the MC DC coverage. In order to ensure completeness, for each API driver we generate execution traces that satisfy MC DC coverage. V. FINDING CONCURRENCY BUGS IN AUTOSAR API DRIVERS Even if the software implementation conforms to the ar- chitecture design (i.e., no mismatch among data dependencies and operations on the shared memory between the architecture design and the implementation), this does not guarantee that the software will execute as expected. Concurrency bugs, of which the most predominant ones are data races, still could be present in the software. Therefore, it is necessary to test if the implementation of the API drivers is race-free. A. Eraser Lockset Algorithm One of the most popular algorithms for finding data races today is the Eraser Lockset algorithm 3 . It takes as input the execution trace, which is a stream of executed instruction records. The Eraser Lockset algorithm has two parts. The first part identifies shared memory using a state memory model as shown in Fig. 5-a (originally, the state is virgin instead of isShared) and as explained in section IV-B. The second part of the Eraser Lockset is the algorithm for the identification of data races, based on the correctness criterion that a common set of locks should always protect a variable (i.e., a memory location) modified by several tasks. Lockset maintains a set of currently held locks for every task (Fig. 6). Lockset associates each variable with a candidate set of locks, which represents the set of locks that have protected the variable so far. At the beginning of the analysis, the candidate set of each variable contains all locks that exist in the tested program. Until a variable reaches the shared state, its candidate set remains unchanged. If the variable is shared, on each access to it, Lockset retrieves the list of candidate set locks and currently held locks of the executing task. Lockset creates a new candidate set for the associated variable by intersecting its candidate set with the currently held locks set of the task performing the memory access (candidate set(new) candidate set currently held locks set). If the result of the intersection is an empty set (candidate set(new) ) and if the variable is in a shared-modified state, Lockset identifies a potential data race. B. Improving Performance During their execution, threads access local only and shared memory. The original Lockset model assumes that every memory location can be potentially shared (which is generally a valid assumption), and every variable that a thread accesses would be saved in its list of variables (Fig. 6). In order to update a variables state, according to the Lockset memory model, it would be necessary to find that variable in the list of variables. Even short software executions result in huge traces (e.g., an application that executes for half a second produces an execution trace of 1 GB 32 ). To achieve good coverage, it would be necessary to execute a thread several times. Therefore, the number of variables in the list of variables would be huge. Finding a variable in the list of variables introduces overhead because it is necessary to find the variable in this huge list and update its status. If a thread accesses a variable for the first time, the algorithm would have to inspect every variable in the list of variables, only to conclude that it is necessary to add a new input to the list. The outcome of the verification of concurrency-related architecture decisions (Fig. 3, section IV-B) is a list of memory locations that API drivers can possibly share, verified by the combination of static and dynamic analysis. If a variable is not on the list of possibly shared memory locations, it will be discarded according to the modified Lockset model we proposed (Fig. 5-a). By using the list of shared variables from the previous step of the analysis (Fig.3-b, find memory operation specification mismatches), we reduce the input for the next analysis step (Fig. 3-b, find data races), by reducing the possible number of variables in the list of variables of each API driver to the number of possibly shared variables among all tasks. Consequently, we reduce the time required to find a variable in that list and update its state. We also reduce the amount of memory required by the algorithm because the list of variables does not contain irrelevant memory locations that can never be shared. C. Improving Precision In its original form, the Eraser Lockset algorithm considers only lock-based synchronization. If an API driver accesses the Fig. 7. The modified Lockset algorithm, with enhancements (darkened parts). shared memory using an atomic operation, Lockset will report a false positive. Therefore, we modified Lockset to consider atomic instructions as a synchronization mechanism (Fig. 7). Modifications include two new blocks. If the address of a memory access is not among the possibly shared memory locations (i.e., isShared), this instruction will be discarded from further processing. If an instruction is an atomic op- eration, the algorithm will update the state of the variable. However, it will not calculate a new candidate set, nor will it reason on whether the access is a data race because we assume that the atomic update protects the variable from races. This assumption (i.e., Atomic instruction? in Fig. 7) also resolves the case of combining locks with atomic instructions. For example, if within a critical section of the var1 variable, there is an atomic update of the var2 variable, the algorithm will not update candidate set of the var2. If it did, the algorithm would lead to a wrong conclusion, namely that the candidate set of var1 should also protect var2, which is not intended because the atomic operation provides enough synchronization. VI. IMPLEMENTATION The architecture model was developed using Enterprise Architect (EA). An example of the model with syntax is shown in Figure 4. It covers assignment of memory locations to an API driver, along with the memory operations. For the EA, we developed a plugin that generates a textual representation of the model. In order to obtain the execution trace, we used a testing tool to generate unit test cases for each function of the API drivers. The test cases satisfy the MC DC coverage criteria. The same tool instruments the API drivers at the source code level, inserting statements that enable tracing the execution. The API driver runs on an instruction set simulator, which is a software application that mimics the targeted hardware. This setup provides a software-based platform for executing binaries in a virtual environment (without the need for real hardware). The instruction set simulator provides a debugger interface to communicate with the unit test tool. By using this interface, the unit test tool can load executable and read write values according to the memory map configuration. The simulator generates the execution traces while executing the API drivers with unit tests. Once the tests are completed, we combine the execution traces. If an API driver can have several instances, unit test cases are performed twice to create two independent execution traces (i.e., different addresses for the local variables). Finally, our modified Lockset algorithm (Fig. 7) processes the execution trace to find mismatches between specified operations on the memory and the im- plementation of the API drivers (section IV-B), and also to find data races (section V). After a replay of the execution trace, the list of variables of each API driver contains the accessed variables from the set of possibly shared variables extracted and validated statically. By comparing these lists and the specification, we additionally verify whether some shared memory was specified to be used, but in practice (although declared) was never used (e.g., due to unreachable code). Therefore, the architecture specifications are verified against the implementation using static and dynamic analysis. VII. EVALUATION A. Setup Industrial AUTOSAR-alike software is very hard to obtain, as it almost always contains confidential information. To the best of our knowledge, there does not exist any open source benchmark with AUTOSAR software and the architectural model containing concurrency-related properties. Therefore, we were very lucky to obtain three peripheral API drivers (driver1, driver2, driver3) with their architecture models from our industry partner. The purpose and the names of drivers are anonymized, due to the confidentiality issues. Since several AUTOSAR tasks can use the same API driver, two or more instances of the same API driver can execute concurrently, using shared resources. The execution traces of these APIs were gathered using source code instrumentation, as explained in section IV-C. On these traces, we applied implementations of the original Eraser Lockset and our mod- ified Lockset for AUTOSAR. The architecture models of the tested API drivers served as additional input for the modified Lockset. We counted the number of data races that the Lockset and the modified Lockset reported. By analyzing the reported races, we identified false positives and reported their number. The modified Lockset also reported the number of mismatches between the specifications in the architecture models and the implementation. Finally, we compared the time needed by each of the two algorithms to process the execution trace and reported the reduced analysis time that our modified Lockset achieved compared to the original Lockset. B. Results and Discussion TABLE II REPORTED DATA RACES WITH ORIGINAL LOCKSET (L) AND MODIFIED LOCKSET (L ), NUMBER OF DATA RACES (FROM REPORTED DATA RACES) THAT WERE FALSE POSITIVES, REPORTED NUMBER OF ARCHITECTURE MISMATCHES, AND OVERHEAD REDUCTION OF MODFIED LOCKSET COMPARED TO THE ORIGINAL LOCKSET. Test case reported data races (L) false positives (L) reported data races (L ) false positives (L ) architecture mismatches overhead reduction(L L) Driver 1 5 0 5 0 1 -9 Driver 2 0 0 0 0 0 -10 Driver 3 1 1 0 0 0 -0.1 The results in the table II show that our approach detected one mismatch between the architecture model and the imple- mentation for driver1. Driver1 uses only lock-based synchro- nization. Therefore, both algorithms reported the same number of potential data races., and all reported data races were real. Driver2 was implemented as specified in the architecture, and the algorithms detected no data races (the driver used lock- based synchronization only). Driver3 used atomic operations and lock-based synchronization. The original Lockset reported one data race. After the inspection of the code, we concluded that the reported race was, in fact a false positive. In all three cases, our modified Lockset performed faster. The higher speed depends on the ratio between the numbers of local variables and global variables. In cases where an API hardly uses any local variables (Driver3), the gain in performances was minimal. In cases of runtime verification of embedded cyclic soft- ware, threads are triggered with a predefined period (T), in a predefined scheduling order, and such software executes indefinitely. If we consider that each memory location is potentially shared, the Locksets list of all variables would become huge after several executions. Therefore, searching for a variable in such a list in order to update its status would introduce huge overhead. However, if the software is developed according to AUTOSAR and MISRA-C standards (a valid assumption in the automotive industry), our approach will reduce the list of variables to potentially shared memory only. It that case, it is possible to perform runtime verification efficiently. In order to assure completeness of the execution traces, our solution generates test cases that ensure MC DC coverage. VIII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK Operations on shared memory performed by concurrently executing software components are important architecture de- cisions. These decisions have far-reaching consequences for different aspects of the system, including its schedulability. If developers instead of architects make decisions about the usage of shared memory followed by the decision which synchronization primitive type to use, the consequences can be execution delays. These can jeopardize the correct functioning of the system, as some tasks might miss their deadlines. Therefore, it needs to be verified whether the implementation follows the specified concurrency-related architecture deci- sions. In this paper, we presented an approach for finding mismatches between specified shared memory operations and the implementation. We used a modified Lockset algorithm and took advantage of the fact that the intentions of concurrent execution are known in the form of an architecture model. Verification of the model results in information about the set of shared memory locations and the atomic operations used, which we use to improve the performance and precision of the Lockset algorithm. Our approach enables verification of the concurrency-related architecture decisions as well as verification whether the implementation is race free, and provides confidence in the results by generating execution traces that satisfy MC DC coverage (required in safety-critical software). This setup relates the high-level architecture decisions to the low-level implementation, and benefits from this in terms of performance and precision improvements. Because of the complexity of the shared-memory concurrent software, caused by implicit high coupling between components, we consider that it is absolutely necessary to have such relationship. Oth- erwise, architects and developers will fail to properly manage the development of the concurrent software. We showed that the suggested approach is able to find mismatches between architecture specifications and implementation in industrial software. We have implemented it on top of the existing in- dustrial development and testing infrastructure, demonstrating its applicability in practice. While the paper explores a use case of the widely accepted AUTOSAR standard for the automotive industry, we believe it is applicable for other safety-critical embedded systems that use concurrent software, because in these systems the assumptions we rely on, in this paper, also hold. In the future, we are planning to expand our work and consider other concurrency bugs (e.g., atomicity violations, deadlocks, priority inversion), and other synchronization prim- itives (e.g., barriers, inter-thread communication). papers.author: Tobias W{\"{a}}gemann and Ramin Kolagari and Klaus Schmid
papers.abstract: Product lines of software-intensive systems have a great diversity of features and products, which leads to vast design spaces that are difficult to explore. In addition, finding optimal product line system architectures usually requires a consideration of several quality trade-offs at once, involving both product-level as well as product-line-wide criteria. This challenge cannot be solved manually for all but the smallest problems, and can therefore benefit from automated support. In this paper we propose ADOOPLA, a tool-supported approach for the optimization of product line system architectures. In contrast to existing approaches where product-level approaches only support product-level criteria and product-line oriented approaches only support product-line-wide criteria, our approach integrates criteria from both levels in the optimization of product line architectures. Further, the approach can handle multiple objectives at once, supporting the architect in exploring the multi-dimensional Pareto-front of a given problem. We describe the theoretical principles of the ADOOPLA approach and demonstrate its application to a simplified case study from the automotive domain.
