papers.fulltext:
1 IntroductionThe microservices architecture steadily gained popularity over the last years. Nowadays, it is often used in greenfield projects, but a lot of the times, systems are first developed as monoliths, which are quicker to develop and to test than microservices. Monoliths can then be broken up into microservices, when and if the need arises 
[1]. Doing this may promise high scalability, shorter release cycles or better maintainability. However, missing to identify the right boundaries may hinder reaching these benefits 
[2]. Therefore, an essential part of such a refactoring is the decomposition approach 
[3], which has the end-goal to identify contextually-related functionality and encapsulate it into different services. These should be characterized by a high cohesion inwards and loose coupling outwards. To optimally leverage from the microservices architectural pattern, existing functionality has to be split up with appropriate granularity as well.There have been a number of approaches proposed already to decompose monoliths into microservices 
[4, 5]. However, Fritzsch et al. found that such refactoring approaches were often not considered by practitioners and that identifying suitable service cuts is still perceived as a major challenge 
[3]. They asked 16 practitioners from 10 companies who were in the process of migrating their systems. Participants were either not aware of such tools or even convinced that it would be impossible to automate such a complex task. In a review of refactoring approaches, the same authors ascribed a lack of automation and missing tool support to most approaches proposed by academia 
[5]. This lack of tools inhibits adoption in industrial contexts and makes empirical studies more challenging to conduct.We address this gap by a) identifying a systematic approach that combines principles of the previously proposed methods, b) using it to create a prototypical implementation, and c) conducting an industry case study with the prototype.In the remainder of the paper, we discuss related work to provide an overview of other approaches, and describe our own approach, which relies on static and dynamic analysis. We introduce a prototype – MonoBreaker – that embodies this approach, and that identifies service boundaries for monoliths based on the Django web framework. Afterward, we present a case study, in which we contrast the results of MonoBreaker with ServiceCutter by surveying three developers of the project.2 Related WorkThe subject of decomposing and migrating monolithic applications to microservices is addressed in books such as Building Microservices 
[6], Monolith to Microservices 
[7] and Microservices Patterns 
[8]. Likewise, a variety of research papers describe ways to tackle such transformations.Building microservices ideally means to create services that are highly cohesive and loosely coupled. Tyszberowicz 
[9] confirms that Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is the most common technique for modeling microservices. With DDD, the software mirrors business domains and sub-domains as well as the related domain models and bounded contexts. Each bounded context implements a small set of strongly-related behaviors and conforms to the Common Closure Principle 
[10]. These sets of behaviors shape individual units, resulting in cohesive designs of loosely-coupled services 
[11]. A system following DDD supports a higher degree of team independence as well as better scalability, testability and changeability 
[12].Meta-studies. Ponce et al. provide an up-to-date overview in their review of 20 papers of migration and refactoring techniques 
[4]. Their study focuses on the approaches, the applicability to certain system types, validations of the techniques, and the associated challenges. The authors group works by their underlying decomposition approaches: model-driven (involving design elements, e.g., DDD), static analysis (based on source code) and dynamic analysis (based on runtime data).Fritzsch et al. similarly compare 10 refactoring approaches and likewise provide a classification 
[5]. They distinguish decompositions based on Static Code Analysis, Meta-Data, Workload-Data, and Dynamic Microservice Composition. While the first three classes imply a fixed decomposition result, a dynamic composition of services would be continuously re-calculated, e.g., based on workload constraints. The study moreover reveals that most approaches are only applicable to certain types of applications, require significant amounts of input, or have limited and prototypical tool support.Concrete Approaches and Tools. Nunes et al. pursue an approach based on identifying transactional contexts of business applications and using a clustering algorithm to determine service candidates 
[13]. Chen et al. similarly base the decomposition on the data flow of the business logic 
[14]. They compare the resulting service cut with the output of ServiceCutter 
[15], a freely-available tool implementing the approach by Gysel et al. 
[16]. ServiceCutter applies a clustering algorithm to identify new services and currently supports the Girvan-Newman and Leung algorithms for this purpose. To calculate the service cut, it requires that an Entity-Relationship Model (ERM) of the system is given in a specific format along with User Representations and Coupling Criteria. The collection of these partly-exhaustive system specifications is done in a manual process and requires the help of domain experts.Ren et al. acknowledge the inadequacy of approaches only relying on static analysis 
[17]. They recognize that not analyzing the runtime behavior would hinder the calculation of a complete and accurate service cut. Therefore, they combine static and dynamic analysis based on the applications’ runtime behavior. A subsequent clustering calculates the candidate service cut. Likewise, Taibi et al. propose a combined approach based on dependency analysis and process mining techniques 
[18]. The decomposition encompasses execution path and frequency analysis. After removing circular dependencies, additionally specified decomposition options are ranked based on coupling and granularity metrics to produce the candidate service cut. The authors employ a toolFootnote 1 that is capable of generating graphical visualizations to represent the business processes. Although a tool is referenced to capture the dynamic behavior of the system, the suggestion of service cuts is outside the scope of the work and must be done by experts, even if the authors mention that the process can somehow be automated.Implications for our Approach. The methods described by Richardson
[8] (Decompose by business capability and Decompose by subdomain) provide general guidelines for a partly-automated decomposition process. They support architects in choosing appropriate input values and assessing the resulting candidate service cuts.The two meta-studies by Ponce and Fritzsch yield a variety of strategies to break down a monolith. Most do not combine static and dynamic analysis to steer the decomposition. As such, the works by Ren et al. and Taibi et al. comprise the core concepts of the approach described in our work. These works do not provide tools for service decomposition, or for any form of automation, but we will build on the concept of gathering runtime behavior and its analysis.ServiceCutter is also of importance to our work, as it too implements the deterministic Girvan-Newman algorithm. In some aspects, our work is less sophisticated than ServiceCutter, as it does not yet consider quality attributes like security, scalability, and business ownership. However, it trades that for the benefit of being independent from extraneous, subjective, information provided by experts to determine the service cuts.3 ApproachDecomposing a monolith is often done based on insights from software developers on the specific context of the problem domain and of the application’s architecture. The challenge that we aim to address is to reduce subjectivity, making the process more systematic and automated. The approach described below is based on ideas that have been documented before 
[16,17,18], but are employed here for determining service boundaries with minimal to no manual input, which so far has not been feasibly demonstrated. Therefore, the approach is described as a hypothesis, and the case study in Sect. 5 as a first step to provide support for its effectiveness.In more concrete terms, this approach aims to be data-driven and to be independent of sophisticated input from experts. To do this, we do not take into account all the intricacies of the process as it is often done manually today. Instead, we focus on what information can be obtained from the application itself via static and dynamic analysis to find beneficial service cuts. We rely on the availability of a) static software artifacts, namely source code, and b) operational data, such as the use of API endpoints, of datastores, and of issued method calls.Static Analysis. Software artifacts are analyzed and the collected information used to build a graph-like model of the system, representing components as nodes and the dependencies between them as edges. Components and dependencies can be of different types, and identifying them will depend on the used programming languages, frameworks and environments. For example, components can refer to classes, packages or modules, and dependencies to imports or method calls.Each edge is assigned a weight to represent the strength of the dependency. This is a function of the number and quality of connections between the two components. The weight of edges after static analysis can, for example, be the sum of the number of imports and method calls between its two components.Dynamic Analysis. The system is then monitored at runtime to gather operational data, which is analyzed to identify how the dependencies are exercised during execution, and gain an understanding of how the system is actually used. Such information is used to compute a new weight for each edge of the graph. The final weight values are a function of the static and dynamic weights, and are a measure for how the components in the system are mutually bound. The underlying assumption is that a high amount of interaction between two components correlates with belonging to a common bounded context. Including them in different microservices would imply higher costs in latency and in maintaining resilience and fault tolerance.Clustering. A graph of the service composition will support identifying different clusters of components. The nodes connected by the edges with higher weight values will be grouped to form clusters of relatively high cohesion. These clusters will depend on each other through edges with low weight values, representing relatively low coupling. The clusters can, therefore, be used to determine a set of possible service cuts. The specific clustering algorithm to be used is outside the scope of this approach, but would be interesting to explore (see Sect. 6).Decomposition Suggestion. The identified service cuts serve as a foundation for assigning existing software artifacts to each of the new services and advise on the architectural refactoring process.4 The MonoBreaker ToolMonoBreaker aims to demonstrate the feasibility of the approach and was used in the case study described in Sect. 5. It is a prototypeFootnote 2 and currently works with applications using the Django web framework. It takes a project’s directory as input and does a static analysis of the source code to identify the overall project structure. This information is mapped to a graph-like model together with associated files and their dependencies. The same graph is populated with data collected through dynamic analysis to quantify the strength of the dependencies. The graph is then traversed to suggest a decomposition into new services, highlighting the source code files that will be involved and how the resulting services should communicate. This workflow is depicted in Fig. 1 and the several steps are exemplified below.Fig. 1.Operation flow of MonoBreaker with inputs and outputs.Full size image
4.1 Collect Operational DataOperational data is gathered using Silk, which is a profiling tool for DjangoFootnote 3. The tool is capable of supplying information about the usage of entrypoint methods (the ones invoked when a URL is requested), and the model classes and queries involved in the process of returning results from the database. It uses this information to infer some of the internal method calls, as we will see in the next section.4.2 Build Model of the SystemThe static analysis inspects the domain model, the views, and the dependencies between them. In particular, it tracks the use of Django’s Model class, identifying its subclasses (i.e., the domain model of the application) and how they are connected through the declared foreign keys. It also tracks the use of the ModelViewSet class by identifying its subclasses (i.e., the views of the application) as well as the connections between these views and the model classes, via the import statements.To illustrate the process, we present a minimalist example and the steps involved in suggesting a service decomposition using MonoBreaker. The file exemplified in Listing 1.1 results in the extraction of the ViewItem class as a new graph node. The imports of Attribute (line 4) and Item (line 6) refer to subclasses of Django’s Model class, therefore, these are also extracted as nodes, with graph edges connecting them to the ViewItem node. Both the model subclasses Attribute and Item have a connection to ViewItem because it imports them and invokes their methods.
Monobreaker uses the graph resulting from the analysis described thus far to generate the visual representation depicted by Fig. 2a. The weight values associated to the edges represent the strength of the dependencies and are determined by:$$\begin{aligned} StaticEdgeWeight = { NumImports } + { NumMethodCalls } \end{aligned}$$After the analysis of all source code files, a global dependency graph of the project is built. In this example, these files would also include Listing 1.2.
Figure 2b represents the updated version of the graph after the static analysis of the second view class. Note also the dependency between ViewOrder and Item via the call to the get_order_items() method. Detecting it could be attempted through deeper static analysis, in particular of chains of method calls that jump into framework code. The static detection of this dependency is a limitation of the current implementation of MonoBreaker, but it is one of little consequence, as it can still be detected through dynamic analysis, as we will see next.The static analysis of the system is followed by the runtime analysis. The operational data that was previously collected (see Sect. 4.1) is processed and the result used to update the graph with a) previously undetected dependencies (in this example, the one between ViewOrder and Item) and b) with updated weight values. This ensures that we also consider the existence and the strength of dependencies that cannot be determined solely by inspecting the source code.The requests received by the application may result in multiple method calls that eventually touch specific model classes. These are determined by MonoBreaker via the database queries that are issued during the processing of a specific request. Table 1 shows some of the data resulting from the dynamic analysis, which is used to compute the dynamic weights.Table 1. Data determined through dynamic analysis for this example.Full size table
To keep the weight values calculated by the dynamic analysis in the same order of magnitude as those calculated from static analysis, MonoBreaker normalizes them – the highest weight determined from the dynamic analysis will be at most as high as the highest one calculated from static analysis. Therefore, the equation representing the weight that arises from dynamic analysis becomes:$$\begin{aligned} DynaEdgeWeight = NumMethodCalls \times \frac{MaxStaticWeight}{MaxNumMethodCalls} \end{aligned}$$In this implementation, the weights from the static and dynamic analyses were considered in equal parts for determining the final weights, resulting in:$$\begin{aligned} EdgeWeight = StaticEdgeWeight + DynaEdgeWeight \end{aligned}$$Figure 2c depicts the resulting graph, showing the computed DynaEdgeWeight in green and the final EdgeWeight in black.Fig. 2.Each graph shows a different stage of the example, (a) is after analysing the ViewItem class, (b) after analysing the ViewOrder class, and (b) after incorporating the results from the dynamic analysis. Values in green are the weights determined by dynamic analysis alone, and those in black are the total weight produced up to that stage.Full size image
4.3 ClusteringThe dependencies collected through the static and dynamic analyses are used by MonoBreaker to create a graph-like model of the system. Nodes consist mainly of Django model and view classes. A clustering algorithm is then applied to break the network down into smaller communities, thus grouping nodes according to the weights of the edges. We have chosen the Girvan-Newman algorithmFootnote 4 
[19] given its apparent successful use in tools such as ServiceCutter. The resulting clusters indicate a set of potential service cuts.4.4 Generate Decomposition SuggestionsAfter clustering the nodes, MonoBreaker provides an overview of the decomposition. It obtains the service cuts through the Girvan-Newman algorithm and provides the lists of the classes that will be needed for each service. These can be used by the developers to guide the refactoring process. Listing 1.3 shows the output for our simple example.
4.5 LimitationsThe approach described in Sect. 3 is designed to apply to a wide range of contexts. The tool described in this section, on the other hand, was designed with a narrower scope and it is worth highlighting some of its limitations.Technologies. The opportunity, of using a fully developed monolith built with Django to conduct a case study in the industry, led us to develop MonoBreaker specifically for Django-based monoliths that use the object-relational mapper. At this point, the tool will work only for systems developed using these technologies.Design Assumptions. The implementation makes simplistic assumptions about the system to decompose, such as that it was designed around a domain model, and that it avoids cyclic dependencies and other kinds of unnecessary complexity. Such design problems should be approached before running MonoBreaker.Operational Time Frame. The quality of the decomposition is sensible to the choice of an appropriate time frame for collecting operational data, as it should be representative of how the system is normally used. Functionality not used during the dynamic analysis time frame will not be considered for calculating dynamic weights.Balancing Quality Attributes. Another assumption is that there is a single optimal set of service cuts, but we know that there are often trade-offs when refactoring. Users of MonoBreaker are still not able to specify, for e.g., how the maintainability of the resulting system should be weighed against its scalability.5 Case StudyTo assess the feasibility and benefits of a systematic approach to decomposition that combines static and dynamic analysis, we conducted an industry case study using the developed prototype. We were interested in generating insights about the approach, in particular, in understanding its effectiveness for identifying good service boundaries when refactoring a monolith, and the impact that dynamic analysis has on the decomposition result. For the latter part of the study, we turned to ServiceCutter for a comparison.5.1 ContextThe case study focused on a web application for supporting the collaboration between two centers of a logistics startup company. The application had 15 KLOC and more than 40 domain-model elements, and had recently gone through significant growth in its use, making it an interesting candidate for the study.We achieved the participation of three of the four developers that form the team responsible for this application. Their professional experience was in the range of 1–5 years for two of the developers and 5–15 years for the third developer.5.2 ProcessMonoBreaker was used to analyze the project and produced a suggestion for decomposing it into different services. The process consisted of four steps: 

a)
Run MonoBreaker – We gathered the project source code and the runtime data collected through Silk and provided them as input to MonoBreaker, which used both static and dynamic analysis to produce a suggestion of how the system could be decomposed.


b)
Run ServiceCutter – The data statically-collected in step a) was transformed to the ERM format expected by ServiceCutter and was provided as input to produce an alternative decomposition using static analysis only.


c)
Present MonoBreaker – A session was scheduled with the development team and included an introduction that explained the goal of the experiment and a showcase of MonoBreaker using an example project.


d)
Questionnaire – Following the MonoBreaker demo, a questionnaire was handed out to the participants. It aimed to assess how the feasibility of the approach and the impact of dynamic analysis on the quality of the results were perceived by the team. The participants did not have access to the source code during the questionnaire, and the two service decompositions were presented visually as dependency graphs. Participants were given 30 min to analyze the graphs and answer the questionnaire.


Table 2. Questions and answers in the approach group.Full size table
Table 3. Questions and answers in the feasibility group.Full size table
5.3 Data SourcesThe case study used as data sources: a) the source code of the project, b) operational data collected through Silk during one week in a production environment and c) the answers to the questionnaire that were given by the team of the project.The source code was obtained from the company’s code repository. The operational information was collected in two tables created by Silk in the application’s database (silk_request and silk_sqlquery). The questionnaire was built using Google Forms and the answers were gathered in a spreadsheet.5.4 Data AnalysisMost questions were based on a Likert scale 
[20], ranging from (1) Strongly Disagree to (5) Strongly Agree. Questions were organized into four groups. Below, we summarize the answers provided by the three interviewees for each group of questions.Fig. 3.MonoBreaker decomposition result as depicted in the questionnaire.Full size image
Personal Experience. These questions support understanding the team’s professional experience, its familiarity with the case study project and with the process of migrating monoliths to microservices. The answers reveal that all team members have some experience migrating monoliths to microservices (3, 4, 3)Footnote 5 and that they were very familiar with the case study project (5, 5, 5), as expected. This ensures their ability to evaluate the decomposition approach.Approach. The questions in this group aim to assess the perceived importance of different aspects when decomposing a monolith into microservices. If the understanding of these aspects by the study participants revealed to be different from our own, it could explain differences in the answers to questions in the next groups of questions. The questions and answers from the three developers are shown in Table 2. The results show unanimous agreement in that identifying the domain objects, the relationships between components, how these relationships are used in production and the schema of the data store are very important factors when determining potential new services (5,5,5).The answers to the remaining questions were not unanimous, but still show that significant importance is attributed to knowing what operations are made to the database/datastore (5,4,4).These results show the relevance, as perceived by the members of this team, of both structural and behavioral information for service decomposition, and therefore are aligned with the concepts that we used to define our approach.Feasibility. The questions in this group evaluate the perceived feasibility of the approach regarding the quality attributes of the application. Namely, the questions focus on the scalability, ease of deployment, and ease of maintenance. They are supported by the decomposition created by MonoBreaker, which was visually presented as depicted by Fig. 3. Both the questions and the answers are shown in Table 3.The participants did not agree in their answer to these questions but answered consistently to all the questions (4,3,2). This led us to inspect more closely the answers for the justification question (the open-ended question where they could provide further context to their answers) and conclude that the decomposition was perceived as a good basis, but insufficient. Namely, the decomposition consists of 3 services, but team members argued in favor of a more aggressive decomposition. Looking closely at Fig. 3, we can see clusters around three different classes – CargoMovement, MasterdataProducts and ShippingTransfer. From their answers, we understood that the team was expecting the ShippingTransfer cluster to be further decomposed into two distinct services. Section 6 outlines a few factors that can be explored in future work to improve the decomposition.Comparison With Using Only Static Analysis. This group has two Likert-scale questions, each accompanied by an open-ended justification question.The first question compared the decomposition using both dynamic and static analysis with the one using only static analysis. To ease the comparison between the outputs, we transported the information to GephiFootnote 6 and extracted both graphs. The graphs were depicted in the beginning of this group of questions as Decomposition A and Decomposition B (respectively, Fig. 4 and Fig. 3).The second question directly addressed the usefulness of the output provided by MonoBreaker, listing the classes that would be required by each service.Table 4 shows the two questions and the associated answers.Table 4. Questions and answers in the “comparing with the state-of-the-art" group.Full size table
Fig. 4.ServiceCutter decomposition result as depicted in the questionnaire.Full size image
The answers dismiss Decomposition A as the best, concluding that combining static and dynamic analysis provided a better decomposition when compared to using static only.Regarding the output provided by MonoBreaker for guidance on the refactoring, the answers were unanimous in that it would be helpful.5.5 Threats to ValidityThe purpose of this case study is to gather evidence to support the approach. The design described in Section 5 tries to minimize possible threats to validity, but those that exist need a closer look.Projects and Participants. The sample of our case study was limited to one project and three software developers. The answers to the questionnaire’s approach group can be used to confirm if this team valued both structural and behavioral information when decomposing services, as these were base assumptions used to design our approach, but the small scale doesn’t allow to generalize conclusions. We would certainly like to see this case study replicated for other products and larger organizations with different backgrounds, to verify if these preliminary results hold in other contexts.Possible Biases from Respondents. The partnership with the startup company for this case study was only possible due to good working and personal relationships and commitment between the company and the researchers. Therefore, there is always the possibility that the participants may have been inadvertently influenced. During the MonoBreaker presentation (Sect. 5.2), we took particular caution to take an impartial stance regarding the merits of the tool and of its underlying approach and to not interfere in any way when participants were responding to the questionnaire. Moreover, they didn’t know which decomposition had been made using only static analysis or using both static and dynamic analysis. For these reasons, we are confident in discarding this as a threat to validity.Representativeness of Sampled Data. The company supplied the project source code and allowed to alter it to enable the collection of operational data that otherwise would not be possible. As already mentioned, the operational data covered only one week of the application’s run time information and collecting data for a longer period may have led to different results. All the relevant functionality of the application seems to have been used during this time, and we believe the amount of data to be sufficient to base a decomposition decision on. For this reason, we are confident in discarding this as a threat to validity.Suboptimal Baseline. To assess the impact of dynamic analysis in the decomposition, we compared the result of MonoBreaker (using static and dynamic analysis) with that of ServiceCutter (using static analysis only). The choice of ServiceCutter stemmed from the intention to compare MonoBreaker with leading tools from the current state of the art. ServiceCutter is the only freely-available tool that we could run to automate the decomposition process with minimal manual inputFootnote 7.However, we realized that the specific purpose of assessing the impact of dynamic analysis would have been better served by comparing the output of MonoBreaker when run with static and dynamic analysis with its output when run with static analysis only. We believe that when the Girvan-Newman algorithm is chosen when running ServiceCutter, the resulting output should be identical to MonoBreaker’s if only static analysis is used, as MonoBreaker uses the same algorithm for clustering dependent components. Notwithstanding, running MonoBreaker with and without dynamic analysis would provide more robust evidence that no other factors had a significant influence on the decomposition result.6 Conclusions and Future WorkIn this work we contribute, a) a systematic approach to decompose monolithic applications to microservices, b) a tool prototype (MonoBreaker) that implements this approach and c) the design and results of an industry case study.The approach is based on previous ideas but differs in its focus on fully automating the process of determining service boundaries. It does so by relying on static and dynamic software analysis. The case study uses MonoBreaker to assess the feasibility and merits of the approach. The decomposition obtained by the tool was regarded positively by the participants and seen as an improvement over using only static analysis. MonoBreaker is freely available, and the methodological design is documented to enable the replication of the case study by other researchers.To improve these contributions, several aspects will be addressed in future work:Model Building. The approach doesn’t define a specific way to build the model of the application using the results of static and dynamic analysis. Future work will evaluate if other algorithms for calculating the weight of dependencies may perform better than our current implementation, which is currently based on a set of simple heuristics.Clustering Algorithms. The approach is also not prescriptive of a particular clustering algorithm. It will be interesting to evaluate if others render better results than Girvan-Newman, the one currently used by MonoBreaker.Evaluation Metrics. To enable a more objective evaluation of the proposed decomposition, the approach could be extended with service-based metrics – e.g., coupling and cohesion 
[21]. The approach of Taibi et al. 
[18] already includes metrics to rank decomposition candidates. A set of suitable service-based metrics for our approach would have to be determined, and can help to drive the search for better model-building and clustering algorithms.Comparison with Human Experts. Future studies will evaluate if a data-driven approach such as ours is, not only able to automate the decomposition process fully, but will also provide a better decomposition than human experts.Further Studies. More industry case studies will need to be conducted to improve our understanding of the effectiveness and limitations of the approach, ideally with a diverse and significant number of applications and participants.Representativeness of Sampled Data. Future studies will compare the number of requests – per request type – that are received during the collection of operational data with those of more extended periods where operational data wasn’t captured, but for which we are able to collect request statistics nonetheless. This will reinforce our confidence that the operational data collected is representative enough of a normal use of the application.Fully Automatic Decomposition. MonoBreaker can identify file contents affected by the suggested decomposition, e.g., which class has to be extracted for each resulting service. The next step could be to suggest a sequence of lower-level refactorings required for the decomposition or even to automatically apply such refactorings to decompose the system.

papers.fulltext: View-Centric Context Modeling to Foster the Engineering of Cyber-Physical System Networks Bastian Tenbergen Department of Computer Science State University of New York at Oswego United States of America bastian.tenbergen oswego.edu Marian Daun, Patricia Aluko Obe, Jennifer Brings paluno The Ruhr Institute for Software Technology University of Duisburg-Essen, Germany marian.daun patricia.aluko-obe jennifer.brings paluno.uni-due.de AbstractCyber-physical systems interact closely at runtime with their operational context, i.e., other systems, users, and external entities. Therefore, eliciting and documenting interactions with the operational context allows documenting rationales for design decisions, which is essential to define a system architecture that suits the systems purpose. For cyber- physical systems acting in system networks, this task becomes challenging since these networks can change at runtime, because individual systems can leave or join a network spontaneously. Hence, it becomes impossible to predict at design time the operational contexts at runtime. To aid context analysis and specification of such systems, this paper contributes a solution approach where the context of a system is not defined based on a static system boundary but depends on the specific intended use. We propose a view-centric perception of the operational context to leverage the functionality of external systems. This allows differentiating between functionality offered by the cyber- physical system network as a whole and the functionality provided by each individual system. An evaluation with an industrial case example and industry collaboration shows that this approach allows making suitable assumptions of the operational context at design time to guide architecture decisions. KeywordsCyber-Physical Systems; Collaborative System Networks; Context; Architecture Views; Requirements Engineering I. INTRODUCTION It is commonly acknowledged that for the development of any system under development (SUD) the context plays an important role. Only complete consideration of organizational aspects pertaining to, among others, development, regulations, social and environmental impact of the SUD, physical constrains, user characteristics, market- and sales-specific concerns (cf. e.g., 1 ) allows for eliciting suitable requirements and architecture that document adequate functionality with regard to stakeholder needs 2 . For instance, an adaptive cruise control system (ACC, a driver assistance system which maintains a certain speed and distance to some vehicle driving ahead) could be designed with the ability to recognize speed signs. In this case, the speed signs to be recognized by the ACC are hence a part of the ACCs organizational context, as country-specific differences in sign design (e.g., between the US and Europe) impact functionality. This organizational context hence constrains the system and its development. In prior work, we have used the term context of knowledge to refer to such organizational context information 3 . Nevertheless consideration of runtime interactions between the SUD and entities within its context (e.g., human users, external systems) is also of importance, as the system must later be able to function with these context entities 4 . In the example above, the ACC may be designed to automatically slow down the car when entering a speed-restricted area by instructing the engine control unit and the brake system to reduce torque and apply brake force. In prior work, we have used the term operational context to refer to the interaction between the SUD and context entities such as the engine control unit and the brake system at runtime 5 . Especially for cyber-physical systems (CPS), considering the operational context also poses significant challenges. CPS are systems that observe the context through sensors and act upon it through actuators (like an embedded system), but also communicate with one another through powerful networks 6 . For example, a cooperative ACC (CACC, see 7 ), may be designed such that it communicates the change of speed to other nearby vehicles so they may be able to adjust their own velocity as well 8 . The operational context of a CPS hence includes interactions, which will take place at runtime. For instance, the operational context comprises interactions with sensors, actuators, other CPS, and external systems. Runtime interaction of CPSs allows all CPS together to achieve a common goal that individual CPS are unable to achieve on their own 9 , 10 , 11 . For example, in a situation, when a phantom traffic jam 12 occurs (e.g., due to a reduction of speed of a car far ahead), CACCs of several cars relay their desired speed, maximum allowed speed, and relative distance between cars to form a convoy and quickly resolve the traffic jam. In the following, we call CPS that collaborate in this way, a CPS network (see also 13 , 14 ). In CPS networks, interactions between CPS and their operational context give rise to several challenges. One challenge we will particularly emphasize within this paper is functional dependencies of collaborating systems such as the CACC. These functional dependencies emerge from the interplay of independent systems 15 . This contrasts with other paradigms (e.g., systems of systems, see 16 ), where functional dependencies are typically designed top-down. Functional dependencies become complex as the operation of one CPS within the network impacts the operation of another CPS within the same network. For instance, if an electronic stability control of one of the cars in the traffic jam reduces the cars speed to ensure safe driving through a curve, it is of importance for other systems, such as the CACC, to not interfere by increasing the speed again (because the CPS network consisting of other CACCs demands it). Hence, in 206 2018 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture 978-1-5386-6398-1 18 31.00 2018 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. order to develop CPS that will be part of a CPS network, documenting the operational context is imperative, as the cyber-physical SUD must not only be adequate regarding stakeholder needs, but must also function verifiably correct 2 and safely together with other systems 9 , 10 , 17 , 18 . This paper contributes a solution approach to foster context analysis and specification of CPS that participate in CPS networks. The approach leverages architecture views that document the functionality of systems partaking in a CPS network to gain insights into shared, emergent context functions within the CPS network. To this end, the approach considers the differentiation on type level between the system and its context, the system and the system network, as well as the dynamicity between different systems joining and leaving the CPS networks, thus allowing to make assumptions about the availability of functionality in the context of a cyber- physical SUD at runtime (i.e. on instance level). Evaluation results show that the approach is applicable to the engineering of industrial case examples from the automotive domain. Industry collaboration has shown that the approach can considerably aid the traceable documentation of rationales for architecture decisions and the identification of specification defects already in early phases. This paper is structured as follows. The following section gives a discussion of existing approaches and their ability to contribute a solution to the problem outlined above. Section III describes our solution approach. Section IV illustrates and evaluates the benefit of our solution in the automotive domain before Section V concludes this paper. II.BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK In the following, we will discuss areas of research that may bear a contribution to development of CPS in dynamic contexts as outlined in Section I. A. Architecture and Context Context serves as important rationale for architecture decisions 19 . A myriad of approaches (e.g., 20 , 21 , 22 ; see 23 for a recent and comprehensive summary) have identified the need to elicit context information to drive good architectures. Literature commonly deals with organizational contexts, e.g., the project context, placing particular emphasis on the stakeholders therein (cf. 24 , 25 ). However, in engineering of embedded and cyber-physical systems, the operational context (i.e. the context the built system will later on operate in) must also be considered (cf. 26 , 27 ). This is because the operational context is source of important design decisions 19 and insufficient consideration of interactions with the operational context could lead to major safety defects 28 . To alleviate such issues, for example, the automotive industry is concerned with developing what is called Safety Elements out of Context (SEooCs, see 29 ). These SEooCs are vehicle systems, which are developed by suppliers, typically in cooperation with several vehicle manufacturers, such that manufacturers can purchase and integrate these SEooCs into their own vehicles. In this sense, the SEooC is not actually developed without context (in contrast to what the name suggests), but without a specific context in mind (i.e. a specific context in a specific car). SEooCs can hence be integrated into any car, in which certain safe preconditions are met 30 (e.g., interface compatibility). To do so, contract- based development (see, e.g., 31 , 32 ) can be applied. However, the context of SEooC is still static. In this sense, the ACC from the example in Section I can been safely integrated into the car, but it cannot be known at design time, whether it will safely interact with ACCs of other cars (since their make and model is unknown at design time). In other words, in CPS networks, the concept of a SEooC (or other contract-based approaches) become inapplicable. B. Architecture Views, Concerns, and Context Views According to IEEE 42010 1 , a view is a work product expressing the architecture of a system from a specific set of concerns (p. 2, Definition 3.5). A concern refers to the interest in a system relevant to ... stakeholders ( 1 , p. 2, Definition 3.7), however, quite recently the relationship between architecture views and stakeholder concerns have been extended to the domain of systems of systems (see, e.g., 33 , 34 ). In particular, in 33 concerns are understood as overarching with regard to the interaction of systems within a swarm. Moreover, in 35 , it is pointed out that concerns are framed from a stakeholders perspective but can be interrelated through common forces (p. 124). Such common forces could be, for instance, child safety (like in 35 ), deployment, shared knowledge, or functional dependencies between individual CPS within a CPS network, as outlined in Section I. Hence, view-centric approaches like in 35 can be used to document the context of individual systems within system networks (be it systems of systems or CPSs). For example, in 36 , an approach was suggested intended to capture information about the context of the organization (see also Section II.A). In this sense, 36 is very similar to the idea of the Context of Knowledge proposed in 3 , which has been proposed as an extension of the SPES modeling framework 37 . The SPES modeling framework provides four viewpoints (requirements, functional architecture, logical architecture, and technical architecture) to systematically enrich the system specification with design decisions and technical solution details. The SPES modeling framework has furthermore been extended with the ability to capture assumptions about the operational context 38 . Yet, in 38 , the focus is on documenting context information corresponding to a single SUD (e.g., in order to foster the development of, for example, SEooCs as discussed in Section II.A, see 31 ). Dynamicity of the context, like it would occur in CPS networks (see Section I) is not considered, nor is there a focus on documenting functional dependencies between context entities. Other approaches to construct views and viewpoints on software architecture, which may allow capturing context information are, for instance, 39 , 35 , 40 , 41 , and 42 . In contrast to Kruchtens 4 1 model 39 , in the approaches in 40 , 41 , and 35 , the focus is less on providing views for system architecture and more on stakeholder concerns. In particular, in 35 , the primary purpose of documenting context information is to provide a rationale for design decisions, much like the approaches outlined in Section II.A. Similar to 33 , an IEEE 42010-compliant architecture framework for intelligent, in part adaptive systems is proposed in 42 . Yet again, the inherent assumption is that the context of the intelligent system is static and known at design time. C. Documenting the Operational Context for Adaptation The need to make explicit assumptions about implicit knowledge of the problem domain as well as dynamically changing runtime properties of a SUD has been established at length in the past (e.g., 43 ), for example with regard to self- adaptive systems. This term typically refers to systems, which observe context conditions and adapt, when conditions change (see 44 for a comprehensive overview). For example, such adaptation could occur when execution times of a service- oriented architecture are increasing beyond a desired point. For such adaptation to occur, the context interactions (i.e. interactions of the SUD with the operational context) must be considered. To do so, ontology-based modeling approaches have been proposed (e.g., 14 , 45 ). These approaches often take a stateful perspective on the context. This allows applying model-checking to verify the coherence between the functionality of the SUD within the context for which it was developed (see, e.g., 46 , 47 ). Again, the implicit assumption of such approaches is that the operational context is fully known at design time, meaning that the developers design the specific adaptations that the system can undertake. Like in previous sections, this requires that the operational context is static and doesnt change at runtime. Moreover, the context must be documented for each individual system within the context and regarding each possible adaptation. Even though this allows developing an individual CPS, designing for functional dependencies within a CPS network as outlined in Section I cannot be achieved this way. This is because the perspective of the CPS network, i.e. the operational context subsuming all CPSs is not documented at any point during development. This means that functional dependencies remain covert und the functionality of the CPS network, as it emerges from the functional interplay of several dynamically allocated CPS, cannot be leveraged at runtime. In other words, since the CPS network composition cannot be foreseen, adaptation cannot be foreseen either. D. Variability Management Variability management can be seen as another field of related work, which seemingly harbors a solution to the issue of specifying the operational context for systems within a CPS network (see 48 for a recent overview of the field). Variability management is concerned with developing a baseline for a product during a development phase called domain modeling. This baseline defines aspects of the product, which may be variable. In terms of the example above, this could be, for example, the number of other CACCs within the CPS network, the CACC within one car can communicate with, or the communication protocol used (e.g., NFC or Ethernet). During application engineering, the product baseline is then bound to a specific variant of the product (e.g., ACC type 42 can communicate with up to five external CACCs over wireless Ethernet). At first glance, approaches from the field of variability management hence seem applicable. However, application engineering presupposes the specific operational context, in which the product developed during domain modeling will operate. In other words, much like the approaches described in Sections II.A through II.C, it presupposes a static context that on the one hand doesnt change, and on the other hand, is fully known at design time. Hence, variability management cannot cope with the challenges arising from dynamic operational contexts as they occur in CPS networks. E. Conclusion from the State of the Art As can be seen from the discussions in the previous sections, accounting for static context information during system development has been achieved in the past. However, as can also be seen, the dynamically changing composition of CPS networks at runtime makes it impossible to predict the specific nature of the operational context of every individual CPS. In consequence, existing approaches fall short of leveraging functionality of a CPS network, which means that functional dependencies remain covert (both desirable dependencies and undesirable ones). In the following, we propose a view-centric context modeling approach to remedy these shortcomings. III. DEFINING CONTEXT VIEWS IN THE ENGINEERING OF CYBER-PHYSICAL SYSTEM NETWORKS While frameworks incorporating IEEE 42010-type views and viewpoints have been proposed in the past, in this paper we leverage existing context modeling concepts to document the functionality of individual CPS on a type level, thereby allowing to obtain a new view on the context depicting the emergent functionality of the CPS network. We argue that this (a) supports documenting important rationales and thereby ensuring traceability regarding the architecture design, and (b) assists in making important design decisions, when developing system types that partake in a CPS network. In particular, the use of context views aids the developers designing the system such that functional dependencies can be leveraged on an instance level (i.e. at runtime). Specifically, the approach described in this section allows building specific views that capture functionality emerging from the interplay of different systems collaborating in a CPS network. Since this functionality is an emergent property, it cannot be considered as entirely context nor entirely part of the system. As such views on the context provide additional information about different possible context configurations at various times, the idea is related to variability management (see Section II.D), where also a differentiation is made between common and individual parts and the time of binding a configuration. Yet, in contrast to variability management, it allows making assumptions about context properties, instead of having to create specific variant bindings. In the following, we highlight the differences between context modeling for traditional embedded systems (Section III.A) and CPS networks (Section III.B). We then propose a view-centric context modeling approach based on the modeling framework from 49 in Section III.C. A. Context of Embedded Systems At some point during the development of embedded systems, it is necessary to define the scope of development (i.e. the system boundary). In Figure 1, the example from Section I is taken up and shows a car that includes an adaptive cruise control (ACC). ACCs query sensors to observe current speed and distance, calculates necessary changes therein, and instructs other embedded systems within the car accordingly. For example, the ACC can instruct, the engine to accelerate or the electronic stability program (ESP) to brake (left side of Figure 1). The system boundary of the ACC contains all the necessary functionality to interact with the operational context (i.e. to take driver commands, read sensor information, and communicate with the ESP and engine). The ACCs operational context is defined by the external entities it communicates with (i.e. the driver, ESP, engine, sensors, and even the brakes; see white trapezoids in Figure 1). Over the course of development, safety considerations, changing budget constraints, interoperability issues, other types of uncertainty, or changes in requirements may necessitate functionality to be added or removed from the scope of the ACC. For example, in the right side of Figure 1, the ACC could directly act upon the brakes, rather than instructing the ESP to do so. In this case, the ESP might still be part of the car, but no longer within the context of the ACC (and hence depicted as a black triangle in Figure 1). Fig. 1. Changing system boundary over the course of development Changes in requirements during development hence motivate a shift in system boundary. But once each SUD is deployed, each SUD will only function within an operational context consisting of the systems considered during the engineering of the SUD. In the example above, the ACC will hence only work in a car, in which it can directly interact with the brakes. Reusing the ACC in a different car may require re- engineering of the ACC (i.e. regarding its interfaces and, presumably, some of the functionality). Embedded systems development hence assumes a closed world 50 . B. Context in Cyber-Physical System Networks In CPS development, however, the closed world assumption no longer holds. Among other things, the functionality in a CPS network is not restricted to individual systems but can also emerge from their interplay (e.g., 11 , 14 ). CPS make use of sophisticated communication networks (e.g., wireless ad-hoc connections) to access each others functionality. Albeit other forms of coupling between CPS are conceivable (e.g., sharing sensor data or domain observations at runtime), accessing functionality of individual CPS within the CPS network means that a cyber-physical SUD interacts not only with other systems in the same car, but possibly also within other cars. This collaboration is often unbeknownst to the individual systems (see 9 for a detailed account of such an interplay). As we have outlined in Section I, the key difference to embedded systems lies in the fact that in CPS, the network can be dynamically created at runtime. In consequence, the specific external CPS an individual CPS interacts with at runtime dynamically changes as well. This may result in heterogeneous CPS networks 18 , where the CPS network is composed of individual CPS of different manufacturers and different functional capabilities. This is exemplified in Figure 2, where our ACC example from Figure 1 is now forming a CPS network with other cars. In Figure 2, every ACC observes the stop-and-go behavior of its own vehicle in a traffic jam and propagates information about sudden stops (to reduce rear-end collisions) or to coordinates convoy velocity (to resolve the traffic jam more quickly, see also 7 , 12 ). Fig. 2. A CPS network of adaptive cruise controls Figure 2 shows how the ACC from Figure 1 (the car depicted in dark grey) is now not only communicating with the sensors, brakes, and engine, but also with ACCs of other cars (depicted in light grey). Moreover, some of the light grey cars also exchange information with other, non-vehicular CPS, e.g., smart road signs, which transmit the maximum allowed velocity. Hence, in this example, the system boundary and the operational context of the CPS network emerges from the union of overlapping contexts of the individual CPSs. Moreover, since networks are created dynamically, the system boundary is subject to change at runtime. This is because a CPS might be added or removed from the network (i.e. a car drives out of communication range with the smart road sign or other cars), thereby adding or removing functionality, and hence impacting the overall functionality of the CPS network. Obviously, a static perception of a systems context is not applicable. As outlined in 50 , closed-world assumption fails. C. Context Views in Cyber-Physical System Networks Instead, the operational context of a CPS must be defined under consideration of the scope of the CPS network, and furthermore, dependent on the specific intended use in a concrete operational situation (see, e.g., 11 ). Albeit each CPS can be regarded individually using the same principles as embedded systems, the cyber-physical SUD and its context cannot be separated by a single system boundary, as the boundary changes with the runtime properties of the CPS network. Therefore, we propose documenting the context for functionally interdependent CPS in CPS networks in a view- centric way, i.e. from the view of functional interaction. The context for each function available within the CPS network consists of the overlap of the context of individual CPS. The concern expressed in the view is hence the assumed functional dependency between the types of CPS and the functions they make accessible to the CPS network. Since views typically document the whole system for a specific concern (in this case, the entire CPS network with all properties of all contained CPS, common abstractions can be applied, e.g., to only document the externally observable functions of each individual CPS. This way, necessary preconditions that must be met for the CPS functionality to be applicable are made explicit and fosters descriptions of the purpose and benefit of the functionality offered to the CPS network. Figure 3 shows an example. In Figure 3 cooperative ACCs (CACCs, cf. 51 ) are shown, which extend common ACCs by building platoons of cars dynamically (i.e. at runtime), in order to coordinate speed and lane changes in dense traffic. In Figure 3, the CACCs perform some internal functions, provide functions to other CACCs in the network, and rely on functions of other CACCs. For instance, each CACC publishes its own vehicles current and desired speed across the network. This allows other CACCs to adapt their speed accordingly. In doing so, forming and coordinating platoons becomes an emergent functionality of the CPS network made up of several CACCs. This emergent functionality, does not belong to one single CACC, but is deployed within the CPS network. Hence, to leverage emergent functionality, the individual CACCs functions of altering and publishing their own speeds must be taken into account. This is done by documenting the operational context of individual CACCs. As can be seen in Figure 3, we use simplified UML activity diagrams to document functionality of each CACC. Hence, in Figure 3, the rounded-corner rectangles represent functions of the SUD and double-ended solid arrows document interactions between them. This yields a view of the functionality within a system; one activity diagram is used for each CPS within the CPS network. Similarly, the functionality within the operational context of each CACC is also documented using rounded-edge UML activities. Again, double-ended solid arrows represent interaction between the context functionality the individual CACCs can make use of. This yields another view of the functionality within the context. To combine the views and therefore leverage functional dependencies between individual CPS and the CPS network, double-ended dashed are used to symbolize an interaction with the context. It is to note that the functionality within the context is not explicitly designed by a developer but emerges through context interactions of several CPS (see Sections I and III.B). Therefore, the context functions depicted in Figure 3 represent assumptions on type level about how the interaction will take place at runtime on instance level. Using this simple visualization of functionality within the systems as well as the context, these assumptions are now made explicit. During development of individual CPS, context views of each individual CPS under development (i.e. CACC1 and CACC2 in Figure 3) can be merged to generate and investigate emergent functionality within the CPS network. This fosters the documentation of assumptions about functionality within the operational context of any individual CPS under development. This approach hence may alleviate the limitations of the closed-world assumption inherent in embedded systems development by showing what the mutual influence of two or more CPS on the same physical property in the context is (e.g., platoon speed in Figure 3). Architecture rationales during system design can leverage this information. The view-centric context modeling approach does not necessarily imply the use from a functional perspective, however, as we will see in Section IV, at present, we placed emphasis on investigating and evaluating the use of such a functional perspective to leverage functional interplay within the CPS network. As stated above, other forms of coupling than functional dependency are conceivable, even likely to occur in practice. Fig. 3. Overlapping functional contexts of two cooperative ACCs (CACCs) of the same type collaborating in a CPS network However, it was a key concern to our industry partners to focus on functional dependency in the current stages of this research. In detail, such a view-centric context modeling approach allows for building purpose specific views for documenting design rationales as well as for analyzing the functionality of the system under development within its context. This is fostered by differentiating between views specific for the individual system within the CPS network (which is the context of the individual system) and views for the CPS network and its context. Furthermore, not necessarily must a view be centered on the system or the system network as a whole but can, for instance, focus on overarching concerns 33 , such as safety or variability. IV. INDUSTRY CASE STUDY To illustrate the idea of view-centric context modeling and evaluate the benefit to the development process, we conducted an industrial case study. The focus of investigation in the case was the functional perspective of a CPS, the CPS network the single system partakes in, and the context of an individual CPS. We used an industry specification of a cyber-physical adaptive cruise control system as the case example. A. Industrial Case Example We obtained a specification of a simplified adaptive cruise control system from our industrial partners. To foster generalizability to the domain, the specification was created and supplied by several industry partners from companies, who serve as suppliers and manufacturers in the German automotive domain. The ACC specification is based on currently existing industry-typical ACC but was anonymized to protect our partners intellectual property. We have extended the specification of the ACC with the ability to form a platoon of cars going at the same speed at runtime, hence making the ACC cyber-physical. In close collaboration with our industrial partners, we quality assured the CACC specification to correspond to industry-typical quality. This served as the baseline for our case example. Therefore, it must be noted, that the CACC that is used as the case example in the following can at best serve as a realistic example, but not as a real example, due to the modifications made to account for cyber-physicality (which, of course, is not market-ready at the time of writing this article). Specifically, the cyber-physical functionality comprises: building a system network at runtime; negotiating the forming of a platoon with some common speed for all partaking vehicles; controlling the own cars speed to match this negotiated speed; and maintain distance to the vehicle ahead. Furthermore, the CACC is specified to consider weather information as well as speed limits transmitted by specifically equipped smart road signs when negotiating an optimized platoon speed. B. Functional Modeling using the Context Views In modern system development, functions are designed to be shared between the different embedded systems (e.g., 52 , 53 , 54 ). Hence, modeling of a functional design needs to allow for separation between system functions and context functions (see 51 ). The term system function refers to a logical function, which is part of the context subject. Context functions refer to logical functions, which are available to the context subject, but are part of context objects. For example, an automotive adaptive cruise control system makes use of braking functions provided by the electronic stability control to maintain a safe distance to preceding vehicles. We applied the context modeling framework 38 to an existing functional modeling technique, whose meta model is given in Figure 4. As can be seen, functions are structurally connected and are defined by a specific function behavior. Figure 5 shows the extensions made to the meta model shown in Figure 4 to account for the different types of functions in CPS networks. It is no longer sufficient to distinguish only between system and context function; CPS network functions must also be considered. CPS network functions comprise collaborative functions that are provided by the various CPS of the CPS network. Depending on which system in the network is considered the context subject (i.e. the subject, upon which the context acts, see 55 ), these collaborative functions are either collaborative system functions (i.e. Exchange Speed in Figure 3) or collaborative context functions (i.e. Control Platoons Speed in Figure 3). Beside collaborative system functions, CPS also have traditional system functions with no collaborative properties, which are referred to as pure system functions (i.e. Determine Desired Speed in Figure 3). Furthermore, the context of CPS also comprises traditional context functions or non-collaborative context functions. This means functions that are not provided by another collaborative system in the same system network, but by some other context entity. In case this context entity is part of the same super system as the context subject, we refer to this function as a local context function, otherwise these functions are considered pure context functions. These distinctions between context functions of the system, which are part of the same super system and context functions, which are part of other systems within the system network, must be made as those functions are typically not constantly available and must be considered volatile, less reliable, less dependable, and less trustworthy. Based on the functional meta model in Figures 4 and 5, we can depict the functional interplay between the functionality of the CPS under development and the functionality of the context. In Figure 3, this leads to three different views (i.e. two views of the interacting CACCs and one of the context). Based on these three views, a fourth view can be derived, which depicts the interaction of system functions and context functions, as shown in Figure 6. In Figure 6, the displayed CPS network documents the functional design of the CACC. As can be seen, to optimize the vehicles speeds, the CACC receives (among others not depicted here for simplicity) information about the current weather (from some remote weather service via an inbuilt transponder) and requests to reduce the speed (from other cars in the vicinity, i.e. in the system network). It also, receives information about the vehicles current speed from an embedded system in the same vehicle, making Determine Current Speed a local context function. Fig. 4. Benefit of View-Centric Context Modeling In addition to aiding the structured documentation of system and context functionalities, the functional modeling approach outlined above fosters several analyses. These analyses include safety analyses, compatibility analyses with neighboring systems, impact analyses, etc. In other words, this structured documentation of system and context functionality of a CPS network can be used as a prerequisite for design approaches, such as contract-based design. In the following subsections, we will outline the major analysis benefits resulting from view-centric context modeling, which we identified in close collaboration with industry partners. 1) Compatibility Checking of a System within the Network One benefit of the application of view-centric context modeling is the use for compatibility checking of the single CPS with the other partaking CPS and with the CPS network. On one hand, compatibility checking between the system and its context is supported as it is clear what the non-collaborative context is, and how the collaborative context differs from it. For the CACC case example, this means that it must be checked whether the CACC is compatible with other CPS and locally connected (e.g., through traditional CANBUS) embedded systems. This can aid in ascertaining whether, for example, the CACC can properly cooperate with the engine control unit to ensure functionality of the context function Regulate Engine Torque or, for another example, if the chosen weather service provides a function Broadcast Weather Information that is compatible with the system function Receive Weather Information. On the other hand, it becomes clear that the functionalities Reduce Speed and Determine Optimal Speed depend on collaboration with other CPSs in the same CPS network. Hence, compatibility of these functions with the CPS network must be ensured. In this case, compatibility checks must take both directions into account. First, it must be ensured the CACC under development can achieve its own goals and is provided with all necessary information to correctly accelerate and decelerate its own car. Second, it must be ensured the entire CPS network can properly work so the overall goal of the CPS network is achieved (i.e. the platoon moves with optimal speed and minimal distance without abrupt braking or collisions). 2) Definition and Validation of CPS Network Safety Goals Through safety analyses, such as the FMEA 56 , potential failures are identified and safety goals and safety requirements are defined as mitigations to prevent the occurrence of these failures 17 . For safety analyses, a certain closed-world must be assumed for the simple reason that absolute safety is usually unattainable. Hence, safety claims typically argue a certain level of safety, given some explicitly assumed operational context at runtime. In the engineering of CPS, which collaborate in a CPS network, the fact that the closed world assumption fails impairs the ability to make safety claims about functionally dependent CPS. For example, safety engineers might identify rear-end collisions as a potential hazard and will, therefore, check whether the CPS as specified can reach a state where such a collision is possible. Using view-centric context modeling, which considers the different aspects of functionality belonging to the CPS as well as to the CPS network, hazards from the collaboration can be detected during safety analyses by considering the overlap of system functions. Moreover, safety claims can be made for system network functions. By making assumptions about functional dependencies using the approach proposed above limits the open world enough to make certain statements about the safety of the CPS network (albeit this may be too much of a simplification). For instance, in Figure 6, the safety engineer can easily identify the system network function Avoid Collisions. One aspect of the safety analysis will be to investigate whether this function properly ensures the avoidance of collisions. In this case, it can easily be perceived that the proper functioning of Avoid Collisions does not only depend on a single CPS (i.e. the CPS under development) but also on other CPSs in the CPS network. The CPSs in the CPS network might be CACCs of the same type (i.e. other instances of the system under development) or CACCs by different vendors. Ensuring compliance with the safety requirement must, among others, consider the possibility of error prone implementations of other CACCs as well as the loss of communication channels at runtime (e.g., due to poor wireless signal reception). Hence, safety requirements might deal with the reliability of communication and safe behavior to be exhibited in case of communication loss but also with standardization or runtime compatibility checks to ensure proper interplay of different CACCs. 3) Detection of Emergent Behavior In the interplay of multiple CPS, emergent behavior describes behavior, which does not result from one single system but emerges from the interplay of multiple systems 57 . Obviously, this is a common situation in CPS networks, where the partaking systems shall contribute to an overall CPS network goal. However, it is often the case that behavior emerges in the interplay, which was not intended during requirements engineering and system specification 58 . For example, while specifying scenarios the system shall be able to execute, implicit scenarios may arise, which typically are a combination of several parts of the specified scenarios 59 . It is important to detect such emergent behavior already in early phases (cf. 60 ). Detected emergent behavior might either hint at defects in the specification or at additional requirements that have been undetected so far. The application of view-centric context modeling to the functional design of the CACCs has shown that the detection of such emergent behavior is supported. For instance, different CACCs might request to reduce the platoons speed for different reasons at the same time: one CACC might request a reduction due to weather conditions, another due to a speed limit in place and a third due to a slow-moving vehicle ahead. While this situation is desired (i.e. all reductions are reasonable and must result in speed reduction of the platoon), it might also result in undesired behavior stemming from the collaboration of the platoon. If the CACC that requested a speed reduction due to a slow-moving vehicle ahead, recognizes that the vehicle is no longer an obstacle, the CACC would request to resume the platoons originally higher speed. However, another CACCs request to reduce the platoons speed are still in place and valid. If the reason for their speed reduction requests is still in place, increasing the platoons speed is obviously undesired. In this situation, this functional dependency must not remain covert but made explicit using the view-centric context modeling approach proposed above. V. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION In this paper, we have proposed a view-centric context modeling approach to leverage functional dependencies in CPS networks. CPS networks are formed at runtime when traditional embedded systems within, for example, automotive vehicles, communicate with one another through powerful communication networks. These traditional embedded systems hence become cyber-physical and work together to achieve a common goal. To do so, CPS networks can form, change, and break up dynamically at runtime, e.g., when individual CPS leave the networks range. In this paper, we have argued that this can be problematic, as proper operation of functionally dependent and networked CPS depends on all functionality of all individual CPS to be present (and reliable). Moreover, we have shown through analysis of existing literature, that common approaches in architecture design, context modeling, view-oriented software engineering, and variability management are unsuitable due to their explicit consideration of organizational context aspects. However, the dynamic behavior of CPS networks requires functional dependencies to be considered during development. We argued the need to engineer the operational context systematically and illustrated the differences in context engineering for embedded systems versus CPS. We proposed a view-centric context modeling approach, which can be understood as an extension of existing context modeling facilities, which adopts one view for the functionality of each individual CPS and one view for the relevant context functions within the CPS network. This allows making otherwise covert functional dependencies explicit, which we assumed to aid in the architecture design of individual CPS under development. To investigate this claim and to illustrate our approach, we developed a realistic industrial case example with industry partners to uncover the specific benefits of view-centric context modeling. Results show that view-centric context modeling aids developers in ascertaining the compatibility of CPS to suit a functional architecture within a car and within a CPS network, defining and verifying safety properties for the functionality within a CPS network as well as individual CPS, and making explicit desired as well as undesired emerging functionality. This work has thus far been successful in theory and, to some extent, in practice. However, a considerable limitation of our findings is the fact that the industry case example was limited to a realistic, not a real system. In consequence, conclusions drawn regarding the specific benefits are preliminary and must be confirmed with a real case study. This is part of ongoing work using a surrogate platform to simulate CPS networks. Moreover, the motivation for this work and case study are based on considerations of the automotive domain. Nevertheless, the same challenges exist for CPS of other domains. Examples include traffic collision avoidance systems and dependent aircraft surveillance systems in the avionics domain 18 , configurable manufacturing spaces in Industry 4.0 61 , prosumer architectures in the electrical engineering domain 62 , or intelligent robotic agents. Future work will be concerned with the application of the view-centric context modeling approach in these areas.
