papers.fulltext: Architectural Patterns for Cross-Domain Personalised Automotive Functions Stefan Kugele, Christoph Segler and Thomas Hubregtsen Department of Informatics, Technical University of Munich, Garching b. M unchen, Germany Email: stefan.kugele tum.de BMW Group Research, New Technologies, Innovations, Garching b. M unchen, Germany Email: Christoph.Segler, Thomas.Hubregtsen bmwgroup.com Quantum Computer Engineering Department, Delft University of Technology, Delft, Netherlands AbstractContext: Future automotive customer functions will be highly personalisable and adapt their settings proactively in an intelligent way. Aim: We aim at designing generic architec- tural patterns for functional architectures containing machine learning components. Method: We first formalise a new archi- tectural model. Based on this model, we present and discuss three alternative architectural patterns: (1) concurrent learning, (2) end-to-end learning, and (3) user shadow learning. For these patterns, three alternative integration approaches are discussed: (i) centralised holistic approach, (ii) domain-specific approach, and (iii) dedicated approach. Moreover, we conduct an evaluation using real car data for different customer functions. Conclusion: We propose the use of the user shadow learning pattern in the dynamic architectural model. The user shadow learning pattern is not affected by safety constraints, as is usually the case for integrating artificial intelligence, as it only models user behaviour while leaving the original function intact. To integrate the multitude of models, we propose a domain-specific approach. This approach provides a balance between the trade-offs in the dedicated approach and the holistic approach, being high computational overhead and design complexity, respectively. Index Termsarchitectural patterns, automotive, personalisa- tion, intelligent functions, artificial intelligence I. INTRODUCTION During the last decades, thousands of software-controlled functions running on a large number of electronic control units (ECUs) were included in modern cars. Their particular characteristics range from non-safety-critical to high safety and real-time critical functions. Driving forces are (i) safety requirements, (ii) customer demand for more comfort and the newest infotainment systems, and (iii) advanced driver assistance systems allowing to reach hitherto unrivalled levels of driving automation (cf. 1 ). Moreover, sophisticated intel- ligent capabilities and highly personalised functions are no longer a future vision. Machine intelligence is an emerging and cross-disciplinary application area which is advancing with great strides also in in-vehicle functions. Examples are computer vision for obstacle detection, traffic sign recognition, drivers emotion recognition, and of course, automated driving. This paper focuses on functions that can be controlled by the driver; for example switched on off, configured, or person- alised. We call them customer functions. The term user will be used instead of driver, since the approach is extendable to The authors contributed equally to this work. any passenger in the vehicle; moreover, in a fully automated scenario users will only occasionally be driversif at all. Rooted in the consumer electronics industry, customers demand new levels of personalisation (and individualisation) for their vehicles. This extends the traditional aspects of personalisation such as vehicle colour, interior equipment, or options by far. Analyses of recorded real vehicle data of a field study showed that different customers are using functions in similar driving situations differently 2 . For instance, the driving dynamics control mode sport (available: sport, comfort, and eco) strongly correlates with the road type and weekday for one user; for another user, the tire temperature, the seat heating, and whether a co-driver is present was relevant. Therefore, we provide architectural patterns that facilitate the development of intelligent, context- aware functions based on existing functions with minimally invasive architectural interventions. This is crucial since especially the re-development of safety-critical functions is very time- and cost-intensive due to comprehensive quality and safety assurance activities demanded by standards such as ISO 26262 3 when required to reach the highest automotive safety integrity level, ASIL D. Usually, technical systems such as vehicles are equipped with sensors for monitoring and controlling tasks. The sensing capability is, however, limited either because of economic reasons or of technological limitations. In our setting, besides the technical system s, there is also a user u interacting with the system embedded into a context c (cf. Fig. 2). There are objects, events, situations, or physical phenomena that cannot be sensed by the system itself but experienced or anticipated by the user. Personalised functions improve their user experience by profiting from that at first obscured and then used knowledge. We propose to use architectural patterns to capture this recurrent problem when architecting future personalisable functions. Each pattern describes a problem which occurs over and over again in our environment, and then describes the core of the solution to that problem, in such a way that you can use this solution a million times over, without ever doing it the same way twice 4 . Gamma et al. 5 use this quote in their seminal work on design patterns to describe the core of design patterns. In this work, we present and discuss three 191 2020 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA) 978-1-7281-4659-1 20 31.00 2020 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA different architectural patterns usable for the design of intelli- gent, highly personalised functions. Note, we demonstrate the approach using automotive functions; however, the patterns are domain-agnostic and can, therefore, be applied in any cyber- physical or IoT system. For the most promising, we conduct an empirical evaluation using real vehicle data to train Neural Networks (NNs). We use four different customer functions from the two domains comfort and driving to evaluate our cross-domain personalisation approach. Research Questions: For this work we pose following research questions: RQ1 How to integrate intelligent functions into automotive software architectures? RQ2 Which architectural patterns facilitate the design of intelligent, highly personalised functions? RQ3 Do different implementation alternatives (centralised holistic, domain-specific, dedicated) significantly influ- ence the accuracy of the approach? Contributions: This paper provides the following scien- tific contributions, but also contributes to the state of practice: (i) We provide architectural patterns for the design of intelligent, highly personalised automotive functions; (ii) We discuss different alternatives for cross-domain func- tion integration; (iii) We conduct experiments and infer from them design recommendations for function architects. Outline: The remainder of this paper is structured as fol- lows. Section II contains preliminaries. Section III summarises related work followed by the main approach in Sect. IV. There we introduce architectural patterns for the design of cross- domain personalised functions. In Sect. V, we evaluate dif- ferent architectures and architectural patterns. For one pattern, we conduct experiments for cross-domain integration methods using NNs trained with real in-vehicle data from customer functions of different domains. Finally, we discuss our findings in Sect. VI and conclude in Sect. VII. II. PRELIMINARIES 1) Notation: Let s be an element of the set S and S SET. We denote with (S) the power set of S, which is the set of all subsets of S. We denote with s the system under consideration which is operated by a user u in a context c. 2) Modelling: We use the modelling approach introduced by Broy and Stlen 6 and briefly introduce notions necessary for an easier understanding of this paper. s s1 s2 Fig. 1: System s consisting of subsystems s1 and s2: s s1s2. A system s is formally specified by its syntac- tic and semantic interface and graphically modelled as depicted in Fig. 1. The subsystems s1 and s2 are mutually exchanging in- formation via their syntactic interfaces. Let CHANNEL denote the set of all available typed channels. There is a function type: CHANNEL TYPE, which assigns a type to each channel and TYPE denotes the set of all types. Simple types, for example, might be int containing all integers. There might also be more complex types, such as intcontaining all sequences over int or sequences of 8 bit (B8 0, . . . , 28 1 ) RGB pictures of dimension x, y: ((B8, B8, B8)yx). Definition 1 (Syntactic Interface): Let I be a set of typed input channels and O be the set of typed output channels, I, O CHANNEL. The pair (I, O) characterises the syntactic interface of a system s, denoted by (I O). The syntactic interface defines which data a system consumes and which data it produces. The behaviour is defined by the semantic interface. Definition 2 (Semantic Interface): The logical behaviour, i. e., the semantic interface of a system s with syntactic interface (I O) is given by the function f : I ( O). Note that I denotes the history of ingoing streams on input channels and O denotes the history of streams on output channels. III. RELATED WORK With the advance of intelligent systems, customer demand adaptive and intelligent functions which learn according to their behaviour. These intelligent functions capture hidden knowledge for continuously improving their capabilities and provide a highly personalised user experience and are known as Context Aware Systems 7 . In the automotive domain, these functions range from intelligent window levers 8 , intelligent in-car infotainment systems 9 , intelligent suspension controls 10 to intelligent cruise controls 11 . The principal function- ality of these functions is already present in current vehicles except for the intelligent adaptation to the user. Functions follow the general pattern of measuring the input of physical effects with sensors, e. g. force and buttons, processing this input, and controlling actuators based on the logic of the processing unit 12 , 13 . As seen in the example of the intelligent adaptive cruise, many different patterns can be used to implement this functionality 11 , 14 . These, on the one hand, perform direct end-to-end learning of the output parameters of the vehicles longitudinal positive and negative acceleration based on sensor data 11 and, on the other hand, perform learning of a single configuration value for a hand-crafted function which controls the longitudinal positive and negative acceleration of the vehicle 14 . These works solely focus on the implementation of a specific function and do not include any general pattern for the implementation of adaptive and intelligent functions. This work focuses on a general-purpose pattern for the implementation of such functions and not on the specific functionality. Currently used patterns for function design follow the sense-process-actuate loop; however, in general, this pattern does not include any adaption to the user. This work partially uses the formal model of dynamic systems introduced by Broy 15 using the FOCUS theory. Moreover, parts of the dynamic model were inspired by Marmsoler 16 . As the dynamic architectural model is not the primary contribution, we refer to both works elaborating in any detail dynamic systems and architectures. IV. APPROACH We present architectural models in Sect. IV-A, introduce three architectural patterns in Sect. IV-B, and discuss alter- natives for cross-domain integration of personalised customer functions in Sect. IV-C. A. Architectural Models We briefly introduce the current static architectural model followed by the future dynamic one proposed in this work. 1) Current Static Architectural Model: A generic system model consists of an automotive system s, the user u, and the context c and is depicted in Fig. 2. f fAI F f system s user u context c IF f Ius f Ius Osu Ics Osc Icu Ouc Ics f Fig. 2: Generic system model. The automotive system s provides a set F of functionsin this case only function f is of our particular interest. Customer functions are functions that can be controlled and parameterised by users. They are defined as Fu f F Ius f . We denote with C p the set of channels perceivable by entity p, with C p C CHANNEL. The function f has access to an AI-based oracle denoted by f AI. This is a component that has been trained at design time and remains static over the whole system life cycle. Examples are traffic signs recognition and speech and gesture recognition. We assume that f contains failure detection and mitigation tactics such as fail-safe or fail-operational. Moreover, we assume that the function under consideration is always a customer function, i. e., f Fu. The system interacts with a user u and is operating in a context c. Here, context is any information that can be used to characterise the situation of an entity. An entity is a person, place, or object that is considered relevant to the interaction between a user and an application, including the user and application themselves. 17 . The interaction between system and user happens using input (I) and output channels (O). Sensors and actuators are the technical concepts of interaction at the system boundary. Control loops, for instance, are realised by receiving information from the context or user (sensing), process them within the system, and transmit results to the context or user (acting). Note that not all inputs to the system, or from other functions F are relevant for the function f, indicated by dotted arrows. In the following section, we will elaborate more on that point. 2) Future Dynamic Architectural Model: We consider a system to be intelligent if it can extract new insights from input and use that knowledge to solve problems. From a user perspective, this manifests in performing actions that were not user-triggered but are user-observable. Moreover, the user is first astounded by the proactively triggered actions but then does not think about it anymore. To do so, we use feature selection (fs) algorithms (cf. 18 for a recent survey paper) to identify so far unconsidered correlations between user perception and function usage. This is the core of personalisation and allows us in this sense to architect intelligent functions. f fAI s f fs ... ... ... ... ... In the following, we extend the architecture model presented above in a way that we add an AI-based function f , which is able to evolve, facilitating the realisation of intelligent, personalised functions. Figure 3 depicts a system s which is equipped with a customer function f and its personalised, intelligent counterpart f . As indicated in the figure, the input channels are divided into two parts, namely a static part Is (defined by engineers at design time) and a dynamic part Id (identified during runtime). Moreover, there is an intelligent function f that in addition to f has not only access to the static interface but also to the dynamic interface Id, i. e., Ics f Ics f assuming Id . The static part is defined during design time, whereas the dynamic part is determined by first (1) collecting usage data during runtime, (2) selecting feature subsets from the collected data at runtime using, for instance, feature selection algorithms, yielding I d, then (3) verifying the selected features at design time in the backend infrastructure, and finally (4) deploying the updated model of the dynamic interface back into the vehicle if all checks such as bandwidth, computing resources, access control, and safety have been passed. The principle process is shown in Fig. 4. The close interaction between design time and runtime will speed up and streamline the development of intelligent functions with shorter innovation cycles. It extends processes currently followed in the automotive industry to be better aligned with Continuous Integration and Delivery concepts. The interaction with the backend for verification, validation, and safety assurance activities can be omitted in the future if the technical in-vehicle architecture supports correct-by- construction deployment. This means that for instance the technical architecture is centralised as for example proposed by Traub et al. 19 . A unifying data backbone provides all data everywhere such that no additional link load is generated by newly established data paths. As long as there will be complex gateway-based topologies, we will need to ensure a functioning, safe, and secure operation of the intelligent functions requiring assurance measures conducted at the manufacturers side. B. Note that unlike to Gamma et al., we have not derived patterns from existing solutions, but propose them to solve recurrent architectural design challenges in future functions. Cross-Domain Function Integration Methods In current-day cars, we see a variety of opportunities for personalisation functions, ranging from climate control to steering stiffness. In this section, we will address the challenge of integrating a large number of functions into a coherent overall system. Thousands of automotive functions are realised using software. Those incorporating user input are in principle subject to personalisation. From a logical point of view, functions are grouped into logically-related clusters called do- mains. Examples are powertrain, infotainment, driving, ADAS, or comfort. This logical domain-grouping usually is also reflected by the software architecture, where software components are deployed onto wired ECUs (cf. Fig. 5 for a typical domain-oriented network topology). This happens whenever the architecture follows the organisational rather than the technical structure in line with Conways Law DCU1 ECU1 ECU2 ECU3 DCU2 ECU4 ECU5 DCU3 ECU6 ECU7 ECU8 ECU9 CAN FlexRay ETH ETH ETH Fig. 5: Domain controller-based in-vehicle network topology (Domain Control Unit, Electronic Control Unit). We distinguish three methods of integration: (1) a cen- tralised holistic approach, (2) a domain-specific approach, or (3) a dedicated approach. Within these approaches, we discuss the design of the voter v, the learned function f and the learned user shadow u. In the following discussion, any reference of these elements applies to all patterns that incorporate such an element, being patterns Pc and Pu for voter v, patterns Pc and Pe for the learned function f , and the pattern Pu for the learned user shadow u. Figure 6 depicts the three different approaches graphically. In Fig. 6(a), a centralised holistic implementation of f , u, and v for all 20 functions is usedno matter to which of the three domains (blue, green, and red) the functions belong to. In contrast, Fig. 6(b) depicts a per-domain integration (blue, three functions; green: 8 functions; red: 9 functions). Finally, Fig. 6(c) exemplifies the dedicated approach, i. e., for each function a dedicated f , u, and v is realised. 1) Centralised Holistic Approach: This method proposes to centralise and incorporate all logic into a centralised holistic function model. The learned function f (centralised holistic) would have to incorporate all functionalities, even if the functionalities do not share any characteristics. The same conditions apply for the learned user shadow u, where a centralised holistic learned user shadow uwould represent the behaviour of the user for all intelligent functions. For the voter v, we have to implement a centralised holistic voter v to control all intelligent functions. 2) Domain-Specific Approach: This method proposes to cluster functionality belonging to the same domain, such as the functions seat heating and air conditioning are both within the comfort domain. This would require implementing one domain-specific learned function f , learned user shadow u, and or voter v per domain. 3) Dedicated Approach: We propose in our final method a system where every function has its own learned function f , learned user shadow u, or voter v. Comparison of Architectural Models When comparing the current static architecture with the proposed future dynamic architecture, it becomes clear that the later is a systematic development of the static approach. Thus, in principle, any static approach can be extended by adding the learned function f , learned user shadow u, and or voter v depending on the used pattern. Since we expect more and more functions in the future that at least use artificial intelligence as an oracle, increased hardware requirements will become relative. This is especially true with regard to more onboard computing power for highly fully automated driving and in- telligent personal assistants as well as backend connectivity in the light of the upcoming 5G standard. The major advantage over currently used architectural models is the possibility to personalise intelligent functions to the degree that had never been reached before. Cross-domain personalisation is also a novelty in automotive software engineering. Another side of the coin is that increased verification and validation efforts are needed in the backend to meet strict requirements given by regulatory authorities. B. Comparison of Architectural Patterns Next, we discuss and compare the advantages and disad- vantages of the previously sketched patterns Pc, Pe, and Pu. We focus on the training effort required at design and runtime and the resulting hardware requirements. Moreover, we elaborate on safety requirements that need to be met for critical applications using machine learning algorithms. In this context also explainability is considered, meaning if the behaviour of the function can be easily described and interpreted. Table II summarises the main classification figures. 1) Concurrent Learning Pattern Pc: The Concurrent Learning Pattern Pc (cf. Pattern 1) additionally integrates an AI-based function f that is representing the behaviour of the user u and the function f at the same time. Pre-training of f during design time is possible but not required. The pre- training is restricted to the functional scope of f and does not include user preferences. Front loading of training activities increases effort during design time but reduces training effort during runtime. This results in a faster convergence between function f and the desired behaviour in representing the user u and the function f. As there are now two functions with similar functionality (except the user part of function f ), of which only one is used to control the system, there may arise additional hardware requirements, such as additional ECUs, extra memory, or higher bus load. Verification of machine learning functions while taking safety requirements into considerations is still an open research question 24 26 . Engineers have to design the voter, which is a challenging task as the voter has to meet similar, or even stricter safety requirements. At runtime, metrics such as accuracy or values of the confusion matrix from function f can serve as additional decision parameters for the voter. Pat- tern 2) only contains the AI-based function f . This is more efficient, as it is only running one instance at the same time. However, this also adds additional development effort for the pre-training of f . The training set is derived from the specification of function f, which either has not been implemented yet, exists from a pre-development project, or exists from a non-intelligent legacy version. With this pre- training, the training effort during runtime will be minimised, and only the additionally required training is for the behaviour of the user. Since function f directly generates the output for the actuators without a voter to monitor decisions, this function has to cover all requirements of fs specification and has to fulfil the same ASIL requirements. As with the previous pattern, this might be very challenging for safety- critical functions. 3) User Model Pattern Pu: For the user model pattern Pu (cf. Pattern 3), the adaptive part of the function only represents the interaction of the user with the function f and does not cover any behaviour of the function f itself. This has the significant advantage of reusing the complete function f and learning what we initially wanted to learn. By only interacting with the predefined input of function f, the user shadow ucan only represent the interaction of the user with the function (for example pressing buttons) and is not able to learn a more accurate differentiation like the other patterns. These interactions are predefined when function f has been developed and might not fit to represent the behaviour of the user adequately. When using machine learning systems to represent the user shadow u, it is still hard to verify the trained model according to functional safety standards. However, in this case, we only have to consider requirements which are not yet covered by function f, i. e., what an average user would never do, or is not able to do. Capturing these exceptions within function f or voter v is less complicated compared to the other two patterns. 4) Functional Interplay: Since functions are highly inter- connected, a function receiving data from a learned function f needs to rely on the guarantees provided initially by f. As a consequence, the voter v embedded in the concurrent learning pattern needs to do two things: First, it needs to decide which values to forward: that of f or that of f , and second, it needs to fulfil the guarantees of f on which downstream functions rely on. For the user shadow pattern, the functionality of the voter is more straightforward since besides deciding between u and uit only needs to check for plausible input to f. The end-to-end learning pattern shifts responsibilities to the users to verify that the values delivered by the upstream learned functions match the assumptions of the using functions. C. Evaluation of Cross-Domain Integration Methods In this section, we will theoretically evaluate the various integration methods. All findings are summarised in Table III. The part on leveraging correlations for accuracy will be experimentally verified in the next section. 1) Computational Overhead: For our theoretical assess- ment of computational overhead, we will distinguish between classifications that need to happen at the same time interval, as well as computations that happen at a different time interval. For example, a safety-critical system likely requires real-time classification, whereas comfort functions can run in the second to minute domain. We will first evaluate systems that require sensory data at a similar interval. TABLE III: Comparison of the methods. Property Holistic Domain Dedicated Computational Overhead Synchronous Classification Asynchronous Classification Accuracy Leverage Correlations Available Compute Design Complexity Safety Requirements Modular Design Signal Routing Good: , notable: , moderate: , poor: a) Synchronous Classification: In the dedicated ap- proach, where every functionality has its dedicated function, the system will calculate every function individually. Given hundreds or more points of automation, this is a large work- load. Assuming a deep neural network, it is likely that a lot of the initial layers show a resemblance between the different functions. When clustering this functionality per domain, it might be possible to reduce computation. Assuming that features can overlap even across domain boundaries (it is cold, so people drive slowly because of ice, but also turn on the seat heating), one can conclude that even less computation is needed. b) Asynchronous Classification: The downside of clus- tering all computation is that one has to run the classification at the smallest time interval required, creating extra classi- fications for data points that are not required. Here, smaller clusters are preferred over larger clusters. 2) Accuracy: Different integration approaches also differ with respect to their ability to identify correlations between features. Their horizon is limited to the dedicated function, the domain, or the whole vehicle, which also influences the required compute resources. a) Leverage Correlations: As already briefly touched upon above, having an overlap in the input feature set could reduce the overhead of computation. However, it is also possible that the feature selection algorithms selected a feature for the feature input set of model A that did not make it into the feature input set for model B, even though there is a correlation present. Leveraging this correlation is possible in the domain method and the holistic method, but not in the dedicated method, as only one feature is evaluated during classification. b) Available Compute: We have argued that less compu- tation is needed if there exists an overlap in the input feature set that would reduce the amount of computation needed. An alternative approach would be to leave the computational steps equal, but leverage this extra available compute to generate more complex models in order to achieve higher accuracy. This would apply to the holistic and the per-domain method. 3) Design Complexity: The introduced integration ap- proaches need to be discussed in the shade of their impact on the in-vehicle network architecture but also on requirements derived from the given architecture. a) Safety Requirements: Safety-critical computations have to be performed within a particular deadline in order to fulfil guarantees. This would imply that the model from the holistic method needs to be run as often and within the time budget as required by the strongest safety requirement. The model from the dedicated approach does not have this limitation; the per-domain approach can be designed to overlap domain and safety classes. b) Modular Design: Another difficulty is modularisation. As soon as one would want to add a new feature, such as mirror heating, one would have to retrain and reverify the func- tionality in the holistic approach, especially the safety-critical functionality. This problem is not present in the dedicated method, and might not be present in the per-domain method if there is an overlap between the separation of domains and the level of safety requirements for this group. c) Signal Routing: For a holistic integration method to work, one would have to route all input channels to a single point of computation. For a variety of reasons, such as single- point-of-failure, real-time deadlines, and modularisation, this is currently not the state-of-the-art in automotive architectures. The domain-specific method does also require aggregation of input channels, but a grouping of input channels per domain is a common approach, already today. Generating functions for every single functionality does allow the function to sit anywhere in the architecture, allowing it to be flexible. D. DISCUSSION When comparing the results between the functions, we can see in three out of four cases that the accuracy is not improved when combining functions of the same domain. However, it significantly improves when combining all functions. Only in one out of four cases (Seat Heating) the accuracy was improved when combining functions of the same domain but was not further improved when all functions where combined. Here, we would like to point out the structure of our network. We have two first layers which remain equal width regardless of the number of input features. The more functions we combine, the more input features are available for the net- work to train on. On the last layer, there are either one or more similar layers that binary-classify the 4096 neurons. For this reason, the benefit of training all functions cannot be attributed to a wider network, but to the additional input information available for the network. Another reason for the improvement in accuracy could also result from the learning interaction between the different functions. Since neural network are known as black boxes and are not easy to assess, we cannot clearly determine the exact reason for this improvement. When comparing the improvement in accuracy, the holistic approach outperformed the domain-based approach in three out of four functions (cf. Table V). However, when compar- ing the mean difference between the centralised holistic and domain-specific approach, we observe only a slight improve- ment of 3 to 1 . But a combination of all functions in one overall system would lead to a significant increase in the design complexity of this system. Following this, we propose a per-domain approach. This approach provides a balance between the trade-off of the lim- itations in the dedicated approach, being high computational overhead, and the design complexity in the holistic approach, as one can make design choices in the domain-specific ap- proach that reduce the impact. As seen in the results in one out of four functions, a domain-based combination leads to a slight improvement but does not imply the design complexity as in the centralised holistic approach. The drawn conclusions rely on the assumptions made for current in-vehicle architectures, which usually are also structured according to domains. In the future, however, also more centralised approaches with multi- core high-performance computing units are possible requiring a reevaluation of the approach. Threats to the Validity: A major threat to validity con- cerns the selection of vehicles. There is a considerable amount of in-house test vehicles data. However, the approach has to be evaluated on real customer data due to the behaviour we want to learn from the user. Real customer data is hard to collect, as a premium car manufacturer, we highly consider the privacy of the customers. Hence, it is very difficulteven as an OEMto get a high number of full real customer car traces. We minimised the impact of these limitations by using traces from different world regions. We are aware of this issue and try to gather more data for future work. VII. CONCLUSION We introduced an architectural model for dynamic systems and studied different architectural patterns and integration methods. The Concurrent Learning Pattern Pc and the End-to- End Learning Pattern Pe will have high safety requirements even for simple functionsand currently, the development of machine learning functions with high safety requirements within the automotive domain is very complex and requires substantial development effort. The User Shadow Learning Pattern Pu is not affected by this constraint, as the learned user behaviour is mimicked by user shadow u, which feeds into the original function f. As function f remains unchanged, it will still meet all safety requirements. For the integration of all functionality, we do not need to consider accuracy, as we have shown that all integra- tion methods perform similarly, although we see a slight improvement when combining all functions. Following this, we propose a per-domain approach. This approach provides a balance between the trade-off of the limitations in the dedicated approach, being high computational overhead, and the design complexity in the holistic approach, as one can make design choices in the domain-specific approach that reduce the impact. papers.fulltext: InMap: Automated Interactive Code-to-Architecture Mapping Recommendations Zipani Tom Sinkala Mathematics Computer Science Karlstad University Karlstad, Sweden tom.sinkala kau.se Sebastian Herold Mathematics Computer Science Karlstad University Karlstad, Sweden sebastian.herold kau.se AbstractReflexion Modelling is a popular method used in industry for Software Architectural Consistency Checking (SACC). However, it involves a mapping step that is manual and tedious. There exist techniques and tools that attempt to automate mapping, yet they are either limited in their approach or they require an initial set of manually pre-mapped entities. This study proposes a novel technique, InMap, that improves the mapping process in reflexion modelling by both providing versatility and eliminating the constraint of needing a set of manually pre-mapped entities in order to automate mapping. Using a softwares architecture descriptions, InMap applies information retrieval concepts to the softwares source code to interactively provide mapping recommendations to an architect. For the six systems InMap was evaluated on, the recommendations it provided achieved an average recall of 0.97, and an average precision of 0.82. InMap also achieved higher, f1-scores in comparison to existing techniques that require pre- mapping. This provides a basis for improving industry tools that use reflexion modelling or similar SACC methods. Keywords automating architecture conformance, software architecture descriptions, source code mapping, reflexion modelling, software architecture consistency checking, software maintenance, information retrieval I. INTRODUCTION A software developer can use a software architecture to define the structure of a software system that will help it achieve desired quality attributes, such as security, performance, scalability or reliability 18 . However, as the software evolves, it may degrade or erode 1, 3 that is, its implementation may no longer conform to its architecture 22, 23 . This in turn threatens the ability of the software to fulfil its architectural design goals or to continue meeting its desired quality attributes 3 . These problems can be costly to resolve 20, 21 . To combat this, practitioners use Software Architecture Consistency Checking (SACC), also known as Software Architecture Conformance, which is a practice of checking if a software implementation conforms-to or deviates-from its intended software architecture 1 . The intended software architecture of a system, which is the architecture as it was originally designed, differs from the as- is architecture which is the architecture as has been implemented in code. SACC research looks for ways of improving the processes, methods and tools software engineers have available to allow them to discover or explore software architecture degradation erosion 3, 7 . One technique that has proven effective in this field, with regard to industry acceptance and tool support, is Reflexion Modelling 24, 25 . In this technique, a softwares implementation is compared against its architectural design. The architectural design is expressed in a graphical model of the softwares architectural modules and the allowed dependencies among them 2 . Reflexion modelling uses three steps to detect and represent the architectural inconsistencies in software. The first step defines the static architectural modules (or module- view architecture) of a software system. The second step maps units of source code to the architectural modules. The third step automatically computes the differences between the allowed dependencies of the architectural modules and the actual dependencies in the software implementation, and visually represents them in a reflexion model. Step 1, architectural module definition, and step 2, mapping code to architecture, of reflexion modelling are both manual. However step 2 is also labour-intensive especially for large complex software systems, which are commonplace in todays heavily software-dependent industries. Ali et al. highlight that practitioners cite the huge effort...required to map the system to the architecture as one of the main barriers to adoption of SACC techniques like reflexion modelling 1 . Because of these factors, SACC may become too costly to consider, or may be over-looked altogether, by software engineering practitioners 1, 3 . To minimize the effort needed to do reflexion modelling due to the manual mapping process, there are techniques that attempt to automate the mapping task. However, these techniques require that an initial set of the source code still be mapped manually by a software architect 4, 5, 6 . In large complex systems, these existing techniques still demand significant manual work as the initial pre-mapped set needs to be of a certain minimum size in order to achieve good results 6 . There also exist tools that assist architects with reflexion modelling; even so, mapping is still a manual drag-drop task 8, 29, 30 . A few provide automated mapping support through name patterns that require no initial pre-mapped set 29, 30 . However, because of their simple nature name patterns are not versatile and do not scale well in systems that have complex code-to-architecture mapping configurations. In this paper, we present a novel interactive automated mapping technique, called InMap, which overcomes the pre- mapping constraint of existing automated mapping techniques and the manual and limited approaches of existing reflexion modelling tools. InMap, in an automated routine, interactively produces mapping recommendations to a software architect. It applies information retrieval techniques on the softwares source code using natural language textual descriptions of the architectural modules. The performance (i.e. recall, precision and f1-score) of the technique is evaluated on six test systems. Its performance is also compared with two automated mapping techniques, namely HuGME and NBC, which require a pre-mapping set in order to automate mapping. Section II briefly describes how reflexion modelling works. Section III gives an overview of existing automated mapping techniques and state-of-the-art reflexion modelling industry tools. Section IV gives an in-depth description of the 173 2021 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA) 978-1-7281-6260-7 21 31.00 2021 IEEE DOI 10.1109.2021.00024 2021 IEEE 18th International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA) 978-1-7281-6260-7 20 31.00 2021 IEEE DOI: 10.1109 ICSA InMap technique. Section V describes how the technique was evaluated along with the results obtained. Section VI discusses the results and the paper is concluded in Section VII. II. REFLEXION MODELLING IN A NUTSHELL Reflexion modelling, using a graphical model visualization, compares a softwares architectural module design and their allowed dependencies with the softwares implementation 2 . The software components, referred to as architectural modules, are high-level abstractions of a software system that are of interest to a software architect in line with their preferred architectural views 2 . Fig. 1 shows an example of architectural modules represented as boxed nodes, with solid edges denoting the dependencies permitted between the modules. If the dependencies of the source code entities match the dependencies of modules in the architecture, then the software implementation conforms to its design. If the dependencies do not match, then the software violates its architecture and investigations as to why take place. The reflexion model in Fig. 1 shows dependencies between modules that violate the architecture as dashed edges. Numbers are sometimes included to show the number of violations or correct dependencies. III. AUTOMATED MAPPING TECHNIQUES Automated mapping techniques are necessary to reduce the effort needed by the architect during a SACC exercise, where given a software system there exists its source code and intended architecture but no mapping between the two. The mapping occurs because either it is a greenfield mapping task or due to software evolution, that necessitates re-mapping. A. Dependency-Based Automated Mapping Dependency-Based Mapping (DBM) techniques exploit software-clustering methods, which group software entities according to the dependencies between them. Software clustering and related techniques such as software partitioning are prevalent in Software Architecture Recovery (SAR) techniques and tools 9, 10 . In SAR, software-clustering techniques propose possible architecture modules as clusters or partitions of source code entities based on varying definitions of similarity. However, SACC methods use them differently to automate the mapping step 4 . DBM techniques instead propose mappings of source code entities to pre-defined modules given by the architect or retrieved from the intended architecture. DBM techniques rely on the dependencies that exist between source code entities to decide which module a source file maps-to. Typically, these dependencies between source code entities of a software system are method calls and field or variable access 5 . One successful DBM mapping technique is Human Guided Mapping Generation Method (HuGME). HuGME is a dependency-based automated mapping technique that clusters a software systems source code using an architects hypothesized knowledge about its architecture 5 . HuGME starts with a filtering step that excludes all unmapped entities below a given threshold. The technique uses in- and out-going dependencies between unmapped and mapped entities, so if there exists a high number of dependencies between unmapped entities then no meaningful results is given. Therefore, the filter excludes all unmapped entities whose ratio of dependencies to mapped entities is below the threshold. After filtering, HuGME applies an attraction function, which minimizes coupling and maximizes Fig. 1. A reflexion model showing architecture module dependency violations. Arrow lines that have the same colour as a module belong to it. cohesion, to produce a matrix of attraction scores for unmapped entities to modules 11 . The calculation of the score uses the dependency values between unmapped entities and mapped entities. The higher the score the higher the likelihood that an unmapped entity belongs to a given module. All unmapped entities that result in only one candidate having a similarity score higher than the arithmetic mean of all scores are automatically mapped. All unmapped entities for which two or more candidates exist are presented to the user in ranked order, from highest to lowest, for manual mapping. This process is incremental, in that HuGME does not attempt to map all source code entities in one complete step; rather it maps a subset at a time until no more mapping is possible. For the attraction function, HuGME compares two different kinds, CountAttract and MQAttract. CountAttract applies a local approach to coupling and cohesion, whereas MQAttract uses a global context. Both attraction functions apply weighting to different dependency types like variables, methods, classes, interfaces and types 5, 12, 13 . CountAttract gave better results than MQAttract. In the study by Christl et al. the results for HuGME had on average about 90 recall and 80-90 accuracy 4 . To get these results the technique needed about 20 of the systems source entities pre-mapped before running the algorithm. Of interest is that because this mapping technique is dependency-based, for it to give meaningful results, the 20 pre-mapped source entities need to be spread across various modules. In addition, they must have dependencies to unmapped entities. This presents a problem for architects in that for them to derive the positives of this technique they need to not only dedicate some time for pre-mapping but must also ensure that the mapping has a balance of mapped entities spread across the modules and ensure they have dependencies to unmapped entities. This is a labour intensive exercise to say the least. Furthermore, because it is using clustering algorithms based on high cohesion and low coupling, if developers do not follow this principle in the softwares implementation then the mapping of the algorithm will be affected 14 . B. Information Retrieval Automated Mapping Information Retrieval (IR) based techniques use concepts from the field of IR to map source entities to architectural modules by searching using differently defined similarity functions. If we define source entities to be a softwares source code files containing object-oriented code and if we make these files represent classes in the software system then we can take advantage of concepts in IR to automate the mapping process 15 . The source file is essentially text with class variables, methods, code comments and class names, which can then be used as input into existing IR techniques. Bittencourt et al. propose an IR based technique that uses the same automated mapping approach as HuGME. It replaces the dependency-based CountAttract and MQAttract attraction functions with the IR based IRAttract and LSIAttract similarity functions 15 . IRAttract is a function that calculates the similarity of an unmapped source entity to a module by searching for specific terms (the modules name and its mapped class names, methods and fields) within the source code of the unmapped class. Before the search, the unmapped class is stripped of stop words (e.g. and, is, the) and tokenized into stemmed class names, methods, fields, and module names. IRAttract uses relative term weights to compute class- module similarity scores. LSIAttract, on the other hand, uses Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI) also known as Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), which introduces understanding of the meaning of a word or groups of words in natural language by grouping terms into concepts 15, 16 . This approach is similar to the studies done by Maletic et al., which investigate applying LSA to program source code and associated documentation (code comments) within the context of SAR for the purposes of program understanding 16 . Similar to HuGME, Bittencourt et al.s technique needs some manual pre-mapping before it can automate mapping. Olsson et al. use Bayes theorem of probability in their IR based technique called Naive Bayes Classification (NBC) 6 . NBC builds a probabilistic model of classifications using words taken from the source code entities. The model gives the probability of words belonging to a source file entity. To derive the words, the technique splits camel case words into single words, and then retrieves stemmed package names, file names, attribute names and variable names. Code comments along with words below three characters are not used. This augmented with syntactical information of the dependencies, a method called Concrete Dependency Approach 6 . To create the probabilistic model, NBC does not use word frequencies, but rather whether a word exists or not. As is the case with HuGME, Olsson et al.s proposed techniques require a pre-mapped set in order to perform well. Both Bittencourt et al.s and Olsson et al.s results showed that when there was a smaller pre-mapped set there was a decreasing trend in the f1-score of their techniques 6, 15 . Naim et al. present a technique called Coordinated Clustering of Heterogeneous Datasets (CCHD), that combines both dependency-based and information retrieval techniques to compute a similarity score of source code files 17 . It uses as input, class names, comments, method calls and identifiers in source code to produce a method call-graph, extract method to class dependence, and construct term-class relations. After obtaining results, CCHD uses an architects feedback on the recovered architecture to iteratively adjust the results until there are no suggestion for change. These adjusted results train a classifier that automatically places new code added to a codebase in the right architectural module. However, the technique is not necessarily meant for automated mapping in SACC but rather for SAR tasks. C. Industry Tools Todays SACC state-of-the-art industry tools provide support for reflexion modelling in various ways. Axivion Architecture Analysis is an industry tool that provides support for reflexion modelling and architectural verification. To automate mapping it uses work based on HuGME and therefore has the same limitations as the technique 28 . More common among industry tools is using naming patterns. Sonargraph-Architect allows a software architect to specify the intended architecture by defining the modules using Sonargraph's Architecture DSL. Source code entities are then mapped to the architecture modules using class package naming patterns e.g. gui to map source classes packages that match the given naming pattern to the GUI architecture module. Structure101 Studio provides drag-drop functionality to map source entities. However, it also allows specifying a class package name pattern to map classes packages to a given module to produce dependency validation architecture diagrams that show any dependencies in the implementation that violate the intended architecture. For example, classes packages that map to module GUI could be represented by the pattern net.java.gui. or .gui. . The drawback of using naming pattern techniques is due to their 1- 1 class package mapping style defining the patterns can be a tedious exercise especially for large software systems that have complex mapping configurations. It is not always the case that packages and their members directly map to modules in a 1-1 manner that naming patterns demand. In such circumstances, specifying the cases where package members are spread across multiple modules requires a long pattern list. Recently programming languages such as Java and C have introduced support for architectural modules, in their programming constructs. For instance, Java introduced the Java Platform Module System, in version 9 of its JDK where developers can define a software systems architectural modules and all the modules they depend on 31 . The modules are defined using Java Application Packages in a separate file called module-info.java which explicitly declares which packages a module depends on and which it exports 32 . For example, the following declares that the module net.java.gui depends on the module net.java.ui, and exports the packages net.java.gui.buttons and net.java.gui.windows module net.java.gui requires net.java.ui; exports net.java.gui.buttons; exports net.java.gui.windows; The addition of explicit module and dependency declaration in programming languages such as Java in version 9 and C in version 20 33 makes it easier to reason about software systems. However, in terms of code to architecture module mapping there are numerous examples of software systems that have an architectural module decomposition that deviates from its defined packages structures. Just like with naming patterns, Programming Language Modules Systems have flexibility limitations. It is not always the case that packages directly map to modules in a 1-1 manner that these methods assume. D. Limitations Available techniques that are designed specifically to automate the mapping step in reflexion modelling either require an initial set of the source code to be pre-mapped manually by a software architect or do not afford mapping flexibility. The automated mapping techniques that have no versatility constraint require pre-mapped source code in order to jump-start mapping as well as to give worthwhile results, that is, with a precision of 70 and above. At minimum, these techniques require about 15-20 of the source code to be pre- mapped in order to give worthwhile results 4, 5, 6, 15 . Though this is better than an entirely manual mapping process, e.g. drag and drop, for large systems with a high number of source code files, this 15-20 pre-mapped source code prerequisite becomes a barrier for adoption of successful software architecture consistency checking methods. We hence believe that the effort in mapping has to be further reduced. From our experience in applying reflexion modelling in industrial contexts, we noticed that current techniques do not exploit one commonly provided and potentially helpful type of information: short descriptions of the purpose of the architectural modules articulated in natural language. To explore this we had the following research question: Can we use natural language descriptions of software architecture modules to overcome the pre-requisite of having an initial pre-mapped set in order to automate mapping in SACC methods like Reflexion Modelling? In the following section, we describe how InMap makes use of such descriptions to recommend mappings without needing an initial set of pre-mapped entities. IV. INMAP A. The Technique InMap is an interactive code-to-architecture automated mapping recommendation technique for SACC methods that involve a mapping step. Specifically, it proposes an improvement to the mapping process in reflexion modelling by eliminating the need for an initial set of pre-mapped source code in order to automate mapping. Using concepts from the field of information retrieval, the technique interactively maps a software systems source code to its architectural modules. The technique takes as inputs, a systems source code files and the systems architectural modules along with their natural language descriptions to produce, as output, class-to-module mapping recommendations. Architectural module description can be obtained from wherever they can be found. For example, they can be obtained from existing software architecture documentation or they can be prepared by the software architect who may also choose to provide them as audio recordings that eventually can be transcribed to text. The source of the descriptions is not necessarily important; the point being stressed is that they are easily retrievable making them cheap information that can be exploited for automating the mapping task. Table I shows examples of some of the architectural module descriptions provided by the development team of ProM, an open source process mining application. The central idea of the proposed technique is to consider descriptions of architectural modules as a piece of information for mapping a systems source code to its modules. The source code files of the system correspond to documents, which in the terminology of information retrieval are well-defined units of text consisting of words 18 . The module descriptions, as well as their names, correspond to terms, that is, keywords that are being searched for in a set of documents. To illustrate this, the source code file ObjectArray.java is a document and the module name basic-utils is a term we can use to search for in the said document. Intuitively speaking, this approach translates the question of what are the source code files belonging to a module, to a textual query, comprising of the modules name and description, made against a body of documents that are the systems source code files. Applicability. There are three predominant scenarios in which InMap can be applied. (1) The first is the case where the softwares intended architecture along with its TABLE I. SAMPLE ARCHITECTURE MODULE DESCRIPTIONS Module Description apache-utils That's a utility package containing apache-licensed third- party libraries. logs log contains the implementation of the event logs in ProM which includes a third-party library called "OpenXES" that we also developed. That the handling of the event logs basically. The model is there, a lot of plugins are there that handle the logs. log-skeleton log-skeleton contains the implementation of the log skeleton model with the useful plugins like creating a log skeleton from a log, importing, exporting and visualizing. models prom-models contains support for graph visualization or modelling. Basically it contains an abstract directed graph model that the developers can use. documentation exists but there exists no mapping between the source code and the architecture. (2) The other is the case where there is no intended architecture or documentation nor mapping, but the architect is present who can provide the intended architecture along with some descriptions either as hand-written notes or verbal descriptions that are transcribed into textual architecture documentation. In these two greenfield mapping scenarios InMap can be used by the architect to map the softwares implementation to its intended architecture. (3) The third scenario is in the context of software evolution where a mapping exists however, the software implementation has undergone some changes. In such a scenario, the intended architecture along with its documentation exists, similar to the first greenfield mapping scenario, however, use of InMap is still applicable as this is considered as a new mapping task or as a re-mapping exercise. InMap similar to other automated approaches can be used to map any newly created classes. InMap is currently implemented to support Java source code only; it is, however, conceptually not limited to the Java programming language. The concepts InMap uses can be applied to other programming languages that follow the object-oriented programming paradigm. The technique works in seven steps, which are summarised in Fig. 2, as follows: STEP 1 Filtering. The software architect can provide InMap with an exclusion list, that is, a list of source code files that should be excluded from the mapping process, and for which no recommendations are to be made. This exclusion list is often desirable, for system or other third-party libraries like the Java system library packages java. , javax. , and javafx. . STEP 2 Pre-Processing. InMap splits each source file that passes STEP 1 into two parts: code and comments. The code is stripped of import statements, private statements, and programming language specific keywords e.g. int, enum, and switch in Java. The comments are stripped of stop words. Both the code and comments are stripped of special characters, after which, the resulting cleaned tokens are then stored. Using a code extract from ProM as an example, the following code, This is used to contain third-party libraries package org.processmining.basicutils.help public class LGPLLicenseHelp public final static String TEXT "" "Retrieves and shows the L-GPL License."; after pre-processing becomes, contain third-party libraries org processmining basicutils help lgpllicensehelp text retrieves and shows the l-gpl license The motivation behind what is done in the pre-processing step is to make sure InMap strips away words that add noise when a term-document similarity calculation is done. However, it must be noted that although stop words are removed from code comments they are not removed from the code because how they are used by developers in variable naming or in method naming, is unpredictable. For example, a developer could use the stop word about as part of a method name. Whereas removing it from comments reduces noise, removing it from code would lead to loss of valuable method name information that InMap uses in the query formation described in STEP 4. This was evidenced by the significant reduction in precision for some of the systems tested when stop words were removed from code. STEP 3 Indexing. In this step, InMap indexes all the pre-processed (or cleaned) documents. It creates an inverted index for the documents resulting in STEP 2. In an inverted index, for each term, the index stores a list of those documents that contain the term 18 . Fig. 3 shows an example of an inverted index for ProM. InMap uses the open source tool Apache Lucene for indexing, and later for searching. STEP 4 Query Formation. In this step, InMap creates a search query string for each architectural module. If there are nine modules then it will create nine independent search query strings for each module. Each module search query string is used, in STEP 5 to search the cleaned documents that were indexed in STEP 3. The search queries are a combination of four parts: (i) the name of the module the class could be mapped to; (ii) the modules textual description, which is stripped of stop words and special characters; (iii) names of classes that are mapped to the module; and (iv) names of methods that belong to classes that are mapped to the module. At a basic level the query appears as follows, (module name) (module description) (mapped class names) (mapped method names) The module name and description terms are performed as wildcard searches. A wildcard search query such as gui looks for documents containing any terms that start with gui e.g. guiButton or guiFrame 18 . Lucene supports single and multiple character wildcard searches. The module name and module description terms are also added as fuzzy search terms. A fuzzy query looks for a term similar in spelling to a given term e.g. affect for effect or "redButton" for "blueButton". Lucene supports fuzzy searches using the Damerau-Levenshtein Distance 26 , which is a string-edit distance metric commonly, used in spell checkers 27 . The query with wildcard and fuzzy search appears as follows, (module name ) (module description ) (mapped class names) (mapped method names) Additionally, InMap specifies the relevance of each term in a query by means of a boost factor. The higher the boost factor, the more relevant the term will be. InMap assigns boost factors to the module name, the Module Name Boost Factor (MNBF) as well as to the module description terms, the Fig. 2. An illustration of the steps in the InMap mapping technique. Fig. 3. Sample inverted index of ProM. Module Description Boost Factor (MDBF). The module name and module descriptions are assigned boost factors as they have the greatest probability of influencing the similarity score between an architectural module and an unmapped source code entity. This is especially the case if the module description and code comments are elaborate explanations of the software system architecture. With boost factors added the query changes as follows, (module name ) MNBF (module description ) MDBF (mapped class names) (mapped method names) InMap retrieves the class and method names from a call- dependency graph. Each source code file is considered as a class. Nested classes are ignored as they are considered to map to the same module as their parent classes. Multiple classes in the same source code file are also considered to map to the same module. The method names are stripped of common accessor method prefixes such as get-, set- and is-. They are then ranked in order of the most frequently occurring within a module and then added to the remaining query space after query formation items (i)-(iii) have been added - Lucenes query size limit is 1,024 terms. A query is automatically created for each architectural module and is submitted to Lucene to search the inverted index. By including mapped class and module names in the search query each time a new class is mapped to a given module the architecture textual representation of the module is updated. This means the query changes each time new classes are mapped allowing InMaps hit-rate to broaden progressively with each new mapping iteration. This occurs after the architect accepts any of the class-module mapping recommendations given by InMap in STEP 7. Below is an example, taken from ProM of what the resulting query produced in STEP 4 looks like. (apache-utils ) 36.0 (utility package containing apache-licensed third-party libraries ) 2.0 (Boot PathHackerRunnable AddJarsForPackageRunnable) (bestRepository latestReleaseInstalled addJarsFromPackageDirectory run) STEP 5 Similarity Scoring. InMap submits the multipart query to Lucene to search the inverted index of the source code files and returns all source code files (specifically classes) that have a hit. Each term in the query and in a given document defines a vector in an n-dimensional space. There are various schemes for calculating each vector 18 . InMap uses term frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf) as the similarity scoring function because it gives more importance to a term that frequently occurs in a few documents relative to the collection than one that occurs in many documents. That is to say, given a software source code base, we would rather give more importance to a term like security occurring frequently in a few source code files as opposed to the name of the software e.g. chromium which is likely to occur in almost every source code file of the software. Formally, tf-idf is defined as follows: given that term frequency (tttttt,dd) refers to the number of occurrences of term t in document d; and document frequency (ddddtt) refers to the number of documents in the collection that contain a term t; and inverse document frequency (idf) is defined as: iiiiiitt log NN ddddtt (1) with N denoting the total number of documents in a collection; then the tf-idf is defined as: ttttiiiiiitt,dd tttttt,dd iiiiiitt (2) tf-idf is highest when t occurs many times within a small number of documents (implying these documents are more important); lower when the term occurs fewer times in a document, or occurs in many documents (implying these documents are less relevant); and lowest when the term occurs in, in essence, all documents (implying these documents are the least relevant). Lucene returns tf-idf weightings for each search query string, which represents a module as defined in STEP 4 that has a hit on one or more classes in the source code base. InMap uses the tf-idf weightings of the unmapped classes as class- module similarity scores and produces a class-module similarity matrix. That is, given a set of classes C c1, c2, c3, ..., cn and a set of modules M m1, m2, m3, ..., mn we get a set of similarity scores SS c1,m1, c1,m2, c1,m3, ..., c1,mn, c2,m1, ..., cnmn where cnmn is a tf-idf weighting as defined in Eq. 2. The classes are represented by the source code files, as described in STEP 4. STEP 6 Mapping Recommendations. For each unmapped class InMap retains the highest class-module similarity score SScnmn and discards the others. In other words, a set of suggested mappings are produced where for each unmapped class we have only one mapping the highest scoring one. The idea is that the module that an unmapped class has the highest similarity score for is the most likely candidate that it maps to. However, InMap does some further filtering before presenting them to the user architect. First, if a class has two or more modules with the same highest score then none is put forth, to avoid arbitrary recommendations. That is to say, using ProM as an example, if the unmapped class ObjectArray has a class-module similarity score of 88.85 to the architectural module framework and the same similarity score to the architectural module contexts then InMap does not present any mapping recommendation for ObjectArray to the architect. InMap only includes, to the list of recommended mappings, a suggested mapping of an unmapped class if the similarity score of the class to a module is the single highest scoring among all the modules in a given iteration. Secondly, all suggested mappings below the arithmetic mean of the set are discarded. That is, given the set of suggested mappings, of the best module similarity scores for each unmapped class, only those that above the arithmetic mean of the set are presented as recommendations. Thirdly, InMap uses what we call a Page Size (PS) to determine how many recommendations at a time should be presented to the architect e.g. 10, 20, or 50 per page. InMap ranks the list of suggested mappings according to their score in, descending order, and presents to the architect no more than the x highest scoring pairs, where x is the page size. The list of suggested mappings that make it this far through the similarity scores filtering process become the list of recommended class-to- module mappings for the given iteration i.e. the first set of recommendations R or more specifically R1 (recommendations in iteration 1). The number of recommendations given per page is sometimes less than the PS. This may happen in two situations. Firstly, when the number of unmapped classes remaining is less than PS. Secondly, when within the set of suggested mappings produced the number of mappings with a score greater than the arithmetic mean of the set is less than PS. Fig. 4 shows an example, using ProM, of how the class-module mapping recommendations are presented to the architect. STEP 7 Accept Reject Mappings. The architect reviews the recommendations agreeing and disagreeing based on his her knowledge of the software system. Once this is completed, InMap returns to STEP 4 with new information about the module architectures, that is, the newly mapped classes that the architect accepted. The names of these mapped classes along with names of their methods are used to update the query, which is passed to Lucene to search the remaining set of unmapped classes and produce similarity scores for them, STEP 5. This culminates into a set of recommendations R2 for the set of unmapped classes with the highest scoring pairs, STEP 6. The architect again accepts and rejects the recommendations in R2, STEP 7. The algorithm returns to STEP 4 once more with new terms to add to the search query. As STEP 4 - 7 continue to repeat, InMap keeps track of rejected mappings and does not present them to the user as recommendations again. The algorithm ends when the mapping is complete (Rn ) or when either the architect or InMap can make no more decisions. Fig. 2 shows an illustration summarizing InMaps steps. All steps in the algorithm are automated with the exception of STEP 7, which allows the architect to accept or reject mappings. B. Replication Package A replication package of the study and its results can be found here https: doi.org 10.6084.figshare.1371410. V. EVALUATION To determine the effectiveness of InMap we evaluated the technique with the intent of measuring its performance in terms of accuracy using a prototypical tool we developed. A. Case Selection We conducted six case studies on Java-based systems. Table II shows the attributes of the different systems under the study. It specifies factors such as system size, number of modules and length of architectural descriptions. Ant is a command line and API-based tool for process automation; ArgoUML is a desktop-based application for UML modelling; JabRef is a desktop-based bibliographic reference manager; Jittac is an eclipse plugin for reflexion modelling tasks; ProM is a desktop-based processes mining tool; and TeamMates is a web-based application for handling peer reviews and feedback. For the evaluation of InMap Oracle Mappings, that is, the correct list of which classes map to which modules were obtained for the six identified systems from experts involved in developing each respective open source project. Additionally Architectural Module Descriptions for the six chosen systems were gathered. For JabRef this was obtained from the project development team; for ProM, these were as the result of a software architecture documentation exercise at a Software Architecture Erosion Conference (SAEroCon) workshop with the software architect; and for Jittac these were produced by an expert who had contributed to development of the tool. The architectural module descriptions for Ant, ArgoUML and TeamMates were derived from system architectural documentation by a researcher independent of this study to avoid bias. An evaluator (also included in the replication package) was built to automatically simulate a human architect accepting and rejecting the recommendations InMap produces using the Oracle Mapping. This allowed us to maintain accuracy and efficiency during our numerous experiments. B. Discussion of the Findings From the results, we observe most importantly that InMap was able to map the three software test systems without requiring a pre-mapped set of entities. This is possible due to the use of information retrieval techniques. InMap assumes any combination of the four parts of the query that make up the textual representation of a module, that is, its name; its natural language description; names of classes mapped to it; and names of methods mapped to it; could be closely related to both or any two parts of a source file, namely, the code comments and the actual code. The results in Table VI demonstrate this idea albeit with varying precision and accuracy depending on what is included in the query and what parts of a source code file is searched. InMap is able to find class-module mapping recommendations in its first iteration using only a softwares module names and or module architectural descriptions.
