papers.fulltext: COCOS: a Scalable Architecture for Containerized Heterogeneous Systems Luciano Baresi, Giovanni Quattrocchi Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica, Informazione e Bioingegneria, Milan, Italy name.surname polimi.it Abstract Nowadays software systems are organized around several and heterogeneous components. For example, a modern application can be composed of different microservices, along with dedicated components for machine learning analytics and recurring batch processing jobs. While containers offer a means to deploy the system and tackle heterogeneity, these components have different execution models, can exploit different resource types (e.g., CPUs and GPUs) and result in completely different execution times (milliseconds vs hours). This complexity calls for a new, scalable architecture to allow the systems to operate efficiently. This paper presents COCOS, an architecture, based on con- tainers and control-theory, that is able to manage large and het- erogeneous software systems. The architecture is based on a three- level hierarchy of controllers that cooperatively enforce user- defined requirements on execution times and consumed resources. The paper also shows a prototype implementation of COCOS based on Kubernetes, a well-known container orchestrator. The evaluation shows the efficiency of COCOS when dealing with microservices, Spark jobs and machine learning applications. Index Termscontainers, kubernetes, heterogeneous architec- tures, microservices, batch processing I. INTRODUCTION Software systems are evolving rapidly and becoming increas- ingly more distributed, complex and heterogeneous. Modern software systems are often composed of different sub-systems that cooperatively form a complete application. Each sub- system is distributed and performs a specific task such as running a web service, executing a data analysis job, or exploiting a GPU-powered machine learning model 1 , 2 . This evolution was caused by different factors, including the need of serving several concurrent users, processing increasingly larger data quantities, and fulfilling different heterogeneous task types. One of the main enablers of this evolution was cloud computing 3 . Cloud infrastructures ease the deployment of different resources types, the automated installation of software on them, and the execution of distributed and heterogeneous applications. This flexibility is allowed by the use of virtualization techniques that abstract several details of the underlying hardware layer. Historically, Virtual Machines (VMs) were the main virtual- ization technique used in the cloud. More recently, containers, a lightweight virtualization technology, are becoming the main means to deploy software systems in the cloud. One of the This work has been partially supported by the European project SODALITE (grant agreement 825480) and by the national research project SISMA (MIUR, PRIN 2017, Contract 201752ENY B) advantages of containers is that they do not contain a guest operating system (OS) which makes them faster to boot and more portable. Instead they exploit features of the host OS that segregate the execution of different processes that run on the same (physical or virtual) machine 4 , 5 . Practitioners usually deploy each sub-system as a set of containers onto a cluster of machines that could be shared with other sub-systems of the same application or even of different ones 6 . Despite the fact that the complexity of managing heterogeneous and distributed systems is increasing, users want to have guarantees on the performance of these applications 7 . Non-functional requirements, such as con- straints on execution response times, are usually defined as Service Level Agreements (SLAs). The response time of a software system mainly depends on its intrinsic structure, on the computational resources allocated to it, and on the incoming workload. Given that the structure is given and the workload is only partially foreseeable, resource allocation plays a key role in helping meet set SLAs 8 . Static resource allocation is done before operating the system, while dynamic allocation capabilities can scale resources as needed while the system executes and the context changes. Horizontal scalability deals with the addition (removal) of executors (e.g., adding removing containers), while vertical scalability is about reconfiguring existing resources while in use (e.g., changing the number of cores allocated to a container) 9 , 10 . Existiing approaches 11 , 8 , 12 , 13 differ in terms of addressing static, dynamic, horizontal, vertical management capabilities, the enabling means they exploit (e.g., rule-based, combinatorial optimization), the type of resources they use (VMs or containers), and the systems they target (e.g., web or big data applications). Since, as mentioned earlier, a single system often comprises heterogeneous components, we advocate that existing solutions lack a comprehensive architecture that allows for the efficient control of the system as whole. The works on containers are still in their infancy since most of the solutions were thought for being used with VMs. The solutions that support dynamic resource allocation are usually limited in scalability since they use combinatorial formulations or because they reason on allocating VMs, which is inherently slower than allocating containers (e.g., minutes vs seconds) 14 . This paper presents COCOS (COntainerized COntrolled Systems), an architecture for heterogeneous software systems that supports their fast, efficient, and distributed operation. 103 2020 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA) 978-1-7281-4659-1 20 31.00 2020 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA COCOS targets systems that are composed of sub-systems of different kinds deployed as containers on a cluster of physical machines. COCOS aims to: i) provide a generic architecture that allows for the control of different types of systems that share resources ii) allow for the lightweight, fast (in the order of seconds), fine-grained, and reliable resource scalability iii) to manage resources at the level of both containers (vertical and horizontal scalability) and VMs (horizontal scalability). COCOS is organized around three hierarchical control layers. The lowest associates each container with a dedicated control theory-based planner and addresses vertical scalability to fulfill requirements on execution times. The mid layer is based on heuristics and operates at machine level to deal with resource contention among containers. At the highest level, the cluster control layer is dedicated to horizontally adding and removing machines and instantiating containers on them. The paper also presents a prototype of COCOS as an extension of Kubernetes1 and the Docker runtime2. Googles Kubernetes, a popular container orchestrator, provides different built-in capabilities for managing containers (e.g, automatic recovery and load balancing). Finally, the evaluation shows how COCOS helps operate containerized heterogeneous systems. It shows results on managing and (partially) mixing three types of systems: microservices, machine learning TensorFlow applications, and big-data Spark applications. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II defines the systems we target with COCOS. Section III presents COCOS and its features. Section IV focuses on how COCOS controls the different containers. Section V describes how we extended Kubernetes to implement our prototype. Section VI shows the assessment we conducted. Section VII discusses some relevant related work and Section VIII concludes the paper. II. CONTAINERIZED HETEROGENEOUS SYSTEMS Containers are often adopted for different reasons. They are used to wrap complete applications in virtualized environments since they simplify software management, deployment, and migration. They are also the preferred means to enact modern architectures that split complex (monolith) systems into diverse sub-systems. For example, the microservice architecture 15 slices a complex application into separate components that can be developed and deployed independently. Also, frameworks for data analysis and machine learning such as Spark 16 and TensorFlow 17 exploit a distributed, component-based architecture to parallelize computation where components (called executors) are deployed independently of one another. Being lightweight and easy to manage, containers are well- suited to deploy these systems. Diverse components (containers) can easily coexist on a single machine (node). Deploying each part of the system as a full VM could result in higher 1https: kubernetes.io 2https: www.docker.com System SLA Sub-System Component VM Container Resource CPU Memory Disk GPU 1 N 1 N 1 N 1 N Dispatcher Executor Data Node deployed into Figure 1: Containerized Software Systems. overhead and slower management. While containers could be deployed onto physical machines, to reduce almost any performance overhead 5 , they are usually deployed onto VMs to exploit the benefits of the cloud. This solution complicates resulting systems, but permits a finer-grained usage of available resources. Containers thus play a key role in modern deployment architectures because they are both lighter and easier to manage than VMs. The different heterogeneous parts of a complex application can easily be accommodated in a container-based system. Figure 1 shows the key elements of the systems we want to address. A system is the composition of one or more sub-systems. A sub-system can then be organized in different components. These components can belong to one of the following three classes: A Dispatcher is a single component that serves as main entry-point to the sub-system and allows users or other sub- systems to connect to and use it. It is usually implemented as an HTTP endpoint that collects incoming requests and dispatches them to the inner components. Note that a dispatcher can be shared among different sub-systems. An Executor provides the actual functionality of the sub- system. It implements its business logic and is usually scalable, that is, multiple instances of the same executor can be deployed for the same sub-system. In this case the dispatcher redirects the requests to one of the instances given a user-defined strategy (e.g., round-robin). In some cases, the different instances can communicate among them to share information or data. A Data Node is deputed to storing data, and it is then used by executors properly. An executor needs no data node if it is not supposed to store any persistent data, while it could require some if distributed data management is required (e.g., SQL and NoSQL DBMS). All these components are deployed as a container but they can be highly heterogeneous. They can be built on top of independent technology stacks, exploit different frameworks, and use diverse resource types (e.g., CPUs or GPUs). As already said, the different sub-systems can be subject to different non-functional requirements (SLAs in the model)3. While many dimensions can be addressed, this paper focuses on response time, that is, the time the system takes to answer one request or an aggregated set. Different sub-systems may have to obey to very diverse SLAs. If the sub-system is interactive, the thresholds are specified as constraints over the time needed to serve incoming requests in a given time window 8 . If the sub-system requires a significant amount of time (i.e., minutes, hours) for processing a single request (e.g., big-data batch applications), usually we set a deadline (maximum foreseen duration) for each execution 18 . The enforcement of these requirements depends mainly on the resources allocated to these sub-systems. An easy approach is to allocate resources statically and decide everything before- hand. Unfortunately, actual workloads are not always easy to predict, and the resulting allocation would always be inefficient, and unnecessarily costly. Efficient resource allocation calls for means for probing the different sub-systems and assigning them resources in a coordinated way only when needed. This means that these systems must be able to manage heterogeneity and be self-adaptive with respect to resource management. As examples, in the following we describe three types of exemplar systems that could be deployed onto the same shared cluster of VMs if the tenant be it the owner of the application or of the cloud infrastructure wants to optimize the use of resources. Microservices. Each microservice is a sub-system since it can be deployed independently of the others and it must fulfill its own SLA defined as a constraint on response time. The dispatcher is a load balancer that sends the requests to different web servers (executors) of the microservices. Each microservice could contain one or more data nodes (e.g., relational or NoSQL databases). Big-data batch applications. These applications usually ex- ploit a shared framework, like Apache Spark, to run the code. The dispatcher is the Spark Master node that organizes the execution in optimized phases of computation (a.k.a. stages). The Spark Master can be shared among different applications sub-systems. The executors are Spark Executors that receive instructions from the master node and execute the single tasks of each stage. Executors could share data when needed (data shuffling). Finally the data nodes are implemented as HDFS nodes, a distributed file-system for big-sized files. Machine-learning applications. As in the previous example, these applications use a framework, such as TensorFlow, for training and inference. While training can be seen as an instance of the previous case, inference consists of deploying models (derived from the training phase) as interactive applications sub- systems. The dispatcher is again a load balancer that distributes requests to the various executors (e.g, TensorFlow servers). In this case, the executors can exploit both CPUs and GPUs, besides memory, and they require no data node since trained models can be stored in memory. A single company (like Netflix 19 ) could use all of them: 3Note that the SLA of a sub-system could be computed as the combination of the SLAs of its components. a set of microservices for their web and mobile applications, multiple recurring big-data jobs for analyzing user behaviors, and a machine learning based recommender system to provide a personalized experience. III. COCOS ARCHITECTURE COCOS (COntainerized COntrolled Systems) is the architec- ture we propose for the control of heterogeneous containerized systems. This paper assumes that containers are already monitored and only focuses on control features. COCOS does not only use containers as deployment means, but they also help manage system operation. They support the realization of fast reaction cycles and allow for vertical scalability, while VMs do not. According to 14 VMs take about 6 minutes to boot, and thus control loops cannot be faster than that; containers only require seconds, and milliseconds for vertical scalability. Containers can scale in a quite sophisticated way by exploiting cgroups provided by the Linux kernel. cgroups provide means to allocate CPU cores exclusively or to allocate them for specific time windows (CPU fractions). They also allow one to set upper and lower bounds to allocated memory, and to reserve GPUs. Control-theory provides a viable, lightweight means to compute the next decision, that is, the next allocation, in constant time (with some assumptions discussed later). It also supplies formal design-time guarantees of controlled systems, their stability, and their properties. Control-theory requires that a system be described as a set of differential equations that only specify its main characteristics. What is not in the model is treated as disturbance by the controller. Since the effectiveness of a planner is proportional to the frequency with which it can update its plans, the combination of control theory and containers can provide valuable means to controlling software systems. Control theory allows for decisions in a few seconds and containers can actuate them, thus enabling control cycles in the order of seconds (and not in the order of minutes as with many other approaches). Figure 2 shows an overview of the COCOS architecture, based on three control levels. Container Level. The lowest level is dedicated to containers and to the main control decisions. At this level the control period is in the range of seconds. Each container is paired with a dedicated control-theoretical Controller, which decides the resources to allocate to the container and exploits its vertical scalability to provision them. Each controller has a local scope: it can only use monitoring data (e.g., incoming workload, response time) related to its container and it cannot interact with the other controllers containers. This means that no synchronization among controllers is required: they can work faster, and the whole approach scales better (see Section IV for an in-depth description of how controllers work). Each container is also deployed with an optional set of Adaptation Hooks (AH). They are triggered after scaling a container and are in charge of reconfiguring the software in the container to make it fully exploit assigned resources (e.g., it could change CONTAINER LEVEL Actuator SUPERVISOR Containerized Component Adaptation Hooks CONTROLLER Disturbance component P I D - SLA e allocation allocations, demands ORCHESTRATOR HEURISTICS VM LEVEL Cloud Provider CLUSTER LEVEL HORIZONTAL SCALING demand update state feedback metrics Figure 2: The three control levels of COCOS. the thread pool of an application server given the number of available cores). VM Level. Containers are deployed onto fix-sized virtual machines. Each VM comprises a Supervisor, responsible for three activities. First, it defines the control period to trigger each Controller of the containers in that machine to compute a new possible allocation of resources. Second, it gathers all the resource demands from the Controllers and solves possible contentions. Since Controllers are independent, the sum of their demands may be greater than available resources (e.g., in the case of traffic peaks or overshooting by Controllers). In this case, resources are allocated by using either a fair user-defined policy or the priorities associated with sub-systems. Then, given the different requests, it computes a plausible resource allocation, then enacted at container level (more details about the heuristics used by the Supervisor can be found in our previous work 18 ). Third, it interacts with the upper-level controller to add or remove containers on specific machines. Cluster Level. At the highest level, a centralized Orchestrator manages the overall evolution of the system. The Orchestrator uses a heuristic to perform horizontal scalability of containers and VMs. At each user-defined control period, which is usually in the order of minutes, it collects the requests from each Supervisor, thus from each Controller, and reacts properly. If used resources are fewer than provisioned ones4, some containers and or VMs are switched off. If the system requires more resources than those available, the Orchestrator can ask the Supervisors to instantiate new containers and or the Cloud Provider to deploy new VMs. As for deployment, in COCOS each machine can host diverse components. However, COCOS does not allow two containers of the same type (e.g., two executors of the same sub-system) to be deployed on the same machine since: (a) they would 4The user can always be conservative and define a proper threshold to avoid the continuous switching off and on of containers and VMs. probably compete for the same resources at the same time and (b) given vertical scalability one can always add resources to the existing container5 without creating a new one. A. Possible scenarios COCOS provides a general-purpose solution to the operation of container-based complex systems and offers the following characteristics: Fast control: the architecture provides means for the fast creation of allocation plans and for their fast actuation; Fine-grained control: containers provide means to allocate resources with high precision (i.e., fractions of CPUs); Heterogeneity: different types of Controllers and con- tainers can be instantiated on the same machine, and Supervisors can handle resource contentions among them. Vertical and horizontal scalability: the architecture exploits vertical scalability of containers and horizontal scalability of both containers and VMs. Scalable control: the hierarchical organization makes CO- COS highly scalable by design since the most complex part of the control is completely distributed, and Controllers are not synchronized. These characteristics are extremely important. For example, let us consider a user who wants to deploy his her application on a IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) platform. The user clearly wants to minimize the costs of operating the application, but s he also wants to offer some reasonable SLAs to the customers. COCOS provides a solution that is proven to be more efficient than both naive and static solutions (see Section VI). Since cloud resources are billed per second 20 , 21 , 22 , efficient vertical and horizontal scalability helps limit costs, while the priorities offered by Supervisors allow for the implementation of user-specific policies. If we flip the perspective, COCOS can also be useful to IaaS providers that want to operate the infrastructure in a smart and efficient way: fewer resources pre-allocated to the different users, to meet agreed SLAs, mean higher profits. The provider can use COCOS to deploy and control the different containerized heterogeneous systems. Similarly to what happens with serverless computing, users would not manage resources directly, COCOS would do it automatically and in an optimized way. The IaaS provider could then both optimize the use of its infrastructure and offer a higher-level service to its clients. IV. CONTROLLERS Different sub-system types and different user requests may require different controllers. This is why COCOS comes with a library of control policies, mainly taken from our previous experiences, but additional control solutions can be added. The different types of Controllers share the common structure shown in Figure 2. Given a controlled metric (e.g., response time), the goal is to make equal to a set-point SLA at each control period. Controllers cannot directly fulfill requirements 5The assumption here is that the component can scale properly and thus exploit provisioned resources. in the form of inequality (e.g., SLA) but they can only aim to target thresholds ( SLA). The set-point SLA could be constant or a time-related function. Inequalities are then translated into SLA, where (0, 1 is a constant that renders the level of conservativeness the user wants to adopt. For example, if the SLA states that the response time RT must always be less than .5 seconds, the inequality RT .5 is transformed into RT .5, where could be set to .9 to have a 10 margin. This way, Controllers compute the amount of resources needed to reach the set-point, then the Supervisor can either downscale the resources to allocate in the case of resource contention or upscale if the system is set to over perform up a certain degree with respect to the computed allocation 18 . At each control period, error e is computed as the difference between SLA and . e is then processed by the actual Controller that is characterized by function fcomponent which identifies the dynamic (i.e., the physics) of the controlled, containerized component. Function fcomponent can use specific metrics (e.g., workload) gathered from the monitoring system. Given e and fcomponent, the controller produces a resource demand as the sum of three contributions: one proportional to e, an integral, and a derivative one (PID controllers 23 ). The computed resource demand is then processed by the Supervisor that, in turn, produces the actual allocation to actuate and updates the state of Controllers if needed (i.e., when demand and allocation are not equal). The allocation is then enacted through the container runtime along with the execution of Adaptation Hooks. After the actuation, the new allocation and unforeseen disturbances affect the value of , which is then processed through the feedback loop at the subsequent control period. Since replicas must satisfy a common SLA cooperatively, for example a threshold over the response time, COCOS adopts a divide et impera solution. It distributes the workload fairly among the containers, that is, each replica receives the same amount of requests or data to process. In case of skew workloads, Controllers remain independent but they probably compute significantly different resource demands 18 . This means that if each Controller can satisfy the shared SLA on its partition of the inputs, then the global SLA is also guaranteed without synchronization. For example, let us consider a microservice, with a workload of 100 incoming requests per second, deployed onto two container replicas, an SLA defined as RT 0.5s and 0.9. The load balancer, which governs the two replicas, can send half the workload, that is, 50 requests per second, to each instance, and the Controller be configured with a set-point equal to 0.45s. This way, if the replicas fulfilled the set-point independently, the average response would be less than 0.5s, and then the global SLA would be met without any synchronization. A. Even if the model exploits other parameters, like the number of incoming requests to the component, the intuition behind this model is that increasing the cores makes the response time decrease down to a certain horizontal asymptote, reached when the degree of parallelism is fully exploited. The Controller for machine learning applications works in a different way. It allocates two types of resources: CPUs and GPUs. Since GPUs are the fastest and preferred resource to exploit, this Controller always saturates the use of GPUs and uses CPUs only to help when the GPUs are not enough to obtain expected results. Given a requirement on the response time, the overall CPU GPU set-point (SLAALL) is set to the inverse of the desired response time (called throughput for simplicity here). At each control step t, given the measured throughput of the GPUs ( GP U), the actual set-point of the Controller that manages the CPU cores is defined as SLA(t) max(0, SLAALL GP U(t)) (as shown in Figure 3b). The relationship between cores and throughput is the inverse of the one described for microservices: the higher the amount of allocated cores is the higher the throughput becomes until we fully exploit the parallelism embedded in the application (Figure 3e). Finally, the requirements for Spark applications are defined as deadlines. Spark divides the execution of an application in stages: optimized phases of computation that do not require the exchange of data among Executors. In our approach, an application deadline is decomposed into multiple stage deadlines. Given a stage deadline, the set-point of the Controller is defined as the expected progress (a linear one, as shown in Figure 3c) at each control step. As for machine learning applications, increasing allocated cores leads to increasing the progress rate up to a horizontal asymptote is reached (Figure 3f), which corresponds to the highest degree of parallelism embedded in the application. This section presents a prototype implementation6 of COCOS as an extension to Kubernetes (probably, the most famous and used open-source container orchestrator). To help the reader better understand the work done, Kuber- netes provides means to deploy containers and to oversee each phase of their life-cycle. It supports different container runtime infrastructures (e.g., Docker, CRI-O, Containerd). Besides containers, volumes provide a plug-in mechanism to connect ephemeral containers with persistent data stores. The main abstraction provided by Kubernetes is pod, that is, a group of co-located containers and volumes. For example, a pod can comprise a container that reads from and writes to files and an associated volume that establishes the interface with the underlying file-system. Pods can then be grouped logically in services. A service is a set of related pods that can communicate one another. Services can be equipped with a front-end load balancer to dispatch incoming requests to the different pods in the service. Kubernetes provides a distributed architecture with a master and multiple workers. The master acts as orchestrator (i.e., it is in charge of deploying and scheduling pods), while the workers carry out the tasks assigned by the master and execute pods. Kubernetes embeds the notion of controller7: a master component that carries out control activities periodically. One of the built-in controllers is the Replication Controller (RC) that allows one to keep the number of replicas of a pod fixed over time and automatically repairs failing ones if needed. Another controller, called Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA), permits one to set the number of replicas, then managed by an RC, at runtime according to monitored built-in or custom 6https: github.com deib-polimi COCOS 7Note the difference between this controller and COCOS Controller. Given this context, Figure 4 shows our prototype. COCOS workers exploit Docker as runtime framework. Each sub-system is deployed as a Kubernetes service, and each containerized component is embedded in a dedicated pod. On each worker, that is on each VM, we deploy an additional pod called COCOS Pod that contains all the Controllers associated with the pods (containers) that belong to the sub-systems on the worker, along with the Supervisor. The vertical scalability of pods is not supported yet in Kubernetes. At the time of writing, Kubernetes offers a beta- versioned Vertical Pod Autoscaler 24 , but it requires that running pods be rebooted, and this is a clear limitation. Therefore, we provide a custom implementation of the vertical scalability of pods by using Docker out of Docker (DooD) 25 . DooD is a volume that provides means to launch Docker commands (e.g., to re-configure a container) within another container. DooD is needed to allow the COCOS Pod control the other pods8. EVALUATION This section shows our evaluation of COCOS and of its Kubernetes implementation to answer the following three research questions: Q1 Do the components introduced by COCOS add overhead to Kubernetes? Q2 Is COCOS able to efficiently control single heterogeneous applications? Q3 Is COCOS able to efficiently control multiple, concurrent, heterogeneous applications? The experiment used a cluster of 4 NV 6 virtual machines. One machine was dedicated to the master node, and three to the workers. Each machine was equipped with 6 cores, 56GB of memory, 340GB of SSD storage and one NVIDIA Tesla M60 GPU. We also used a VM of type HB60rs equipped with 60 cores for generating the client workloads. We used 3 different applications: two of them based on microservices, called Movies9 and Pwitter10, and a machine learning application built with TensorFlow called ResNet 26 . For both the microservice- based applications we used the Ingress loadbalancer provided 9https: github.com Crizstian cinema-microservice tree master movies-service 10https: github.com deib-polimi Pwitter by Kubernetes11 as Dispatcher. Movies allows one to gather information about movies from a database. The Executors are implemented as Node.js components, while the Data Node exploits a Mongo DBMS. Pwitter is a Twitter-like application that exploits instances of Gunicorn12 application servers as Executors and Redis13 as Data Node. Finally, ResNet is a trained convolutional neural network for image classification that can exploit both CPUs and GPUs and has no Data Node. The E-labeled green vertical lines represent the actual stage ends, while the red dashed vertical lines represent stage deadlines; the deadline of the last stage is also the deadline of the entire application. The chart shows how the actual progress of stages adheres to the prescribed one, and the execution of the application terminates almost exactly when desired. COCOS minimizes the resources to achieve this goal, and thus allows other concurrent (heterogeneous) applications to consume them. Finally, to answer Q3, we also carried out a preliminary evaluation of the behavior of COCOS when operating con- current heterogeneous applications (Movies and ResNet) on the same cluster. Figure 8 shows workload, core allocation, and response time, respectively. Figure 8a shows the two consecutive traffic peaks injected into the applications. ResNet is supposed to manage a peak that starts at around second 50 and lasts till second 120, when Movies starts managing its peak, which continues until around second 180. Consequently, Figure 8b describes the reaction of the two controllers in terms of allocated cores. Note that since we have two controllers active at the same time, the Supervisor is charge of keeping allocated resources below (equal to) the available ones (6 cores). The response time (Figure 8c) is stabilized by the dynamic resource allocation: its average value is below the SLA and unwanted behaviors (i.e., violations) are fixed in a few instants. COCOS is thus able to efficiently control heterogeneous applications even when they run simultaneously on the same machines . Being COCOS completely distributed at its core control layer (i.e., the container layer), we are confident that 14This test was executed using another type of VM called Standard D (a) Movies - workload and cores (b) Pwitter - workload and cores (c) ResNet - workload and cores (d) Movies - RT (e) Pwitter - RT (f) ResNet - RT Figure 6: Experiments on Controllers. Figure 7: Spark executor. our solution can scale efficiently also when dealing with bigger, more complex systems compared to the ones shown here. To this end, we have already investigated the scalability of single controllers in our previous works 8 , 18 . VII. RELATED WORK Several works study how control-theory can help operate software systems. For example, Shevtsov et al. 27 observe that control-theory applied to software engineering is still in its infancy but, on the other hand, the interest on it is rapidly increasing. They emphasize also that the research in this area is focused on experimental results without any adequate study of the properties that control theory can ensure a-priori. Brun et al. 28 witness the importance of control loops when dealing with complex software systems. They claim that feedback loops are a key factor in system management and they should be considered as first-class for such systems. In addition, Filieri et al. 29 provide a methodology to generalize the process of automatically analyzing and building a controller with specific properties and behavior. These contributions inspired us on choosing control theory as main enabler of COCOS. Several works focus on the control of single types of systems, but they do not provide a general architecture, as COCOS does. For example, Guerrero et al. 30 present a genetic algorithm, based on the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm-II (NSGA-II), to optimize resource allocation and elasticity management. The work focuses on containerized applications deployed as multiple microservices. They optimize system provisioning and performance while reducing failures, and network overhead. Compared to COCOS, their work only focuses on microservices and does not consider higher- level SLAs based on response times. Kiss et al. 31 present MICADO, a generic architecture for deploying and managing microservices. They use open-source technology to provide the dynamic discovery of microservices, to orchestrate their deployment, and to automatically scale them. The proposed architecture, again, is not as general as COCOS since it only focuses on microservices, and only offers horizontal scalability. Sidhanta et al. 13 introduce OptEx, an optimization model for configuring a Spark cluster according time and cost constraints. Their approach works a-priori, meaning that they do not provide dynamic resource allocation during execution. Moreover they support VM-only clusters. Islam et al. 32 propose a resource allocation system for Spark called dSpark. It exploits an optimization problem to offer different possible resource allocation schemas with different costs and resource quantities; the user must select one of them manually. Given (a) Movies and ResNet - workload (b) Movies and ResNet - cores (c) Movies and ResNet - RT Figure 8: Heterogeneous systems. a schema, the allocation is then static and cannot change at runtime. Both dSpark and OptEx are solutions that only focus on big-data applications. As for machine learning applications, few studies focus on investigating how the training time changes when running on GPUs. The solutions are specific to particular systems and are not integrated in a well-defined architecture as COCOS. For example, Gianniti et al. 33 propose an approach for modeling the execution time of training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) deployed on GPUs, while Lu et al. 34 propose an approach for computing resource requirements for CNNs on mobile devices. Lakew et al. 35 present a more generic, control-based approach. They optimize both application performance and resource utilization given different user-defined KPIs (Key Per- formance Indicators). The evaluation on different applications demonstrates that the proposed solution provides guaranteed performance while avoiding over- and under-provisioning of resources. Compared to COCOS, this solution does not deal with the control of multiple applications deployed onto the same cluster and does not provide horizontal scalability for containers and for VMs. Some approaches propose extensions of Kubernetes to improve its self-adaptive capabilities. To the best of our knowledge, no other solution is able to manage resources at the level of both VMs and containers and, at the same time, to address concurrent heterogeneous applications that share the same resources. For example, Medel et al. 36 present a Petri-net based model of the life-cycle of pods containers in Kubernetes. Their work can be used to analyze the performance of the applications that run in Kubernetes, to identify the amount of resources to allocate to them and to generate a rule-based planner for the control of them at runtime. Compared to COCOS, they do not consider VMs and do not support vertical scalability of resources. Kubow by Aderaldo et al. 37 is an implementation of the Rainbow adaptation framework 38 in Kubernates. Users can define the architecture of the application and its deployment in Acme, a dedicated domain specific language (DSL). The self-adaptation actions are defined using tactics (parametric conditions and actions) and strategies (actual invocations of tactics) written in Stitch (another dedicated DSL). Compared to COCOS, Kubow only manages containers (and not VMs) and only provides their horizontal scalability through statically defined rules. Xu et al. present NBWGuard 39 , a tool that makes network bandwidth manageable as other types of resources (e.g., CPUs, memory) in Kubernetes. They provide three different modes of bandwidth allocation: guaranteed (fixed allocation), burstable (fixed allocation with the possibility of increasing it at runtime) and best effort (takes the bandwidth that is not used by guaranteed and burstable allocations). Our controllers are currently able to only control CPUs, memory and GPUs. VIII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK The paper presents COCOS, a conceptual architecture, along with a prototype implementation based on Kubernetes, for the operation of containerized heterogeneous systems. These systems usually comprise diverse, distributed, and cooperate components, and their operation is not trivial. COCOS originates from the complexity of these systems and the need for guarantees on their operation. The proposed solution is based on containers and control theory. The former allows for the fine-grained, fast control of provisioned resources and also for the addition of resources (vertical scalability) to running executors (containers). Control theory provides the theoretical means to produce new allocation plans in a limited amount of time. Fine-grained, hierarchical control over containers allows COCOS to allocate resources with a control period in the order of seconds. COCOS also takes care of resource contention at VM and cluster levels by means of dedicated heuristics that enact the horizontal scalability of containers and or VMs as needed. All these concepts are embedded in a prototype based on Kubernetes, and an initial evaluation demonstrates the benefits of the proposal. The overhead introduced by COCOS is less than 7 on average and the controllers are able to keep the response time within desired ranges. papers.fulltext: Self-commissioning Industrial IoT-Systems in Process Automation: a Reference Architecture Heiko Koziolek Research Area Software ABB Corporate Research Ladenburg, Germany heiko.koziolek de.abb.com Andreas Burger Research Area Software ABB Corporate Research Ladenburg, Germany andreas.burger de.abb.com Jens Doppelhamer Research Area Software ABB Corporate Research Ladenburg, Germany jens.doppelhamer de.abb.com AbstractDistributed control systems are currently evolving towards Industrial Internet-of-Things (IIoT) systems. However, they still suffer from complex commissioning processes that incur high costs. Researchers have proposed several so-called Plug and Produce (PnP) approaches, where commissioning shall be largely automated, but they have suffered from semantic ambiguities and usually rely on proprietary information models. We propose a novel reference architecture for PnP in IIoT systems, which is based on OPC UA and PLCopen standards and can reduce industrial device commissioning times across vendor products to a few seconds. Our proof-of-concept implementation can handle more than 500 signals per millisecond during runtime, sufficient for most application scenarios. Index TermsSoftware architecture, Client-server systems, Real-time systems, Control engineering, Internet of Things I. INTRODUCTION There is a growing market of distributed control systems (DCS) for industrial process automation with annual rev- enues of more than 14 billion USD 17 . These systems are large-scale (several MLOC) spreading over cloud servers, on- premise servers, embedded real-time controllers, as well as sensors and actuators. Such systems support chemical plants, electric power generation, oil gas industries, pulp and paper production, refining, and other industries. With the emerging Industrial Internet-of-Things (IIoT) 18 , individual devices in such systems provide means for internet connectivity as well as self-description enabling a new range of applications. High costs for such systems often do not only incur from the involved hardware elements, but also from the manual labor to engineer and set them up 4 . Commissioning of devices and systems (i.e., initial network configuration, application-specific device configuration, and integration with other devices) and is cumbersome and laborious today. It often requires substantial manual work and can take hours for each device due the complexity of applications 3 . The overall commissioning process of an industrial plant with thousands of devices can take several months, which delays time-to-market for the production processes. Configuration complexity suffers from heterogeneous communication technologies as well as static architectures requiring costly re-configurations. Researchers have envisioned Plug and Produce (PnP) approaches for industrial automation already for more than 15 years 16 , postulating a similar seamless experience as for Plug and Play for consumer computer devices. However, industrial devices are complex and can have several hundreds of configuration parameters. Due to that, Garlan 6 pointed out that architectures need to become much more flexible to handle dynamic re-configurations. Numerous PnP-approaches have been proposed for fieldbuses and analog connections 5 , 13 , 15 , 16 , but they suffer from semantic ambiguities and usually do not work across vendors. Thanks to the trend towards Industrie 4.0 and IIoT, industry standards are evolving to achieve vendor-independent PnP if combined properly. The contribution of this paper is a reference architecture design for IIoT systems that enables automatic field device pa- rameterization and controller commissioning and aids system architects as well as researchers. The key ideas of the reference architecture are (i) to use partial controller description models based on PLCopen (IEC 61131-3) 23 to also describe controlled devices, (ii) to introduce a PnP service that manages the configuration matching decoupled from controllers and devices, and (iii) to use network discovery technology. It relies on OPC UA (IEC 62541) 19 communication protocols and information modeling capabilities and can be implemented using various programming languages and libraries. The main benefit shall be a faster and more robust commissioning process due to the higher automation. We validate the reference architecture with a proof-of- concept implementation in C and demonstrate its capabili- ties with a sample scenario involving an industrial boiler, four field devices, and one controller. The results show that au- tomatic controller-to-device commissioning is feasible almost automatically upon network connection, if the devices are properly equipped with standard-compliant self-descriptions. We also validate a specific performance aspect of the reference architecture, namely the encoding overhead for OPC UA publish subscribe communication and show that up to 800 signals can be encoded per millisecond on a single-board computer, which is sufficient for many applications 20 . The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Sec- tion 2 provides background information and motivates the reference architecture. Section 3 introduces the architecture and lists the most important architecture decisions and their rationale. Section 4 describes details of our proof-of-concept implementation. Section 5 reports on the validation of the 196 2018 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture 978-1-5386-6398-1 18 31.00 2018 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. reference architecture, before Section 6 puts the architecture in context to related work. II. BACKGROUND Fig. 1 shows the generic structure of an automation system according to ANSI 24 . Dozens of commercial prod- ucts follow this structure, and there are currently more than 130,000 installations world-wide 17 . Fig. 1. Structure of an Automation System (ISA-95) On Level 4, there is an Enterprise Resource Planning system to manage business processes and logistics. Below, on Level 3, a Manufacturing Execution System is responsible for initiation and high-level supervision of production processes and orders. Level 2 consists of workstations for supervision by human operators and for engineering of devices and processes, as well as real-time controllers, for example to execute closed- loop control. A large-scale system can include more than ten operator workstations and dozens of controllers. Level 1 con- sists of field devices, which include sensors and actuators that directly interface with the machines executing the industrial process, for example a heat exchanger in a chemical plant. For example, commissioning a level indicator (sensor) for a heat exchanger, requires roughly the following steps: First, an engineer places the sensor into the device and connects it to power and the network. Then , the engineer sets a fieldbus address manually, so that other network devices can reference the sensor. Ethernet-based fieldbuses, such as PROFINET, can also search for devices in a network segment. Using the address, a configuration tool can retrieve the type and instance identification of the sensor. The engineer then selects an according communication file (e.g., a GSD file for Profibus) that provides protocol-specific data encodings to enable basic communication. The level indicator now requires a parameterization, i.e., setting possibly dozens of parameter values for the application context. For example, the level indicator needs to set maximum ranges for the level value, which is one of the parameters. Based on engineering data, the engineer enters this value into a device parameterization tool, which for example may be based on FDT (field device tool) or FDI (field device integration) standards. After uploading this parameterization to the level indicator, it is ready to operate, but still needs to be connected to a controller. A control logic programmer imports the network configuration into a control logic engineering tool and maps the IEC 61131-3 control logic variables to the bus addresses for the field devices. Hence, step up to step need to be done for every field device which is connected to the network. Afterwards, the programmer deploys the control logic to the controller, which is then installed in the plant and connected. Now, both the controller and level indicator are configured for their specific task with the heat exchanger, and the production process can start. For IIoT, these steps shall be automated to save engineering time and allow changes more easily. Furthermore, device integration shall work across vendor products, which requires multiple industry standards. We extracted the following re- quirements from 28 , 29 in order to meet customers requests for IIoT: R1: Standardized communication protocol R2: Automated network discovery R3: Standardized device description R4: Field devices provide standardized signal interface R5: Standardized control logic language R6: Automated signal matching R7: Human approval step for discovered configurations R8: Real-time communication (1 ms cycle time) R9: Security via authentication and optional encryption There are already several recently emerging technologies and industry standards that potentially aid fulfilling the stated requirements. However, often they have been designed for other requirements and they need to be combined properly to realize the desired PnP scenario. For example, OPC UA (IEC 62541) is both a communication protocol and a generic infor- mation model for industrial assets. OPC UA is client server- based and specifies approx. 40 services for servers, such as connect, read, write, subscribe, call method, add node, etc. Servers expose information items according to an object- oriented type space. While OPC UA was originally designed for monitoring field devices via personal computers (e.g., getting an updated level indicator value once a second), it has a growing number of application scenarios thanks to numerous recent additions. For example, OPC UA Discovery (IEC 62541-12) allows finding OPC UA servers on the network, OPC UA for Devices (IEC 62541-100) provides a generic, standardized syntactic model for field devices, and the PLCOpen Companion standard for OPC UA allows mapping control logic elements to OPC UA servers. OPC UA does not provide standardized semantics for de- vices. For example, properties and configuration parameters of field devices, such as the maximum range of the level indicator, are not covered. However, there are standards, such as the IEC Common Data Dictionary, eCl ss, STEP, and the PA profiles for fieldbuses, which could be combined with OPC UA models to achieve the required semantic unambiguousness. Finally, there are recent standardization activities around TSN (time-sensitive networking, IEEE 802.1), which shall allow de- terministic and low latency communication for Ethernet-based networks and can be combined with different application-level protocols, such as HTTP, OPC UA 27 , or MQTT. III. CONCEPTUAL REFERENCE ARCHITECTURE The reference architecture described in the following is on the one hand motivated by the desire to achieve a faster and more robust commissioning. On the other hand it provides guidance on how recently released standards can be used to achieve PnP in a vendor-neutral way. We describe the architecture from static, dynamic, and deployment viewpoints and then briefly rationalize its most important underlying decisions. A. Static View Fig. 2 depicts a static view of our proposed reference architecture, which focuses on ANSI ISA-95 level 2 and 1 from Fig. 1. Controllers and field devices communicate via OPC UA over Ethernet both for commissioning and operation (addressing requirement R1 from Section II). Existing field buses and analog connections may be included by having an IO gateway node that arbitrates between the different networks. With the OPC UA servers, controllers and field devices become IIoT devices, which can be accessed from the internet if desired by the plant owner and are capable of self-description. !" !" ! " " '(()( Fig. 2. Reference Architecture: Overview (UML Component Diagram) Fig. 2 shows a Controller OPC UA Server that stores control logic programs and controller status information. There is also a Device OPC UA Server providing data and services for the connected field devices. While classical client server connections manage the self-commissioning of controllers and field devices, the cyclic, real-time communication for closed-loop control is supported by OPC UA publish subscribe connections (IEC 62541-14). With TSN-enabled network switches, a deterministic real- time control loop becomes possible (requirement R8). The publish subscribe communication can either be broker-based (e.g., via AMQP or MQTT) or broker-less. In the latter case, publishers send data sets to multicast IP addresses via UDP, to which subscribers listen. Using lower-level network protocols IGMP or MMRP, network traffic can be reduced, so that the network switches only forward network packets for which a subscriber has been registered. For discovery of connected OPC UA servers, the reference architecture suggests an OPC UA Controller Local Discovery server and a Device Local Discovery server according to IEC 62541-12 (R2). Resource-constrained devices can alternatively use Multicast DNS (mDNS) instead of local discovery servers, which is for example also implemented by Apple Bonjour or Spotify Connect. mDNS can use DNS SRV records to advertise discovery URLs for OPC UA servers to clients. A controller in the reference architecture provides an IEC 61131 Runtime that can execute PLCopen control logic programs (R5). The control logic exposes function blocks that require connected input signals, e.g., from a sensor such as a level indicator. The control algorithm then computes output values, e.g., for an actuator such as a valve for a heat exchanger. Control algorithms run cyclically, e.g., every 100 ms, and for special applications even every 1 ms. OPC UA servers expose information about field devices in the reference architecture. Such a server may run on a dedicated network node or directly on a field device, if it has appropriate CPU capability and memory. On a dedicated node such as an IO gateway, the server may manage data and services for numerous field devices. The Field Device is con- nected to the OPC UA server via a Communication Channel. This may encapsulate fieldbus or analog communication. The Device Management is responsible for supplying a Communication Channel with drivers and the field device with a parameterization. It gets the driver from a Public Device Driver Repository, e.g., from specific vendors or other organizations (R3). For example, the Fieldcom Group is in the process of setting up such a server for FDI Device Packages. Parameterization can rely on imported engineering data, and if necessary for fine tuning also be altered via user input from OPC UA clients. To get a device running with basic features, the imported engineering data is however sufficient. The Device Management uploads the parameterization to the field device. Finally, the architecture contains a Plug and Produce Service that looks for connected controllers and handles the signal matching with field devices. It has a built-in OPC UA client to retrieve required signal names from the controller and to browse OPC UA servers for field devices for the matching signal names. It is aware of different semantic standards, such as OPC UA for Devices, IEC 61987, or NAMUR NE B. Dynamic View The device parametrization follows the procedure in Fig. 3. First, the Device OPC UA Server optionally scans its con- nected Communication Channels, in case the field device is connected via an additional network connection. Otherwise, this step can be omitted. Then, it announces itself on the network, which gets picked up by the Device Management component. This corresponds to the automation of step in our example from Section II. , - , ! . . 0 . 0. . , . 0 . 0. . Fig. 3. IEC 62541-100). Using the IDs, it queries the Public Device Driver Repository for device drivers and the Engineering Repository parameterization data, which replaces step in the level indicator example. It uploads the information to the OPC UA server, which forwards it to the actual field devices. Finally, the OPC UA server updates its contents and signals its readiness to the Device Management. After this update process, the field device is automatically in step . Now, signal matching can start (Fig. 4). The Plug and Produce Service constantly searches for Controller OPC UA servers connected to the network. It connects to such servers and retrieves a list of the input and output signals required for the execution of the configured control logic programs. Then, the service connects to any Device OPC UA servers that are already connected or are being connected during plant commissioning. Finally, after processing this phase, the field device and the controller fulfill steps and . The Plug and Produce Service browses the OPC UA servers address space and tries to find a matching tag name for the configured device (R6). Reference Architecture: Signal Matching (UML Interaction Diagram) function blocks with a specification of input signals (mainly for actuators) and output signals (mainly for sensors) (R4). Once found, it attempts to find a match with the signal names from the controller. In case the controller and the device use different signal names, since they have been configured independently, matching may also rely on other information, such as the physical location and network configuration in the OPC UA address space. In case of a match, the Plug and Produce Service sets up a subscription of the controller to the output signals. This can either be an OPC UA client server connection, which then requires handling a client session on the Device OPC UA server, or it can be an OPC UA publish subscribe connection via multicast UDP IP or a broker. For fast cyclic control, the Controller OPC UA Server may bypass writing the signal values into its address space, but instead directly forward them to the 61131 Runtime for calculating the control logic outputs. After setting up the subscription, the Plug and Produce Service disconnects from the Device OPC UA server, and sets a flag in the Controller OPC UA server to query a human engineer for final approval. The found configuration can be relayed to the engineer, who can perform a final checkup, before actually starting the process (R7). C. Deployment View The deployment of the components to hardware nodes is flexible and allows addressing different application contexts and resource constraints. Fig. ' ( !" ( ( ( ( !" ( ( ( )' " !"
