papers.fulltext: Predicting the Performance of Privacy-Preserving Data Analytics Using Architecture Modelling and Simulation Rajitha Yasaweerasinghelage, Mark Staples, Ingo Weber, Hye-Young Paik Data61, CSIRO, Level 5, 13 Garden St, Eveleigh NSW 2015 Australia School of Computer Science and Engineering, University of New South Wales, NSW 2052 Australia Email: firstname.lastname data61.csiro.au Email: Helen.Paik data61.csiro.au AbstractPrivacy-preserving data analytics is an emerging technology which allows multiple parties to perform joint data analytics without disclosing source data to each other or a trusted third-party. A variety of platforms and protocols have been proposed in this domain. However, these systems are not yet widely used, and little is known about them from a software architecture and performance perspective. Here we investigate the feasibility of using architectural performance modelling and simulation tools for predicting the performance of privacy- preserving data analytics systems. We report on a lab-based experimental study of a privacy-preserving credit scoring ap- plication that uses an implementation of a partial homomorphic encryption scheme. The main experiments are on the impact of analytic problem size (number of data items and number of features), and cryptographic key length for the overall system performance. Our modelling approach performed with a relative error consistently under 5 when predicting the median learning time for the scoring application. We find that the use of this approach is feasible in this technology domain, and discuss how it can support architectural decision making on trade-offs between properties such as performance, cost, and security. We expect this to enable the evaluation and optimisation of privacy-preserving data analytics technologies. Index TermsSoftware architecture, Software performance, Data security, Data analysis. I. INTRODUCTION Privacy-preserving data analytics is an emerging technology which allows analytics to be performed on data owned by multiple semi non-trusted parties without data being disclosed to either party or a trusted third-party. A number of privacy- preserving data analytics platforms and protocols have been introduced 1 , 2 , 3 based on a variety of cryptographic building blocks such as Homomorphic Encryption 4 , 5 , Secret Sharing 6 , and Garbled Circuits 7 . These tech- nologies have been studied for a long time in security and cryptographic research communities 7 . However, adoption of industrial applications is limited 8 due to computational expense compared to traditional analytics 8 , and limited help for users in understanding their performance characteristics. Although slower than conventional systems, these tech- niques are expected to be acceptable where the benefits of joint data analytics can be achieved without disclosing confidential data. So, accurate way to predict the performance of a privacy- preserving analytic system before implementing the system is important. But, to best of our knowledge, there is no any previous study on predicting performance characteristics of privacy-preserving data analytics systems accurately. Addi- tionally, there are many subsidiary design decisions related to the selection of a system architecture, such as the number and arrangement of computing nodes, the computing power of each node, and cryptographic key length. So, a methodology for supporting design decisions by allowing to compare potential design decisions is also equally important when adapting privacy-preserving data analytics systems. In this work, we present and evaluate performance model for a new kind of system, namely privacy-preserving data analytics systems based on partial homomorphic encryption. For this work, we explored the possibility of using existing modelling and simulation methods from the literature, and show that these methods also apply to these systems. Our method for performance prediction is based on ar- chitectural performance modelling techniques. In this paper, we evaluate our solution using an implementation of a data analytics application built on the N1 Analytics system 2 . Our method is intended to support the evaluation and comparison of design alternatives early in the development lifecycle. Our contributions are: A performance model for privacy-preserving data analyt- ics systems based on partial homomorphic encryption. A method to micro benchmark privacy-preserving data analytic systems using a profiler. An evaluation of prediction accuracy for the job comple- tion time. Discussion how to use performance models for architec- tural decision making of privacy-preserving data analytics systems. In Section II we outline previous work and related technolo- gies in this research area. Section III presents our approach for modelling privacy-preserving data analytics systems. The accuracy of our approach is evaluated in Section IV by comparing the simulation predictions with measurements of a laboratory-based exemplary system. In Section V-A we discuss 166 2018 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture 978-1-5386-6398-1 18 31.00 2018 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. ! " ! " Fig. 1. N1 Analytics platform distributed architecture the use of performance models for architectural decision mak- ing for privacy-preserving data analytics. Finally, we discuss limitations and future work in Section V-B before concluding the paper in Section VI. II. BACKGROUND Here we describe privacy-preserving data analytics tech- niques and the N1 Analytics system used in our experiments. A. Privacy Preserving Data Analytics This problem is where a set of parties with private inputs wish to jointly compute some function 9 and perform data collaboration without sharing data. Loosely speaking, the parties should learn the correct output and nothing else, even if some of the parties maliciously collude to obtain more information. Discussion on homomorphic encryption is out of scope this work. We refer the reader to 10 for discussion on Homomorphic Encryption. B. N1 Analytics N1 Analytics1 2 is a platform which allows statistical analysis on data distributed between different providers, while maintaining data confidentiality between those providers. 1) Data Privacy Mechanism: The mechanisms used in N1 analytics is mainly Paillier encryption 5 . The adversary model is honest-but-curious, where adversaries try to gain as much information as possible by using but not actively attacking the protocol. N1 Analytics defines actors that hold data and computations as confidentiality domains. In order to guarantee data confiden- tiality, it restricts usual performance optimising across multiple confidentiality domains. 2) Deployment Architecture: The federated deployment ar- chitecture for the N1 Analytics platform is shown in Fig. 1. There are two parts: data providers and coordinators. The coordinators hold the private key to decrypt the computed results, but do not have access to either the plain data or the encrypted input data except for partial output from data providers where the plain text of partial output does not reveal information. Data providers do not have access to the private key so that even though they share encrypted input data, data privacy is maintained. Data providers and coordinators can have multiple worker nodes to perform operations. Data can be moved between nodes but should maintain the protocol that the coordinator should not have access to the encrypted data and data providers should not have access to the private key. C. Performance Modelling Performance modelling has been thoroughly studied and has been shown to be able to predict the performance of various types of software systems. Two main classes of performance models are: Analytical models: represent the performance aspects of a software system as input for analytical solvers. Some popular examples are Petri nets (PN) 11 , Queue- ing Networks (QN) 12 , Layered Queueing networks (LQN) 13 . Architectural models: capture the structure of the system and main factors that influence its performance. Palla- dio Component Model (PCM) 14 , and the Descartes Modelling Language 15 are example frameworks. Ar- chitecture models can be converted to analytical models to be solved using analytical model solver or can be directly simulated using an architectural model simulator for obtaining performance predictions. Simulations can be more time consuming than analytic solvers but provide more flexibility in modelling. Non-functional attributes such as latency, resource usage, cost and throughput related to the structure and behaviour of a software system can be incorporated within architectural models. The resulting models can be fed to simulation engines or analytical solvers to predict non-functional performance at different stages of the development life cycle 16 . Ad- ditionally, Architectural models allow the description of the system on a higher level of abstraction and natural connection of components can be modelled which is not possible with analytical models. In this study, we modelled architecture performance char- acteristics of systems using N1 Analytics with the Palladio workbench 14 . The selection of Palladio was due to its free availability, simulation support, familiar UML-like interface provided for model creation, and the flexibility for incor- porating extensions such as architectural optimisation 17 , 18 , new qualities 19 , and new kinds of systems 20 . Palladio modelling concepts are aligned with component-based development, supporting re-use of modelled components. !! " Fig. 2. Relationship between inputs for the model construction and compo- nents of Palladio Component model D. Related work The studies of performance of privacy-preserving data ana- lytics systems from systems perspective are limited. Most of the discussions focus on computation complexity viewing from a theoretical viewpoint. Archer et al. 8 compare the runtime of multiple secure computing paradigms using AES-128 block cipher and using Levenshtein edit distance computation. The general approach for this work, constructing perfor- mance models using micro benchmark the system on a test environment has been used in domains such as enterprise applications 21 , 22 , cloud-based applications 23 , and blockchain-based applications 20 . III. PERFORMANCE MODEL CONSTRUCTION In this work, we first carry out micro-benchmarking and resource utilisation measurements in a test environment using a parametrically-varied range of test datasets. The data col- lected from this is then used with the architectural model to construct an architectural performance model. The relationship between inputs for the performance model to Components of Palladio is shown in Fig. 2. Here, high-level architecture is from general system design and the deployment architecture. Finally, simulation is used to extrapolate and predict system- level performance. In this work, we explore the applicability of the same approach, for privacy-preserving data analytics applications. While the overall approach is similar to previous work, the structure of system models, participant interactions, and the importance of cryptographic functions are different for privacy-preserving data analytics. These are described below. We have published an abstract version of the performance model which can be used as a template for constructing performance model2. We removed benchmark data and some 2https: doi.org 10.6084.figshare.5960014.v1 architectural components to protect confidential informations of N1Analytics system. A. Micro Benchmarking Privacy-preserving data analytics protocols typically pro- ceed with various stages of computation, as parties iteratively share and or compute portions of the solution. We perform micro-benchmarking on all of the components of the platform to determine time and resource utilisation at each stage. Most prior work on micro-benchmarking for architectural performance modelling use Application Performance Mon- itoring (APM) tools to measure resource usage 21 , 22 or using instrumentation to the test system 24 . However, in our experiments below we have used software profilers instead, and have found that this to be sufficiently accurate. The software profiler we used, Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is free to use, lean, and easy to manage. In our experiments we have considered CPU usage, network usage, and memory usage when constructing the performance model as these key resources may vary across different protocols. Privacy-preserving data analytics can work over datasets of varying numbers of data items and features. Depending on the particular algorithm, these size dimensions may impact the performance in different ways. For micro benchmarking, we only varied one dimension at a time to study changes to the resource utilisation with respect to that dimension. We benchmark the system while systematically varying problem size, to identify the performance characteristic of architectural elements. To illustrate, consider micro-benchmarking results in Section IV which shows change in resource utilisation as we increase the number of features in the test datasets. Each function shows linear response in resource utilisation with a different gradient. These lines are used to parameterise the performance model constructed from the architectural model. Where variable resource utilisation is observed, this can be modelled by probability distribution functions of utilisation. However, some resource utilisations are constant and do not increase with problem size, therefore do not impact modelling. In our experiments below, we observed that the overheads from network latency and bandwidth limits were negligible with respect to the overall task time, and so it would be pos- sible to omit them from the performance model. Nonetheless for the evaluation, we retained network latency for fidelity. We used separate LAN resource between each node for accommo- date scenarios where two parties have dedicated connection and or have different network characteristics. B. Model Construction First, we mapped micro benchmarks to functional compo- nents of the algorithm. To do this, we manually identified the related functions executions from the implementation of the N1 Analytics system, studied the call graph, and the resource utilisations of each branch. We did this varying different dimensions to study the behaviour as we described further with the example used for evaluation (see Section IV-B). This is in contrast to the usual practice of using structural components for performance modelling. We then combined this with the system-level architectural model to construct a performance model. We model each node as a component, and each iterative stage as an individual function. This provides reasonable accuracy, and a reasonable level of granularity for modelling, making the model less coupled with the implementation. A finer granularity might produce better accuracy. However, the model will require more effort to construct and will be more coupled with the implementation, making it difficult to use during the early stages of development. The following are the Palladio Model elements: 1) Component Model: The system structure is modelled as three components: two data providers and one coordinator. Each component (node) communicates with others through defined interfaces. We abstracted the functionality of each component to higher-level functions. These are logical func- tions rather than functions in the concrete implementation. Fig. 3 shows an example abstract model. Each component has a different set of functionalities. For example, the coordinator node initiates computation in re- sponse to an external run command, and starts handshaking with data providers. Some computations are performed by data providers, and are shown as operations in the model. The model diagram shows the different functions performed by each node (component). In this example, we modelled each component as having at least one initialisation function to perform handshaking with other nodes, data initialisation, and initialisation of the iterative computation. Each component also contains at least one iteration function to execute its part of the optimisation after it receives partially-completed results from other nodes. High-level components, interfaces, and component relation- ships are modelled in Palladio as shown in Fig. 3. 2) Resource-Demanding Service Effect Specifications (RD- SEFF): After modelling the components, interfaces, and their relationships, we model the non-functional behaviour of com- ponent operations. The component operation behaviour is specified in an RDSEFF diagram, e.g. as shown in Fig. 4. We assigned the resource utilisation as a function of the different dimensions which we considered in the micro- benchmarking and each sub-component as either a probability distribution function where the resource usage is a variable or as flat function with constant resource utilisation. Component functions resource utilisation is calculated us- ing the micro-benchmarks performed in the test environment as discussed in Section III-A. The type of resources considered here are CPU usage, network usage, and secondary memory usage of each component. As discussed earlier, the logistic regression example is mainly CPU bound. For each function, once its computation is completed, the sub-component triggers an external interface of the various nodes with the output to continue the computation. 3) System Diagram (Model): In a Palladio Component Model, a System Model specifies the connection and data flow between the components specified in the Repository Diagram, and specifies external interfaces. For this work, the System Model is simple to construct as the abstraction level allows us to define the system as three components (the nodes of the system). For simplicity in our current work, we assume that the computation is not distributed among worker nodes. 4) Resource Environments and Allocation Model: In a Palladio Component Model, a Resource Environment diagram and Resource Allocation diagram are where the deployment environment and deployments are defined. So far, the model is constructed using micro-benchmark data obtained from the test environment and the architecture of the implantation. However, for these models, we use parameters based on the intended deployment environment and the component allocations. The main parameters modelled in the resource environment diagram are computation power (CPU resources), secondary memory speed, network bandwidth, and network latency. These can be obtained either from the environment specifica- tion or by performing a simple benchmark on the environment. If the environment resource is not constant, parameters should be modelled as probability distribution functions. The Resource Environment Diagram of our example is shown in Fig. 5. Each component is assigned to three servers according to the deployment specification. Note that we con- figure different network connections between each pair of nodes to reflect real deployment scenarios where latency and bandwidth of network connections can vary. 5) Background workload of the Server: The performance of our application can vary due to background workloads on the nodes. These may be from the operating system, docker (for deployment), background computations of the privacy- preserving system (for N1 Analytics, this is negligible), and other possible background workloads. For better prediction accuracy, we benchmarked each node when idle, to represent the background workload. We inte- grated this into our performance models as a probability distri- bution function in resource environment diagram by assigning variable available resources. If there are other workloads associated with the solution, resource utilisation for these should be benchmarked and integrated with the performance model accordingly for better accuracy. IV. EVALUATING SYSTEM-LEVEL LATENCY PREDICTIONS Here we evaluate the accuracy of performance models using a laboratory-based experiment. This uses an example task of logistic regression learning between two data providers, using one independent coordinator. A. Experiment Setup for Micro-Benchmarking The methodology for micro-benchmarking is discussed in Section III-A. We micro-benchmarked the N1 Analytics sys- tem using the profiler Java Flight Recorder (JFR). We deployed the system in three virtual machines located in the same data centre each running on an Intel Xeon CPU E5-2697 v3 2.60GHz single core virtual CPU. We used a credit history dataset with 5,000 data elements with 5 features each within the two data providers. We used Fig. 3. Basic Repository Model Diagram Fig. 4. Example RDSEFF diagram for an iteration function where the resource demand is defined as a function of data size encryption. A Java profiler instance was run alongside each system instance. We used a custom logging configuration for enabling I O and socket monitoring, collection of all available events, and verbose GC memory management logging. For the micro-benchmark, we executed Java Flight Recorder instances in each node, and these incurred a CPU overhead below 5 throughout. The CPU, HDD, and network usage observed from the micro-benchmarking are detailed in the section IV-B. Note that, in real-world applications, micro-benchmarking may be conducted in a separate test environment and with dummy test data. The dimensions of dummy data may differ from the actual data. We assume that deployment used for micro-benchmarking is analogous to the test environment. B. Micro-Benchmarking Measurements From the micro-benchmarking we observed variable re- source utilisation at different stages. That is due to imple- mentation characteristics such as terminal conditions, caching, and optimisations of some computations. Additionally, we observed a warm-up behaviour of some operations where initial iterations consume more resources compared to later iterations. See Fig. 6 for the CPU usage of the first fifty iterations at different phases of the gradient descent. Resource utilisation of the initialisation and generalised iteration functions obtained from micro-benchmarking, shown in Table I. Some of the functions are CPU heavy while some are I O heavy. CPU utilisation of a function can vary across iterations (note the standard deviation of CPU usage). Each node, after performing a CPU-heavy workload, sends its partial results to another node to continue the computation and waits until receiving partial results from another node. The CPU usage of each node during micro-benchmarking is shown in Fig. 7 for the first 10 iterations of computation with respect to the time. In order to construct the final model, we used the CPU usage profile, network profile, and disk usage profile obtained using Java Flight Recorder. We micro-benchmarked the system, changing the number of rows and features in the dataset and encryption key length, to observe changes in resource utilisation. We added these variables as parameters to the constructed model as they can be used to interpolate resource utilisation for a given dataset, particularly when the exact dimensions of the dataset are not available during design. We observed that network payload and disk utilisation increased linearly with respect to dataset size. Fig. 8 shows the changes to the CPU usage of various abstract functions with respect to dataset size. Fig. 9 and Fig. 10 show the CPU usage for functions with respect to the number of features. Note that CPU usage of some functions stayed constant. Fig. 11 shows an increase of CPU with respect to key length. Fig. 5. An example resource environment diagram with three distinct nodes. The background workload is defined as probability distribution functions. Fig. 6. Model Construction and Simulation The performance model was constructed as discussed in Section III each node is a component and the logical functions of computation are operations. The CPU usage, network usage, and disk usage of each operation were obtained combining resource utilisation from micro-benchmarking. In the RDSEFF diagram (see subsubsection III-B2), we added CPU usage as parameterised probability distribution function. We kept the model abstraction level to a higher level in order to reduce coupling to the implementation. The performance Fig. 10. For simulation, we used the SimuCom engine 25 . Simu- Com is the standard engine for Palladio model simulation. It uses model-to-text transformations to translate Palladio models into Java Code. Eclipse version 4.6.0 (Neon release) and Palladio version 4.0.1 were used for modelling, and SimuCom version 4.0.1 was used for simulations. The resource environment model and allocation model are configured based on the experiment set up for the macro- benchmark discussed in Section IV-D. Fig. 12. Completion time of each iteration for execution of logistic regression learning gradient descent iterations. D. Experiment Setup for Macro-Benchmarking We deployed the N1 Analytics system in a lab-based docker environment to measure system-level results (macro- benchmarking) to evaluate the accuracy of the constructed model. Each node was deployed as a Docker container, which enabled us to change the resource allocations for each node. We benchmarked a varying number of data elements, num- ber of features, amount of resources allocated for each node, and key length used for the encryption. We measured average logistic regression job completion time for each configura- tion over five executions. Job completion time can vary for consecutive executions. So, we compared the predicted job completion time with the mean measured job completion time. We observed from the consecutive executions that the sample size of five is sufficient considering the variance of the samples when calculating the relative error of the mean. Each docker container ran in a virtual machine on an Intel Xeon CPU E5-2697 v3 2.60GHz single virtual core. These were deployed in one data centre, sharing a LAN connection. Job completion time of each iteration is mostly steady after a couple of warm up iterations. The job completion time of the first 90 gradient descent iterations for an example execution is shown in Fig. 12. The measured job completion time for various configurations is discussed in Section IV-E along with the accuracy of the model predictions. E. Comparing Measurement and Simulated Results In this section, we evaluate the prediction accuracy of job completion time against macro-benchmarks as described in Section IV-D. We evaluated prediction accuracy changing properties such as the number of data elements, number of features, resource allocation for each node, and key length. Although it is possible to change multiple properties at once, we changed the one property at a time to limit the configuration space what we consider for this evaluation as the purpose of this work is to measure the accuracy of prediction in general. 1) Prediction Accuracy Versus Number of Data Elements: We measured job completion time while changing the number of rows in the dataset from 5,000 to 80,000. Table II compares predicted and mean measured job completion time. Table III compares predicted and mean measured job completion time. 3) Prediction Accuracy Versus Key Length: The perfor- mance of the computation depends on the key length. We compared the prediction accuracy of the performance model with measurements obtained for various key lengths. Table IV compares the predicted and mean measured completion time. 4) Prediction Accuracy Versus Available Resources: We also examined the accuracy of predictions while changing available CPU resources for a docker container. We tested for arbitrary allocations. Table V shows some configurations. V. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK A. Using the Model for Architectural Decision-Making One of the main advantages of constructing performance models is that they can be used for architectural decision- making for privacy-preserving data analytics systems, to help answer what-if questions. Design alternatives can be eval- uated based on their predicted performance. Performance models can be used to evaluate and optimise against other non-functional requirements such as cost, and security. For privacy-preserving data analytics systems, design con- siderations include the following. 1) Cryptographic Key Length: Paillier encryption is an asymmetric encryption method that relies on the properties of prime numbers for its security. The larger the size of the key, longer it will take to break the encryption. However, the size of the key has an impact on overall performance. Key length can be chosen according to the desired security model. In general, a 512-bit key is considered insecure, and 2048-bit keys are considered secure 26 . However, the optimal key length may be a trade-off between security and overall performance. It is straightforward to compare predicted job completion time of the overall computation using the performance model. Using a range of key lengths, job completion time can be compared in order to identify a key length for adequate security and acceptable job completion time. 2) Dynamic Resource Allocation for Dataset Size: In mod- ern systems, provisioning resources (such as with cloud com- puting) for machine learning will be dynamic depending on TABLE III MEASURED VS SIMULATED JOB COMPLETION TIME WITH RESPECT TO THE NUMBER OF FEATURES OF EACH DATA PROVIDER IN THE DATASET FOR 50 ITERATIONS OF OPTIMISATION of features Data Provider 1 of features Data Provider 2 Predicted Measured Mean Relative Error of Mean ( ) 5 5 787 753 4.3 10 5 892 934 4.7 20 5 1,097 1,141 4.0 50 5 1,715 1,787 4.2 100 5 2,744 2,851 3.9 5 10 865 823 4.8 5 20 1,017 1,063 4.5 5 50 1,474 1,531 3.8 5 100 2,236 2,342 4.7 TABLE IV MEASURED VS SIMULATED JOB COMPLETION TIME WITH RESPECT TO THE KEY LENGTH FOR 50 ITERATIONS OF OPTIMISATION Key-length (bits) Predicted (s) Measured Mean (s) Relative Error of Mean ( ) 256 343 338 1.5 512 787 753 4.3 1024 3,603 3,641 1.0 2048 21,047 21,582 2.5 4096 117,585 119,498 1.6 workload and required performance. Deciding on resourcing to achieve required performance and overall cost is challenging. The performance models we describe should be usable with optimisation tools such as PerOpteryx 17 to identify the optimum deployment architecture given constraints such as maximum available resources and maximum acceptable job completion time for a given configuration and dataset size. 3) Choice of Using Privacy-Preserving Data Analytics: As discussed earlier, privacy-preserving computation can be significantly slower than normal computation. Depending on the size of the dataset, security level, and available resources, job completion time may not be acceptable. Models can be developed using micro-benchmarks in a test environment. This can be used for getting insights into job completion time for a given size of the dataset before deployment. 4) Trade-off Between Infrastructure Cost and Performance: More expensive and powerful infrastructure usually leads to better performance and job completion time. The cost of infrastructure and its performance is another trade-off which can be tackled using performance models. These performance models should be usable with optimi- sation tools such as PerOpteryx 17 to identify the optimum infrastructure for the expected job completion time. 5) Integrating Privacy-Preserving Data Analytics with En- terprise Applications: The performance models constructed in Section III can be used to predict and analyse the perfor- mance overhead caused by integrating privacy-preserving data analytics systems such as N1 Analytics. The generation and construction of performance models for enterprise applications have been thoroughly studied in the literature 22 , 21 . As our work is based on the standard Palladio notation, it should be straightforward to integrate our models with other performance models for enterprise applications. B. Limitations The performance benchmarks reported in Section IV and Section III are not intended to be generalised. In particular, we have used only one example system and one data analytics task (logistic regression) for this initial evaluation. Similarly, our main focus here is on latency (job completion time), not scalability and security constraints. Therefore, we did not evaluate the accuracy of our method on horizontally- scaled systems. In real-world applications, one party may have multiple computing nodes. This approach may not work for the systems based on other types of secure multi-party computing techniques such as secret sharing and garbled circuit. Here, we only considered privacy-preserving data analytics systems based on partial homomorphic encryption. In this paper, we have evaluated a compute-heavy implementation of confidential computation based on partial homomorphic encryption. Systems based on communication-heavy techniques may behave differently. The performance benchmarks we have reported use an early version of N1 Analytics platform which is not optimised for performance. The performance of more recent versions of the N1 Analytics system can be significantly better. The purpose of this paper is not to evaluate the performance of N1 Analytics, but instead to evaluate the accuracy of our performance prediction method. In order to maintain the simplicity of our performance model, we abstracted methods and components in the actual implementation. We do not guarantee that there is a one- to-one mapping to the actual implementation. Rather than a limitation, this may be a strength of our approach, because we achieved reasonable accuracy despite this approximate model. C. Future Work Memory speed may be a significant factor for overall performance. We have assumed that the memory performance characteristics of the micro-benchmark environment are sim- ilar to the deployment environment. Integrating variations in memory speed and specific CPU architecture properties will be future work. For this study, we do not consider security aspects of the deployment. In real-world applications, a number of security TABLE V MEASURED VS SIMULATED JOB COMPLETION TIME WITH RESPECT TO THE AMOUNT OF RESOURCES ALLOCATED FOR A NODE FOR 50 ITERATIONS OF OPTIMISATION CPU for Coordinator CPU for Data Provider 1 CPU for Data Provider 2 Predicted Measured Relative Error of Mean 100 100 100 787 753 4.3 80 80 80 1,074 1,033 3.8 30 30 30 3,055 2,913 4.8 30 50 80 1,794 1,738 3.2 80 30 50 1,878 1,882 0.2 factors need to be addressed. Mitigations taken to prevent security vulnerabilities such as side-channel attacks can affect system performance. Sharing direct benchmarks of real ex- ecutions may lead to security breaches in some confidential applications. In future work, we may integrate a security constraint model with our performance model, in order to optimise performance considering security constraints. VI. CONCLUSION In this paper, we have proposed and evaluated an ap- proach for predicting performance characteristics of privacy- preserving data analytics systems using architectural perfor- mance modelling and simulation techniques. For an illustrative system in a lab environment, our performance model predicts the job completion time of a logistic regression scoring ap- plication with the relative error of mean consistently under 5 . We further demonstrated the accuracy of the performance model under different workloads and key lengths. Addition- ally, we discussed how to compare design alternatives using performance models. The proposed architectural models also provide a basis for optimising deployment architectures, sys- tem configuration, cost, and other non-functional properties. papers.fulltext: Architecture-based Change Impact Analysis in Information Systems and Business Processes Kiana Rostami, Robert Heinrich, Axel Busch, and Ralf Reussner Karlsruhe Institute of Technology Karlsruhe, Germany Email: rostami, heinrich, busch, reussner kit.edu AbstractBusiness processes as well as software systems face various changes during their lifetime. As they mutually influence each other, business processes and software systems have to be modified in co-evolution. Thus, to adequately predict the change impact, it is important to consider the complex mutual dependencies of both domains. However, existing approaches are limited to analyzing the change propagation in software systems or business processes in isolation. In this paper, we present a tool-supported approach to estimate the change propagation caused by a change request in business processes or software systems based on the software architecture and the process design. We focus on the mutual dependencies regarding the change propagation between both domains. In the evaluation, we apply our approach to a community case study to demonstrate the quality of results in terms of precision, recall, and coverage. I. INTRODUCTION Most organizations use enterprise Information Systems (IS) to support their Business Processes (BP). Longevity is one of the most important characteristics of both domains. Long-living systems have to be adapted due to changes during their life cycle. Thus, it is important to understand and predict the impact of a change to these systems. In modern organizations the IS is an integral part of the BP. Hence, there are mutual dependencies between both domains regarding their maintainability: On the one hand, IS has to be adapted to reflect the changes caused in the corresponding BP (e.g., supporting new activities in a BP can cause changes in the corresponding IS). On the other hand, a BP needs to be modified due to changes in the corresponding IS (e.g., replacing software components with components of alternative vendors can cause some services to the customers to be changed). We use a supermarket example to demonstrate the change propagation between both domains according to their mutual dependencies: Exchanging a two-dimensional barcode for product identification by another machine-readable representation of data such as RFID tags leads to changes in the BP (e.g., inventory of products), but also in the IS. Changing the IS again affects the ability of the cashiers who use the IS to sale products (e.g., to register the products which the customers buy). Thus, a BP and the corresponding IS are co-evolving. During the co-evolution a change to one of the both domains can propagate to the other domain due to these mutual dependencies. Thus, to adequately estimate the impact of a change in one domain we need to consider the impact of changes on the other domain. However, the mutual dependencies make the analysis of the change propagation challenging. Business process modeling is used to better understand, structure, and analyze the processes of an organization. Hence, considering only the architecture of an IS or the design of a BP is not sufficient while analyzing the change propagation between the domain of IS and BP, as it neglects the effects of the corresponding domain. Thus, the co-design of BP and IS 1 plays an important role when considering the change propagation during the co-evolution. To reflect the co-evolution of the BP and the corresponding IS we need to metamodel both domains to represents their relationships 2 . Thus, the enterprise architecture 3 is the main artifact during the co- evolution, as it provides a holistic perspective of a BP and of the IS. It allows analyzing the change propagation between activities in an organization and the corresponding IS. To this end, the activities of a BP can be divided into activities that are performed completely manually by actors, called actor steps and activities that are performed completely automatically by the IS, called system steps 4 . Our analysis involves the process (organization layer), the software architecture (software layer), and the infrastructure layer of the enterprise architecture. Existing approaches to the change propagation analysis in the IS (e.g., 5 , 6 ) are based on the architecture of the IS without taking the mutual dependencies to the BP into account. However, these mutual dependencies play a key role in the co- evolution, as changes to an IS highly impacts the activities of the BP and how the customers are able to meet their goals 7 , 1 . Works on change impact analysis in BP consider change propagation from the metamodel of a BP to its instances (e.g., 8 , 9 ), in collaborative processes (e.g., 10 , 11 ), or a set of models of a BP at different abstraction levels (e.g., 12 ). But they neither support the change propagation in one instance of a BP nor in co-evolution with an IS. Several approaches exist that support the analysis of the co-evolution process of BP and IS: There are approaches that describe the importance of considering the mutual dependencies between both domains (e.g., 1 , 13 ) or present two related metamodels (cf. 2 ), but do not take the change propagation into account. Approaches to the change impact analysis in enterprise architectures (e.g., 14 , 15 ) describe a set of coarse-grained rules for the change propagation using the relationship between elements of both domains. However, they either do not support estimating the 2017 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture 978-1-5090-5729-0 17 31.00 2017 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. change efforts as an activity list to implement a change request, or do not offer an automated change impact analysis. In this paper, we present a tool-supported approach the Karlsruhe Architectural Maintainability Prediction for Business Processes (KAMP4BP), to automatically analyze the change propagation in a BP and the corresponding IS caused by an initial change request in one of the domains. Our approach is an extension of the Karlsruhe Architectural Maintainability Prediction (KAMP) 6 . KAMP is a scenario-based approach to calculate the change propagation but is limited to analyzing the IS. In contrast to KAMP, KAMP4BP calculates a more fine- grained change propagation for the IS based on the software architecture. In addition to structural changes in the IS, we consider the change propagation in the BP and between the BP and the corresponding IS to support the co-evolution of both related domains. Our approach results in a task list containing the estimated tasks to be carried out for the change. Thus, KAMP4BP supports change effort estimation and the decision making process by comparing the design alternatives. The contribution of this paper is threefold: i) We describe an approach that considers mutual dependencies between a BP and the corresponding IS regarding the maintainability. ii) We show an automated analysis of change propagation due to an initial change request in a BP and or the corresponding IS. iii) We evaluate our approach using a community case study to demonstrate its applicability and its practical benefits. For the evaluation we use different change scenarios that represent several equivalence classes. Each equivalence class refers to model elements of the BP design and of the IS architecture that are relevant for the change propagation. Using these change scenarios we assess the quality of the task lists for implementing change requests in terms of precision, recall, and coverage. The reminder of this paper is organized as follows: Sec. 2 summarizes the foundation of our approach. In Sec. 3, we introduce our running example to illustrate our approach. Sec. 4 gives an overview of the approach and the application of our approach to the running example. We present the evaluation of our approach in Sec. 5. Sec. 6 summarizes related work. The final Section concludes the paper and discusses future work. II. FOUNDATION A. Change Propagation Analysis When implementing a change request three sets of changing elements can be distinguished: i) Change set is a collection of elements, that are directly affected by a change request. ii) Affected set is a superset of the change set and contains all elements, that have to be changed to implement a change re- quest.iii) Impact set is a superset of the affected set and includes all elements, that a change request potentially affects 16 . Our Approach extends the KAMP approach. KAMP is a scenario-based change propagation analysis approach for the IS, which derives an impact set to implement a change request. KAMP extends the Palladio approach by maintainability analysis of software architectures. Palladio 17 predicts the performance of an IS and is based on the Palladio Compo- nent Model (PCM). PCM is a domain-specific metamodel enabling software architects to model the architecture of a component-based IS especially regarding the performance quality attributes. Reussner et al. 17 defined a software component as a contractually specified building block for software, which can be composed, deployed, and adapted without understanding its internals. A software component can be either a basic component or a composite component. A composite component is a composition of basic components and or other composite components. Components provide or require interfaces. The relation of an interface to components defines its role. Thus, these relations are called provided or required roles, respectively 17 . In our approach, we extended the metamodels of PCM in a modular way, in order to allow metamodeling of maintainability of the BP and IS domain. Our metamodel extensions are based on a reference structure for metamodels for architecture description languages. This reference architecture can be divided into layers of paradigm, domain, quality, and analysis to ease model extension and customization 18 . B. Integrated Business IT Impact Simulation (IntBIIS) The IntBIIS approach 4 extends PCM by metamodels of BPs regarding the performance impact of the BP and the corresponding IS. The BP metamodel extends the usage profile of PCM and consists of a set of linked activities, where an activity can be either an actor step or a system step, as illustrated in Fig 1 (cf. 4 ). An actor step can be completed by an actor, whereas a system step is a call to a provided role of a component by the user, called entry level system call 17 , 4 . However, neither Palladio nor IntBIIS, nor KAMP consider the maintainability of a BP and the corresponding IS in terms of change propagation. Excerpt from PCM usage model and IntBIIS metamodel extension 4 III. EXAMPLE SCENARIO In this section, we use the hybrid cloud-based Common Component Modeling Example (CoCoME) (cf. 20 , 21 ) as our running example to illustrate the idea of our approach. A. System Overview Fig. 2 shows a simplified component diagram of the IS architecture of the hybrid cloud-based CoCoME and the corresponding BP design of the sale scenario. CoCoME has been set up in a GI Dagstuhl research seminar as a demonstrator for component-based software engineering and serves as a community case study to which several approaches can be applied. Using CoCoME as a common demonstrator allows comparing the research results regarding evolution. CoCoME is a fully implemented application and represents a trading system of a supermarket and consists of a set of stores. Each IExpress LightModel ::Data CoCoME Enterprise Customer AS: Press startNewSale Acquire barcode scanner AS: Enter good identifier AS: Place goods on the belt Item Good AS: Scan good scanBarcode Release barcode scanner ... Component diagram of CoCoME 19 and an excerpt from the adjacent sale business process store has a store server controlling a cash desk line consisting a set of cash desks. A cash desk contains a computer and hardware resources (e.g., barcode scanner) connected to the computer. The store servers of all stores are connected to an enterprise store server 20 , 19 . The IS architecture of the hybrid cloud-based CoCoME is a three-tier architecture and is composed of a composition of several composite components, namely TradingSystem::Inventory, WebService:: Inventory, TradingSystem::CashDeskLine, WebService::CashDeskService, and WebFrontend. The TradingSystem::Inventory component comprises other composite components, namely ::Application and ::Data. They model the business logic and data layer of the three-tier architecture. The WebFrontend component provides a JavaServer-Faces-based user interface. The composite component WebService::CashDeskService provides the WebFrontend component access for the components of TradingSystem::CashDeskLine. The TradingSystem::CashDeskLine component is composed of ::CashDesk components that in turn comprises all components at a cash desk such as ::BarcodeScanner or ::CardReader. The composite component WebService::Inventory provides WebFrontend access to enterprise components 19 . CoCoME supports several processes (e.g., sale or reporting). In the following, we use the main BP of CoCoME, namely the sale process. Fig. 2 illustrates an excerpt from the simplified sale process starting with placing goods on the belt of the cash desk. Actor steps are marked with AS. All other activities are system steps and represent the services of CoCoME. After a customer placed the goods on the checkout belt of the sale process, the cashier scans or types out the bar code. At the end, the customer pays by cash or by credit card. Finally, the stock will be updated due to successful sales 20 . B. Change Scenario In order to illustrate how our approach automatically supports the change propagation between a BP and the corresponding IS, let us assume, that we have to speed up the scanning process according to a new requirement. Thus, we decide to modify the business process by exchanging the machine-readable data representation of goods from barcode tags to RFID tags. IV. APPROACH Our approach calculates the change propagation in the BP design and the corresponding IS model caused by an initial change request to these domains. To this end, it considers the mutual dependencies between a BP and the corresponding IS. Change Request Temporary Task List Impact Phase Impact on Business Process Impact on Software Change Propagation in Business Process Design Change Propagation in Software Architecture Postanalyze Phase Merge Tasks ( 1 Change Request) Duplicate Detection Task List Recalculation of Task List User Decision on Fig. 3. Approach Overview Fig. 3 gives an overview of KAMP4BP. KAMP4BP is composed of three phases: i) preparation phase, ii) impact phase, and iii) postanalyze phase. In the preparation phase, we model the design of the BP and the IS architecture. The impact phase automatically calculates the change propagation in the IS architecture model and in the model of BP design, and between both models. This phase results in a temporary task list representing an impact set to implement the change request. The postanalyze phase eliminates the duplicates and merges the task lists, if more than one change request was selected. Additionally, the approach allows users to reject single tasks referring to elements, that are not affected by the change. Based on decisions of the user KAMP4BP recalculates the task list. In the following, we refer to CoCoME to demonstrate the phases and the algorithms of KAMP4BP. A. Preparation Phase In the preparation phase, the design of the BP and the architecture of the corresponding IS are modeled. Model-based approaches can lead to a higher effort in the early development stages. However, it is expected, that this higher effort reduces the rework in the subsequent stages 22 . We can either model the architecture of the IS manually or automatically using a reverse engineering approach to reduce the effort (e.g., SOftware MOdel eXtractor (SoMoX) 23 ). The BP design can be modeled using the extended usage profile of PCM as a set of actor steps and system steps 4 . Additionally, we annotate the model of the IS architecture or BP design with additional information regarding IS (e.g., test cases) or BP (e.g., organizational units). KAMP uses annotations related to IS to calculate the impact resulted by changing other elements than code (e.g., test cases) 6 . Our approach uses additional information in a BP to give its user feedback about elements, that are possibly affected (e.g., organizational units) or about the implicit impact due to changing some activities (e.g., training the employees). In the next step, we select the initial change request(s) in the model of an IS architecture and or the corresponding BP design. To avoid overestimation of the derived task list, only a minimal set of the initial change requests has to be selected. For example, if only one signature was modified initially, we have to select only the signature and not the whole interface. Further, deciding which element has to be initially modified in the IS architecture model and or in the BP model due to an initial change request is not a trivial task and can be defined in different ways depending on the change scenario. Additionally, a change request can result in more than one initial changing element in the IS architecture model and or the BP design model (hereafter referred to as seed modification). Further, the granularity of the model is an important factor for selecting the seed modification in the models. Application to CoCoME: In the first step, we model the IS architecture and the design of the sale BP of CoCoME. In our change scenario, replacing barcode with RFID can be implemented in different ways. One possible seed modification can be replacing the barcode of all products in the BP with RFID tags and using RFID scanners instead of barcode scanners. However, replacing the barcode of all products can impact the model at different levels of granularity: i) If the physical Barcode has been modeled as a data object and the Goods have explicitly barcode tags, the Barcode data object is marked as modified. ii) If the Barcode is not explicitly represented in the BP model, maybe the data object Goods has to be marked as modified. For the application of our approach to CoCoME we explicitly modeled the physical Barcode. Therefore, the seed modification is the data object Barcode and the resource device Barcode scanner. B. Impact Phase In the impact phase, KAMP4BP automatically analyzes the propagation of the initial change requests in the BP and the corresponding IS. In particular, the change propagates from the modified elements of the model of the BP design and the architecture model of the IS to other elements in the models based on change propagation rules. When considering a BP, the corresponding IS, and their mutual dependencies change propagation analysis can be divided into three groups: i) Intra- domain change propagation between the elements of the BP (cf. Algorithm 1). ii) Inter-domain change propagation: from the IS to the BP and from the BP to the IS (cf. Algorithm 2) iii) Intra-domain change propagation between the elements of the IS (cf. Algorithm 3). In the following, we present the algorithms for the aforementioned groups. We describe the phases of each algorithm by the application to CoCoME. 1) Impact Analysis in BP: Algorithm 1 presents the analysis of the change propagation in the model of a BP design. The seed modification in a BP model can be device resources, roles, actor steps, or data objects. Device resources represent devices or machines needed for an activity or a sequence of activities (e.g., barcode scanner) 4 . In order to model a physical data object in a BP, we extend the PCM to include the data object. The data object concept is inspired by Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 24 but reflects only the physical elements which actors need as input or output to perform their actor steps. In our scenario, Goods is an example of a data object and represents the goods the customers bought. A physical data object can correspond to one or many data types and vice versa. For example a physical invoice can map to a table or to an object in a database. Further, a data object can be a composed data object or a collection data object. A collection data object can only include several data objects of the same type (i.e., collection of different invoices can only include invoices and no other types, such as goods.). Thus, a data object can be mapped either to a composed data type or to a collection data type. Each phase of Algorithm 1 describes how a change propagates from an element in a BP model to other elements in the BP model. Application to CoCoME: If we apply the first phase of the Algorithm 1 to the sale BP model of CoCoME, a change to the data object Barcode propagates to the composite data object Good that contains the Barcode. After the composite data object Good was modified, the collection of Goods representing the purchases or the goods in the stock has also to be modified. Applying the second phase leads to changing the actor step scan items performed by the cashier, since this actor step uses Goods as input. By applying the final phase the change propagates from the device resource Barcode scanner to all related activities, such as acquire barcode scanner and release barcode scanner, depicted in Fig. 2. 2) Impact Analysis between BP and IS: Change propagation between the BP and the corresponding IS is calculated using Algorithm 2. The change between both domains can propagate due to the data objects or data types dependencies and system steps. If a data type is changed, the change can propagate to the corresponding data object and vice versa. As the system steps in the BP model are calls to the provided roles, a change to a signature in a provided role propagates to the system step of the BP model. Application to CoCoME: As the data object Barcode and Goods were modified in the previous step, the second phase of Algorithm 2 marks the corresponding data types in the IS architecture model Barcode and Products as modified. Another example is the signature addDigitToBarcode of ICashDeskView that represents a system step (i.e., entry level system call). If the algorithm marks this signature as modified, the change would propagate from the IS architecture model to the corresponding model of the BP design. 3) Impact Analysis in IS: Algorithm 3 extends the KAMP algorithms for change propagation in an IS and refines the Algorithm 1 Algorithm for the Change Propagation Analysis in a BP Model Require: Model of BP design, change request 1: Calculate the change propagation from a data object to the other data objects while There is at least one new modified data object do Determine composed data objects that contain the modified data object. Mark them as modified. Determine collection data objects that contain the modified data object. Mark them as modified. end while 2: Calculate the change propagation from data objects to actor steps using the modified data objects as input 3: Calculate the change propagation from a role to the correspond- ing actor steps 4: Calculate the change propagation from a modified actor step to the directly following actor step while There is at least one new modified actor step A do Determine the actor step B directly following the modified actor step A. if The same data object serves as input of B and output of A then Mark B as modified. end if end while 5: Calculate the change propagation from a modified actor step to the directly following system step 6: Calculate change propagation from modified device resources Identify modified device resources. for all Acquire- ReleaseDeviceResource activities using these device resources do Mark Acquire- ReleaseDeviceResource activities as modified. for all activities between two corresponding AcquireDeviceRe- source and ReleaseDeviceResource do Mark the activities between as modified. end for end for Algorithm 2 Algorithm for the Change Propagation Analysis between the Model of IS Architecture and BP and vice versa Require: model of IS architecture and BP design, change request 1: Calculate the change propagation from data types to the corresponding data objects 2: Calculate the change propagation from data objects to the corresponding data types 3: Calculate the change propagation from modified signatures to the system steps (entry level system calls in the usage model) 4: Calculate the change propagation from modified system steps (entry level system calls in the usage model) to the signatures existing steps to enable the change propagation from the architecture model of an IS to the model of the corresponding BP design. The seed modifications in an IS architecture model are interfaces and their signatures, components, data types, event types, and event groups. KAMP analyzes the change propagation at the granularity of interfaces. However, to support the change propagation to and from the domain of the BP we extend KAMP to signature-based change propagation within a component and between two components (cf. the first phase of Algorithm 3 Apply modified KAMP). Additionally, KAMP4BP supports change propagation in the case of event- based communication between components, as in an event- based communication, the components can fire (i.e., source role) or handle (i.e., sink role) event groups, which are composed of single events (i.e., event types) 17 . Further, the algorithm supports change propagation analysis from a data type to the composite data type, collection data type, and event types. Algorithm 3 Algorithm of the Change Propagation Analysis in IS Architecture Model Require: IS architecture model, change request 1: Apply modified KAMP at the level of signatures 2: Calculate the change propagation from a modified data type to the other data types while There is at least one new modified data type do Determine composed data types that contain the modified data type. Mark them as modified. Determine collection data types that contain the modified data type. The rest of the Algorithm 3 calculates the change propagation due to interfaces, signatures, data types, or events to signatures, interfaces, events, or data types that use or relate to the changing elements. For example, the data type ProductTO has to be changed, as it composed of other changing data types, in particular the data type Barcode (cf. the second phase of Al- gorithm 3). Following the third phase of Algorithm 3, the event type ProductBarcodeScannedEvent has to be modified, since it uses the data type Barcode. Changing the event type ProductBarcodeScannedEvent requires to change the event group handleProductBarcodeScannedEvent of the CashDeskEventHandler component (cf. the fourth phase of Algorithm 3). Thus, according to the fifth phase, the component CashDeskEventHandler has to be changed in order to apply the changes in its interfaces. An example of the application of the sixth phase of Algorithm 3 is the change propagation to the getBarcode signature of the provided ICashDesk interface of Web::Data::CashDeskData component. getBarcode is modified due to the data de- pendency to the Barcode data type. ICashDesk contains at least one changing signature getBarcode. According to the seventh phase of the Algorithm 3, we need to change the interface ICashDesk. The addDigitToBarcode sig- nature of ICashDeskView interface calls getBarcode. Thus, the refinement of KAMP results in changing addDigitToBarCode (cf. the first phase of Algorithm 3). The last three steps are not used for the change propagation in this example, but in the change scenarios in the evaluation. The Algorithms 1, 2, and 3 are repeated as long as the algorithms result in new changes. The change propagation terminates if there are no new changes in the previous iteration. Thus, this phase of the approach predicts all elements of the IS architecture model and the BP design model which are potentially affected by the change request. The impact phase results in a temporary task list. Application to CoCoME: Tab. I illustrates the output of KAMP4BP as a task list required to implement the initial change requests based on the CoCoME models. C. Postanalyze Phase If we select more than one change request as modified in the preparation phase, KAMP4BP merges the tasks of the temporary task list and removes duplicates in the post-analyze phase. Further, a task can refer to an element that cannot be modified (e.g., if a component is a third party component). As the element referred by the task can be the cause for the change propagation in other elements, the user has the possibility to mark this task as rejected. The approach can reanalyze the task list based on the user decisions and calculates a modified change propagation task list according to these decisions. The result of this phase is a merged task list. V. EVALUATION KAMP4BP analyzes how a change request affects the model of a BP design and the model of the IS architecture. To this end, we consider the IS architecture and the BP design and the mutual dependencies between both domains. Using our approach, software architects and process designers can compare the design alternatives and the ways in which a change can be implemented. For the change impact analysis, first, the user has to model the BP design and the corresponding IS architecture and select the seed modifications in the models. Then, KAMP4BP analyzes the potentially affected elements of the models due to the seed modifications. The main contribution of our approach is the automatic identification of tasks required to implement a change request regarding the complex mutual dependencies between BP and IS. Additionally, a tool-supported approach allows the analysis of the change propagation in a Initial Change Request 1: Device barcode scanner Initial Change Request 2: Data Object barcode Propagation due to Data Dependencies Modify Interface ICashDeskDAO Modify Signature enterBarcode Modify Interface ICashDesk Modify Signature getBarcode Modify Signature setBarcode Modify Interface ICashDeskQuery Modify Signature enterBarcode . ..
