papers.fulltext: Continuous Architecture: Towards the Goldilocks Zone and Away from Vicious Circles Torvald Martensson Saab AB Linkoping, Sweden torvald.martensson saabgroup.com Daniel Stahl Ericsson AB Linkoping, Sweden daniel.stahl ericsson.com Antonio Martini University of Oslo Oslo, Norway antonima ifi.uio.no Jan Bosch Chalmers University of Technology Gothenburg, Sweden jan janbosch.com AbstractThis paper identifies three improvement areas related to system design and architecture, where an organization can change to better support continuous integration and continuous delivery: The products architecture, Ways to work with system design and architecture, and The role of the architect. The three improvement areas are based on a literature review, two series of interviews and a cross-company workshop with three case- study companies. Furthermore, the paper proposes three actionable strategies corresponding to the three identified improvement areas: Systems with a modular and loosely coupled architecture, A balanced approach where system design and architecture is focused on the systems most important characteristics, and Architects shifting perspective from control to facilitation. Keywords-agile; architecture; continuous architecting; continuous delivery; continuous integration; large-scale I. INTRODUCTION In industry projects we have studied or ourselves participated in, we find an inherent conflict between the doctrine of continuous practices and the need to plan system design and architecture ahead of time. We frequently encounter engineers who struggle with this conflict in their day-to-day work. Meanwhile, much of the literature on Agile development or continuous practices implicitly assumes a steady state where small features or partial features can be added one on top of the other in a continuous fashion. When that is not the case, however, it is less than obvious how to apply continuous practices by the book. Parts of published literature address this problem. As Coplien and Bjrnvig 1 put it: While we must acknowledge emergence in design and system development, a little planning can avoid much waste. Leffingwell 2 describes this as the problem of constructing an architectural runway: before developers can efficiently and effectively implement features, there needs to be a minimum of code and infrastructure on which to build. Oftentimes, these types of planning and runway-building are not one-off activities, though. Particularly in long-lived large-scale systems, there is a need for continual re-planning and re-architecting, but on a scale much larger than what a strict interpretation of continuous integration doctrine would appear to permit. As a result, multiple strata of development tend to form in a large-scale development project: the larger and slower fundamental systemization and architectural design activities, and the faster and more frequently integrated software development activities. Where these strata meet there is a high risk of conflict. Examples of this include change synchronization problems and architects playing catch-up with developers rather than leading the way 3 . That being said, we argue that there is a need for these conflicting strata to co-exist. We observe that the quest for balance between pragmatism and continuous practices doctrine when it comes to architectural design and systemization is an area of frequent struggle in the industry. In our previous work, we have also identified architecture not adapted to continuous integration as an impediment which can prevent developers from frequently integrating their software 4 . Based on this reasoning, we phrase the following research question: How can the way companies work with system design and architecture change to better support continuous integration and continuous delivery? The contribution of this paper is two-fold: First, it presents interview results and experiences from three case study companies, showing how they currently combine system design and architecture with continuous integration and delivery. Second, it proposes actionable strategies corresponding to three identified improvement areas, which can help organizations to better implementations of continuous integration and continuous delivery. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section we present the research method. This is followed by a summary of related work in Section III. Section IV presents the two series of interviews, and Section V presents the results from the cross-company workshop. 131 2019 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA) 978-1-7281-0528-4 19 31.00 2019 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. The results from the interviews and the cross-company workshop are discussed in Section VI. Threats to validity are discussed in Section VII. Finally, the paper is concluded in Section VIII. II. RESEARCH METHOD A. Overview of the Research Method To answer the research question from Section I, an exploratory approach was deemed appropriate, where each step of the study informed the next. An overview of the steps of the study is shown in Fig. 1. Figure 1. An overview of the steps in the research study. The study started with a literature review, in order to look for answers to the research question in published literature. In parallel, a series of interviews was conducted to give the researchers an overview of the three case study companies involved in the study (which we will refer to as Company A, Company B and Company C). Based on the first series of interviews, the second series of interviews aimed at identifying problems and solutions in order to answer the research question. The literature review and the results from the analysis of the two series of interviews were presented at a cross-company workshop, in order to validate the findings from the interviews and further identify the mechanisms involved. B. Literature Review The first step was to conduct a literature review. The literature review continued in parallel with the two series of interviews and the cross-company workshop. Instead of doing a new full systematic literature review (according to the guidelines from Kitchenham 5 ), the study used a previous systematic literature review by Qureshi et al. 6 as a starting point. Qureshi et al. conduct a systematic literature review based on 247 primary studies to evaluate empirical studies of software architecture. As a complement to the review from Qureshi et al. we also analyzed other published work (identified in our previous work) which in different ways discuss architecture in combination with Agile or continuous practices. C. Interview Series 1: An Overview of the Companies The purpose of the first series of interviews was to give the researchers an overview of the companies current ways of working. The interviews included four individuals, two from one of the case study companies (interviewed together) and one from each of the other two case study companies. The interviewees had senior roles in their organizations such as product manager or technical manager. All interviews were conducted as semi-structured interviews with pre- defined questions, and lasted for one hour each. The questions in the interview guide were: Q1.1: Briefly describe the product that your organization is developing Q1.2: Briefly describe your role in the organization Q1.3: How do you in your organization work with system design and architecture when a new feature and or sub-system should be introduced in one of your products? Q1.4: How do you in your organization utilize continuous integration and continuous delivery? As we have identified in our previous work 7 that there is confusion regarding the terms continuous integration and continuous delivery, clear definitions of the terms (from published literature 7 ) were also included in the background material which was sent to the interviewees: Continuous integration is a developer practice where developers integrate their work frequently, usually each person integrates at least daily, leading to multiple integrations per day. Continuous delivery is a development practice where every change is treated as a potential release candidate to be frequently and rapidly evaluated through ones continuous delivery pipeline, and that one is always able to deploy and or release the latest working version, but may decide not to, e.g. for business reasons. D. Interview Series 2: Identifying Problems and Solutions The purpose of the second series of interviews was to investigate how the companies could change the way they work with system design and architecture in order to better support continuous integration and continuous delivery. The interview series included twenty individual interviews. Six interviewees participated from Company A, eight from Company B, and six from Company C. The interviewees had roles as developer, architect, technical manager specialist and product project manager. The interviews were conducted as semi-structured interviews, using an interview guide with pre-defined questions. They lasted from half an hour up to (in most cases) one hour. The questions in the interview guide were: Q2.1: How many years of industry experience with regards to software development do you have? Q2.2: How would you describe your individual role and responsibilities? Q2.3: How do you on a scale from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high) value how software development of large-scale systems benefits from continuous integration and continuous delivery? Q2.4: How does your organization currently combine system design and architecture with continuous integration and delivery? Q2.5: How can the way your organization works with system design and architecture change to better support continuous integration and continuous delivery? Q2.6: Which activities related to architecture and system design do you think should be completed before starting the implementation in the software? The interviewees were provided with the same definitions of continuous integration and continuous delivery as the interviewees in interview series 1. After the first answer from the interviewee on question Q2.6, the interviewee was encouraged to consider different descriptions of what architecture means. Three descriptions of architecture and system design (selected to cover different perspectives) were presented to the interviewees: Six Architectural Views (from The Art of Systems Architecting 8 ). Three Kinds of Architectural Structures (from Software Architecture in Practice 9 ). Product Quality Properties (from System and Software Quality Models 10 ). The complete material is not presented here due to formatting constraints. The results from the two series of interviews (described in Sections II-C and II-D) were analyzed with exploratory analysis. Thematic coding analysis (as described by Robson and McCartan 11 ) was used to analyze the interview results from questions Q2.5 and Q2.6, as the responses from these two questions included a large amount of statements and comments. E. Cross-Company Workshop The cross-company workshop included ten participants from the case study companies and two of the researchers. The two researchers took turns in presenting the results from the literature review, and the analysis of the interview results. The researchers had also prepared a number of questions (presented in Section V) designed to promote discussions among the workshop participants. The workshop resulted in good discussions, which were moderated by the researchers to allow all participants to express their opinions, and perspectives from all case study companies to be heard. Responses and significant comments were transcribed during the workshop, and read back to the participants (before moving on to the next part of the presentation) in order to validate that the transcribed responses and comments reflected what had been said during the workshop. After the workshop, the researchers summarized the new findings, and analyzed these together with the results from the interviews and the literature review. III. LITERATURE REVIEW A. Identiying Relevant Literature for the Review The first step in the study was to conduct a literature review, using the systematic literature review by Qureshi et al. 6 as a starting point. According to Qureshi et al. (who investigates empirical studies of software architecture) only one percent of the identified papers were related to Agile and architecture. Instead, published literature tends to discuss architecture within the context of longer update cycles, e.g. Breivold et al. 12 describe that systems are continuously changing, but discuss this from a perspective of 10-30 years. Continuous architecting is a recent phenomenon that has emerged from the shift towards the application of more iterative and Agile practices in large-scale organizations, such as continuous integration and continuous delivery. Being such a recent topic, there are only a few papers available in published literature related to continuous architecting. The only definition that we have found in published literature for continuous architecting was architecting that supports continuous delivery 13 (in a non-peer reviewed manuscript). However, our previous work 4 has shown that absence of a modular and loosely coupled architecture can prevent developers from integrating their software. Therefore we argue that continuous architecting should be defined as architecting that supports continuous integration (a developer practice where developers integrate their work frequently leading to multiple integrations per day) as well as continuous delivery (a development practice where every change is treated as a potential release candidate to be frequently and rapidly evaluated through ones continuous delivery pipeline) 7 . We have not found any definition in published literature of the distinction between Agile architecting and continuous architecting, and observe that the two terms are being used interchangeably. B. Results from the Literature Review In the literature review we found papers that in different ways discussed problems and challenges related to architecture combined with Agile methods (Agile architecting) or continuous practices (continuous architecting). Bellomo 14 focuses on the architectural process, and asks for An Agile way to define an architecture, using an iterative lifecycle, allowing the architectural design to tactically evolve over time, as the problem and the constraints are better understood. The paper suggests an iterative process for architecture that is parallel to the iterations related to requirements and implementation, and is synchronized via integration points. Bellomo 14 also discusses the characteristics of the actual product architecture: A system or software architecture that is versatile, easy to evolve, and easy to modify, while resilient enough not to degrade after a few changes. The paper reports several tactics to make the product architecture more Agile, such as service-oriented architecture and layered architecture. Other papers take a different approach and focus on architecture decisions: Van Vliet and Tang 15 argue that the process of architecting suffers from several biases, as many human decisions are not fully rational. An example is the anchoring bias, for which the context in which the architect is when he or she takes a decision, influences all the further decisions. The anchoring points are not rational ones, but usually belong to the latest experiences that the architect has been involved in. Poort and van Vliet 16 argue that the risk of an architectural decision being wrong decreases as time passes, since more information is available. In conclusion, early architectural decisions have high probability to be wrong, and therefore need to be postponed and re-evaluated as more information becomes available. Architecture risk management is discussed by Waterman et al. 17 . According to Waterman et al., addressing risks is in conflict with responding to change, as technical risks mean that more up-front architecture design is required. The authors propose the use of template and framework architecture to mitigate the gap. Poort and van Vliet 16 take a different perspective and argue that a way to make architecting more continuous is to consider the whole process as a cost- and risk management discipline. The authors suggest that architectural concerns should be collected via the main stakeholders. The architectural backlog can then be re-prioritized iteratively, according to additional information elicited during requirement and implementation activities. Another perspective is architecture communication: In our previous work 18 we found that it is important to pay attention to the fact that the architects and the development teams communicate iteratively (in both directions). In particular, architects need to communicate clearly and continuously the importance of the main architectural significant requirements, while they need to have feedback (from the team or from analysis tools) on the status of the system, to understand if the architectural requirements are at risk. Our previous work 18 also highlights several roles, responsibilities and practices that are considered necessary in an Agile environment by Agile teams and architects. Some practices and responsibilities are shared by different roles, which means that teams (intended as group of roles with the same goal, in this case carrying out a practice or sharing a responsibility) are needed. The paper also proposes an organizational framework (CAFFEA) which includes roles, teams and practices to support continuous architecting. IV. INTERVIEW RESULTS A. General Information The study reported in this research paper included three case study companies (referred to as Company A, Company B and Company C). The case study companies are all multi- national organizations with more than 2,000 employees. All companies develop large-scale and complex software systems for products which also include a significant amount of mechanical and electronic systems. All companies have on different levels and in different ways adopted Agile ways of working and continuous practices such as private builds, integration build servers, integration pipelines and automated testing. The companies operate in the following industry segments: Aeronautical systems Cars and services for cars Video surveillance cameras and systems Detailed descriptions of the case study companies way of working and detailed interview results are not included in this research paper due to non-disclosure agreements with the case study companies. The interviewees in the second series of interviews had on average 15.6 years of experience of the software industry. They had all a positive or very positive attitude to continuous integration and delivery, responding 4 (six interviewees) or 5 (fourteen interviewees) on the question How do you on a scale from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high) value how software development of large-scale systems benefit from continuous integration and continuous delivery? (Q2.3). B. Identified Problems The analysis of the interview results showed that the case study companies had quite different ways of working. Despite this, interviewees from all three case study companies described in different ways that problems related to architecture were found late in their development projects. Company A integrated software frequently on a component and subsystem level, and all teams had at least a nightly build of their subsystem. Most of the teams also had automated tests executed at a commit, and test suites executed on the nightly build. The interviewees from Company A described that they were integrating frequently on a component or subsystem level, but they had very long feedback loops on a product level. Due to this, it could take as long as several months before the software that the developers had committed was tested in the complete product, giving the developers feedback on whether their design and architecture were actually working. The problem was described as being partly related to how the company was working with subcontractors, which were responsible for some of the subsystems in the product. The interviewees from Company A also described that they had a stage-gated way of working. One interviewee even described it as we work according to waterfall. Company B had implemented continuous integration and continuous delivery on a slightly higher level. The developers committed frequently to their team branches, where in most cases test suites on component and system level were repeatedly executed. The teams delivered their software to a common main track (the software mainline) where tests were frequently executed in both simulators and test environments with real hardware. Interviewees from Company B described that system and software were seen as two separate disciplines, which also affected how the employees worked together (e.g. people who work with system design and software work in two completely different tracks). Furthermore, the interviewees from Company B described problems related to an extensive system design phase, which was conducted before starting implementation in software. One interviewee described the problem with a lack of feedback from implementation as we are working with detailed architecture for stuff where we dont have a clue if it will work at all. The work in the extensive system design phase also seemed to be a bit circular. To quote one of the interviewees: In the design phase we write a lot of documents which specify how we should do the implementation. That means that a lot of documents must be updated if we change the implementation. So we continue the design phase to make sure that everything will be absolutely correct. It goes around in circles. Company C had embraced a more agile way of working. Developers were working with new features and sometimes subsystems on branches, and delivered software to a main track guarded by a QA (Quality Assurance) department. The QA department executed different types of tests on the main track. System design and architecture were seen as something that primarily emerged during implementation in software, not in a separate design phase. Despite this, the interviewees from Company C described that problems with architecture were found late during implementation, as it seems much due to the fact that the teams worked on separated branches. There was little coordination between the development teams, which then tended to isolate themselves. One interviewee described the problem as the teams are out on a branch for between one and two years, then they have huge problems when they try to integrate which causes delays or technical debt. Another voice described similar situations with the words it works on the branch, but not together with other functions or on all hardware configurations on the main track. Some problems were related to compliance to the rules and guidelines given by the companys architects. As one interviewee said: When you are almost done you have to refactor the software is in the wrong components which causes delays and security problems. C. Possible Improvement Areas The interviewees described a range of suggestions and ideas related to how system design and architecture could better support continuous integration and continuous delivery. The interview results were analyzed with thematic coding analysis (as described by Robson and McCartan 11 ) which resulted in the following three themes: The products architecture Ways to work with system design and architecture The role of the architect The products architecture was supported by statements from 12 of the 20 interviewees (including interviewees from all three case study companies). Interviewees described the benefits from modular architecture (10 interviewees) and loosely coupled architecture (7 interviewees). A modular and loosely coupled architecture was considered to make it easier to break down the work in smaller chunks, and then work in parallel. Other topics related to the products architecture were also brought up by the interviewees: layers and services (two interviewees) and systems easy to change (one interviewee). One interviewee answered the question (Q2.5 in Section II-D) with I dont know. Ways to work with system design and architecture was supported by statements from all of the 20 interviewees, but the interviewees described quite different situations in the case study companies. Ten interviewees from Company A and Company B requested a more light-weight design phase, followed by shorter iterations with earlier and more frequent feedback from implementation. Other voices described that we should work with architecture and system design in smaller steps this way of working slows us down or it would be better to have feedback on the architecture earlier. The six interviewees from Company C had a somewhat opposite approach, which is reasonable as Company Cs way of working in many ways differs from that of Company A and Company B (as described in Section IV-B). The interviewees from Company C asked for more design and planning before starting the implementation. The interviewees requested a more thought-through design or at least a vision for the architecture. The interviewees also described that it was important to plan the integration in steps and requested a model for how we should work during development. Furthermore, five of the interviewees (from Company A and Company B) asked for that people from system and software could work better together, e.g. that the architects should talk more frequently with the developers. There were also comments (from one or two interviewees) related to several other areas, e.g. cross- functional teams, better tools, less centralization, and using design patterns. The role of the architect was supported by statements from 13 interviewees (from all three case study companies). The most common viewpoint was that the architects should support the development teams better (eleven interviewees). One interviewee described it as: The architect is on the other side of a wall. If focus is on working software, shouldnt the architect be serving me then? Now it feels like it is the other way around. Another viewpoint was that the architects in the organization must work better together (four interviewees), e.g. working as an expert council. Other voices asked for the architects to provide a vision for the architecture (four interviewees) and provide good examples (three interviewees). D. Activities Before Implementation in Software The interviewees from the three companies did in various ways describe which activities that they thought should be completed before starting the implementation in the software. The interviewees described very different approaches, which also were sometimes difficult to interpret due to the terminology seemingly being used differently by the different interviewees. Especially terms like function or behavior were clearly used differently by the interviewees, some of the interviewees referring to more high-level functions whereas other referred to detailed functions in a component. The interview results were analyzed to find patterns related to the three perspectives described in Section II-D (Six Architectural Views, Three Kinds of Architectural Structures, and Product Quality Properties). Six of the interviewees proposed in different ways that the components and or interfaces should be defined before starting implementation in the software. Three interviewees took the opposite approach, and described that you only have to decide which characteristics that should be considered to be most important in the system (e.g. usability, security, maintainability). Nine interviewees talked about both component interfaces and characteristics as areas that must be handled before starting implementation in the software. One interviewee described that the developers should start coding day one, and that all aspects of architecture and system design should be handled in parallel with the implementation. One interviewee answered the question (Q2.6 in Section II-D) with I dont know. No pattern was found in the analysis of the interview results related to interviewee responses and the interviewees role and or case study company. Seven of the interviewees talked about one or two characteristics (typically safety and or security) as more important than others. Another five interviewees stated that the characteristics that are most important in a system differs between different types of systems. We argue that the perspective that some of the characteristics of the system should be seen as more important than others could enable a more iterative way of working (as requested by the interviewees from Company A and Company B). This must then be balanced with good planning of the iterations (in order to avoid the problems described by the interviewees from Company C). V. CROSS-COMPANY WORKSHOP A. Validating the Analysis of the Interview Results The cross-company workshop included ten participants, representing all three case study companies. The workshop started with a presentation from the researchers of related work, based on the literature review (presented in Section III). This was followed by a presentation of the analysis of the interview results, in order to validate that the analysis in a good way summarized the conditions at each of the case study companies. The workshop participants were generally confirming the analysis of the interview results, only adding minor comments or additional information. After the presentation of each section of the analysis (following the same structure as in Section IV) the workshop participants discussed around one of the questions that was prepared by the researchers before the workshop: All three companies have long feedback loops: problems related to architecture are found late in the project. Is this only the same symptom, or is it the same problem? Are these improvement areas described here in Section IV-C relevant for every type of development project? Is something missing? Why are there so mixed opinions on which activities should be completed before starting the implementation in the software? The participants were confirming the summary of the status in each case study company (presented in Section IV- B). The workshop participants from Company A agreed that they had a history of integrating stuff (i.e. hardware components) which was seen as at least part of the explanation for their current situation. One workshop participant from Company B commented that although the description of an extensive system design phase was correct for some subprojects, other subprojects worked more with system design and implementation in parallel. Another workshop participant from Company B fully agreed with the description in Section IV-B, and even commented we are stuck in the system design phase. One workshop participant from Company C described the presentation as representative and added there are a lot of problems with communication between teams. The workshop participants agreed on that the three case study companies had the same symptoms (problems related to architecture are found late in the project) but due to that the companies had different types of products and different ways of working, this should not be seen as the same problem (which could be solved in the same way in all three companies). The three improvement areas (presented in Section IV-C) were well received by the workshop participants, and the three areas were intensively discussed from different perspectives. The participants agreed that The products architecture was the most important area, but an organization must succeed with the two other areas first (Ways to work with system design and architecture and The role of the architect) in order to have a good architecture. The participants also agreed on that development tools was something which might be missing in the description of the three improvement areas, but that this should be seen as part of The products architecture (not a separate improvement area). That is, as architectural decisions could affect the development environment and the tool chain, this must be also be considered in a decision. The workshop participants confirmed the viewpoint that due to different interpretations of terminology it was difficult to discuss the results from interview question Q2.6 (as described in Section IV-D) regarding which activities should be completed before starting the implementation in the software. However, the approach to focus on the most important characteristics in the system was well received by the workshop participants. B. A Balanced Approach Based on the findings from the case study companies (in particular the perspective to focus on the most important characteristics in the system), the need for a new balanced approach was discussed at the workshop. With this balanced approach, the primary activities before starting the implementation in the software are: Defining the most important characteristics: Which characteristics (e.g. safety and security) are most important How are these characteristics handled in the architecture Planning of the integration in steps: Work breakdown into development steps (to be integrated into the main track) Activity sequencing (including synchronization between development teams) Planning for in-house development as well as handling of subcontractors The workshop participants discussed this balanced approach in comparison to a waterfall approach (design and architecture specified in a separate design phase prior to implementation) and a 100 Agile approach (start coding immediately). The participants were then asked to place their organization in relation to the three approaches, and also mark what they saw as their wanted position. The responses from each company are presented in Fig. 2. The participants from each case study company were then asked what they considered most important to change, in order to go to the wanted position. Finally, the representatives from each case study company were asked how they wanted to prioritize what to take care of during an initial phase (i.e. which are the most important characteristics). The workshop participants representing Company A placed themselves quite close to the waterfall alternative, and their wanted position close to the balanced approach. One participant from Company A described that we must define the most necessary architecture before starting the implementation. Another voice from Company A added that it is important to synchronize between all affected teams when you introduce a new feature. The participants from Company A agreed on that culture was the main factor that prevented a change towards the balanced approach. One individual explained: people are afraid to change and afraid to lose control control which they in reality dont have. Another voice stated that we dont agree on what we should do its frustrating. Security was considered to be the most important characteristic to deal with early, as it is most difficult to change later in the project. Figure 2. The case study companies current position (marked with an x) in relation to the three approaches, and their wanted position (marked with a ring). The participants representing Company B also placed themselves quite close to the waterfall alternative, and their wanted position close to the balanced approach (similar to Company A). The Company B participants described that we must focus on the most important characteristics for each delta we implement, as that could depend on which feature or other change that was to be implemented. Another comment was to limit the number of reviewers, and not include all aspects or characteristics. One of the participants from Company B proposed frequent light-weight reviews of the architecture in parallel with the development, instead of a full-scale review after an upfront design phase. The response from Company C placed the current position quite close to the 100 Agile alternative (start coding immediately), and the wanted position as a field around the balanced approach. Visibility for the architectural team was considered to be the most important factor to enable change (to promote an architectural vision). The biggest obstacle was that people will not listen anyway our problem is communication. Compliance to standard APIs was described as most important because of our business model. Security was also described as very important due to requirements from the customers (a necessity to survive). All workshop participants agreed that a key factor to enable change towards the balanced alternative was that the architects attitude shifted from controlling the organization to facilitating good design principles and good examples. Communication within the organization was also considered to be an important factor by all workshop participants. Culture and the attitude of the employees were seen as most important factor that prevented change, and not so much problems in the product itself. VI. DISCUSSION A. Three Improvement Areas for Continuous Architecting In the second series of interviews we identified three improvement areas related to system design and architecture, showing how an organization can change to better support continuous integration and continuous delivery (presented in Section IV-C). A comparison with the literature review (presented in Section III-B) shows that the three areas are discussed in previous work (often with other terminology). However, the research papers identified in the literature review tend to focus on one of the three areas, leaving out areas that other authors consider to be the core issues. According to the results from this study, an organization should address all three areas (shown in Fig. 3) in order to succeed with continuous architecting (architecting that supports continuous integration and continuous delivery). The participants in the cross-company workshop identified The products architecture as the most important area, but an organization must start with the two other areas as they enable the third (as described in Section V-A). That is, in order to succeed with a shift to a new modular and loosely coupled architecture (perfectly adapted to support continuous integration and continuous delivery), the organization must first change its ways of working, and change the role of the architect. Figure 3. The three improvement areas which can enable continuous architecting. An unexpected result from the interviews was that we were not able to isolate a set of activities that should be completed before starting the implementation in the software (as presented in Section IV-D). We believe that this is partly due to that the case study companies operate in different industry segments (although this could not be shown from the interview results), but primarily due to the lack of clear definitions of terms like function or behavior. B. Vicious Circles Different factors might also be connected and strengthen each other. Three examples of vicious circles related to the three improvement areas described in Section IV-C were identified during the interviews and the workshop (shown in Fig. 4). Figure 4. Vicious circles identified in the study. The first vicious circle is about developers or teams that deliver their software with low frequency, which will make it difficult to integrate the software due to changed interfaces and other prerequisites in the software on the main track. Due to this, the team waits even longer to integrate (focusing on development of their new feature on time on their branch), which will make the integration problems even bigger. The second vicious circle is about that the design phase is extended repeatedly, due to that new and more detailed questions are raised. The result is, as one interviewee put it, that the design teams work with detailed architecture for stuff where we do not have a clue if it will work at all. One of the workshop participants described the solution for this to be more frequent evaluations of the architecture instead of one giant step. The third vicious circle is related to the role of the architect: as the developers ignore to the architects (as the developers find the architects disconnected from the development teams), the architects isolate themselves and then become even more disconnected. We argue that the solution must be that the architects move from control to facilitation. This standpoint is in a good way illustrated by the developer who is quoted in Section IV-C: Shouldnt the architect be serving me? Now it feels like it is the other way around. We argue that these vicious circles point out interesting phenomena identified in the study, but as the correlations presented in Fig. 4 are based on statements from only one or two interviewees, they should be seen only as a discussion about interesting topics which call for further investigations and analysis. C. Towards Continuous Architecting Based on the interview results and the cross-company workshop, we propose the following strategies corresponding to the three improvement areas: The products architecture: During the interviews, we identified problems related to teams working on a branch too long, and then having huge problems when they try to integrate (described in described Section IV-B). This phenomenon is also visualized in the first vicious circle. In our previous work 4 , we have identified that a modular and loosely coupled architecture is one of the factors that can enable more frequent integration of software. The idea of modular architecture is well-established in literature, and was described early as an enabler for continuous integration by Owen Rogers 19 and Roberts 20 . A modular architecture makes it easier to break down the work into small chunks, and work in parallel. If the architecture is structured as small components, problems are avoided where many teams need to make changes in the same component. The benefit from a loosely coupled architecture is that the developers can commit changes independently. Otherwise, if you change one thing, it tends to drag in other modules as well. One solution is to split the system into layers, representing e.g. functional applications, common services and infrastructure (as described in Section IV-C). In order to support continuous integration, the system must have a modular and loosely coupled architecture. However, this also calls for further research related to the causality between these two phenomena. Does frequent integration also drive developer behavior to implement functionality in a more modular and loosely coupled architecture? Ways to work with system design and architecture: The cross-company workshop discussed a balanced approach, which outlined an alternative to address the problems reported by the case study companies (as described in Section V-B). The balanced approach outlines a way of working with a small upfront design phase, which focuses on the most important characteristics of the product. Work is broken down into development steps, which include frequent reviews of the architecture and planning the following steps (avoiding problems such as the second vicious circle). We find it very interesting that despite the different contexts (two companies coming from a more waterfall-ish approach and one comping from an almost extreme Agile environment) the companies converged on a Goldilocks zone (as described in Section V-B): The two companies who work with a more upfront design wanted to embrace more Agile ways of workings. The third more Agile company wanted to move in the other direction, asking for more upfront architecture prior to implementation (in the hopes of avoiding some of the integration difficulties they were experiencing). We interpret this as the companies having common needs, despite operating in different industry segments. The solution for companies which develop large-scale and complex software products seems to be a balanced approach where system design and architecture is focused on the systems most important characteristics. The solution does not seem to be as easy as to just be Agile, and let the developers start coding immediately. Instead, companies must find the Goldilocks zone, which also includes influences from upfront design. The role of the architect: The interviews and the discussions at the workshop revealed severe problems with lack of communication between architects and developers. In a traditional waterfall-ish project setup, the architect has a well-defined role, but if the organization changes its ways of working and the upfront design phase disappears, the architects might lose their footing. As a result, they might be dragged along by the developers, trying to catch up. This is also showing in the third vicious circle, which shows how the architects tend to get more and more disconnected from the developers. The gap between architects and developers are described both by developers (in Section IV-C) and by an architect at the cross-company workshop (as described in Section V-B). The problem is not so much caused by the shift to Agile ways of working, instead the problem is just highlighted by the shift. Rather, the problem is about architects who are unable to act as true leaders as individuals to whom the developers will turn for support and guidance. This can be achieved through architects shifting perspective from control to facilitation. This shall not be interpreted as the idea of architects being outdated. Architects still serve an important role, but could now be seen more like traffic planners. The architects primary task is then to create a software structure that enables the autonomy and effectiveness of the developers. VII. THREATS TO VALIDIY A. Threats to Construct Validity One must always consider that a different set of questions and a different context for the interviews can lead to a different focus in the interviewees responses. In order to handle threats against construct validity, the interview guides and the questions for the workshop were designed with open- ended questions to as large extent as possible. In this paper, we also include information about the background for both the interviewees and the case study companies in order to provide as much information as possible about the context. B. Threats to Internal Validity Of the 12 threats to internal validity listed by Cook, Campbell and Day 21 , we consider Selection, Ambiguity about causal direction and Compensatory rivalry relevant to this work: Selection: All interviewees were purposively sampled in line with the guidelines for qualitative data appropriateness, given by Robson and McCartan 11 . The participants in the interviews reported in Section IV were selected as good informants with appropriate roles in the companies. Based on the rationale of these samplings and supported by Robson who considers this type of sampling superior for this type of study, we consider this threat to be mitigated. Ambiguity about causal direction: While we in this study in some cases discuss relationships, we are very careful about making statements regarding causation. Statements that include cause and effect are collected from the interview results, and not introduced in the interpretation of the data. Due to this, we consider this threat to be mitigated. Compensatory rivalry: When performing interviews and comparing scores or performance, the threat of compensatory rivalry must always be considered. Therefore, the questions in the interviews and at the workshop were deliberately designed to be as value neutral as possible, rather than judging performance or skills of the interviewee or the interviewees organization. Generally, all questions were also designed to be opened-ended to avoid any type of bias and ensure answers that were open and accurate. However, our experiences from previous work is that we found the interviewed engineers more prone to self-criticism than to self-praise. C. Threats to External Validity The study is based primarily on qualitative data from three case study companies. It is conceivable that the ndings in this study are only valid for these companies, or only for companies that develop large-scale and complex software products which also include a significant amount of mechanical and electronic parts (software-intensive embedded systems). However, as described in the comparison with the literature review in Section VI-A, many of the problems described in this paper are evidently not isolated to our three case study companies. VIII. CONCLUSION The purpose of the study reported in this research paper was to investigate how the way companies work with system design and architecture can change to better support continuous integration and continuous delivery. The interview results showed that although the case study companies had quite different ways of working, they all reported that problems related to architecture were found late in their development projects (described in Section IV-B). Company A was integrating frequently on a component or subsystem level, but had very long feedback loops on a product level. Company B described problems related to an extensive system design phase, which was conducted before starting implementation in software. Company C described that problems with architecture were found late during the implementation due to that the teams worked on separated branches (as the teams tended to isolate themselves due to a lack of coordination). From the interview results we identified three improvement areas related to system design and architecture, where an organization can change to better support continuous integration and continuous delivery: The products architecture Ways to work with system design and architecture The role of the architect The three improvement areas (further described in Section IV-C) were well received by the participants at the cross-company workshop (as described in Section V-A). The products architecture was seen as the most important area, but an organization must succeed with the two other areas first in order to attain an architecture adapted to continuous integration and continuous delivery. Based on the interview results and the cross-company workshop, we have proposed actionable strategies (further described in Section VI-C) corresponding to the three improvement areas: Product: Systems with a modular and loosely coupled architecture, which allows developers (and development teams) to work independently and in parallel. Ways of working: A balanced approach where system design and architecture is focused on the systems most important characteristics and each development step include frequent architectural reviews and planning of the following steps. Role: Architects shifting perspective from control to facilitation, with the primary task to create a software structure that enables the autonomy of the developers. A systems architecture could both prevent and enable continuous integration. We believe that the results from this study are valuable for both researchers and practitioners in their struggle to help organizations to better implementations of continuous integration and continuous delivery. A. Further Work This study does not include any external validation of the results from the interviews and the cross-company workshop. Further work could include an extended study, where the three improvement areas (described in Section IV- C) and the strategies corresponding to the improvement areas (described in Section VI-C) are validated in companies separate from the case study companies in this study. In the same way, further work could build upon the idea of a balanced approach (described in Section V-B) and further expand this to a method or a model. This method (or model) could then be introduced in one or several case study companies to be evaluated. Another topic for further work is to further examine the mechanisms laying behind the vicious circles which are presented in Fig. 4 (in Section VI-B). Are the factors presented in the figure truly correlated, and if so are there an unambiguous causal direction? papers.abstract: There are widespread and increasing interest in big data analytics (BDA) solutions to enable data collection, transformation, and predictive analyses. The development and operation of BDA application involve business innovation, advanced analytics and cutting-edge technologies which add new complexities to the traditional software development. Although there is a growing interest in BDA adoption, successful deployments are still scarce (a.k.a., the “Deployment Gap” phenomenon). This paper reports an empirical study on BDA deployment practices, techniques and tools in the industry from both the software architecture and data science perspectives to understand research challenges that emerge in this context. Our results suggest new research directions to be tackled by the software architecture community. In particular, competing architectural drivers, interoperability, and deployment procedures in the BDA field are still immature or have not been adopted in practice.
