papers.fulltext: Reducing Development Overheads with a Generic and Model-Centric Architecture for Online Games Sebastian Apel Department of Computer Science, Friedrich Schiller University Jena Jena, Germany Email: sebastian.apel uni-jena.de AbstractThe development of an online game requires not only the content, visual and auditory design but also a considerable amount of effort for planning, creating and operating the infrastructure for exchanging information between players and backend. Within the context of building an own browser-based massively multiplayer online game, questions like how information of this kind can be exchanged arise. Within this paper, various strategies were planned, developed and evaluated to provide the helpful basis for a platform decision. These strategies do not feel very game-like. As a result of this, we created an alternative approach as a runtime environment for games of this kind, which has to simplify the conventional strategies for making games: our GameEngine. This environment combines code generation for clients, automated data transformation, platform independent remote procedure calls and lifecycle management for entities. This paper targets to outline the different strategies for game realisation, and analyses the efforts in comparison to our approach in various applications. Proprietary TCP-based approaches are taken into account, as well as standardised web technologies and currently available runtime environments for game development. All approaches indicated a significant increase in effort for the implementation of various examples. An additional effort that can be nearly avoided, and is achieved with our approach. I. INTRODUCTION Developing a Game, in our case a massively multiplayer online game (MMOG), is Harder than you think 1, P. 35 . Such a development can include topics like graphic, audio, music, 3D model and animation, as well as rendering, physics and collision. Further, there are topics about authentification, development tools, game state persistence, communication protocols, data formats for transportation, serverside gameplay code and its ongoing simulation, as well as analytics, artificial intelligence, static content and configurations which are handled by a wide range of professions as outlined in 2, P. 63 and 3, P. 5 . This kind of online game development is a creative process which makes use of a rising amount of third-party technologies which has to consider software architecture 4 . When we started to create our MMOG, we were confronted with an extensive amount of tools. Ignoring the artistic-like tasks, the architecture and infrastructure challenges were a central concern for us. The intended game Viechers 5 is designed as a browser-based game and requires to think about technical challenges and underlying toolsets. These challenges are primarily about infrastructure and architecture to exchange information between visualisation and centralised instance which keeps this game persistent. An initial insight can be gained through various architectural approaches for the realisation of games in 6 10 , by using experience reports like 1 , 11 as well as utilising a reference-architecture like 12 with a focus on games, multiplayer games and MMOG. However, we will demonstrate an example in Section III and which efforts have to be done to build a game on top of them. But, as you will notice, a not inconsiderable portion of efforts for communication infrastructure that are not relevant to the game is included in these approaches, our so-called overhead. As a result of our reflections from a technical point of view, we have designed an alternative approach and implemented it as a runtime environment for (browser- and mobile-based) MMOG games; our middleware called GameEngine. This runtime environment avoids the overhead, which means redundant parts of architectural and infrastructural implementation tasks when creating games like Viechers. The main research question of this paper is regarding the technical focus on the architectural and infrastructural implementation tasks, the identification and classification of overheads, as well as the presentation of our approach as an alternative. Within this paper, we want to analyse conventional strategies in Section III to implement communication infrastructure for online games and compare them with the presented GameEngine in Section IV. The evaluation in Section V is done by application onto game realisations and discuss the achieved amount of overhead reduction. The primary focus when evaluating is on reviewing this application and rate their implementation effort for communication infrastructure and game logic. This rating is done by analysing the resulting code base by measuring logical lines of code (LLoC) defined within the COCOMO II 13 and tagged them in various dimensions. However, within this paper, we do not want to go into detail about the performance achieved with this runtime environment. II. RELATED WORK The topic of this paper refers to architectural aspects and how online games can be realised. On the one hand, this can be achieved by considering research about software architecture and game development and on the other hand by reviewing available solutions to create online games. A first insight into the challenges for network infrastructure in online and multiplayer play are provided by 7 and 10 . 21 2018 IEEE International Conference on Software Architecture 978-1-5386-6398-1 18 31.00 2018 IEEE DOI 10.1109 ICSA. They identify common algorithms (like pathfinding, decision making, randomness) and tasks (like cheating preventing, network infrastructure and information filtering). Further, game-related network infrastructure, e. g., in 6 , illustrates mostly client-server infrastructures which focus on information exchange by using, e. g., TCP or UDP. That setup can be found in the publisher subscriber communication layer from 8 , as well as in 9 which helps to distribute s dynamic game-play state and computation while adhering to tight latency constraints and maintaining scalable communication costs. The architectures presented in 12 and 14 illustrate another client-server infrastructure with an abstract point of view. Client and server related tasks are placed on top of the message processing which interacts through the network layer itself. Centralised, distributed and replicated architecture, as well as resource management and areas of interest, are discussed in 15 . Apart from that, 16 presents object-oriented design patterns in game development, which cover various patterns to realise recurring game elements, and reference a generic game architecture from 17 . This architecture targets, independent from communication, the correlation between platform, inputs, graphics and audio, as well as a centralised game logic which holds the story of the game. However, 4 points out the importance of software architecture and the creative process in game development. This is backed up by a survey among game developers, which shows that software architecture is of central importance and influences itself up to a certain degree of gameplay. The references considered indicate a focus for exchanging messages regarding a centralised game mechanic. In addition to this review, an insight into available tools is helpful. Primary, tools like SmartFoxServer 2X 18 and Photon Server 19 , as well as tools like BigWorld 20 , the Unreal Engine 21 and the Unity Engine 22 , are well-known. The SmartFoxServer and Photon Server are Java- and C -based solutions. These tools support the implementation of client-server based games by using TCP or UDP sockets and key-value-based proprietary protocols for data (de-) serialisation. Further, these tools offer a room-based communication infrastructure to manage the distribution of data packets to connected and listening players. An alternative to this room based communication is the location-based mapping of listening individuals. Each could have one or more positions, and each position will have a specific range to listen for events. Tools like that can be used somewhere between two strategies. The first strategy might be to realise all game-mechanic implementations in the client and use this room-like infrastructure to broadcast information to related players. The second strategy might be to add game-mechanic into so-called extension points within the server environment. This extension point offers capabilities to interact with the communication infrastructure by using a specified API. The BigWorld Server 20 as another is a dynamic real-time load-balancing system to remove arbitrary zone limitations. The specific customisation can be done by adding Python or C based behaviours. Fig. 1. Simple game example for moving around to find an unknown position. Furthermore, the API with functions required to use this game model. The Unreal Engine 21 and the Unity Engine 22 mentioned above, are development and runtime environments focusing on the client-side development. Those tools organise projects within multiple scenes or levels which contain various kinds of game entities as instances of a project-wide set of assets. They allow synchronising game entity states across participating clients in a multiplayer session. However, they are not the primary focus. III. CONVENTIONAL STRATEGIES Networking in online game development seems to be, beside the basic game-mechanic and client related presentation, about infrastructure, information exchange and broadcasting as shown in Section II. This section goes more in-depth into five realised strategies: (1) Java TCP, (2) Java EE, (3) SmartFoxServer, (4) JS REST and (5) JS WebSocket. These strategies range from low-level implementations up to high-level networking tools. The simplified example used within our strategies, shown in Fig. 1 and from now on called BasicGame, contains an avatar, which has a position and moves around in our so-called AvatarWorld. This example and its complexity are oriented toward common definitions as they can be found, e. g., in 23 , which describes games within a pretended reality with at least one arbitrary, nontrivial goal by acting in accordance with rules 23, P. 2 , as well as in 14 which says, that a user plays the game in a world view and each world has a consistent model of physical laws and rules that apply to all players within that world. Our BasicGame finishes when one of the players finds a hidden, unknown position, by using its only possible action-rule: moving left or right. However, this BasicGame is neither meaningful nor fun. Implementing this BasicGame requires creating the class Avatar, the AvatarWorld and the Position as well as all of its attributes and constructors. This example contains five functionalities: getAvatar, getAvatars, moveAvatar, newAvatar and updateAvatar. These functionalities cover requests and information broadcasts and are accessed through an API, which acts as controlled access or proxy. This API-interface is shown in Fig. 1 and the implementation should hold the reference to the current simulated AvatarWorld instance. Before going into the strategies, we need to mark common characteristics for each server-side strategy. These characteristics can be found in various implementations as introduced in Section II and are based on the architecture presented in 12 and 14 . On top, there is (1) the game model, which contains the game mechanic implementation, e. g., the BasicGame from Fig. 1. Additionally, (2) an API to access this game model. Further, there is (3) the controller, which has to manage events within the game model as well as incoming requests, forwarded through (5) the message handler. The message handler itself maps data packages from the network layer onto (4) local communication objects and vice versa as well as manages active (6) sessions. The first strategy, Java TCP, is about a plain TCP socket server implementation as motivated by 6, P. 216 as the most basic strategy to implement the infrastructure. This strategy enforces to implement or integrate each component by self. Our example uses the embedded TCP API in Java to construct connections, manage sessions and handle messages. Each data package is JSON de- and encoded by using JAXB and Jettison. JAXB is a descriptive way to mark objects with annotations to transform instances of them automatically into the data format XML. Jettison uses JAXB to transform this XML format into the JSON format. Finally, the local communication objects (annotated to use them with JAXB), the controller to dispatch received communication objects, the API from Fig. 1 and the game model is implemented straightforward. Our Java EE strategy, the second one, targets a server implementation using Java EE version 7 for web services based on REST. This strategy offers the usage of well-accepted standards to realise components independently from runtime environments. Different kinds of specifications within Java EE like EJBs, Java API for RESTful Web Services (JAX-RS) and Contexts and Dependency Injection (CDI) can be used to describe controller, API, model and the interaction between them. Those components can be packed up and deployed to a runtime environment which supports the used Java EE standards, e.g. WildFly from redhat 24 . This strategy has to implement several parts as done in the first Java TCP strategy: the communication objects (JAX-RS use JAXB as well to map between data format and communication objects), the API specialised to an EJB and the model implementation instantiated within this bean. Additionally, we need to implement our controller, which uses JAX-RS to define one method per exposed API functionality and annotates them correctly. Finally, the JAX-RS service has to define a dependency to our EJB by using CDI where a local attribute is annotated, and the runtime environment will inject the corresponding dependency. Once it is deployed, we get this EJB as an access point for our model and an HTTP based REST service based on JAX-RS. The runtime environment will add all required characteristics to establish the TCP server, handle the HTTP protocol, specific of REST interface, extract our data to communication objects, inject the bean into our service and calls a JAX-RS method where our controller starts. Our third strategy makes use of a game related network engine. There are several engines available which support the development of MMOGs, e. g., the Photon Server 19 and the SmartFoxServer 18 , Unreal Engine 21 and Unity Engine 22 as well as BigWorld Server 20 . Unreal and Unity were rejected because of their focus on multiplayer games, not massively, and BigWorld Server was not available for comparison and might be taken into consideration in future. The remaining engines, Photon Server and the SmartFoxServer, have monolithic architectures, their data format for transportation and offer wide ranges of available client technologies. Embedding our game model can be done by implementing so-called extensions. This extension might be compared to the Java EE strategy, but it is less standardised. This third strategy uses the SmartFoxServer strategy, because of its possibility to use Java for extension implementations. In comparison to the Java EE strategy, there is nothing else to do. Strategy three implements the controller, as well as API and model precisely as done in our first strategy. However, this strategy has to create individual communication objects to use the data format from SmartFoxServer. The next strategy, implemente the whole setup by using JavaScript (JS) and execute this within Node.js. JS is used because of it is easy to use and its ability for fast prototyping as well as the fact that the client and server can be implemented within the same language. The fourth strategy, the JS REST, creates a REST service by using express 25 to define a specific handling description for each functionality. This implementation is comparable to the second and third one. It contains controller and model implementations, as well as the API for our example model, which has to be implemented. Thanks to JS, no specific declared communication objects are required. These objects will exist at runtime and do not have to be implemented. Finally, the fifth strategy, the JS WebSocket, is based on WebSocket implemented in JS. These WebSockets are an upgraded HTTP-based communication which allows bidirectional ongoing message exchange for client-side web applications. This strategy requires an implementation of the model and the API for this model which is the same as in the fourth strategy as well as a controller, which has to identify incoming data packages and map them to the corresponding API method. All described strategies and required implementation parts are condensed in Table I. The table uses the already mentioned six characteristics. Additionally, this tables contains the entry Configuration which is related to characteristics within the implementation like annotations or additional configuration files. Until now, we can conclude the easiest strategies are the JS-based ones, which is because it is not necessary to implement communication objects. IV. GAMEENGINE MMOG game development seems to be not very game like. As we have experienced with our strategies to implement the example game in Section III, it is all about providing TABLE I COMAPRISON OF THE FIVE STRATEGY IMPLEMENTATIONS JAVA TCP (S1), JS REST (S2), JS WEBSOCKET (S3), JAVA REST (S4) AND SMARTFOXSERVER (S5) OF THE BASICGAME-EXAMPLE. MARKS ARE PLACED, IF THE RELATED CHARACTERISTIC HAS TO BE IMPLEMENTATED FOR THIS PARTICULAR STRATEGY. S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 1 Game Model 2 Game Model API 3 Controller 4 Communication Objects () () 5 Message Handler 6 Session Management 7 Configuration information for clients and think about how to get them. This can be noticed in implementations from scratch (Java TCP), as well as by using high-level APIs (Java EE, JS REST, JS WebSocket) or a game related tool (SmartFoxServer). In detail, the primary task is managing message handling, defining communication objects and implementing controllers to access the game model. In contrast, all strategies avoid interaction with network layers and provide session management to allow focusing on the handling of messages. Our approach, the GameEngine, focuses on creativity by reducing the amount of communication infrastructure. The goal is to develop the game-mechanic, add meta information, e. g., mark methods within this mechanic which has to be used by the client and finally execute this by using the runtime environment of the GameEngine. The result is a generated client-side proxy which abstracts the communication between client and server. The GameEngine is a combination of platform-independent remote method invocation, automated data transformation, automated code generation for clients (mainly if the client environment differs from the server environment) and lifecycle management for entities based on a generic game model as well as its tracking of state changes and broadcasting to related clients. The GameEngine is written in Java and describes components by using the Java Management Extension (JMX). It is designed to run in a Java EE environment as an additional container beside, e. g., business logic (like EJBs) and frontend (like Servlets). A. Architecture The GameEngine, as its Level 1 component visualisation in Fig. 2 shows, is primarily a client-server architecture enhanced by components that derive the communication infrastructure from a provided game model. Each game is instantiated and executed in its container like environment. The further architectural decisions are based on the approaches outlined in Section II and manually used in Section III. The components and their function are briefly explained below. The server-side outline a multi-tier application with essential features of a model-view-controller. In this case, the Message Handler is the view on the information, the Request Handling takes over the functionalities of the controller, and the components Sessions, Services and Game Model Container are available for processing the requests. The Message Handler handle encoding and decoding of messages on top of the network infrastructure. The handler provides a single communication port to handle various transport protocols like WebSockets, HTTP, plain TCP as well as proper handshake handling. The identification is made automatically when a new client connects. While the component is capable of processing XML- and JSON-based messages, it uses an optimised mapping format which will be introduced later. The component Request Handling realises the processing of received requests, supplements the session context and translates the request to call the functionality in the corresponding container with our actual game model. Further, this component saves changes made by invoking entities. The additional game-related services, e. g., payment, authentification and authorisation, are bundled in the Services component. Communication between the client and services for this component is done via the additional ServicePort because, e. g., authentication must be processed before entering a game world. The next component, Sessions, manages active client connections, especially data to be stored for later request handlings, e. g., state of authentification and authorisation. Finally, the Game Model Container which acts as the runtime environment for a game model. The game model is kept in memory and, if necessary, further simulated without user interaction. Finally, there is a provided Game Meta Model for the development of games which can be used optionally. This model supports basic entity types of a game and offers preconfigured properties required by the GameEngine. The client-side is the counterpart to the server. It is also based on a multi-tier layout: The client-side message handler performs the same tasks as on the server-side to establish a working communication infrastructure; the Game Model Proxy grants access to all published functionalities, as well as synchronised states of attributes of communicable entity types; the Game State buffers already communicated entities, e. g., attribute states; and the controller processes communication, user events and controls necessary visualization updates. Finally, required information is visualised within the view. Apart from client and server, additional components are involved. The Client Code Generator is a black box code analysing tool. This tool generates client facades, so-called Game Model Proxies, which implement published functionalities with related network engine calls, e. g., platform-independent remote procedure calls. The database is used as a persistent image, while the game model state is held in memory. B. Communication The previously sketched strategies in Section III outline that each exposed functionality of our game model requires a specific development effort. The aim is to avoid this infrastructure overhead. The idea is to derive the communication infrastructure for the game model from the same. For example, in case of exposing the newAvatar function from Fig. 1 as shown in Fig. Fig. 2. Level 1 component visualization of the GameEngine. NewAvatarRequest name : String newAvatar(name : String) : Avatar NewAvatarResponse AvatarData id : int name : String NewAvatarHandler handle(call : NewAvatarRequest) PositionData x : int y : int - position 1 1 - avatar CallHandler abstract handle(call : T) bind T- NewPlayerCall T Fig. 3. Generic request, response and handling entities to expose the newAvatar functionality. Fig. 4. Abstract game model useable to specialise into a particular game idea. and the related context the currently executed game world. The derived request object contains all required parameters of the specific method, e. g., the name for the new avatar as well as an identifier for some specific context, e. g., when exposing avatar functionalities. This identifier helps to find the correct instance within the handling description and redirects the invocation as intended. The response object, on the other side, encapsulates the return value of the method, e. g., the avatar in case of newAvatar. Finally, the handling description contains every required processing instruction to validate received parameters, find the related instance, call the related method and reply with a new instance of the corresponding response object. This concept can be expanded to support the client development as well. This expansion is done by translating the communication objects derived from the game model into the desired client language. Additionally, we can generate all required entities to recreate a client subset of our game model. Those entities act as proxies for their real counterparts on the server-side. To reduce the communication overhead, the client-side remembers the last state of each requested instance as long as they are required, i. e., an entity is within view range. Finally, mapping entities on data streams can be automated as well. If the communication objects are known, and our processes generate the client source code, the GameEngine has finally full control over the entire process. As a result of this, we have created our mapping format which avoids overheads when describing structures in data streams. This format can communicate the state of an entity by only using a type identifier. The remaining information, like attribute type, name and order, is synchronised between client and server when the code is generated. Annotations apply the different components of the GameEngine in Java. In particular, this means that entity types must be selected if they are interchangeable between client and server. This also means that each function must be selected if it should be callable by the client. Also, a marker can be added to define its distribution to clients that are also active. C. Abstract Game Model The GameEngine offers an optional abstract game model which offers a basic concept based on the definition of a typical game as outlined in the example of Section III. Thus, our abstract game model contains a pretended reality, the game world. This world is the central entry point. Further, this model covers various types of rules. Adams 23, P. 8 categorises these rules in semiotics of the game, gameplay, sequence of play, goal(s) of the game, termination condition and metarules. We have decided to provide an abstract game object to cover semiotics of the game, which are the required symbols that the game employs 23, P. 8 . Further, gameplay, sequence of play, goal(s) of the game and termination condition is all about functionalities, events and timing. Thus, this model contains an observer pattern to allow entities the sending of notifications or to receive them. Additionally, we have added the Timer which simulates ongoing ticks. However, further functionalities should be added through specific methods within game object specialisations. The remaining metarules might be embedded within particular implementations. The resulting abstract game model is visualised in Fig. 4. However, this game model applies required configuration to use the GameEngine. This means that there are prepared identifiers, object creator methods, associations and annotation markers to configure the communication layer. If this model is used as an entry point, it can help speed up the implementation of a specific game. However, while the GameEngine itself is designed to be replaceable, this abstract model would bind a specific implementation to this development tool, which has to be taken into consideration. We used the GameEngine to realise the example from Section III. In summary, the development effort is reduced to the annotating of our five functionalities, as well as the annotating of all entity types for transferability. (a) Comparison of the common elements (b) Accumulated efforts (c) Comparison of the common elements (d) Accumulated efforts Fig. 5. Results of the analyses of the BasicGame example and the MMO-Meischta project. V. EVALUATION Our analyses of efforts to implement the overhead characteristics, are considered in three steps: (1) comparing the efforts of the already mentioned example in Section III, (2) comparing an independent example and finally (3) taking a closer look on a more comprehensive example, as mentioned earlier, the game Viechers. This analyses of efforts for each step can be done in two significant ways: analyse the lines of codes (LoCs) of a game implementation or analyse the amount of time used to create this implementation. While the experience of developers influences time-based analyses, LoC based analyses are influenced not only by experience but also by the programming style. However, we have decided to use LoC as a rating criterion. This rating criterion is also used in the cost estimation model COCOMO II 13 which is used to rate software projects. This model describes a standardised way to determine so-called LLoC. These LLoCs clean up the count result of language-specific characteristics to obtain a comparable result. This clean up equalises the analysis based on time and LoC. Thus, both ways are mainly influenced by the experience and should be taken into consideration in case of discussing and rating results. For this evaluation, a rule-based tool was developed and used which supports the evaluation in three dimensions and utilises the Unified Code Counter (UCC) 26 to count LLoC. The first dimension describes the set S of possible strategies, which contains Java TCP, Java EE, JS REST, JS WebSocket and SmartFoxServer. The second dimension describes the set C of characteristics which contains the game model, API, controller, communication objects, message handler, session management and configuration (referring to Table I). Finally, the third dimension targets the set F of functionalities the code line is required for. In case of the BasicGame, those are the functionalities, getAvatar, getAvatars, moveAvatar, newAvatar and updateAvatar in combination with an initial state. ZJava TCP, ZJS REST, ZJS WebSocket, ZJava EE and ZSmartFoxServer are the sets of source code lines of the respective strategy. For s S, c C and f F we will use the cnt function in Equation 1. The equation uses three functions characteristic ch, functionality fu and countable co to estimate the already mentioned characteristics, functionality and finally if we have to count this line. Further, we can use this cnt function to accumulate by functionalities the overall amount of LLoC and use this to calculate the trend as shown in Equation 2. The function scc is used to select the successor of f. cnt(s, c, f) x x Zs ch(x) c fu(x) f co(x) 1 (1) acc(s, f) cC cnt(s, c, f) acc(s, scc(f)) if f init cC cnt(s, c, f) otherwise (2) Comparing the measurement result for each characteristic for the BasicGame example from Section III results in Fig. 5a as the final implementation state. As already presumed, the JS-based strategies JS REST and JS WebSockets require the least effort, i. e., the least amount of code. The ratio for JS REST between game model and the sum of everything else, the so-called overhead, is 1:1.711 and the ratio for the JS WebSocket is 1:1.267. The most extensive implementation is used for the Java TCP strategy with a ratio of 1:5.404. However, the average ratio between model and overhead is 1:3.01. In return, the overhead could be reduced to a ratio of 1:0.113 using the GameEngine. Another view on the measurement values is done within the Fig. 5b. This figure uses the acc function shown in Equation 2. It finally allows to show, regardless which conventional strategy we have used, a measurable overhead can be shown per additional exposed functionality, or rather, it applies to each s S and f F that acc(s, scc(f)) acc(s, f) if f init. Next to the BasicGame example, further games using the GameEngine were created in student projects. The teams start without initial knowledge of the GameEngine and have to sketch an own game project, as well as model and implement the game mechanics as their game model. In the final step, the resulting game model was combined with the GameEngine. For this purpose, the various projects were examined concerning the components used from the GameEngine. It was analysed whether the designed game ideas can be realised by using an abstract approach and only via remote procedure calls by using the game model proxy on the client-side, or whether additional low-level communication objects and request handlings are necessary to handle individual cases. The projects have a code length of 767 to 904 LLoC and expose 13 to 19 functionalities. We noticed that no additional communication object nor request handlers are required. Everything could be done simply by using the game model proxy translated into the client environment. We analysed one of these student projects in detail: MMO-Meischta. This one has a wide variety of game objects and exposed functionalities. The implementation was cleaned from all annotations and dependencies to the GameEngine and then implemented using the Java TCP, Java EE and SmartFoxServer strategy again. Each strategy exposes each functionality as it would be done within this specific tool stack. These stacks are the same as they are used within the BasicGame. Fig. 5c shows the final MMO-Meischta implementation state and compares each characteristic. Beside the GameEngine, the strategy with the least effort is SmartFoxServer with a ratio between model and overhead of 1:1.061. The ratio between model and overhead for conventional strategies is at 1:1.422. Using the GameEngine reduces this ratio to 1:0.033. Further, there is the accumulate effort plot in Fig. 5d outlines again that each conventional strategy has its specific effort to expose additional functionality and behaves like the BasicGame example: acc(s, scc(f)) acc(s, f) for each s S and f F if f init. The last step of analysis refers to the initial motivated game project called Viechers. This game is created as the reference implementation to the GameEngine, and further is grown in parallel and could not make use of generic features. Viechers uses the basic mechanics of the GameEngine, and the analysis evaluates each finally provided functionality. The motivation to evaluate the implementation after a development time of approx. 2 years lies in the complexity range. It is not just an example; it is a project developed to the point of maturity with approx. 120 kLoC (excepted the GameEngine) that uses the communication infrastructure implemented in the GameEngine in productive operation and tests it under load. Using this game allows taking a closer look on two aspects: (1) request handlings which might be realised by using the generative processes in combination with platform-independent remote procedure calls and (2) the ratio between particular parts of this implementation. Viechers has an overall of 119 request handlings. Each has its specific request communication object which describes required and optional parameters. These handlings range from already observed requests, used to invoke functionalities within the game model, up to handlings which are required to realise payment methods, authentication and authorisation which partly interact with the game model as well with providers to handle these kinds of services. We have identified an overall of 108 handlings, or rather 91 , which are realisable by using our game model-based approach. The remaining 11 handlings require an API from the GameEngine to realise this kind of handler related to the game model, without being part of the same. Finally, the last analyses focus on the ratios between different parts of the implementation of Viechers. The server part has a ratio between game model implementation and overhead of 1:0.809 and the client part has a ratio of 1:0.577. VI. DISCUSSION The realisation of an MMOG involves a multitude of tasks steps were assumed. The focus was on the communication infrastructure, which organises the processing of requests and the distribution of responses between the player (client) and the central instance (server). This covers APIs for the game model, controller to handle events and requests, communication objects for storing data related to communication, the message handler as well as session management. To reduce the infrastructure related effort, we have relied on the use of well-known strategies, especially in the area of Java EE, NodeJS and a game related networking engine. However, the presented measurements and resulting ratios in the game implementations cannot be generalised. They indicate the assumption that conventional strategies require a development effort for infrastructural overhead, which is derived from the corresponding functionalities. One possible reason for this is that these strategies require typical steps: based on a provided game logic, the implementation of the infrastructure for establishing the communication between visualisation and game logic has to be done manually. This part of development is technology-dependent. As soon as the technology is mastered it is a craft whose steps are derived from the business logic. For example, create communication objects which contain attributes from exposed functionalities or handle incoming packages to call related game logic. On the one hand, this is due to the fact that it results in an identifiable overhead in addition to the game logic for the conventional strategies and, on the other hand, because it was possible to avoid this overhead in the context of the GameEngine. The avoidance achieved with the GameEngine has been demonstrated both conceptually and in practice. We believe that this is possible because the alternative strategies provide a set of tools, mostly APIs, which force to use them. Tools that derive the necessary steps to establish the infrastructure from an available model are not the general practice in the area of game development. Approaches like this help to focus on the implementation of the mechanisms of an application. Direct contact with technological conditions is avoided. The remaining task for the developer is to mark functionality. In practice, this allows, for example, the uncomplicated use of modelling and code generation tools. Design required entity types, realise associations and generate source code without dependencies. Further, this allows simplifying the definition of unit tests. Complicated mock-up construction is not necessary. Apart from that, the number of required skills is lowered, and user errors might be reduced, especially in small teams and targeting knowledge about architecture and communication infrastructure, as we could notice within our student projects. Finally, the concentration on modelling and implementing game logic mechanics helps to focus on the creative part of games. However, based on the architectural layer, the application to game independent applications is also conceivable. This can be done either by using the primary infrastructure components or by creating a domain-specific model that supports application development as well as the abstract game model does. Other aspects of the approach include performance and scalability. The generative approach to providing the infrastructure allows efficient algorithms for data exchange, without the developer of the game logic having to be confronted with the characteristics of the same. Scalability of our infrastructure can also be achieved independently of the game logic. For example, game entities can be distributed location-based, and communication infrastructure can be separated from the game simulation environment. This enables horizontal scaling of the communication infrastructure and vertical scaling of the game logic. Viechers makes use of this without touching the game logic. VII. CONCLUSION The GameEngine was not only realised as a prototype but brought to a productive stage and applied in different game projects, e. g., Viechers as well as game projects made with students. However, the aim of this paper was to analyse conventional strategies for exchanging in-game information from a technical point of view, identify efforts for communication infrastructure and avoid them within the own approach. As shown above, there is a considerable amount of effort that has to be planned for realisation. The shown overhead is not surprising and can be expected quite easy, but for us, it was essential to determine a scale and to trace the source. This scale is an average ratio of 1:1, and the source can be found in redundant implementation steps for connecting game logics with communication infrastructure. Using this gathered knowledge in combination with platform-independent remote method invocation, automated data transformation, automated code generation for clients, an optimised data mapping format for transportation and lifecycle management for entities results in our alternative technology stack which reduces the overhead on simple markups. This is achieved by inverting the usage. While the conventional strategies offered the abstracted communication infrastructure via an API, the GameEngine focused on the analysis of an independently created model containing the mechanics of the game idea. This engine can be used to support model-driven approaches, use generative approaches to avoid technology-related implementation efforts from specific implementation cases, lower test complexity, reduce required development skills and finally help to focus on creative parts.
